the appellants would be entitled to claim credit because the explosives were used for the manufacture of the intermediate product, namely, limestone which, in turn, was used for the manufacture of cement. The appeal of the manufacturer was, accordingly, allowed and it was held that the MODVAT credit was allowable on the use of the explosives in the manufacture of cement irrespective of the fact that the explosives were used directly in the mines and never entered the factory of the manufacturer of cement. [Para 8] In 2000, the MODVAT Rules were replaced by the CENVAT Rules by the Central Excise (Second Amendment) Rules, 2000. Basically there was a re-arrangement of the earlier rules which in substance remained the same.

It is clear that sub-rule (d ) of rule 57AA (as introduced in 2000) had merely reframed rule 57B to include all the ingredients of inputs while at the same time broadening the base not only by referring to ‘all goods’ but also by using the word ‘includes’. [Para 9]

Rule 57AC provides for the conditions for allowing CENVAT credit in respect of inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer. [Para 10]

Initially, rule 57J of the MODVAT Rules was deleted. Consequently, with the intention of re-introducing the benefit granted earlier under rule 57J, rule 57AB was introduced under the heading ‘CENVAT credit’. [Para 11]

Rule 57AB effectively duplicates the substance of rule 57J(1) and (2) and deals with a situation where inputs are received by a job worker for production of intermediate goods which are used in the manufacture of a final product. [Para 12]

In J.K. Udyog Ltd.’s case (supra), three reasons were given by the Supreme Court for holding that credit could be taken only on inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer of the final product. First, the Court held that the definition of input given in sub-rule(d) of rule 57AA was entirely different from the manner in which the said word had been expounded in the Explanation to rule 57A of the MODVAT Rules. However, there was only a re-arrangement of the several provisions of rule 57B in rule 57AA. Rule 57AA is in fact more broad based than rule 57B.

Second, the Court proceeded on the basis that under the CENVAT scheme, there was no provision similar to rule 57J of the MODVAT scheme. However, rule 57J was replaced in substance by rule 57AB. That provision was overlooked.

Another reason given by the Court in J.K. Udaipur Udyog case (supra ) for holding that the CENVAT scheme was different from the MODVAT Scheme was rule 57AC(1). However, that rule was limited to inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer and did not impinge on rule 57AB at all.

The schemes of MODVAT and CENVAT Credit are not, therefore, different and the conclusion of the Court in J.K. Udaipur Udyog that the decision in Jaypee Rewa Cement (supra ) would have no application to CENVAT Rules could not be accepted. [Para 14]

The CENVAT Rules in effect substitute the MODVAT Rules and the decision in Jaypee Rewa Cement would continue to apply. The decision in CCE v. J.K. Udaipur Udyog Ltd. (supra ) holding to the contrary, was not good law. [Para 15]

HEADNOTE: Rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Input service - Whether assessee was entitled to input credit on LPG used in its canteen where such canteen, as per Factories Act, was necessarily required to run manufacturing activity - Held, yes [Para 6]

FACT: The assessee was the manufacturer of Scooters. It had availed the Cenvat credit on Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG). LPG was also used in its canteen for providing meals to the workers and staff members. The department held that the quantity of LPG which was used in canteen was not eligible for the Modvat credit as it was not used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final products. The assessee was asked to reverse inadmissible credit of LPG used in the canteen. However, on appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the demand of duty.

On appeal :

HELD: In the instant case, there was no doubt that the assessee was required to maintain a canteen in its factory as per the Factories Act and to provide canteen facilities to its workers to run its factory which was a statutory requirement. In M.M.R. Khan v. Union of India AIR 1990 SC 937, the Apex Court had given a clear-cut findings that providing canteen was an integral part of the manufacturing activity of the assessee and as per the decision in Maruti Suzuki Ltd.'s v. CCE [2009] 22 STT 54 (SC) also any input which has gone into manufacturing of the final product directly or indirectly is entitled to input credit. Relying on both the decisions, it was to be held in the instant case also that the assessee was entitled to input credit on LPG used in the canteen, which as per the Factories Act was necessarily required to run its manufacturing activity. Accordingly, there was no infirmity in the impugned order and the same was to be upheld and the appeal filed by the revenue was to rejected. [Para 6]

of insurance of money in transit was covered by the definition of ‘Input service’. [Para 6]

As regards the follow-up services, the same were business auxiliary services availed by the assessee in connection with installation of captive power plant. Since these services were in connection with installation of captive power plant and since the services in relation to setting up or modernization are specifically covered by the definition of ‘input service’, these services were also eligible for Cenvat credit. [Para 7] As regards the Cenvat credit of service tax paid in respect of telephone installed in the residence of General Manager and company’s guest house, the assessee had not shown as to how these services were in relation to his manufacturing business/or in relation to manufacture of finished goods. The use of these telephones may be substantially for non-business purposes also; while for being covered by the definition of ‘input service’ the service availed must be in or in relation to manufacturing business of the assessee. Service tax credit in respect of telephone services in respect of telephone installed in the G.M.’s residence and the company’s guest house had, therefore, been rightly denied. [Para 8]

As regards the Cenvat credit of service tax on the premium for insurance of the personnel working in the assessee’s factory, the assessee pleaded that as per the provisions of the Factory Act, it as principal employer had vicarious liability for any compensation in the case of injury, etc., to even contract workers and for that reason, the accident insurance cover was provided even to the workers supplied by the contractors. The Tribunal held in Millipore India Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 22 STT 536 (Bang. - CESTAT) that, medical and personnel accident policy, group personnel accident policy, etc., are covered by the definition of ‘input service’ and Cenvat credit of service tax paid on them is available. In view of this, the assessee was eligible for Cenvat credit of service tax on the insurance premium paid for the insurance of the personnel working in the factory. [Para 9]

In view of the above discussion, except for the portion of the impugned order upholding the denial of Cenvat credit taken in respect of telephone services, in respect of telephone installed at the residence of the General Manager and at the assessee’s guest house, the rest of the order upholding the Cenvat credit demand by denying Cenvat credit in respect of marine inland transit insurance, money insurance for money in transit from bank to factory to & fro, follow-up services in connection with installation of plant & machinery of captive power plant and insurance of personnel working in the factory and upholding the penalty on the assessee, was to be set aside. HEADNOTE: Rule  3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, read with Rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 - Cenvat Credit - General - Whether it is permissible for input service distributor being head office of appellant, to distribute credit before obtaining registration - Held, yes - Whether where appellant has taken credit not on valid invoice but on allocation chart which contains all information as required under Rule 4A of Service Tax Rules, 1994, said document should be accepted and credit cannot be denied - Held, yes [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat: Input service distributor can distribute credit before obtaining registration; credit can validly be availed on basis of allocation chart if it contains all relevant information; valid invoice is not a must  Cenvat: For Rent-a-cab service received by assessee for to and fro transportation of assessee's employees to job worker's place for purpose of assessee's manufacturing activity there, cenvat credit would be available  Cenvat: For security service received at job worker's place in relation to activity carried out for assessee's manufacturing, cenvat credit would be available

Rule  3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Input (Rent a cab service) - Job worker was carrying out cutting process of paper supplied by appellant on job work basis - Appellant received rent-a-cab service - Vehicle was used for transportation of assessee's employees to and fro factory of job worker for purpose of factory activity - Whether rent-a-cab service would fall within ambit of definition of input service and appellant was entitled to avail cenvat credit on said input - Held, yes [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]

Rule  3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Input (Security service) - Input service distributor can distribute credit before obtaining registration - Appellant received security service at job worker's place - Whether since service was received in relation to job work activity carried out on behalf of appellant, job work activity being part and parcel of overall manufacturing of final products, credit would be admissible on security service - Held, yes [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee availed cenvat credit in respect of distribution of credit by the Head Office, an input service distributor [ISD], which was distributed by the Head Office before obtaining registration. The assessee also availed credit of service tax paid on rent-a-cab service and security service.

The Adjudicating Authority denied cenvat credit in respect of distribution of credit by the Head Office on the plea that the credit was distributed by the Head Office before obtaining registration and the assessee had taken credit not on basis valid invoice but on basis the allocation chart. He also denied cenvat credit of tax paid on rent-a-cab service and security service on the plea that the services were provided at job worker's place, where the job worker was carrying out cutting process of paper on behalf of the assessee.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the original order.

On appeal to Tribunal:

HELD: As regard the registration issue whether the ISD can distribute the credit before obtaining registration has been settled by the Gujarat High Court in the case of CCE v. Dashion Ltd.[2016] 66 taxmann.com 31/54 GST 32, Ahemdabad Bench of Tribunal in the case of CCE v. Smita Conductors Ltd. 2012 (278) ELT 492 and Delhi Bench of Tribunal in the case of Bhansali Engg. Polymers Ltd. v. CCE[2015] 53 taxmann.com 448/49 GST 697. From the said judgments, it is observed that even if the credit is distributed by input service distributor before obtaining registration, it is permissible.

As regards the issue, where the assessee has taken the credit not on valid invoice but on the allocation chart, if the document on which credit was passed on contains all the information as required under rule 4A of Service tax Rules, 1994, the said document should be accepted and the credit could not be denied. The allocation chart on record contains the details as required under rule 4A of the 1994 Rules. Further the said issue has been considered by the various Tribunals in the cases of Shriram Pistons & Rings Ltd. v. CCE 2012 (281) ELT 90 ( Trib. - Delhi ), CCE v. Tikmani Steel Co. Ltd. 2005 (192) ELT 413 (Trib. - Bang.) and Vodafone Cellular Ltd. v. CCE [2016] 55 GST 610/69 taxmann.com 112 (Mum. - CESTAT).

FACT: "In fact the invoices issued by T1SC0 Depots (though registered as dealers) for effecting inter-depot transfers are merely stock transfer invoices and can not be categorized as Dealer's invoices, because there is no sale by one Depot to another depot. The sale from TISCO to the appellants constitutes the first sale. HEADNOTE: Rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, read with Rule 11, of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 - Cenvat Credit - Documents and accounts - Whether Cenvat credit can be availed by manufacturer on invoices issued by supplier for clearance of inputs or capital goods, showing manufacturer's name as consignee and name of dealers as buyer - Held, yes - Whether for claiming Cenvat credit on input, it is not mandatory that payment towards purchase of input had to be made - Held, yes - Appellant being manufacturer availed Cenvat credit on invoices wherein appellant's name was mentioned as consignee and dealers name as buyer - Credit was denied on ground that invoices showing appellant's name as consignee was invalid - Whether since there were number of transactions in trade where there was no transaction of any payments towards supply, despite this, Cenvat credit was admissible and could not be disputed so long input duty was paid, goods were received in factory and used in manufacture - Held, yes - Whether appellant had correctly and legally availed Cenvat credit - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]CENVAT : Cenvat credit can be availed by manufacturer on strength of invoices issued by supplier for clearance of inputs or capital goods, showing manufacturer's name as consignee and name of dealers as buyer

FACT: The appellant being manufacturer availed Cenvat credit on the invoices wherein the appellant's name appeared as consignee and in the column of the buyer, names of the dealers were mentioned.

The Revenue alleged that, since the appellant was not buyer as per the invoices and the appellant was not making payment of said invoices to the manufacturer-supplier, documents were invalid and credit was not admissible on such documents. Accordingly, it was proposed that Cenvat credit should not be allowed.

The Adjudicating Authority confirmed the demand of imposition of penalty of equal amount and Cenvat credit including interest.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) modified the order inasmuch maintained confirmation of demand of Cenvat Credit. However, he reduced the penalty and maintained the demand of interest.

On second appeal before the Tribunal:

HELD: One of the documents on which Cenvat credit is allowed as mentioned in clause (a) of subject rule 9(1) is an invoice issued by manufacturer for clearance of inputs or capital goods from his factory. In the instant case, invoices, on which credit was disputed was issued by manufacturer and the appellant's name is clearly appearing as consignee. Therefore, the invoices in question squarely covered by clause (a) of sub-rule 1 of Rule 9. The Revenue's contention that in case of purchase of input from dealer, invoices should be issued by first stage dealer or second stage dealer, is not agreeable. Only in case where the input is purchased directly from a dealer on his invoices and the manufacturer invoices does not indicate the name of the recipient as consignee, the first stage dealer or second stage dealer, as case may be, who is registered with Central Excise, should issue invoices as provided under rule 11 of Central Excise Rules, 2002. However, in the instant case invoices on which credit was taken issued by manufacturer and appellant's name is appearing as consignee, in such cases credit is admissible on these invoices and there is no need of separate invoices to be issued by the registered dealer for taking credit. The contention of the Revenue that since appellant has not made payment for purchase of the input of the manufacturer supplier, Cenvat credit is not admissible, is absurd for the reason that manufacturer supplier as per the invoices, sold the goods to the dealers and in turn dealers sold the goods to appellant in such transactions there are sale purchase transactions is involved, i.e., one from manufacturer supplier to dealers and second from dealers to the appellant. Therefore, the appellant made payment to dealers and cannot make payment of the bills to manufacturer supplier. Therefore, contention of the Revenue on this count is not acceptable. However, for taking Cenvat credit on input it is not mandatory that payment towards purchase of the input has to be made. There are number of transactions in the trade such as procurement input from group company, sister concern on payment of duty, procurement of input for job work, etc. In such transaction there is no transaction of any payments towards supply of inputs. Despite this position, Cenvat credit is admissible and cannot be disputed so long input is duty paid, received in the factory and used in the manufacture. The appellant has correctly and legally availed the Cenvat credit on the invoices wherein appellant name is appearing as consignee and name of the dealers as buyer; therefore, the impugned order is set aside. [Para 5]

material and used capital goods on which credit was taken from DTA unit to EHTP unit, after duly obtaining permission from the department.

The assessee reversed credit under protest and applied for refund thereof.

Tribunal, relying upon its own order, held that : (a) credit reversal is not required in case of used capital goods; and (b) even otherwise, said clearance was exempt under Notification No. 22/2003-CE.

The High Court confirmed order of Tribunal. On revenue's appeal, Supreme Court remanded matter back to the High Court as in CCE v. Solectron Centum Electronics Ltd. [2014] 46 taxmann.com 43/45 GST 722 (SC).

Revenue's Arguments

As the assessee has not received the excisable goods directly from the factory of manufacture or warehouse, the condition stipulated in the Notification No.22/2003 is not fulfilled. In the instant case, the assessee has imported the impugned capital goods on which Cenvat credit has been availed and cleared without payment of duty to EHTP under the cover of CT-3 and therefore, the impugned order passed by the Tribunal is not legal and requires to be set aside.

Assessee's Arguments

The assessee is having the DTA unit in the ground floor and EHTP unit in the First floor. When the assessee purchased the capital goods as well as raw material, it has paid excise duty. With the permission of the authority, it has transmitted or shifted the capital goods after its use and raw material as such to the EHTP unit.

When authorities have permitted the transmission of raw material and used capital goods which have suffered duty to EHTP unit, it was not liable to reverse credit.

Issue Involved

Whether assessee was liable to reverse credit ?

HELD: The EOU is entitled to procure goods duty free. Such procurement is permissible only subject to fulfillment of condition of the exemption notification.

Further, the decision of Larger Bench of the Tribunal in Lakshmi Automatic Loom Works Ltd. (supra) deals with only reversal of input as such and not removal of used capital goods.

In the instant case, the assessee is having Domestic Tariff Area (DTA) Unit in the ground floor. It is having Electronic Hardware Technology Parks (EHTP) Unit in the first floor. The assessee while purchasing the capital goods as well as inputs to its DTA unit has paid duty. Therefore, it has availed Cenvat credit.

In so far as the capital goods are concerned, it was used by the assessee in DTA unit. Thereafter, with the permission of the authorities in terms of the Rules 11 and 20 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 and clause (6) of the Notification No.22/2003, the assessee removed the said goods from DTA unit to EHTP unit. As the said removal of used capital goods was done before the amendment to rule 3(4)/(5) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 during November 2007, no credit was reversible on removal of used capital goods and as such they were not liable to pay duty.

In so far as the inputs are concerned, with the permission of the authorities as reflected in Form CT-3 they were also removed to EHTP unit. The assessee had purchased those inputs for its DTA unit. It was not liable to reverse credit as it had paid duty as it was purchased for DTA unit and thereafter with the permission of the authority removed to EOU unit.

In the instant case, when it removed goods to EHTP unit, it was not bringing excisable goods directly from the factory of manufacture or warehouse and therefore they are not entitled to the benefit of Notification No.22/2003. This is not a case where the assessee was purchasing those goods for its EHTP unit for the first time. It purchased the capital goods as well as inputs for its DTA unit. Therefore, duty was paid. Thereafter, with the permission of the authorities as reflected in CT-3, the inputs were removed from DTA unit to the EHTP unit. Similarly, the capital goods purchased for DTA unit was used, it was not removed as such and when it was removed to EHTP unit again, they have no liability to pay the credit. This aspect has been completely missed by the authority.

They proceeded on the assumption that user industry thereby mean EHTP unit was not bringing excisable goods directly from the factory of manufacture or warehouse and therefore they are not eligible for exemption.

In the light of the aforesaid Notification which granted exemption, it is very clear that EHTP unit is entitled to exemption of payment of duty. Therefore, the assessee rightly availed the Cenvat credit and then reversed it when those goods were moved to EHTP unit and claimed refund. [Para 8]

It has been further held that the Tribunal is correct in allowing Modvat credit on capital goods received when endorsement is made in the Bill of Entry by the importer. In the present case, Cenvat invoices were consigned in favour of SISCOL. [Para 64.1] Power plant supplying exclusively to factory for manufacture - Treated as part of factory : Capital goods/input/input service used on power plant situated at a different premises CENVAT credit is admissible subject to exclusive supply of power by the impugned plant to the assessee manufacturing unit. In the present case, the capital goods were used to set up power plant for generation of electricity primarily for use in the manufacture of the final product within the factory of SISCOL. So, if the power plant is situated outside the factory premises, Cenvat credit on capital goods used for setting up power plant cannot be denied as the electricity is captively consumed within the factory of SISCOL. [Para 64.4]

Lease agreement : On perusal of the lease agreement, it is seen that the Lessor (SISCOL) requested to the Lessee (JSWPL) to set up a power plant in the premises of the Lessor (SISCOL) to take care of the power generation of the Lessor to which Lessee has agreed. The lease of the immovable property is determined for a limited period conditionally on the happenings of some events. The tenure of the lease agreement depends upon the happenings of the future events. In the instant case, it is a conditional transfer of the property with an interest created on a transfer of the property and dependent upon the fulfilment of the condition. Thus, it is clearly evident that SISCOL had provided their land to JSWPL with a condition to set up a power plant and the electricity generated would be consumed in manufacturing activities of SISCOL. [Para 68.1]

Lease agreement was financing arrangement : An agreement should also be examined with actual state of affairs and its implementation from the records. In the present case, it may be seen from the documents and records that in 2004, SISCOL was declared as sick unit under SICA, 1985. CDR Cell report would show that SJG came forward for financing the sick unit SISCOL, as finance acts as an engine of growth. It appears from the Show Cause Notices that JSWPL, one of the companies of SJG, have expertise in constructing and operating Power Plants and JSW Steel Ltd. another company of SJG, is one of the purchasers of the final product of SISCOL. It is recorded in the CDR Cell report that there was proposal of merger of SISCOL with SJG, which is corroborated by Director's report dated 26-4-2005 of JSWPL balance sheet. It is mentioned in "Unit III Debentures Trust Deed" dated 22-9-2005 of JSWPL that with a view to finance its 2 x 30 MW plant at SISCOL, the company has approached the Debenture holders. Further, TNEB approved as SISCOL Captive Power Plant located in the company's premises. [Para 68.2]

Rule 4(3) - Capital goods were acquired under loan/lease agreement : Rule 4 (3) of CCR 2004 provides that the Cenvat credit in respect of the capital goods shall be allowed to a manufacturer, even if the capital goods are acquired by him on lease, hire purchase or loan agreement, from a financing company. Rule 4(3) has a wide amplitude in so far as it would cover the cases of various types of financial arrangements for availing credit on the capital goods. It is contemplated that under this sub-rule (3) of rule 4 would cover the cases where the ownership of the capital goods does not vest in the manufacturer until the loan is repaid. There must be an agreement for the purpose of acquiring the capital goods. Variations/unusual features in the agreement covering the lease agreement were not relevant for determining the eligibility of credit. It is clear that title of the property is not relevant for availing Cenvat credit on capital goods. [Para 68.3]

Plant was captive power plant : Even prior to 31-8-2006, it was a Captive Power Plant of SISCOL as approved by TNEB under the Electricity Act. SISCOL was a sick unit. They entered into lease agreement with JSWPL, a relationship had already been developed prior to October 2005, as evident from CDR Cell report, JSWPL balance sheet etc., for financial accommodation to get loan from UTI Bank Ltd. for setting up C.P.P. and one of the considerations is that electricity would be supplied to SISCOL, which is an integral part of manufacturing activities of SISCOL. HEADNOTE: II. Rule 57-O of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Capital goods - Whether incorrect classification done by supplier cannot be a ground for denial of Modvat credit - Held, yes - Whether fuel storage tanks are eligible capital goods for Modvat credit - Held, yes [Para 4]

FACT: The assessee claimed benefit of Modvat credit on fuel storage tanks purchased by it from the material obtained from ship breaking company and falling under sub-head 72.30. The revenue denied claim on the ground that since said heading does not apply to machinery or tanks, fuel storage tanks received under said invoices were not to be treated as capital goods for Modvat credit. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the credit.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: The charges only on classification of the input under heading 72.30 and not under the machinery or fuel storage tank or steel tanks headings, would not deter from granting capital goods credit; as the incorrect classification done by the supplier cannot be a ground for denial of Modvat credit. The credit can be obtained if the input is used in relation to the manufacture of the goods. Fuel storage tanks have been held to be eligible capital goods by catena of decisions of the Tribunal. Therefore, there was no reason to deny the credit on fuel storage tanks eligibility. [Para 4]

HEADNOTE: I. Section 16 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Rule 3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Input tax credit - Eligibility and conditions for taking credit - Period 2008-09 - Assessee was engaged in manufacture of car seats - Its premises was located within premises of one 'H' - It procured capital goods, i.e., two machines for use in manufacture of car seats - It installed said machines within premises of 'H' and availed cenvat credit of duty paid on these machines - Adjudicating Authority denied cenvat credit on plea that machines were not installed in premises of assessee - Whether since assessee stood merged with 'H' later on, it was eligible for cenvat credit - Held, yes [Para 5.2][In favour of assessee]GST/Cenvat: Where assessee was engaged in manufacture of car seats and it procured two machines for use in manufacture of car seats and installed same in premises of one 'H', since assessee stood merged with 'H' later on, it was eligible for cenvat credit of duty on machines   GST/Cenvat: Where assessee imported 'Auto Ware House System' a complete automated storing system, it was eligible for cenvat credit of duty paid on said machinery

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of car seats. Its premises was located within the premises of one 'H'. During the year 2008-09, it had procured capital goods, i.e., two machines for use in the manufacture of car seats. It had not installed the said machines in its premises but within the premises of 'H', since it did not have facilities for keeping them in air-conditioned atmosphere as was required.

It availed cenvat credit of duty paid on these machines.

The Adjudicating Authority held that since the machines were not installed in the premises of the assessee but in the premises of 'H' which had separate Central Excise Registration, availment of credit by the assessee was not in order. He accordingly denied the cenvat credit availed by assessee.

On appeal to Tribunal:

HELD: No doubt, for availing credit of capital goods the conditionalities of rule 2(a) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 will require to be satisfied, inter alia, that goods should be used 'in the factory of manufacture of final products'. Strictly interpreting this provision would no doubt appear, at first sight, that in respect of machines which were installed not in the premises of the assessee but in an adjacent unit of 'H', cenvat credit would ordinarily not be available. However, it should also be kept in mind that the assessee stood merged with 'H' with effect from 1-4-2009 and as a result both these premises became a common entity from that date. From the facts on record, it appears that the assessee has availed credit under cover of invoice dated 1-11-2008, which was around five months prior to the date of the said merger. However, at the same time if the assessee had not taken the credit on or around 1-11-2008, but only on or after 1-4-2009, the availment of credit would not have excited any controversy. Therefore, the assessee's right to avail the credit on the said capital goods is very much available with effect from 1-4-2009 and the availment of credit prior to that date does not extinguish such eligibility. At the most, there will arise an interest liability for the period 1-11-2008 to 1-4-2009, i.e., for the period between the date when the credit was availed and the effective date of merger of two entities. This being so, the availment of cenvat credit by the assessee cannot be disturbed. However, the assessee will require to discharge interest liability at applicable rates for the period 1-11-2008 to 1-4-2009. [Para 5.2]

HEADNOTE: Rule 4, read with rules 2(a) and 3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Conditions for allowing of - Capital Goods - Period from September 2005 to October 2006 - SISCOL, a sick unit engaged in manufacture of iron and steel, leased out its land to JSWPL for setting up Captive Power Plant (CPP) - JSWPL took loan on said premises and using said funds, purchased various machineries for setting up CPP - Purchase invoices were endorsed in name of SISCOL and resultant electricity was also exclusively captively used by SISCOL for manufacture work - From 31-8-2006, lease agreement was terminated - SISCOL took credit of purchases made by JSWPL during Sept. 2005 to March 2006 as 'capital goods' : 50% during year 2005-06 and balance in July 2006 - Department denied said credit on ground that purchases were made by JSWPL and same was never received in factory of SISCOL - HELD : 'CPP' for generation of electricity was not an independent entity from SISCOL; Section 35D of the Central Excise Act, 1944 read with rule 23 of the CESTAT (Procedure) Rules, 1982, section 86 of the Finance Act, 1994 and 129C of the Customs Act, 1962 - Appeals - Procedure - Appellate Tribunal - Assessee filed a miscellaneous application for placing additional evidence on record - HELD : Since evidence produced by assessee was available at time of adjudication and is very much relevant for arriving at correct conclusion in matter, same was allowed [Paras 2 and 3] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: Facts

The main assessee JSWSL was having an integrated steel plant with facilities for production of 'pig iron', 'steel billet', 'bar', 'rod with virgin iron ore' as the basic raw material.

HEADNOTE: Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - CENVAT credit - Procedure to be observed by manufacturer - Assessee was availing MODVAT credit on basis of invoices issued by dealers/traders - MODVAT credit was denied to assessee on ground that duty paying documents did not show required details - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed said order - As per relevant Board Circular, Assistant Commissioner should ignore minor procedural lapses as long as it is verified that inputs/capital goods have suffered duty and are being used in manufacturing process - Whether Commissioner (Appeals), while disposing of appeal, should have considered Board’s Circular - Held, yes - Whether since assessee demonstrated that it had received duty paid inputs and consumed same in its factory, assessee was eligible for MODVAT credit - Held, yes [Para 5] Circular and notification : Circular No. 441/7/99-CX dated 23-2-1999

FACT: The assessee availed MODVAT credit on the invoices issued by the dealers/traders during the period July, 1994 to December, 1994. A show-cause notice was issued to the assessee denying the MODVAT credit on the ground that these dealers/traders were not registered dealers with the Central Excise department. Though the assessee contested the show-cause notice on the ground that these dealers/traders got themselves registered, the adjudicating authority confirmed the demand on the assessee and imposed penalty on the ground that addresses of the traders were different and duty paying documents did not show the required details. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), in respect of the credit availed by the assessee on the invoices issued by Indian Oil Corporation, allowed the appeal but in respect of other dealers/traders, denied the MODVAT credit and upheld imposition of penalty. He, however, reduced the quantum of penalty.

On appeal :

HELD: It was undisputed that the inputs covered under all the orders were received in the factory of the assessee and consumed by it in its factory. From the plain reading of the Board’s Circular No. 441/7/99-CX dated 23-2-1999, it is very clear that the Assistant Commissioner should ignore minor procedural lapses as long as it is verified that inputs/capital goods have suffered duty and are being used in the manufacturing process. The Board, in the above Circular had clearly mentioned for disposal of pending cases accordingly. The Commissioner (Appeals), while disposing of the appeal, should have considered the Board’s Circular while dismissing the appeal filed by the assessee. Accordingly, the assessee demonstrated that it had received the duty paid inputs and consumed the same in its factory and, hence, it was eligible for MODVAT credit. [Para 5]

HEADNOTE: Rule 57 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat Credit - Modvat - Job work - Modvat--Input sent directly even before Modvat benefit announced, eligible. Notfn. 351/86-CE

HELD: Modvat--Inputs sent directly to job worker by suppliers and thereafter received by the manufacturers in their factory are eligible for credit, even before issue of Notification No. 351/86-CE dated 20.6.1986 allowing the benefit of this facility, in case the manufacturer discharges the onus of establishing the identity of the inputs in question after the same were sent to the intermediate processor and received back in the factory. Matter remanded to original authority for reconsideration, and due verification of the above fact, in accordance with law. "..........the burden is on the appellant to establish the identity of the input in question after the same were sent to the job worker and received back in the appellant's factory. Since the appellant undertakes to discharge this onus with reference to the input in question with necessary evidence, without expressing any opinion on the merits of the issue and in the interest of justice we set aside the impugned order and remit the matter to the original authority for consideration of the issues in the light of our observations above and in accordance with law".

38A of the Central Excise Act, provides saving clause in respect of rules, notifications and orders made or issued under Central Excise Act, 1944 and the said section has been given retrospective effect with effect from 1944 and the proceedings initiated have been validated vide section 132 of the Finance Act, 2001. In these circumstances, the challenge to the issue of show cause notice and the proceedings would not sustain. [Para 6.2]

Issue No. 2 Assessee has not disputed the fact that they did not receive the material and therefore, they raised debit notes on the supplier/transporter towards non-receipt of the goods and recovered the charges for the value of the materials not received. It is clear from this factual position, as admitted, the assessee wants to avail credit in respect of material not received. This contention of the assessee cannot be accepted at all. The Cenvat Scheme envisages receipt of duty paid inputs and its utilization in the manufacture of dutiable final products. Therefore, credit was denied. [Para 6.3]

Issue No. 3

The assessee cleared the goods under rule 57F(4). Under rule 57F(5) the assessee was required to bring back the waste generated at the job-worker's factory premises and the only situation where the assessee was exempted from bringing back the waste generated was when the waste was cleared on payment of duty at the job-worker's end. In the present case, there is no evidence led to show that the waste generated at the job-worker's end was cleared on payment of duty. In these circumstances, the confirmation of duty demand is sustainable in law. [Para 6.4]

Issue No. 4

The revenue has proceeded to confirm the demand on the ground that the goods were sold to ISMTL. Excise duty is on manufacture and not on sale; whether the goods are sold or not, the liability to excise duty would arise on manufacture of the goods and the liability has to be discharged at the time of removal of goods from the factory. In the present case, in respect of 78 Nos. of DSRM Rolls manufactured by the assessee and captively used within the factory of production, Notification No. 67/95-C.E., dated 16-3-1995 provided for exemption on the capital goods captively used within the factory in the production or manufacture of excisable goods. It is not in dispute' that the assessee used the capital goods in the manufacture of final products specified in Notification No. 67/95-C.E. If that be so, the demand on the ground that capital goods were sold, would not sustain at all. Similarly, in respect of 38 Nos. of DSRM Rolls imported by the assessee and used within the factory of production and sold to ISMTL, reversal of credit is envisaged only when the capital goods are removed as such or removed after use or removed as waste and scrap under the provisions of rule 57S(2) of the Central Excise Rules, as it stood at the relevant time. In these circumstances, reversal of credit taken on the capital goods captively used in the manufacture of final products is not warranted. [Para 6.5]

Issue No. 5

Imposition of penalty was quite harsh and a penalty of 10 per cent of duty demand would suffice for violation of statutory provisions. Accordingly, the penalty was reduced.

As regards the penalty of Rs. 15 lakhs imposed on General Manager (Finance), he was only an employee of the assessee and did not stand to gain personally by the wrong credit availed by the assessee firm. Therefore, there is no reason to impose any penalty on him under rule 209A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. Accordingly, the penalty imposed on employee was set aside. [Para 6.7]

HEADNOTE: Rule 9, read with rule 4, of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Documents on which credit may be taken - Cenvat Credit was denied on ground that credit has been taken on strength of invoices where owner is person other than assessee and since owner of capital goods was not financing company, credit was ineligible - HELD : Duty paying documents clearly indicated name of contractors i.e. Essar Projects Ltd. and as also name and address of assessee as a consignee - Since it was not disputed that capital goods/other goods which were received at site of assessee, were used in refinery and documents indicated correct duty paying nature, demand was set aside [Para 7(i)] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Consumables such as enamels, paints, polyester resins, electrodes and chemicals used/consumed by assessee during installation/erection or setting up or maintenance of factory are eligible for credit

Rule 3, of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - General - Non-submission of intimation of receipt of capital goods and other goods to Jurisdictional Superintendent is a procedural violation and where it has been accepted and undisputed that capital goods and other goods were received and consumed as per law, mere non-filing of declaration cannot be a ground for denial of credit - Moreover, credit cannot be denied only on ground that same is availed on original copy and/or extra copy of invoice [Paras 7(ii) and 7(iii)] [In favour of assessee]

Rule 2(a) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Capital Goods - HTPE sheets, insulation packages, domestic (refractory) anchors etc. though not falling under specific Chapters of 84, 85 and 90, are used in refinery as either components or spares in plant and machinery which are used for manufacturing of final products - Hence, items were consumed/used as components, spares or parts of various machineries which were either fabricated and installed alongwith bought out items for setting up of refinery - Accordingly, they were eligible for credit as capital goods [Para 7(iv)] [In favour of assessee]

Rule 2(k), read with Rule 2(a), of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Input - Consumables such as enamels, paints, polyester resins, electrodes and chemicals used/consumed by assessee during installation/erection or setting up of factory are eligible for credit - This is because said items were used in factory premises for maintaining of plant and machinery, fabrication of machinery [Para 7(v)] [In favour of assessee]

Rule 15 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Confiscation and penalty - Where Cenvat Credit is allowed on merits, penalty under rule 15 is to be set aside [Para 8] [In favour of assessee]

Rule 14 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Recovery of cenvat credit wrongly taken or erroneously refunded - Even if credit is taken and subsequently reversed, interest liability arises [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: Facts

The assessee being refinery unit, had undertaken activity of constructing the refinery from October 1996.

For construction of such a refinery, they received various capital goods, consumables, inputs, etc. which were accounted by them in the books of account. The said refinery was commissioned and assessee got Central Excise registration and started manufacturing activities from November, 2006.

Assessee availed Cenvat Credit of the duty paid on the various items used and consumed by them for setting up such a refinery in the month of November, 2006.

On the scrutiny of the monthly returns filed by the assessee in December, 2006, the lower authorities were of the view that the assessee is not eligible for availing Cenvat Credit and directed them to show cause why such credit be not denied.

The adjudicating authority denied the Cenvat Credit of an amount of Rs.26,11,20,838/- on various grounds as ineligible Cenvat Credit, demanded interest thereof and imposed a penalty under Rule 15(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004; also demanded interest on an amount of Rs.39,02,938/- reversed by the assessee during the scrutiny of the records admitting that such credit is ineligible.

Cenvat credit had been taken by its manufacturing unit at Hapur. A show-cause notice was issued to the assessee for recovery of allegedly wrongly taken Cenvat credit along with interest and penalty on ground that Delhi office of the assessee could not issue invoices to factory at Hapur for passing on service tax credit as Input Service Distributor when no registration in that regard had been obtained. The Commissioner confirmed the Cenvat credit demand along with interest and also imposed penalty.

On appeal : HELD: Concept of Input Service Distributor was introduced for the first time in 2004 Rules effective from 10-9-2004, read with 1994 Rules. Rule 2(m ) of the 2004 Rules, defines an ‘Input Service Distributor’ as an office of the manufacturer or producer of final product or provider of output service, which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the 1994 Rules, towards purchases of input services and issues invoices, bills or, as the case may be, challans for the purpose of distributing the credit of service tax paid on such services to such manufacturer or producer or provider, as the case may be. Rule 4 of the 1994 Rules, provides for obtaining registration by the persons liable for paying the service tax. This rule does not contain any provision regarding obtaining of registration by Input Service Distributor and it provides for registration of only the persons liable for paying the service tax.

From a plain reading of sub-rule (2) of rule 4A of the 1994 Rules, it is clear that there is no provision in this sub-rule that an Input Service Distributor before issue of invoice, bill or challan for passing on the service tax credit must have a registration and should quote such registration number in the invoices, bills or challans issued by him. Though rule 4A in its present form had come into effect from 10-9-2004, there is no provision in sub-rule (2) of rule 4A that this sub-rule will be effective only when the procedure for obtaining registration by Input Service Distributor is notified or that it is necessary for an Input Service Distributor as defined in rule 2(1)(ccc) of the 1994 Rules, read with rule 2(m) of the 2004 Rules, to obtain registration before he could issue the invoices, bills or challans for passing on the Cenvat credit.

By Notification No. 27/05-ST, dated 7-6-2005, the Service Tax (Registration of Special Category of Persons) Rules, 2005 were notified and rule 3(1) of these Rules provided for an Input Service Distributor to make an application to the Jurisdictional Central Excise Superintendent for obtaining registration within the period of thirty days from the commencement of business or 16-6-2005, whichever is later. Simultaneous with the issue of Notification No. 27/05-CE (NT), dated 7-6-2005, another Notification No. 28/05-CE (NT), dated 7-6-2005 was issued by which 2004 Rules were amended and in rule 9(1) of the 2004 Rules clause (e) was amended and sub-rule (10) of rule 9 was substituted by new rule which provided that the Input Service Distributor would furnish a half yearly return in such form as may be prescribed by notification issued by the Board.

HEADNOTE: Rule  4 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Conditions for allowing - Whether where expenditure was incurred by assessee company, even though invoices were not in name of company but in name of directors/employees of company and same had been booked as expenditure in books of assessee, credit was admissible - Held, yes - Whether where services of construction of foundation in factory, construction of security cabin, construction of scrap yard and shifting of machines directly related to activity of manufacturing unit and were clearly included in inclusion part of definition of input services credit was admissible on these services - Held, yes - Whether as regards air fair and cleaning services, they were related to business activity of assessee company, hence credit was admissible - Held, yes - Whether where there was no dispute that services were received by assessee and invoices raised to assessee, Cenvat credit could not have been denied for mere non mention of registration number on invoice - Held, yes - Whether further, in Cenvat Credit Rules, relaxation was specifically provided for banking services, hence, Cenvat credit on banking charges could not have been disallowed - Held, yes - Whether therefore, assessee would be prima facie entitled for Cenvat credit which was disallowed for various reasons, subject to verification of invoices to be produced by assessee - Held, yes [Paras 6, 6.1, 6.2, 6.3, 6.4  7] [In favour of assessee/Matter remanded]CENVAT : Where expenditure was incurred by assessee company, even though invoices were not in name of company but in name of directors/employees and same had been booked as expenditure in books of assessee, Cenvat credit could not have been denied

FACT: As per the impugned order Cenvat credit was denied on the following grounds:

(a)

Certain Cenvatable invoices were not in the name of the assessee

(b)

Some of the Cenvatable bills/invoices were not available /traceable.

(c)

Some of the invoices which could not be traced, in this regard certificate had been obtained.

(d)

Some of the services were held not to be input services.

(e)

In some of the Cenvatable invoices, service tax registration number was not mentioned.

(f)

Cenvat credit was availed on GAR7 Challan. In respect of banking services, no bills were available.

On appeal the assessee submitted that the Cenvat credit had been denied only on technical infraction, however there was no dispute that Cenvatable bills were accounted for in the books of the assessee and services were received by the assessee, therefore merely on technical errors, substantial benefit of Cenvat credit should not have been denied.

HELD: Though the invoices are not in the name of the assessee but it is in the name of the directors and the employees of the company, credit should be allowed for the reason that all these expenditure were incurred by the assessee company and the same is not under dispute, therefore even though the invoices are not in the name of the company but in the name of the directors/employees and the same has been booked as expenditure in the books of assessee, credit is admissible. [Para 6]

As regard the reason for denying the credit that cenvatable bills/invoices were not available, assessee submitted that now they are in possession of most of the invoices which can be produced before the authority for verification. In such cases the matter needs to be remanded so that assessee can produce invoices before the adjudicating authority and the adjudicating authority after verifying the same can allow the credit to the assessee. [Para 6.1]

As regard the services which were not considered as input services, it is found that services involved are of construction of foundation in the factory, construction of security cabin, construction of scrap yard, shifting of machines, these services are directly related to activity of the manufacturing unit and the same are clearly included in the inclusion part of the definition of the input services therefore credit is admissible on these services. As regard the services of civil work at Mohannagar quarters, Misc. Civil work in HDFC colony, these services are not related to the factory but it is related to the staff quarters, therefore civil work of staff quarters and civil work in HDFC colony cannot be treated as input service. As regard the air fair and cleaning services, it is related to the business activity of the assessee company hence the credit is admissible. [Para 6.2]
