a supplementary invoice, bill or challan issued by a provider of output service, in terms of the provisions of Service Tax Rules, 1994 except where the additional amount of tax became recoverable from the provider of service on account of non-levy or non-payment or short-levy or short-payment by reason of fraud or collusion or wilful mis-statement or suppression of facts or contravention of any of the provisions of the Finance Act or of the rules made thereunder with the intent to evade payment of service tax; or]

(c)

a bill of entry; or

(d)

a certificate issued by an appraiser of customs in respect of goods imported through a Foreign Post Office 94a[or, as the case may be, an Authorized Courier, registered with the Principal Commissioner of Customs or the Commissioner of Customs in-charge of the customs airport]; or

95[(e)

a challan evidencing payment of service tax, by the service recipient as the person liable to pay service tax; or]

(f)

an invoice, a bill or challan issued by a provider of input service on or after the 10th day of September, 2004; or

95a[(fa)

a Service Tax Certificate for Transportation of goods by rail issued by the Indian Railways; or]

(g)

an invoice, bill or challan issued by an input service distributor under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 :

96[Provided that the credit of additional duty of customs levied under sub-section (5) of section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 (51 of 1975) shall not be allowed if the invoice or the supplementary invoice, as the case may be, bears an indication to the effect that no credit of the said additional duty shall be admissible.]

obtained.

In Krishna Wire Products v. CCE 2003 (158) ELT 491 (CESTAT), the goods were dispatched directly to place of manufacturer-buyer directly from place of import, but the dealer's invoice showed that goods were dispatched from godown of the dealer. However, there was co-relation between duty paying documents and invoice of dealer. It was held that buyer can avail Cenvat is available, so long as duty paid nature of goods is not in dispute. In Bellary Steels v. CCE 2003 (157) ELT 324 (CESTAT), the applicant was manufacturer as well as dealer. The purchased goods were dispatched directly but it was shown as received in factory. Invoice was raised by the assessee as if he is manufacturer. This was done as the assessee did not want buyers to know who is the actual manufacturer. Thus, though the procedure was wrong, there was no loss to revenue. Hence, penalty imposed was set aside. [Lucky they got relief. Otherwise, it is a border line case, as assessee had thrown all prescribed procedures to the wind].

In V K Enterprises v. CCE (2010) 249 ELT 462 (CESTAT), goods were neither received nor supplied. Only invoices were issued (to pass on credit). It was rightly held that penalty is imposable.

a gate pass, the gate pass book was required to be authenticated by Excise Officer. Later, in April 1994, gate pass was replaced by invoice and pre-authentication by excise officer was replaced by self authentication. A person who authenticates invoice at the top can also sign the invoice at bottom. This did not seem to serve any useful purpose. Thus, 'authentication' was a hangover of the past. It took 16 years to department to get over the hangover]. Invoice should be in book form - Rule 11(4) of Central Excise Rules [earlier rule 52A(7)] refers to 'Invoice Book'. Hence, invoices should be in book form i.e. bound form. Original and duplicate should be delivered to the consignee and triplicate copy should be retained in the Invoice Book. The invoices can be 'loose leaf' only if Invoices are computerised. Rule 11(3) [earlier rule 52A(3)] states that Invoice shall be marked as ORIGINAL FOR BUYER etc.

Invoice can be taken out for typing - When invoices are type written, the leafs have to be first taken out from book for typing. In such cases, the triplicate copy should be retained in bound book form. - Chapter 4 Part I Para 5.4 of CBE&C's CE Manual, 2005.

Cenvat credit cannot be denied for minor defects - Cenvat credit cannot be denied for minor defects in invoice. See case law under Cenvat.

Invoice required even for exempted goods - Invoice is required for clearance of all 'excisable goods'. The manufactured goods continue to be 'excisable goods' even if they are chargeable to 'Nil' rate of duty or are exempt from duty. Thus, 'excise invoice' is required even if goods are exempt from duty. However no 'invoice' is required if goods are not 'excisable goods'. In CCE v. Pawan Tyres P Ltd. 1998 (101) ELT 140 (CEGAT) and CCE v. Govind Rubber Ltd. 1998(102) ELT 67 (CEGAT), it was held that 'clearance' means removal of both dutiable and exempt goods from approved premises. Both dutiable and exempt goods are 'excisable goods'.

Invoice required only for removal from factory and not from dealer's godown - Excise Invoice is required only for removal of goods from factory. There is no such requirement in respect of goods removed from a dealer's place. A transporter carrying goods delivered by a dealer is under no obligation to produce any duty paying document. - Inland Road Service v. CCE - 1992 (60) ELT 571 (CEGAT). All goods lying in market are presumed to be duty paid. [for case law - refer under 'Demand']

Provisions in respect of computerisation of Invoices - Computerisation of Invoices is freely permitted and no permission is required. If running stationary is used, the stationary should be pre-printed with distinctive names and marks of the assessee. After invoices are prepared, triplicate copy shall be retained in bound book form. - Chapter 4 Part I Para 5.4 of CBE&C's CE Manual, 2005.

If invoices are prepared on computer, generation of serial number by computer at the time of printing of invoice on blank stationery of computer is permitted. However, this is so only if the software is such that computer automatically generates number and same number cannot be generated more than once. - Chapter 4 Part I Para 3.3 of CBE&C's CE Manual, 2005.

In case of computerised invoices, authentication at top and signing of invoice at bottom can be done simultaneously. As per earlier instructions, estimated serial number of invoices likely to be used should be intimated.

No specific requirement that Invoice should accompany goods upto destination - Earlier rule 52A(2) provided that duplicate copy of invoice should be produced en route to destination from the factory. Now, there is no parallel provision in new rules. Hence, in the opinion of author, goods cannot be confiscated merely because they are not accompanied by Invoice. Of course, it is highly advisable to ensure that goods are accompanied by duty paying documents, which in any case, are required under provisions of law relating to sales tax, octroi, entry tax, Motor Vehicles Act etc.

Direct dispatch of goods from manufacturer or importer to final consignee

17.4-2 Often, a person procures inputs or capital goods from a manufacturer or registered dealer but these are to be directly despatched to consignee. In such cases, following are the provisions.

Manufacturer to job worker of buyer-manufacturer - If a buyer-manufacturer or provider of output services purchases the inputs and intends to send the same directly to premises of job worker, the invoice of supplier-manufacturer should indicate name of job worker as consignee - second proviso to rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2015.

41.4

Cenvat on Goods purchased from trader

When the inputs are purchased directly from factory of original manufacturer, there is proof regarding amount of duty paid, in the form of Invoice of manufacturer. If goods are imported directly by manufacturer (who is user of inputs), Bill of Entry is proof of payment of CVD.

However, sometimes, goods are purchased from depot/consignment agent of the manufacturer and not directly from the factory. In some cases, indigenous or imported goods (inputs or capital goods) are purchased by the user of inputs (who wants to avail Cenvat) through trade channel i.e. wholesaler and retailer.

In such cases, a provision has been made to allow dealers/depots/consignment agents to issue Invoice to enable manufacturer (buyer of inputs) to avail Cenvat credit. This Invoice will be documentary evidence enabling the manufacturer to avail Cenvat credit.

All dealers/depots/consignment agents issuing invoice for Cenvat purposes will have to register with central excise authorities under Rule 9 of CE Rules. Only first stage and second stage dealers are allowed to issue Cenvatable Invoices.

41.4-1 Direct dispatch of goods by manufacturer i.e. transit sale

In certain cases, direct dispatch of goods without bringing in the premises of dealer is permitted.

Direct dispatch from manufacturer to final buyer, but sale is through dealer i.e. Transit sale - If whole consignment is despatched to buyer from manufacturer, Cenvat will be permissible, if name of the final buyer is shown as consignee. (Invoice will be in name of dealer). The consignee can avail Cenvat on the basis of duplicate copy of manufacturer issued under rule 11 (that time rule 52A). In such cases, the goods need not be brought to the premises of registered person. Invoice of Registered person (dealer) is not required for availing Cenvat by the consignee -CBE&C Circular No. 96/7/95-CX dated 13-2-1995.

This was also held permissible in CCE v. SSPE Cotton 1999(106) ELT 102 (CEGAT), SWILL Ltd. v. CCE (2008) 232 ELT 802 (CESTAT SMB), CCE v. REC Ispat (2009) 240 ELT 101 (CESTAT).

41.4-2 Buyer cannot be penalised for dealer's mistake or wrong doing

In Elveety Industries v. CCE 2001(130) ELT 199 (CEGAT SMB), assessee had taken Cenvat credit on basis of dealer's invoice. The dealer had taken credit on basis of original invoice of manufacturer (and not on duplicate copy of invoice as was required during that time). It was held that assessee cannot be denied Cenvat credit even if dealer had taken credit wrongly. - similar views in CCE v. Unichem Trading Co. 1998(102) ELT 284 (CEGAT).

Assessee buying goods from registered dealer cannot be expected to go beyond checking identity and address of manufacturer or supplier. He cannot examine whether supplier/manufacturer has actually paid the duty - Transpek Industry v. CCE (2010) 249 ELT 91 (CESTAT SMB).

41.4-3 Receiver not liable if supplier does not pay duty or service tax

CBE&C, vide Circular No. 766/82/2003-CX dated 15-12-2003, has clarified that Cenvat should not be denied to user-manufacturer as long as bona fide nature of the consignee's transaction is not doubted. Further, if the manufacturer-supplier has received payment from the buyer in respect of goods supplied including excise duty, action should be initiated against manufacturer-supplier u/ss 11D and 11DD - same view in Prachi Poly Products v. CCE 2005 (186) ELT 100 (CESTAT SMB) - followed in Bhuwalka Steel Industries v. CCE (2007) 212 ELT 63 (CESTAT SMB) - same view in CCE v. Anand Arc Electrodes (2010) 252 ELT 411 (CESTAT SMB) * CCE v. Muzaffarnagar Pipe Industries (2011) 265 ELT 182 (All HC DB) * CCE v. D P Singh (2011) 270 ELT 321 (Guj HC DB) * Lason India v. CST (2010) 27 STT 27 = 32 VST 156 (CESTAT SMB) * CCE v. Wilson Engineering (2013) 288 ELT 436 (CESTAT SMB).

rewritten_query: May a factory claim excise input credit when the supplier's invoice names the company's head office but the goods reached the factory and the office endorsed the invoice to it?

case_summary.text: II. Credit may be taken in one factory based on duty paying documents addressed to main office of company or documents in old name of company assessee, subject to utilization of input services for dutiable goods.
Cenvat credit available even if challan and invoices were in name of head office

ST : Procedural lapses and absence of all particulars are rectifiable errors, hence, credit was to be allowed subject to rectification by assessee; further, credit is allowable even if invoices are in name of head office
ST : Credit of input service cannot be denied merely because invoice was in name of assessee's Head Office, especially when receipt and utilization of input service were not under challenge

Cenvat Credit : It is natural that Customs House Agent (CHA) invoice would be in name of Head Office where clearance of goods through Customs is centralized; hence, in absence of doubt as to actual receipt of services, credit cannot be denied merely because Head Office is not registered as Input Service Distributor (ISD)

Excise/ST/VAT: Cenvat Credit could not be denied to branch office merely because bill of entry was in name of head office when capital goods had been used in branch office and head office had not availed Cenvat Credit on such goods

Cenvat Credit : Where two units are located adjacent to each other and have common service tax registration, practice of taking credit belonging to either of units without considering whether invoice was addressed to Head Office or to units is valid; department cannot seek segregation of credit along with separate registration
Credit can't be denied to input service distributor even if its invoices bear name of head office

Cenvat Credit : Credit may be taken on basis of invoices issued by manufacturer or importer or their distributor/dealer and said requirement is mandatory; since endorsement of invoice is not provided in rules, hence, job-worker cannot take credit on basis of invoices endorsed by principal-manufacturer
Cenvat Credit can not be denied to branch office just because bill of entry was in name of head office: CESTAT

II. CENVAT Credit, otherwise admissible, cannot be denied merely on ground that it was availed on basis of invoices raised by their head office, which was not registered under central registration during material period
GST/CENVAT : Cenvat credit of service tax paid by assessee could not be denied on ground that in invoices address given was that of Head Office, Delhi and not of registered premises at NOIDA

ST : Where receipt of input service and use thereof along with identity of service provider and service recipient are established, credit cannot be denied merely because invoice thereof bears address of Head Office, which is not registered as ISD.

Excise & Customs : Word "factory" includes "all units/premises at same place"; therefore, if steam/electricity generated out of fuel (furnace oil) is used for more than one units (DTA & EOU) in same "factory", entire fuel/furnace oil would be eligible for input credit

EXCISE/CENVAT : Supplier was duly registered with Central excise department and paid Central excise duty on capital goods and cleared same from his factory; since receipt of capital goods was also not in dispute, Cenvat credit on same could not be denied to recipient unit
Manufacture can claim Cenvat credit even on basis of invoice showing him as consignee

Cenvat Credit : If particulars relating to payment of tax on input services are genuine, then, credit cannot be denied merely because input service provider had quoted incorrect address of assessee in invoice.

ST : In case of centralized purchases of capital goods by Head Office, credit can be allowed to individual units/branch only if Cenvat credit was passed to such unit/branch under proper authorisation and there is no multiple claim by other units
Credit of ST couldn't be denied merely on ground that address of registered office wasn't mentioned in invoice

Cenvat Credit : Where three separately registered units are using a common input in continuous, interconnected and integrated process for common share, they constitute a single factory and CENVAT cannot be denied on ground that credit is being availed by one factory and material inputs are used by three factories

Cenvat Credit : Where lessee is manufacturing goods under lease agreement with lessor and lessor supplies capital goods to lessee, lessee may take credit on basis of supplier's invoice in name of lessor but endorsed by lessor in favour of lesse.

GST/Cenvat: Where invoices were in name of appellant themselves and receipt of service by appellant had not been challenged, credit on same could not be denied merely because of a different address being shown

Cenvat Credit : Merely because transporter's records contain different description of goods, department cannot deny credit especially when all parties in chain and even check-post records evidence receipt of inputs by assessee

Cenvat Credit : Credit of duty-paid returned goods can be allowed only if invoice is in name of person availing credit or invoice is endorsed in favour of assessee; credit cannot be taken on invoice in name of a third party
EXICSE/ST/VAT : Cenvat credit taken by assessee not on basis of invoices issued to their Mumbai office but on ISD invoice; Further, credit cannot be denied on ground of nexus; Matter remanded.

ST : Being a manufacturer having one factory and setting up second factory, assessee can easily and correctly take credit of services availed at Unit-2 in Unit-1 also, but since assessee took a separate registration for Unit-2, credit could only be taken in Unit-2
No denial of Cenvat Credit even if invoices are in name of employees: Mumbai CESTAT

Cenvat Credit : Where imported consignment is directly received in factory of job-worker, job-worker may take credit of CVD paid on imports, on strength of bill of entry, even if said bill of entry is in name of principal manufacturer

CENVAT : Where expenditure was incurred by assessee company, even though invoices were not in name of company but in name of directors/employees and same had been booked as expenditure in books of assessee, Cenvat credit could not have been denied
Manufacturer may take credit on basis of its own invoice in case of return of duty-paid goods to factory
Credit of CHA service allowable even if bill is issued to Head Office which isn’t ‘Input Service Distributor’

CENVAT : Cenvat credit can be availed by manufacturer on strength of invoices issued by supplier for clearance of inputs or capital goods, showing manufacturer's name as consignee and name of dealers as buyer
EXCISE : Cenvat credit on capital goods used in beneficiation plant cannot be denied on ground of separate registration as it is an integral part of factory

Cenvat Credit : Where supplier factories and recipient factories, both, belonged to assessee only, demand of Cenvat reversal from recipient factories on ground of excess duty payment by supplier factories, was dropped on undertaking from supplier factories that they would not claim refund of such excess duty

Cenvat Credit : Where there is no dispute that assessee had received input services and utilised them for providing output services, credit cannot be denied merely on ground that address of assessee was not mentioned on invoices on which credit was availed
No credit can be taken on basis of invoices neither addressed to assessee nor endorsed in his favour

GST: Where a manufacturer with regular registration in Tamil Nadu and separate ISD registration for its Head Office received common input service invoices in the name of regular registration and distributed ITC based on Board circular till March 2025, amendments effective 1 April 2025 mandate that such ITC can only be received and distributed through ISD registration, making invoice receipt in regular registration and subsequent credit transfer to ISD impermissible.

Cenvat Credit: Where applicant gas transporter will engage contractor to lay pipelines and contractor will procure pipes and valves from manufacturer who will issue invoice to contractor showing applicant as consignee and pipes will be delivered directly at applicant's work-site, applicant can avail cenvat credit on pipes and valves on basis of invoice issued by contractor, if contractor is a registered dealer

GST/Cenvat: Where assessee was engaged in manufacture of car seats and it procured two machines for use in manufacture of car seats and installed same in premises of one 'H', since assessee stood merged with 'H' later on, it was eligible for cenvat credit of duty on machines
Cenvat Credit : Where there is no dispute about receipt of material and payment of duty thereon, credit taken based on 'endorsed bill of entry' is valid
CENVAT: Where there was specific inclusion of input services for construction of factory, assessee-manufacturer would be eligible to avail credit of service tax paid on such input services

Cenvat Credit : Burden of proof to take credit lies on assessee; hence, where department found that input supplier did not have manufacturing facilities and was passing on credit without supply of goods and even assessee failed to prove receipt and consumption of goods in his factory, credit could not be allowed to assessee

Cenvat Credit : In case of return of duty-paid goods to factory following procedure under Rule 16 of Central Excise Rules, 2002, assessee may take credit of duty paid on returned goods, based on manufacturer's own invoice
No denial of credit just because input service provider had quoted wrong address of assessee in invoice
No reversal of credit on excess duty paid by supplier if factory of supplier/recipient was owned by assessee

EXCISE : One Autoconer machine out of two imported at Baddi Plant, transferred to Guna Plant but Baddi Plant availed 50 per cent of credit of duty paid on both Autoconers at Baddi in year 2001-02; Right course would have been to debit full credit pertaining to transfer of Autoconer, and to take its full credit at Guna Plant in terms of Rule 4(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002

GST/EXCISE/VAT/ST : Where High Court upheld Tribunal's order that raw material allegedly purchased by assessee never reached its factory and, thus, assessee's claim for CENVAT credit was bogus, SLP filed against said order was to be dismissed
No denial of input credit merely due to absence of assessee’s address in invoices
Cenvat credit on capital goods purchased by HO would be allowed on prorated basis to each unit
Claim of Cenvat credit was bogus where raw material purchased by the assessee did not reach factory premises

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: Rule 2(l), read with rule 15, of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Input service - Period October, 2005 to March, 2006 - Assessee availed credit of service tax on basis of invoices which were in name of head office - Original authority denied said credit on ground that invoices were not in name of factory - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) held that mistake was only a procedural omission and dropped demand - However, he imposed a penalty under rule 15(1) - Whether since there was no allegation of non-receipt of input service in factory or no allegation that input service was not relatable to factory and further since invoice was in name of head office of same factory and not in name of some one else, Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in holding that assessee was eligible for Cenvat credit - Held, yes - Whether since assessee was eligible for credit and there was no suppression of facts and extended period was not invocable, question of imposing penalty did not arise - Held, yes [Para 4]

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of polyester filament yarn. It availed credit of service tax during the period from October, 2005 to March, 2006 on the basis of invoices which were not in the name of its factory. In the impugned order, the Commissioner (Appeals) had held that it was only a procedural omission and therefore, the credit taken by the assessee was in order. On that ground as well as on the ground of limitation, he had dropped the demand and also set aside the penalty but had imposed a penalty of Rs. 10,000 under rule 15(1).

On cross-appeals :

HELD: The Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly followed the decision of the Tribunal in the case of CCE&CE v. DNH Spinners [2010] 25 STT 295 (Ahd. - CESTAT). Even though the assessee had multiple divisions, in the absence of any dispute about the receipt of the services in question by the factory to whom credit had been passed on, the ratio of the cited decision was applicable. In fact, the Commissioner(Appeals) proceeded to say that the assessee should have followed the procedure of issue of invoices by the head office as an input service distributor but observed that as far as the present appeal was concerned, the proceedings were limited by the ground taken in the show-cause notice and the order-in-original which had held that assessee had taken credit wrongly since invoice was not in its name but in the name of its head office. In view of the fact that the invoice was in the name of the head office and there was no dispute raised in the show-cause notice as to the admissibility of input service credit to the factory on the ground that the input service was not relatable to the factory, the omission became a totally curable defect and was a condonable one. Under those circumstances, the conclusion reached by the Commissioner (Appeals) to drop the demand could not be found fault with. The Commissioner (Appeals) also had taken a view that merely because the assessee did not disclose to the department that it had availed credit on the basis of documents not prescribed under rule 9(2), it could not be said that there was suppression of fact, wilful misstatement, etc. He had relied upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (211) ELT 513. In view of the fact that there was no allegation of non-receipt of input service or the allegation of service not relatable to the factory and also in view of the fact that invoice was in the name of head office of the same factory and not in the name of someone else, the decision of the Commissioner (Appeals) that extended period was not invocable also had to be upheld. Since the assessee was eligible for the credit and there was no suppression of facts, extended period was not invocable and, hence, the question of penalty did not arise. Accordingly, the penalty imposed was to be set aside. In view of the above, the appeal filed by the revenue was to be rejected and appeal filed by the assessee was to be allowed. [Para 2]

HEADNOTE: Rule 9, read with Rules 2(a), 3 and 4 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, Rule 4A and Rule 4B of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 and Rule 11 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 - Cenvat Credit - Documents on which credit may be taken - Assessee was manufacturing dutiable products under lease agreement with DSM - DSM had provided capital goods to assessee and said capital goods were installed and used by assessee - Assessee took credit of duty paid on capital goods on basis of supplier's invoice, which was in name of DSM and was endorsed by DSM to effect that 'goods covered under these invoices are transferred to assessee in view of lease agreement' - Department denied credit on ground that Endorsed invoices which are in name of DSM Sugars cannot be held to be proper Cenvatable document - HELD : Since there was no dispute that said capital goods were : (a) received by assessee, (b) duly installed in their factory and (c) used for manufacture of final product cleared by assessee, revenue's objection that such CENVAT credit is not available on basis of endorsed invoices cannot be upheld - Since this was not a case of 'sale' by one manufacturer to another and was a case of lessor buying and supplying capital goods to assessee-lessee's factory, certificate by lessor DSM as endorsement on invoice would be sufficient to take credit [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Where lessee is manufacturing goods under lease agreement with lessor and lessor supplies capital goods to lessee, lessee may take credit on basis of supplier's invoice in name of lessor but endorsed by lessor in favour of lesse.

FACT: Facts

The assessee is engaged in the manufacture of mould steel ingots and runners and risers under an agreement entered into by them with DSM Sugar Asmoli.

Under the said lease agreement dated 26-09-2002, the facility of land and machinery stands provided by DSM Sugar, Asmoli and the capital goods were received by them are required to be installed by the assessee and the duty on the final product required to be paid by the assessee.

DSM Sugars, Asmoli had endorsed the said invoices indicating as "certified that the goods covered under these invoices transferred to Kailash Steel, Asmoli in view of lease agreement dated 20-09-2002".

The Department denied CENVAT credit to the assessee on the ground that the invoices issued by the supplier are in the name of DSM Sugars, Asmoli, though there is no dispute that the said capital goods were received by the assessee and were duly erected and installed in their premises and were used for the manufacture of dutiable and excisable goods.

Revenue's Arguments

Endorsed invoices which are in the name of DSM Sugars cannot be held to be proper Cenvatable document so as to allow the CENVAT credit in respect of the same, to the assessee.

Assessee's Arguments

Even though DSM Sugars are the owners of the capital goods in question, there is no sale purchase of the capital goods and the same only stands transferred to their unit under the lease agreement, in which case, the effect of endorsement would not be of much relevance.

HELD: In as much as there is no dispute that the said capital goods stand received by the assessees and further duly installed in their factory and were being used for the manufacture of the final product, which was being cleared by the assessee, the revenue's objection that such CENVAT credit is not available in as much as the same was taken on the basis of the endorsed invoices cannot be upheld.

Admittedly, this is not a case of sale of capital goods from one manufacturer unit to another. It is a case where the capital goods are bought by the lessor and transferred to the lessee's factory, under lease agreement for further manufacture of the final product. As such, the certificate given by DSM Sugars, Asmoli on the invoices indicating that are being transferred and in the absence of any dispute to the factual aspect, the assessee is entitled to the CENVAT credit involved in the present appeal. [Para 4]

and all transactions of movement and receipt are maintained by the assessee.

The original payment of duty on the inputs is made by the principal manufacturer, the duty paying documents is in the name of assessee and the final receipt of the goods from the job workers to the assessee's factory is not disputed by the department.

It is relevant to state that the substantial condition for availing credit on inputs is :

(1)

evidence of duty payment of inputs

(2)

receipt of the inputs and (3)

usage of the inputs in the excisable goods.

In the present case, all the three conditions have been satisfied. Though the goods have been directly supplied from the principal manufacturer to the job workers premises, the invoices are raised by the principal supplier is in the name of assessee. It is also not in dispute that the assessee had duly received the goods from the job workers premises after carrying out the job work. [Para 8]

Credit cannot be denied on the ground that the inputs were supplied directly to the job workers premises from the principal manufacturers.

The Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly observed the revenue neutrality as there is no loss of revenue and also there is no dispute on the duty paid nature of the inputs duly received by the assessee from the job workers premises.

Therefore, there was no infirmity in the order of the Commissioner (Appeals), in allowing credit on the inputs directly supplied to the job workers premises from the principal manufacturer and subsequently received by the assessee. [Para 10]

HEADNOTE: Rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Documents and accounts - Assessee took Cenvat credit of inputs/capital goods on basis of invoices wherein supplier had mentioned its brand name and address - Adjudicating authority denied said credit on ground that invoices did not bear assessee’s name - Whether since there was no dispute that inputs/capital goods had suffered duty and were used in manufacture of final products and further since brand name of assessee with its address instead of companies’ name in invoices established ownership of goods, Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly allowed credit - Held, yes [Para 4] Circulars & Notifications : CBEC Circular No. 441/7/99-CX, dated 23-2-1999.

FACT: The assessee availed Cenvat credit on inputs/capital goods on basis of the invoices, wherein the suppliers had mentioned the brand name and address of the assessee. The adjudicating authority denied credit on the ground that the invoices did not bear the assessee’s name. The Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the adjudication order.

On appeal :

HELD: There was no dispute that the goods in question were received by the assessee and were used in the manufacture of the final product and duly recorded in the register. The Central Board of Excise & Customs vide Circular No. 441/7/99-CX, dated 23-2-1999 clarified that in terms of sub-rule (11) in rule 57G, and sub-rule (13) of rule 57T of the erstwhile Central Excise Rules, 1944, the Assistant Commissioner of Central Excise may allow the credit of duty paid on inputs/capital goods in minor procedural lapses in filing the declaration or in the invoices/documents, based on which credit is to be taken. However, the Assistant Commissioner should ensure that inputs/capital goods have suffered duty and are being used/are to be used in the process of manufacture. In the instant case, there was no dispute that inputs/capital goods had suffered duty and were used in the manufacture of final products. In any event, brand name of the assessee with its address instead of company’s name in the invoices established ownership of the goods. So, the Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly allowed the credit. Accordingly, no reason was found to interfere with the order of the Commissioner (Appeals). The appeal filed by the revenue was to be rejected. [Para 4]

A.K. Rastogi for the Appellant. V.K. Agarwal for the Respondent.

scrap, was not doubted by the Excise authorities. Similarly, the certificate issued by another Superintendent to the effect that the quantity of shredded steel scrap received by the appellant from ‘E’ Ltd. had been used as inputs in the factory of the appellant, was also not doubted by the Excise authorities. In these circumstances, the appellant had established that the credit of duty on receipt of imported shredded steel scrap from ‘E’ Ltd. had been taken in accordance with law. [Para 9] For availing the credit of duty, what is required to be established under rule 57G is that the inputs received are in fact duty paid. The procedure set out in rule 57G is to ensure that the credit is taken on the basis of duty paid documents. The bill of entry is one such document set out in rule 57G. The said rule does not require that the bill of entry should be in the name of the person claiming credit of duty. It is not in dispute that the goods imported and cleared on payment of duty by one person can be used as inputs and credit of duty can be claimed by another person by establishing that the imported duty paid goods have been received as inputs and that the importer has not taken credit of that duty. In the instant case, it was established that the duty paid goods were received as inputs, however, the credit was denied on the ground that the Bill of entry was not endorsed in the name of the appellant. Rule 57G does not require that for taking credit of duty, the bill of entry should be endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the absence of any provision regarding endorsement on the bill of entry, the credit of duty cannot be denied on the ground that the bill of entry is not endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the facts of the instant case, the evidence on record i.e., the bills of entry together with the certificates issued by excise authorities, clearly showed that the goods imported and cleared under the bills of entry on payment of duty were received and utilized by the appellant as inputs in its factory and that the importer had not utilized the credit of duty paid on the said goods. Thus, the appellant had established that the inputs received under the bills of entry were duty paid and, therefore, the authorities below were not justified in denying the credit of duty to the appellant. [Para 10]

HEADNOTE: Section 2(e), of the Central Excise Act, 1944, read with Rules 2(a), 2(k), 3 and  4 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Factory - Meaning of - Definition of "factory" is an inclusive definition and more than one premises - If assessee owns more than one unit, all units, if they are situated at a place, would constitute "a factory" - Hence, where assessee had DTA unit and another EOU unit situated in same factory premises, both of them constituted same "factory" [Paras 9, 15 and 16] [In favour of assessee]Excise  Customs : Word "factory" includes "all units/premises at same place"; therefore, if steam/electricity generated out of fuel (furnace oil) is used for more than one units (DTA  EOU) in same "factory", entire fuel/furnace oil would be eligible for input credit

FACT: Facts

Assessee-manufacturer was procuring the furnace oil for use in generation of steam/electricity and was availing CENVAT Credit on the furnace oil.

The assessee was also utilizing the furnace oil for generation of steam/electricity which was used in another unit, an EOU situated in the same compound.

A part of the Steam/Electricity was cleared to EOU unit.

The Department contended that proportionate CENVAT Credit on furnace oil utilized in the generation of Steam/Electricity cleared to their EOU was reversible in terms of rule 57AD(2) of Central Excise Rules 1944, read with rule 6(2) & (3) of CENVAT Credit Rules 2001/2002/2004.

The assessee argued that electricity generated has been used in their EOU unit which is the same factory premises, which was also factory of production. Even if the EOU procures inputs/capital goods for generation electricity, the EOU could procure the same without payment of duty in terms of the Foreign Trade Policy.

The Tribunal allowed credit.

Assessee's Arguments

When the assessee establishes two units in the same compound, both of them falls within the definition of "premises" under the Act and when both the units are manufacturing excisable goods, the steam manufactured in the factory of production even if it is used in the other unit, is eligible for CENVAT Credit.

Revenue's Arguments

Having regard to the definition of "input", the assessee would be entitled to the benefit of CENVAT Credit only to the extent of steam manufactured out of furnace oil is used in the factory for its production.

Even if such a steam is utilized by it in it other unit in the same compound, it amounts to wheeling out or diverting the steam to another unit and the assessee is not liable for CENVAT Credit.

Issue Involved

When the assessee who manufacture the steam, use the same in the factory of manufacturing and also utilized the steam in its another unit which is situated in the same compound, is he entitled to CENVAT Credit proportionately to the extent which was used in the other unit ?

(NT), dated 9-2-1999 - Circular No. 441/7/1999-CX, dated 23-2-1999

FACT: The assessee, namely, ‘G’, Ghaziabad availed MODVAT credit on the strength of invoice, which was in the name of ‘G’, Kota. The assessee also availed MODVAT credit on the strength of other invoice in which the buyer’s name was ‘P’, Faridabad; whereas the goods had been consigned to the assessee at Delhi. The Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the MODVAT credit taken by the assessee on the strength of the aforesaid invoices. He held that though there was cutting in consignees’ address but the same had been authenticated by the same person who had prepared the invoice and the address was changed from Kota to Ghaziabad.

He further held that a certificate issued by ‘P’ was also brought on record to show that the goods had been supplied by it to the assessee at Delhi address.

On appeal to the Tribunal by the revenue:

HELD: The benefit of MODVAT credit could not be denied to the assessee merely on the ground that there was change in the address from Kota to Ghaziabad. Further, it had not been disputed by the revenue that the inputs sent by ‘P’ were duty-paid and the same were received in the factory for being used in the manufacture of the final products. Thus, in view of the subsequent amendment made in rule 57G by Notification No. 7/1999-CE (NT) dated 9-2-1999, the MODVAT credit cannot be denied on account of some minor procedural lapses in the duty-paying documents. The Board had also clarified, vide Circular No. 441/7/1999-CX dated 23-2-1999, that Notification No. 7/1999-CE (NT), has been issued so as to empower the Assistant Commissioner, having jurisdiction over the factory of the manufacturer, to allow the credit ignoring minor procedural lapses provided the inputs have suffered duty and are being used in the process of manufacture. Hence, the appeal was liable to be rejected. [Para 3]

Issue Involved

When the assessee who manufacture the steam, use the same in the factory of manufacturing and also utilized the steam in its another unit which is situated in the same compound, is he entitled to CENVAT Credit proportionately to the extent which was used in the other unit ? HELD: The definition of "input" makes it clear that, "input" means all goods used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final products or not and includes lubricating oils, greases, cutting oils, coolants, accessories of the final products cleared along with the final product, goods used as paint, or as packing material, or as fuel, or for generation of electricity or steam used in or in relation to manufacture of final products or for any other purpose, within the factory of production. [Para 8]

The word "factory" has been defined in the Central Excise Act at section 2(e). It is an inclusive definition. For the purpose of Central Excise Act, a 'factory' means more than one premises. [Para 9]

Rule 6, of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 makes it clear that the CENVAT Credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of goods which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods. However, exception is carved out in sub-Rule (2). Sub-Rule (2) of Rule 6 provides- where a manufacturer or provider of output service avails CENVAT Credit in respect of any inputs except the input intended to be used as fuel and manufactures such final products or provides such output service which are chargeable to duty or tax as well as exempted goods or services, then, an obligation is cast on the assessee to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory or input and input service meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service and the quantity of input meant for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services. However he would be entitled to CENVAT credit only on that quantity of input or input service which is intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods. Therefore, it is clear that the assessee manufacturer is entitled to CENVAT Credit on "inputs" which is used in the manufacture of dutiable goods. [Para 11]

In view of clear language in the statutory provisions coupled with the fact that the factory includes more than one premises to be eligible for CENVAT Credit, an assessee has to use the input in the manufacture of dutiable goods in his factory. If the factory includes more than one unit and if the assessee uses this input in the manufacturing of excisable goods in both the units, he would be entitled to CENVAT Credit. [Para 12]

The definition of 'input' brings within its fold the inputs used for generation of electricity or steam, provided such electricity or steam is used within the factory of production for manufacture of final products or for any other purpose. Therefore, it follows the term "within the factory of production" cannot be confined to a single unit. In view of the definition of factory in the act which means more than one premises, it has to be construed as the factory owned by the assessee. If the assessee owns more than one unit, all the units if they are situated at a place would constitute "a factory". If the electricity or steam generated within the factory of production means within the factory premises which may include more than one unit. If such electricity or steam generated within the factory of production is utilized by the assessee in more than one unit and if those units are manufacturing excisable goods, then, the assessee would be entitled to the benefit of CENVAT credit to the entire extent of utilization of such electricity or steam in all the units of its factory premises. Therefore, whatever goes into generation of electricity or steam which is placed within the factory which may consists of more than one unit would be an input for the purposes of obtaining credit on the duty payable thereon. [Para 15]

In the instant case, the assessee is having two units; one DTA unit and another EOU unit. Both are situated in the same factory premises. Both are manufacturing excisable goods. The assessee has purchased furnace oil from which, the steam is generated within the said factory premises. The said steam is utilized by the assessee in manufacturing excisable goods in both the units which are situated within the same compound, which falls within the definition of the word "factory" and therefore, the assessee is entitled to CENVAT credit in respect of entire volume of steam used in the manufacture of excisable goods by both the units. That is precisely what the appellate authorities have held and granted relief to the assessee. [Para 16]

Hence, impugned order was confirmed. [Para 17]

HEADNOTE: Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Procedure to be observed by manufacturer- ‘E’ Ltd. imported a consignment of shredded steel which was cleared under bill of entry on payment of countervailing duty - A portion of said goods imported was given as loan to appellant - Appellant availed credit of duty on goods received from ‘E’ Ltd. - Revenue denied credit of duty to appellant on ground that bill of entry was not endorsed in its name - However, Superintendent of Central Excise issued certificate that ‘E’ Ltd. had not taken credit of duty paid on goods which were given as loan to appellant and goods received by appellant were used in its factory as input - Whether since rule 57G does not require that for taking credit of duty, bill of entry should be endorsed in name of claimant, credit of duty could not be denied on that ground to appellant - Held, yes - Whether, further, since bill of entry together with certificate issued by authority clearly showed that goods imported and cleared under bills of entry on payment of duty, were received and utilized by appellant as inputs in its factory and that assessee had not utilized credit of duty paid on said goods, authorities below were not justified in denying credit of duty to appellant - Held, yes

FACT: E Ltd. had imported a consignment of shredded scrap and cleared the same on payment of duty. Out of the said consignment, ‘E’ Ltd. gave certain quantity of shredded scrap to the appellant as a loan. On receipt of said goods, the appellant took credit of duty of the amount equivalent to customs duty paid by ‘E’ Ltd. on those goods. However, the revenue denied credit of duty to the appellant on the ground that it had taken credit of duty on basis of delivery challans issued by ‘E’ Ltd. but credit of duty could not be taken under rule 57G on that basis. On adjudication, the Commissioner confirmed the demand of duty on the appellant along with penalty. On appeal, the Tribunal also confirmed the demand on the ground that bills of entry were not endorsed in the name of the appellant.

On appeal :

HELD: Rule 57G clearly shows that the credit of duty can be taken on inputs by establishing that the duty has been paid on the said inputs on the basis of documents such as invoice, AR-1, Bill on Entry, etc. In the instant case, it was not in dispute that the appellant had received imported shredded steel scrap from ‘E’ Ltd. on which countervailing duty had been paid by ‘E’ Ltd. It was also not in dispute that ‘E’ Ltd. had not taken credit of the duty paid on shredded steel scrap which was given on loan to the appellant. It was also not in dispute that the appellant had used the said shredded steel scrap taken on loan from ‘E’ Ltd. as inputs in its factory. The certificate issued by a Superintendent of Central Excise to the effect that ‘E’ Ltd. had not taken credit of duty paid on the said shredded steel scrap, was not doubted by the Excise authorities. Similarly, the certificate issued by another Superintendent to the effect that the quantity of shredded steel scrap received by the appellant from ‘E’ Ltd. had been used as inputs in the factory of the appellant, was also not doubted by the Excise authorities. In these circumstances, the appellant had established that the credit of duty on receipt of imported shredded steel scrap from ‘E’ Ltd. had been taken in accordance with law. [Para 9]

HEADNOTE: Rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Documents and accounts - Assessee-manufacturer placed a purchase order with a supplier for procurement of input, i.e., HR sheets - Though assessee physically received H.R. sheets, description mentioned in invoice was CR sheets instead - Whether in absence of any allegation that assessee had procured same clandestinely without cover of invoice, it was entitled to Cenvat credit on same although description of goods did not match with actual receipt of goods - Held, yes [Para 6] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacturing business of motor vehicle parts. During the course of manufacturing activity, it was procuring inputs such as HR sheets. For that, the assessee placed a purchase order with its supplier for HR sheets and the said HR sheets had been supplied by the supplier but in the invoices, these HR sheets were shown as CR sheets and against which the assessee took Cenvat credit. In such circumstances, the revenue alleged that the assessee has contravened Rule 9. Therefore show-cause notice was issued, on adjudication of which demand along with interest and equivalent amount of penalty was confirmed. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the adjudicating authority.

On appeal:

HELD: It is an admitted fact that the assessee has placed a purchase order for HR sheets and physically received HR sheets in its factory which have been used by it in the manufacture of its final products. The only description mentioned in the invoice is CR sheets instead HR sheets. As per provisions of Rule 9 where it has been clarified that the documents contains the details of duty or service tax, description of the goods or assessable value, Central Excise or Service Tax registration number of the person issuing the invoice, name and address of the factory or warehouse or premises, the assessee is entitled to take Cenvat credit. Although the description of the goods does not match with the actual receipt of the goods but the fact is not denied that these HR sheets have been received by the assessee in its factory. Therefore, the assessee is entitled to take Cenvat credit on the goods received by it. It is not the allegation that the assessee had procured HR sheets clandestinely without cover of invoice, therefore, the Cenvat credit cannot be denied. Hence, the impugned order is to be set aside and the appeal is to be allowed. [Para 6]

HEADNOTE: Rule 57 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat Credit (Modvat) - Modvat - Raw material can be transferred to another unit which can get credit - Inputs need not be used directly as per settled law, as there is no requirement of direct use if inputs are fully utilised - CE Rule 57F(2)

FACT: The appellants have their factory at Mandideep in M.P. They have another factory at Ankleshwar in Gujarat. They manufacture Cephalexin and Cephadroxil falling under Chapter 29 of CETA. Penicillin GK is the main input for the final product, which the appellants import as also procure locally. With the approval of the Assistant Collector they sent Penicillin to Ankleshwar factory direct where the same was converted into "7ADCA", which was then received at the factory at Mandideep for manufacture of the final product. They had similar approval in respect of other raw materials used in the manufacture of "7ADCA" for being sent to the factory at Ankleshwar. They were availing of the Modvat credit in respect of all the raw materials at Mandideep when "7ADCA" along with other documents was received from Ankleshwar. The Collector of CE, Indore after issuing a show cause notice and hearing the appellants, held that appellants had wrongly availed of the Modvat credit at Mandideep by deliberately suppressing the fact by not making a proper declaration of use of inputs in as much as "7ADCA" was never declared as an input. According to the Collector, in the absence of such a declaration they were not entitled to Modvat credit which could have been availed of by the Ankleshwar factory which received the declared raw materials. He therefore disallowed Modvat credit of Rs. 79,38,597.50 and also imposed a penalty of Rs. 5 lakhs.

HELD: The appellants were legally entitled to send the raw material to Ankleshwar factory and to avail of Modvat credit when "7ADCA" was received at Mandideep factory. "Since the appellant had filed the declaration the appellant was legally entitled to send the raw materials to Ankleshwar factory and avail of the credit in respect of such raw materials when 7ADCA manufactured by the appellant at its Ankleshwar factory from such raw materials was received by the appellant at its Mandideep factory."

2. Since there was no requirement to use raw material directly in the manufacture of final product the denial of Modvat credit was uncalled for and contrary to judicial pronouncements. "Since there was no requirement to use raw materials directly in the manufacture of final product the denial of modvat credit by the Collector was clearly uncalled for and contrary to judicial pronouncements which has settled this position beyond any pale of doubt."

3. There was no violation of Rule 57F(2). "We, therefore, hold that there was no violation of Rule 57F(2) which postulates that a manufacturer assessee engaged in the manufacture of final product can send the raw materials directly to a job worker, request such job worker to convert the raw materials into an intermediate product and then receive such intermediate product in his factory for manufacture of final dutiable products."

4. No justification for denying the credit because all raw materials were used in the manufacture of final product. "There is no justification for denying the credit because it was not in dispute that the entirety of the raw materials were, in fact, used in the manufacture of final dutiable product. The appellant had filed before the Collector a certificate from the Chartered Accountant certifying that the total quantity of raw materials received at Ankleshwar was used in the manufacture of 7ADCA which, in turn, was used in the manufacture of Cephalexin at Mandideep. Every ounce of the material was thus fully accounted for."

5. Appellants entitled to Modvat credit of Rs. 79,38,597.50. Penalty imposed set side. "We, therefore, hold that the appellants are entitled to the benefit of modvat credit of Rs. 79,38,597.50. For the same reason, we also set aside the penalty imposed by the adjudicating authority."

That heading is identical to heading 21.06 of organised system of nomenclature issued by WCO. In fact the Excise Tariff is based on HSN. Therefore, the Supreme Court has repeatedly emphasized that the Explanatory Notes of HSN are valuable material for understanding the scope of various headings in the Central Excise Tariff. The Explanatory Note of HSN of Heading 21.06 demonstrates that the concentrates contain the flavouring ingredient that are characteristics of a particular beverage. The beverage in question is obtained simply by diluting the preparation with water, sugar and carbondioxide gas. From the Explanatory Note it is, therefore, clear that there is a link between the concentrate and the beverage made from that. The above Explanatory Note also explains the rational for business being arranged in this industry in a particular manner. This method of doing business avoids unnecessary transport of large quantity of water. In addition, the bottles and crates have to be collected back from the shop keepers or dealers and taken back to the factory for filling the fresh batch on a constant basis. At all times, the quality of beverage was maintained and marketing support to the beverages was provided by the brand name holder-cum-concentrate manufacturer. [Para 42]

It follows from the above discussion that the credit is availed on the tax paid on the input service, which is advertisement and not on the contents of the advertisement. Thus, it is not necessary that the contents of the advertisement must be that of the final product manufactured by the person advertising, as long as the manufacturer can demonstrate that the advertisement services availed have an effect or impact on the manufacture of the final product and establish the relationship between the input service and the manufacture of the final product. The manufacturer thereby can avail the credit of the service tax paid by him. Once the cost incurred by the service has to be added to the cost, and is so assessed, it is a recognition by the revenue of the advertisement services having a connection with the manufacture of the final product. This test will also apply in the case of sales promotion. [Para 43]

Therefore, services of advertising and marketing procured by the assessee in respect of advertisements for aerated waters are covered by the definition of the words ‘input services’ as defined in rule 2(l) when admittedly the assessee manufactured concentrates which were exclusively used for the manufacture of the respective aerated waters which were advertised by the assessee. The advertisement or sales promotion of aerated waters undertaken by manufacturer of concentrate was covered by the inclusive part of the definition of ‘input service’ contained in rule 2(l ). [Para 43]

In the light of the above, the impugned order of the Commissioner, and the order of the Tribunal were set aside, and the matter was restored to the Commissioner, to pass appropriate order in the light of what had been set out above. [Para 44]

It was for the Board to take an appropriate action against the Commissioner for issuing the alert circular against the instructions issued by the Board and the remedy did not lie in holding all the proceedings invalid and depriving the statutory powers of the revenue officers and also preventing the officers from performing their statutory functions or holding the proceedings in performance of statutory functions invalid. [Para 4] The provisions of rule 7 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 and rule 12B of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 would show that it is very important to know as to who was the manufacturer and who was responsible to fulfil all the obligations towards central excise. It was contended that rule 12(b) of the Central Excise Rules would not be applicable to the persons who had already been registered earlier and would be applicable only in respect of the new assessees. However, the rule does not prevent the old manufacturers also from utilizing the facility. Rule 12(b) of the Central Excise Rules envisages four types of situations, namely, a merchant- manufacturer may undertake to fulfil all the obligations himself; the job worker may be authorized by the merchant-manufacturer to fulfil the obligations on his behalf in which situation, the job worker would be virtually acting as an agent for the purpose of manufacture of fabrics of the merchant-manufacturer or alternatively, the merchant-manufacturer may be authorized by the job worker in which case the merchant-manufacturer would be the agent of the job worker. In cases where either the merchant-manufacturer or the job worker had authorized either of them to act on his behalf, obvious conclusion would be that the knowledge of the job worker or the merchant-manufacturer about the existence of the other would be irrelevant, since either of them would be an agent of the other. Therefore, in cases where the job worker or the merchant- manufacturer has been authorized as contemplated under rule 12(b) of the Central Excise Rules, the obvious conclusion would be that when the goods are received under the invoice, the fulfilment of obligations under rule 7(2) of the Cenvat Credit Rules is complete only if the obligation is fulfilled in respect of the person who has supplied the goods to the merchant-manufacturer or the job worker who, in turn, supplied goods to the other. Therefore, if the merchant- manufacturer has authorized the job worker to fulfil his obligations under central excise law, the fact that the merchant-manufacturer has supplied the goods under his own invoice or endorsed the invoice issued by another supplier and, therefore, the knowledge of the receiver about the merchant- manufacturer would be sufficient, would not be correct. In such cases the job worker has to necessarily know the supplier and the obligations can be said to be fulfilled only if it is done keeping the supplier of the merchant-manufacturer in mind. In the instant cases this information was not available. The case of the department was that the job worker or the processor was required to know the supplier of the fabrics even where the invoice was endorsed by the merchant- manufacturer or the merchant-manufacturer had issued another invoice. [Para 20.4]

In cases where the invoice is merely endorsed, the issue is settled and in such cases the obligations of the job worker would be fulfilled only if he has taken reasonable steps to ensure that the supplier of the fabrics to the merchant- manufacturer who has endorsed it is in existence. [Para 20.5]

However, where the goods had not travelled directly from the weaver/the manufacturer to the job worker and the invoice had not been endorsed, the question arose as to whether it would be sufficient if the job worker knew the supplier or he was required to know the original manufacturer who had paid the duty, even though another invoice had been issued by the merchant- manufacturer and he had supplied his invoice as well as the original manufacturer’s invoice. In such cases if the job worker was authorized by the merchant-manufacturer for fulfilling of central excise obligations, the job worker would be required to know the supplier of the fabrics to the merchant- manufacturer. Otherwise it would be sufficient if he knew the merchant- manufacturer and was able to show that he had taken the steps envisaged in rule 7 of the Cenvat Credit Rules. [Para 20.6]

Scheme : Under the Cenvat Credit Scheme a manufacturer of excisable goods is allowed to take credit of excise duty paid on inputs and capital goods used in the manufacture of excisable goods and utilize such credit for payment of excise duty on final products manufactured by him. [Para 36]

Rule 4(4) - Credit only by person paying value/duty : There is no specific provision in the Rules to the effect that credit can be taken by a manufacturer only if duty is paid by him to the supplier of goods. HEADNOTE: Rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Documents and accounts - Period May, 2006 to February, 2007 - On verification of records of assessee, department found that assessee had availed input service tax credit on strength of invoices addressed to its branch offices - Department alleged that assessee had availed input service tax credit based upon ineligible documents in contravention of rule 9(2) - Accordingly, a show-cause notice was issued to assessee proposing to recover such amount of input service tax credit irregularly availed by it - Adjudicating authority as well as Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed demand - It was assessee’s case that input service tax credit was availed in accordance with Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 inasmuch as assessee’s name and address of its branch offices were clearly indicated in said invoices - Further, Commissioner (Appeals) had recorded in his order that invoices in question were received under Service Tax Rules, 1994 - Whether rule 4A(1)(ii) of Service Tax Rules, 1994 only requires name of person receiving taxable services and address where taxable services are provided - Held, yes - Whether, under such circumstances, assessee had made out a case for credit of service tax paid on service to its branch offices - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, impugned order was unsustainable - Held, yes [Paras 8 and 9]

FACT: On verification of the records of the assessee by the internal audit party of the department, it was found that the assessee had availed input service tax credit on the strength of the invoices addressed to its branch offices. The department alleged that the assessee had availed input service tax credit based upon ineligible documents in contravention of rule 9(2). Accordingly, a show-cause notice was issued to the assessee proposing to recover such amount of service tax credit irregularly availed by it. The adjudicating authority confirmed the demand as proposed in show-cause notice and also imposed penalty under rule 15. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the adjudicating authority.

On appeal, the assessee contended that credit of service tax was availed in accordance with the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002, inasmuch as the assessee’s name and address of the branch office was clearly indicated in the invoices.

HELD: Rule 9(2) provides for the availment of Cenvat credit by a manufacturer or provider of input/output services on the basis of the documents, which are enumerated in rule 9(1). The said documents on which credit was availed was not in dispute, inasmuch as the delivery invoices on which credit had been availed by the assessee fell within the category of ‘Invoices’ issued by a service provider. The only question was as to whether the provisions of rule 9(2) were attracted in the instant case. Provisions of rule 9(2) can be pressed into service for denial of cenvat credit to the assessee, only if the document does not contain the particulars as required. In the instant case, it was seen from the show-cause notice that only the contravention of rule 9(2) had been indicated, but it was not very clear as to what was the contravention. Proviso to rule 9(2) talks about non-mention of the particulars and the corrective action that can be taken by the jurisdictional Assistant Commissioner and the Deputy Commissioner in the absence of such details. The credit of service tax leviable under section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 is eligible to be taken as Cenvat credit on any input services received by the manufacturer of the final product. The plea of the assessee on provisions of credit rules, invoked for denial of cenvat credit, was not at all addressed by the Commissioner (Appeals) while rejecting the appeal filed by the assessee. It could be seen from the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that the Commissioner had recorded that the invoices in question were received under the Service Tax Rules, 1994. As per rule 4A(1)(ii), the invoices should indicate the name and address of the person who is receiving the taxable services. There was a strong force in the contention of the assessee that the provisions of rule were very clear; it only requires person receiving the taxable services and only address where the taxable services are provided. [Para 7]

office equipment or appliance) are used in the factory of the manufacturer of the final products or for providing of output service. Thus, any item which is covered by the list of the items mentioned in rule 2(a) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, except for office equipment or office appliances, and is used in any manner in the factory of the manufacturer of the final products, would be covered by the definition of the capital goods and, accordingly, would be eligible for Cenvat credit. There is absolutely no requirement that the capital goods at the time of receipt must be owned by manufacturer or that the same would cease to be capital goods, if they are installed in the factory and become fixed to earth. In fact, most of the capital goods the machinery, equipment or instruments covered by Chapters 84, 85 and 90, pipes and tubes, pollution control equipment refractories, and storage tanks are required to be installed and after installation, the same put together constitute a manufacturing plant, which is fixed to earth structure. Just because after being installed in the factory, the capital goods put together become a plant which is fixed to earth structure, the Cenvat credit cannot be denied on the basis that the plant which is fixed to earth structure, is not excisable. This preposition of the Department is, in fact absurd, as there is no such condition in rule 2(a) for capital goods.

For capital goods Cenvat credit, the items must be among those mentioned in this rule and should have been used in the factory of the manufacturer and how the items are not used relevant. The words used in rule 2(a) are "used in the factory of manufacturer of the final product" not "used in the manufacture of final product". Therefore, once any item received in the factory is 'capital goods' in terms of Rule 2(a) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, and is used in the factory, the manufacturer would be entitled to Cenvat credit of excise duty paid in respect of the same.

If the logic of the Commissioner in the impugned order is accepted, no capital goods Cenvat credit can be allowed in respect of any item of capital goods enumerated in rule 2(a) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, as all the items - various items of machinery covered under Chapters 84, 85 and 90 of the Tariff, pipes and tubes, tanks, pollution control equipments refractories, etc., have to be installed in the factory before being put to use and after installation, the same would become fixed to earth plant. Reading the impugned order gives an impression that the same has been passed without any application of mind.

Therefore, prima facie, impugned order is not sustainable and as such the assessee have strong prima facie case in their favour. The requirement of pre-deposit of the Cenvat credit demand, interest thereon and penalty is, therefore, waived for hearing of the appeal and recovery thereof is stayed till the disposal of the appeal.
