Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoices - Forming basis of credit were endorsed in favour of head office and not in the name of factory - No dispute about duty paid nature of inputs, their actual receipt or use in manufacture of the final product - Credit admissible - Appeal allowed (Para 4)
Modvat credit - Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944- Invoice - in name of head office - endorsed by head office to factory - credit admissible - appeal rejected (Paras 4  5)

Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoice - In the name of head office - Address corrected by input manufacturer to show factory address - Credit admissible - Appeal allowed (Paras 4  5)
Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoice - Raised in the name of Head office - Received by Dombivli plant with endorsement by Head office - Credit admissible (Para 2)
Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoice - in the name of head office - no dispute about receipt of inputs into the factory - credit admissible (Para 19)

Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoice - Procedural irregularities - credit not to be denied on the grounds that (i) invoice was in the name of head office whereas the goods were received directly into the factory, and (ii) full consignment covered by the invoice was received in two spells - appeal allowed (Para 4)

Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoice - mentions head office as consignee and does not give mode of transport - invoice not endorsed by head office - credit not to be denied as the goods moved directly in a taxi to the factory and their receipt is evidenced by entries in private records and RG-23A Part I  II - appeal allowed (Paras 4  5)

Rule 9, read with Rules 3 and 4 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Documents on which credit may be taken - Assessee-factory was located at Gurgaon - Assessee's Head Office at Kanpur imported raw materials and goods were received directly at Gurgaon in November 1996 - But, Bill of Entry was mistakenly received at Kanpur and credit was taken at Kanpur in March 1997 - Credit was subsequently reversed by Kanpur, and Kanpur Head Office issued invoices in name of Gurgaon factory and assessee-factory (Gurgaon) took credit in March 1997 on basis of those invoices - Department argued that statutory procedure was not followed and invoices issued by Head Office were not eligible documents for taking credit - Assessee argued that there was procedural lapse, but, credit was otherwise within time - HELD : Since factum of receipt of goods at Gurgaon was not disputed, non-following of procedure by itself cannot be held to be a ground for denial of credit - Since there was mistake, which was rectified by way of invoices issued by Kanpur Office, impugned credit could not be disallowed [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Where factum of receipt and use of goods is not disputed, non-following of procedure by itself cannot be held to be a ground for denial of credit

"Their Calcutta factory ordered for the goods and their Kansbahal factory took the Modvat credit on these inputs which were imported. In such circumstances, it cannot he said that the Modvat Credit was utilised without the authority of law. In fact, even at the time of personal hearing, the appellants filed a certificate dated. 14.9. 1992 from its Calcutta office certifying that all the aforesaid consignments were imported from the foreign countries as per the requirement of its Kansbahal Works. The appellants also filed copies of the purchase Orders placed upon the foreign suppliers in respect of these consignments. Hence merely on the ground that the appellants' name was M/s. L.  T. Ltd. Calcutta and not M/s. L. T. Ltd., Kansbahal, the Modvat Credit could not disallowed. Even if any endorsement is required, the appellants should have been allowed to have such endorsement done which request they had made before the Adjudicating Officer." (Para 23)

Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Bill of entry - In name of Head office - Not endorsed in favour of factory - No dispute about receipt and utilisation of inputs - Credit not deniable - Appeal rejected (Para 3)

Rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Documents and accounts - Cenvat credit of service tax paid was been denied to assessee's factory on ground that invoice issued by service provider was in name of registered office and not in name of factory - Department opined that registered office should have taken registration as an input service distributor to facilitate distribution and availment of Cenvat credit by factory - HELD : It was doubtful whether registered office of assessee was required to be registered at all when they had only one factory and when credit had been taken by factory on basis of invoices issued by service providers - There was no allegation that assessee's factory did not receive input service - If the service was received by the factory, credit was admissible even if document was in name of registered office [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]

Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoice - in name of head office - credit on such invoice admissible as there is no dispute about receipt, utilisation and duty paid character of inputs - appeal allowed (Para 8)

Rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Documents and accounts - Assessee’s unit at Daman imported goods under a bill of entry - On strength of said bill of entry, assessee’s head office at Mumbai availed credit - Revenue denied credit on ground that there was violation of rule 9(1)(a)(iii), read with rule 11 of Central Excise Rules, 2002 - However, Tribunal held that invoices could have been endorsed by Daman Office of same appellant in name of its Mumbai office; it was rectifiable defect and could be rectified at any point of time and there being no dispute otherwise about entitlement of Modvat credit, such procedural lapse should not result in denial of benefits to it otherwise admissible as credit - Accordingly, Tribunal set aside impugned order - Whether no infirmity could be found in impugned order of Tribunal - Held, yes [Para 5]
Modvat credit - Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Invoice - in the name of head office - acceptable (Para 9)

Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat credit - Invoice - Issued by mistake in the name of Noida unit of appellant - Company and the same was transmitted to their Ghaziabad unit with appropriate endorsement - Goods were received directly by the appellant unit from the manufacturer - Credit admissible (Para 5)
Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat Credit - Gate pass - in the name of head office - not endorsed to factory - such non-endorsement not to result in denial of credit (Para 5)
Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoice - credit admissible when invoice is in the name of branch office and inputs are received direct into the factory. (Para 4)

Rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Documents and accounts - Department denied credit of input service on ground that credit was not availed on proper invoice, as invoice was in name of their head office - HELD : Although documents were not in name of assessee's factory/unit but same were in name of head office of assessee and there was no dispute about input service received by assessee - Substantive benefit cannot be denied on procedural grounds - Hence, input service credit was admissible to assessee [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]ST : Credit of input service cannot be denied merely because invoice was in name of assessee's Head Office, especially when receipt and utilization of input service were not under challenge

Rule 57GG of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoice - manufacturer's invoice was in name of dealer's head office while inputs were received directly under invoice by dealer's branch office at a different place - credit not deniable to appellants on basis of invoice issued by dealer's branch office against such manufacturer's invoice when no action is taken against the dealer - appeal allowed (Para 4)

Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoice - gave Mumbai address of consignee while goods were received by Delhi factory - invoice got corrected subsequently - credit admissible - appeal allowed (Para 5)

Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoice - supplier by mistake sent duplicate copy to head office of the appellants and original copy to the factory - credit taken on the basis of original copy not to be denied - appeal allowed (Paras 7, 8, 9  10)

Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Bill of entry - in the name of appellant company's office but the inputs received direct into the factory - credit not deniable on such ground (Para 8)

Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoice - issued by a dealer is proper though irregularity was committed at dealer's end inasmuch as the manufacturer's invoice was in the name of head office of the dealer but invoice was issued from the godown - credit not to be denied for irregularity at dealer's end - appeal allowed (Para 2)

Rule 2(l), read with rule 15, of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Input service - Period October, 2005 to March, 2006 - Assessee availed credit of service tax on basis of invoices which were in name of head office - Original authority denied said credit on ground that invoices were not in name of factory - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) held that mistake was only a procedural omission and dropped demand - However, he imposed a penalty under rule 15(1) - Whether since there was no allegation of non-receipt of input service in factory or no allegation that input service was not relatable to factory and further since invoice was in name of head office of same factory and not in name of some one else, Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in holding that assessee was eligible for Cenvat credit - Held, yes - Whether since assessee was eligible for credit and there was no suppression of facts and extended period was not invocable, question of imposing penalty did not arise - Held, yes [Para 4]

Rule 57GG of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoice - was endorsed by head office to one of their godowns and inputs were also sent to that godown while registration number of another godown was given in the endorsement by mistake - credit not to be denied for such procedural lapse - appeal allowed. (Para 3)

II. Rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Documents and accounts - Department denied credit taken on basis of invoices in name of head office of assessee-company as well as invoices in old name of assessee-company -It was argued that assessee should have followed procedure applicable as Input Service Distributor - HELD : In this case, bills received at Headquarters were transferred to one factory, hence, there was no distribution as such - There is no serious irregularity in taking credit in one factory based on duty paying documents addressed to main office of company, hence, credit cannot be denied in view of proviso to rule 9(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules - However, credit attributable to units located in exempted areas cannot be allowed in view of rule 6 of CENVAT Credit Rules - Further, credit on bills in old name of company could be allowed, as services were received and utilized by assessee only [Paras 10 and 11] [Partly in favour of assessee]
Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoice - In the name of head office - Credit admissible (Para 6)

Modvat credit - Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Invoice - Inputs received on stock transfer from another factory of the manufacturer under endorsed invoice - Such endorsed invoice is valid as no sale is involved - Appeal rejected (Para 4)

Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoice - both Jind and Faridabad mentioned in consignee's address in the invoice - credit not to be denied as respondents have produced evidence of movement and receipt of input into the factory - appeal dismissed (Para 3)

Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Bill of entry - in the name of one factory of the manufacturer - endorsed in favour of another factory of the manufacturer - credit admissible on such endorsed bill of entry - appeal allowed. (Para 8)

Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoice - showed appellants' two factories as consignees - inputs received in one factory - credit not deniable - assessee's appeal allowed (Para 7)

Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoice - issued by IOC in the name of Sturdia Chemicals which had already been amalgamated with appellant company - credit available as there is no other factory by name Sturdia Chemicals, appellant company continued to be known locally by its old name and inputs received were co-related with invoices (Para 3)

Rule 16 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002, read with rule 7 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 and rules 2(k), and 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Return of duty-paid goods to factory - Period January 2002 to August 2002 - Assessee received duty-paid trailers and took credit on basis of invoices issued by Volvo, consigned to Nav - Department denied credit on ground that said invoices were neither addressed to assessee, nor endorsed in his favour - HELD : Credit of duty-paid goods is allowed under rule 16 ibid, as if such goods are 'inputs' under CENVAT Credit Rules - As per rule 6 ibid read with rule 7 ibid, credit is allowed on 'receipt' of duty-paid goods in factory; however, in this case, assessee could not show any documentary proof of said 'receipt' - Rule 7 ibid requires that invoice should be in name of person availing credit; however, in this case, invoices were neither in name of assessee nor endorsed by consignee in favour of assessee - Hence, credit could not be allowed [Paras 10 to 12] [In favour of revenue]Cenvat Credit : Credit of duty-paid returned goods can be allowed only if invoice is in name of person availing credit or invoice is endorsed in favour of assessee; credit cannot be taken on invoice in name of a third party

Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoice - issued by the manufacturer in the name of another manufacturer and subsequently corrected the same incorporating the name of the appellant - no dispute that the goods did not get transported to the appellant's premises - it is not endorsed invoice - Revenue appeal dismissed. (Para 6)

Rule 3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - General - Assessee had more than one manufacturing unit - It received consignment of inputs in its factory - Invoice of said inputs contained address of assessees corporate office - Cenvat credit availed on said inputs was denied to assessee - Whether merely because corporate office address was given in invoice, it could not be made reason to deny credit otherwise available to assessee - Held, yes - Whether since there was no dispute about duty paid character of inputs, their receipt in factory premises and their utilization in manufacture of final products, impugned credit could not be denied - Held, yes [Para 2] [ In favour of assessee]

Rule 57T of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit on capital goods - Invoice - not endorsed by head office - a rectifiable defect - credit to be allowed after the defect is rectified - appeal allowed (Para 4)

Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Limitation - Modvat credit - Invoice - inputs received and entered in RG-23A Part I within six months from the date of issue of invoice - as invoice was in the name of head office, it was sent back for correction and was received after six months from the date of its initial issue - credit taken on receipt of the corrected invoice not to be denied, though taken after six months from the date of its initial issue - appeal rejected (Paras 5  6)

Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoice - shows wrong address of appellants by mentioning Varanasi instead of Rewa since the inputs were sent direct to job worker at Varanasi where head office of appellant was located - credit not to be denied for such lapse. (Para 4)

Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - endorsed invoice - transfer of inputs - inputs received by Central Stores, Patiala and transferred to appellant workshop at Amritser - invoice under which inputs were received, also endorsed - while endorsement of invoice after 1.4.94 is not permissible, the inputs to be treated as received by appellants under the invoice, though the place is different - credit available - penalty set aside - appeal allowed (Para 5)

Rule 57T of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit on capital goods - Bill of entry - in the name of Thane factory but credit taken by Dewas factory without endorsement - credit admissible as declaration says that credit on the said bill of entry would be taken by Dewas factory - appeal allowed (Paras 2  3)

Modvat credit -Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Subsidiary certificate - issued in the name of another factory of the manufacturer -endorsed to appellant-factory of the manufacturer - valid (Para 2)
Modvat credit - Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Invoice - in the name of manufacturer's depot, endorsed by depot in favour of appellant - acceptable valid document (Para 5.2)
Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoice - In favour of one factory but inputs received into another factory of the manufacturer - Credit not deniable (Para 7)

Rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Documents and accounts - Department denied credit taken by assessee only on grounds that : (1) there were procedural lapses and tax invoices did not contain all particulars ; and (2) some challans/invoices were in name of Head Office - HELD : Procedural lapses and absence of all particulars were rectifiable errors; hence, credit was to be allowed subject to rectification by assessee - Further, credit was to be allowed even if challan and invoices were in name of head office - Matter was remanded back to adjudicating authority to satisfy him regarding eligibility of Cenvat credit as provided under rule 9(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 [Paras 6 to 9] [In favour of assessee]ST : Procedural lapses and absence of all particulars are rectifiable errors, hence, credit was to be allowed subject to rectification by assessee; further, credit is allowable even if invoices are in name of head office

Rule 57T of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit on capital goods - Bill of entry - Was in the name of one factory but the goods were received and installed in another factory of the manufacturer by endorsing the bill of entry - Credit admissible even prior to amendment of the Rule vide Notification No. 23/94-CE (NT) dt. 20.5.94 - Appeal rejected (Para 4)

Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat credit - Invoice - Issued by the registered depot of the manufacturer - Name and address of the appellant mentioned on the invoices by deleting name and address of another party - These are not endorsed invoices - Credit admissible - Appeal allowed (Para 5)

Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Invoice - Endorsed invoice is valid in case of transfer of goods to another factory of the manufacturer not involving sale - Appeal rejected (Para 4)

facts.text:
Facts

The assessee is engaged in the manufacture of mould steel ingots and runners and risers under an agreement entered into by them with DSM Sugar Asmoli.

Under the said lease agreement dated 26-09-2002, the facility of land and machinery stands provided by DSM Sugar, Asmoli and the capital goods were received by them are required to be installed by the assessee and the duty on the final product required to be paid by the assessee.

DSM Sugars, Asmoli had endorsed the said invoices indicating as "certified that the goods covered under these invoices transferred to Kailash Steel, Asmoli in view of lease agreement dated 20-09-2002".

The Department denied CENVAT credit to the assessee on the ground that the invoices issued by the supplier are in the name of DSM Sugars, Asmoli, though there is no dispute that the said capital goods were received by the assessee and were duly erected and installed in their premises and were used for the manufacture of dutiable and excisable goods.

Revenue's Arguments

Endorsed invoices which are in the name of DSM Sugars cannot be held to be proper Cenvatable document so as to allow the CENVAT credit in respect of the same, to the assessee.

Assessee's Arguments

Even though DSM Sugars are the owners of the capital goods in question, there is no sale purchase of the capital goods and the same only stands transferred to their unit under the lease agreement, in which case, the effect of endorsement would not be of much relevance.

The assessee, namely, ‘G’, Ghaziabad availed MODVAT credit on the strength of invoice, which was in the name of ‘G’, Kota. The assessee also availed MODVAT credit on the strength of other invoice in which the buyer’s name was ‘P’, Faridabad; whereas the goods had been consigned to the assessee at Delhi. The Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the MODVAT credit taken by the assessee on the strength of the aforesaid invoices. He held that though there was cutting in consignees’ address but the same had been authenticated by the same person who had prepared the invoice and the address was changed from Kota to Ghaziabad.

He further held that a certificate issued by ‘P’ was also brought on record to show that the goods had been supplied by it to the assessee at Delhi address.

On appeal to the Tribunal by the revenue:

The assessee availed Cenvat credit on inputs/capital goods on basis of the invoices, wherein the suppliers had mentioned the brand name and address of the assessee. The adjudicating authority denied credit on the ground that the invoices did not bear the assessee’s name. The Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the adjudication order.

On appeal :

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of automobile parts. It registered itself with Central Excise Department on 28-11-2006 for manufacture of automobile components. The assessee set up its new factory by awarding the contract of construction thereof to a contractor. During the period from January 2007-08, the assessee availed cenvat credit on service tax paid on the construction services on the strength of 12 invoices issued by the contractor. Out of 12 invoices, invoices involving cenvat credit were issued prior to 28-11-2006 and remaining were issued after 28-11-2006, i.e. the date on which the assessee was registered with the Central Department. The Commissioner allowed the credit relating to the invoices which were issued subsequent to 28-11-2006, however, disallowed the credit in relation to the invoices which were issued prior to 28-11-2006 on the ground that the assessee was not registered with the Department at the time of issuance of those invoices and secondly, on the ground that the invoices were issued in the earlier name of assessee and not in the current name of the assessee.

On appeal:

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of excisable goods. It also imported finished goods on payment of duty. During the course of the business, it availed a number of services which were used in relation to the manufacture of final products as well as in relation to selling and marketing of final products, etc. As the assessee was having its head office situated in Mumbai which was registered as ‘Input service distributor’, the assessee received various services which it distributed to various factories as an input service distributor by issue of invoice in terms of rule 4A(2). The credit so distributed and availed by the assessee at various factories was utilized to discharge the excise duty liability of various factories on various final products manufactured by them. The revenue, however, denied said input service credit taken by the assessee on ground that said credit was availed for duty paid final products as well as exempted final products and, hence, it was not entitled to input service credit as per rule 6(2), as it was not maintaining separate account of input service for dutiable as well as exempted goods. Accordingly, demand was confirmed on assessee along with penalties.

On appeal :

Facts

There was no dispute with regard to the compliance with the substantial conditions for availing the Modvat Credit viz., inputs have suffered Central Excise duty, such duty paid goods were received into the factory under the cover of the duty paying document and the said inputs were used in the manufacture of the final product.

Since the goods in question, covered under single invoice, could not be transported as a single consignment, the same were split up into smaller consignments and transported as per the convenience of the supplier. The various split up consignments were transported under the cover of the photocopy of the original invoice.

The Department denied the Modvat Credit to relating to the inputs received from Visakhapatnam Steel Plant, a Government of India undertaking, merely on the ground that the inputs covered under single invoice were transported by various vehicles by splitting up the consignment, as a matter of convenience for the supplier in transporting such inputs.

The Department also denied the Modvat Credit taken on the basis of Original copy of the invoice, as the duplicate for the transporter was lost, though the inputs were received into the factory of manufacture and used in the manufacture.

Issue Involved

Whether denial of Modvat Credit merely on procedural lapses was valid ?

The assessee-company was engaged in the manufacture of aerated waters and mineral water chargeable to central excise duty. It was also availing of the Cenvat credit of central excise duty paid on various inputs and capital goods and of service tax paid on various input services used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final products as per the provisions of 2004 Rules. It applied for registration as an Input Service Distributor (ISD) on 4-5-2006 in respect of its Delhi office and the registration was granted to it on 26-5-2006. In course of scrutiny of central excise records of the assessee, it was found that the Delhi office of the assessee, even prior to the date on which the registration was granted to it, had issued invoices for passing on service tax credit and on the basis of those invoices, the Cenvat credit had been taken by its manufacturing unit at Hapur. A show-cause notice was issued to the assessee for recovery of allegedly wrongly taken Cenvat credit along with interest and penalty on ground that Delhi office of the assessee could not issue invoices to factory at Hapur for passing on service tax credit as Input Service Distributor when no registration in that regard had been obtained. The Commissioner confirmed the Cenvat credit demand along with interest and also imposed penalty.

On appeal :

The assessee availed cenvat credit in respect of distribution of credit by the Head Office, an input service distributor [ISD], which was distributed by the Head Office before obtaining registration. The assessee also availed credit of service tax paid on rent-a-cab service and security service.

The Adjudicating Authority denied cenvat credit in respect of distribution of credit by the Head Office on the plea that the credit was distributed by the Head Office before obtaining registration and the assessee had taken credit not on basis valid invoice but on basis the allocation chart. He also denied cenvat credit of tax paid on rent-a-cab service and security service on the plea that the services were provided at job worker's place, where the job worker was carrying out cutting process of paper on behalf of the assessee.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the original order.

On appeal to Tribunal:

Facts

The assessee was given a show cause notice dated 17-1-2007 asking them to show cause as to why their refund claim of Rs. 11,79,720 should not be rejected. The assessee submitted their reply dated 25-5-2007. The Assistant Commissioner sanctioned said refund claim.

However, the Assistant Commissioner issued a corrigendum (dated 17-7-2007) to the earlier show cause notice -

stating that as the assessee had taken credit to the tune of Rs. 11,18,182 on the strength of the invoices for capital goods issued by their Head Office, the same was not admissible as their Head Office was not registered as a registered dealer and

therefore asking why their refund should not be rejected to the extent of Rs. 11,18,182.

The assessee contended that -

the refund sought was of the excess amount paid by them which should be sanctioned and that the amount of cenvat credit on capital goods (Rs. 11,18,182) was rightly taken on the strength of the documents issued by their Head Office in respect of the capital goods actually used by them for providing the output service and

they and their Head Office are not separate entities.

Issue Involved

Whether unconfirmed demand can be set-off against unconfirmed refund claim ?

Facts

Assessee-manufacturer was procuring the furnace oil for use in generation of steam/electricity and was availing CENVAT Credit on the furnace oil.

The assessee was also utilizing the furnace oil for generation of steam/electricity which was used in another unit, an EOU situated in the same compound.

A part of the Steam/Electricity was cleared to EOU unit.

The Department contended that proportionate CENVAT Credit on furnace oil utilized in the generation of Steam/Electricity cleared to their EOU was reversible in terms of rule 57AD(2) of Central Excise Rules 1944, read with rule 6(2) & (3) of CENVAT Credit Rules 2001/2002/2004.

The assessee argued that electricity generated has been used in their EOU unit which is the same factory premises, which was also factory of production. Even if the EOU procures inputs/capital goods for generation electricity, the EOU could procure the same without payment of duty in terms of the Foreign Trade Policy.

The Tribunal allowed credit.

Assessee's Arguments

When the assessee establishes two units in the same compound, both of them falls within the definition of "premises" under the Act and when both the units are manufacturing excisable goods, the steam manufactured in the factory of production even if it is used in the other unit, is eligible for CENVAT Credit.

Revenue's Arguments

Having regard to the definition of "input", the assessee would be entitled to the benefit of CENVAT Credit only to the extent of steam manufactured out of furnace oil is used in the factory for its production.

Even if such a steam is utilized by it in it other unit in the same compound, it amounts to wheeling out or diverting the steam to another unit and the assessee is not liable for CENVAT Credit.

Issue Involved

When the assessee who manufacture the steam, use the same in the factory of manufacturing and also utilized the steam in its another unit which is situated in the same compound, is he entitled to CENVAT Credit proportionately to the extent which was used in the other unit ?

• The assessee received duty paid Hydrogen and Argon gas from 'P', which were used for welding purposes.

• Before welding, these gases were mixed at assessee's premises using a facility/machinery set up in assessee's premises by supplier 'P'.

• 'P' charged facility charges for such facility/machinery on which 'P' paid excise duty.

• The assessee took credit of such duty paid on facility charges.

• Department denied such credit contending that such duty didn't relate to any inputs received by the assessee.

Issue involved

• Whether the assessee was eligible for credit ?

The assessee was registered as provider of advertisement services. According to the adjudicating officer, it had contravened the provisions of rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 inasmuch as it had availed credit on the documents which were not addressed to its registered premises but addressed to the branch office of the assessee. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the adjudicating authority. Before the Tribunal, the assessee’s case was that it had taken service tax registration with the authorities on the ground that it had got centralized accounting system and centralized billing was done from the address of its registered premises.

The assessee, a manufacturer, availed Cenvat credit on the inputs received by it through registered dealers. The revenue authorities took view that it was a case of irregular availment of Cenvat credit as the dealer from whom the assessee had purchased inputs never existed at the address mentioned in the invoice. Accordingly, demand was confirmed on the assessee along with interest and penalty. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the inputs which were purchased by the assessee were duty paid and consumed by the assessee in the factory premises and it could not be denied the Cenvat credit and, therefore, it set aside the order of the adjudicating authority.

On appeal:

Facts

•

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of excisable goods and provision of output services.

•

The assessee installed ammonia storage tank facility at their premises at Raigad for storage of imported ammonia, which was raw material meant for manufacturing of final product at their Taloja factory.

•

The assessee availed Cenvat Credit of service tax paid on input services (Consulting Engineers, Technical Inspection and certification service, Construction service, erection, commissioning and installation service, etc.) used for installation of said ammonia storage tank.

•

The department denied credit arguing that services received in connection with the activity of installation of storage tank which was immovable property and outside factory premises were not input services.

Issue Involved

•

Whether the assessee was eligible for CENVAT Credit on input services ?

The assessee had leased a land to ‘J’ Ltd. Under lease agreement, ‘J’ Ltd. set up a power plant in the lease premises by making use of components procured by it but consigned to the assessee (lessor). When power plant became ready for commissioning, it was handed over to the assessee on payment of full consideration for the job, and the assessee started using the power plant. The assessee took Cenvat credit to the extent of 50 per cent on the abovesaid components in September, 2005 to March, 2006 and the balance credit was taken in the next financial year. The department disallowed entire credit on the ground that on dates on which capital goods were received by the assessee were not received in the factory of the assessee but in premises of ‘J’ Ltd. and, therefore, the benefit of capital goods credit would not be admissible to the assessee under rule 3. Accordingly, the Commissioner ordered recovery of Cenvat credit wrongly taken by the assessee and also imposed penalty on ‘J’ Ltd.

On appeal :

The appellants have their factory at Mandideep in M.P. They have another factory at Ankleshwar in Gujarat. They manufacture Cephalexin and Cephadroxil falling under Chapter 29 of CETA. Penicillin GK is the main input for the final product, which the appellants import as also procure locally. With the approval of the Assistant Collector they sent Penicillin to Ankleshwar factory direct where the same was converted into "7ADCA", which was then received at the factory at Mandideep for manufacture of the final product. They had similar approval in respect of other raw materials used in the manufacture of "7ADCA" for being sent to the factory at Ankleshwar. They were availing of the Modvat credit in respect of all the raw materials at Mandideep when "7ADCA" along with other documents was received from Ankleshwar. On appeal to the Supreme Court :

held.text: The Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly followed the decision of the Tribunal in the case of CCE&CE v. DNH Spinners [2010] 25 STT 295 (Ahd. - CESTAT). Even though the assessee had multiple divisions, in the absence of any dispute about the receipt of the services in question by the factory to whom credit had been passed on, the ratio of the cited decision was applicable. In fact, the Commissioner(Appeals) proceeded to say that the assessee should have followed the procedure of issue of invoices by the head office as an input service distributor but observed that as far as the present appeal was concerned, the proceedings were limited by the ground taken in the show-cause notice and the order-in-original which had held that assessee had taken credit wrongly since invoice was not in its name but in the name of its head office. In view of the fact that the invoice was in the name of the head office and there was no dispute raised in the show-cause notice as to the admissibility of input service credit to the factory on the ground that the input service was not relatable to the factory, the omission became a totally curable defect and was a condonable one. Under those circumstances, the conclusion reached by the Commissioner (Appeals) to drop the demand could not be found fault with. The Commissioner (Appeals) also had taken a view that merely because the assessee did not disclose to the department that it had availed credit on the basis of documents not prescribed under rule 9(2), it could not be said that there was suppression of fact, wilful misstatement, etc. He had relied upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (211) ELT 513. In view of the fact that there was no allegation of non-receipt of input service or the allegation of service not relatable to the factory and also in view of the fact that invoice was in the name of head office of the same factory and not in the name of someone else, the decision of the Commissioner (Appeals) that extended period was not invocable also had to be upheld. Since the assessee was eligible for the credit and there was no suppression of facts, extended period was not invocable and, hence, the question of penalty did not arise. The definition of "input" makes it clear that, "input" means all goods used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final products or not and includes lubricating oils, greases, cutting oils, coolants, accessories of the final products cleared along with the final product, goods used as paint, or as packing material, or as fuel, or for generation of electricity or steam used in or in relation to manufacture of final products or for any other purpose, within the factory of production. The word "factory" has been defined in the Central Excise Act at section 2(e). It is an inclusive definition. For the purpose of Central Excise Act, a 'factory' means more than one premises. [Para 9]

Rule 6, of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 makes it clear that the CENVAT Credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of goods which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods. However, exception is carved out in sub-Rule (2). Sub-Rule (2) of Rule 6 provides- where a manufacturer or provider of output service avails CENVAT Credit in respect of any inputs except the input intended to be used as fuel and manufactures such final products or provides such output service which are chargeable to duty or tax as well as exempted goods or services, then, an obligation is cast on the assessee to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory or input and input service meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service and the quantity of input meant for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services. However he would be entitled to CENVAT credit only on that quantity of input or input service which is intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods. Therefore, it is clear that the assessee manufacturer is entitled to CENVAT Credit on "inputs" which is used in the manufacture of dutiable goods. [Para 11]

In view of clear language in the statutory provisions coupled with the fact that the factory includes more than one premises to be eligible for CENVAT Credit, an assessee has to use the input in the manufacture of dutiable goods in his factory. The definition of 'input' brings within its fold the inputs used for generation of electricity or steam, provided such electricity or steam is used within the factory of production for manufacture of final products or for any other purpose. Therefore, it follows the term "within the factory of production" cannot be confined to a single unit. In view of the definition of factory in the act which means more than one premises, it has to be construed as the factory owned by the assessee. If the assessee owns more than one unit, all the units if they are situated at a place would constitute "a factory". If the electricity or steam generated within the factory of production means within the factory premises which may include more than one unit. If such electricity or steam generated within the factory of production is utilized by the assessee in more than one unit and if those units are manufacturing excisable goods, then, the assessee would be entitled to the benefit of CENVAT credit to the entire extent of utilization of such electricity or steam in all the units of its factory premises. Therefore, whatever goes into generation of electricity or steam which is placed within the factory which may consists of more than one unit would be an input for the purposes of obtaining credit on the duty payable thereon. [Para 15]

In the instant case, the assessee is having two units; one DTA unit and another EOU unit. Both are situated in the same factory premises. Both are manufacturing excisable goods. The assessee has purchased furnace oil from which, the steam is generated within the said factory premises. The said steam is utilized by the assessee in manufacturing excisable goods in both the units which are situated within the same compound, which falls within the definition of the word "factory" and therefore, the assessee is entitled to CENVAT credit in respect of entire volume of steam used in the manufacture of excisable goods by both the units. That is precisely what the appellate authorities have held and granted relief to the assessee. [Para 16]

Rule 57G clearly shows that the credit of duty can be taken on inputs by establishing that the duty has been paid on the said inputs on the basis of documents such as invoice, AR-1, Bill on Entry, etc. In the instant case, it was not in dispute that the appellant had received imported shredded steel scrap from ‘E’ Ltd. on which countervailing duty had been paid by ‘E’ Ltd. It was also not in dispute that ‘E’ Ltd. had not taken credit of the duty paid on shredded steel scrap which was given on loan to the appellant. It was also not in dispute that the appellant had used the said shredded steel scrap taken on loan from ‘E’ Ltd. as inputs in its factory. The certificate issued by a Superintendent of Central Excise to the effect that ‘E’ Ltd. had not taken credit of duty paid on the said shredded steel scrap, was not doubted by the Excise authorities. Similarly, the certificate issued by another Superintendent to the effect that the quantity of shredded steel scrap received by the appellant from ‘E’ Ltd. had been used as inputs in the factory of the appellant, was also not doubted by the Excise authorities. In these circumstances, the appellant had established that the credit of duty on receipt of imported shredded steel scrap from ‘E’ Ltd. had been taken in accordance with law. [Para 9]

For availing the credit of duty, what is required to be established under rule 57G is that the inputs received are in fact duty paid. The procedure set out in rule 57G is to ensure that the credit is taken on the basis of duty paid documents. The bill of entry is one such document set out in rule 57G. The said rule does not require that the bill of entry should be in the name of the person claiming credit of duty. It is not in dispute that the goods imported and cleared on payment of duty by one person can be used as inputs and credit of duty can be claimed by another person by establishing that the imported duty paid goods have been received as inputs and that the importer has not taken credit of that duty. In the instant case, it was established that the duty paid goods were received as inputs, however, the credit was denied on the ground that the Bill of entry was not endorsed in the name of the appellant. Rule 57G does not require that for taking credit of duty, the bill of entry should be endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the absence of any provision regarding endorsement on the bill of entry, the credit of duty cannot be denied on the ground that the bill of entry is not endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the facts of the instant case, the evidence on record i.e., the bills of entry together with the certificates issued by excise authorities, clearly showed that the goods imported and cleared under the bills of entry on payment of duty were received and utilized by the appellant as inputs in its factory and that the importer had not utilized the credit of duty paid on the said goods. Thus, the appellant had established that the inputs received under the bills of entry were duty paid and, therefore, the authorities below were not justified in denying the credit of duty to the appellant. [Para 10]

Rule 3(1) allows a manufacturer of final products to take credit inter alia of duty/service tax which is paid on :

(i)

any input or capital goods received in the factory of manufacturer of the final product; and

(ii)

any input service received by the manufacturer of the final product.

Rule 3(1) makes a distinction between inputs or capital goods on the one hand and input services on the other hand.

Clause (i) of rule 3(1) provides that duty should be paid on any input or capital goods received in the factory of manufacture of the final product.

Such a restriction, however, is not imposed in regard to input services since the only stipulation in clause (ii) is that the input services should be received by the manufacturer of the final product.

Hence, even as a matter of first principle on a plain and literal construction of rule 3(1), Tribunal was not justified in holding that assessee would not be entitled to avail of CENVAT credit in respect of services utilized in relation to ammonia storage tanks on the ground that they were situated outside the factory of production. Storage of input is a part of process of manufacture - Hence, impugned services were input services under rule 2(l) :

The definition of the expression 'input service' covers any services used by the manufacturer, whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products. The words 'directly or indirectly' and 'in or in relation to' are words of width and amplitude. The subordinate legislation has advisedly used a broad and comprehensive expression while defining the expression 'input service'.

Rule 2(l) initially provides that input service means any services of the description falling in sub-clauses (i) and (ii). Rule 2(l) then provides an inclusive definition by enumerating certain specified services. Among those services are services pertaining to the procurement of inputs and inward transportation of inputs.

The Tribunal's interpretation that legislature restricted the benefit of CENVAT credit for input services used in respect of inputs only to these two categories viz. for the procurement of inputs and for the inward transportation of inputs was ex facie contrary to the provisions contained in Rule 2(l).

The first part of Rule 2(l) inter alia covers any services used by the manufacturer directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products. The inclusive part of the definition enumerates certain specified categories of services. However, it would be far-fetched to interpret rule 2(l) to mean that only two categories of services in relation to inputs viz. for the procurement of inputs and for the inward transportation of inputs were intended to be brought within the purview of Rule 2(l). Rule 2(l) must be read in its entirety.

The input services in the present case were used by the Appellant whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products. The assessee was manufacturing dutiable final products and the storage and use of ammonia is an intrinsic part of that process.

Hence, assessee was eligible for input service credit. [Para 5]

The salient points of the Strategic Alliance Agreement are as follows :

(a)

assessee manufactures alloy and non-alloy steel billets and blooms;

(b)

Kalyani Steels Limited manufacture pig iron (solid) and pig iron (hot metal) which is an intermediary product and in turn this intermediary product is also used by assessee for production of final product in terms of the Strategic Alliance Agreement dated 16-5-1998 for production of steel through an integrated steel plant.

Therefore, logically, the corporate entities had entered to Strategic Alliance Agreement for manufacture of steel in an integrated steel plant. [Para 8]

Admittedly, Praxiar has supplied oxygen and nitrogen in pipelines and the CENVAT credit has been availed of only by the assessee. Though the CENVAT credit was claimed only by the assessee, the input i.e., oxygen and nitrogen were used by both the companies. [Para 9]

It is well settled that a manufacturing unit can have one or more units to manufacture intermediary raw materials to manufacture a final product. In the instant case, by the Strategic Alliance Agreement, the corporate entities had entered into a joint venture agreement to manufacture steel products. The records disclose that whatever was manufactured by Kalyani in the ratio agreed to between the parties was finally made over to the assessee herein for manufacture of final product. Therefore, it appears, the companies joined hands to manufacture the final products in terms of the Strategic Alliance Agreement. In the circumstances, CENVAT cannot be deemed on the ground that credit is being availed by one factory and material inputs are used by three factories, because the CENVAT able input is being used for common share and continuous purpose of manufacturing dutiable goods.

Though there are three separate units with separate registrations, the entire raw material is being converted into final dutiable product in continuous, inter connected and integrated process conforming to the definition of a single factory under section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act. [Para 10]

Hence, Tribunal order was affirmed. [Para 11]

The Supreme Court in Collector of Central Excise v. Dai Karkaria Ltd. 1999 (7) SCC 448 held that where a manufacturer obtains credit for the excise duty paid on raw material to be used by him in the production of an excisable product immediately, it should make the requisite declaration and obtain an acknowledgement thereof. It is entitled to use the credit at any time thereafter while making payment of excise duty on the excisable product. There is no provision in the Rules which provides for a reversal of the credit by the Excise Authorities except where it has been illegally or irregularly taken, in which event it stands cancelled or, if utilized, has to be paid for. Where the credit has been validly taken, its benefit is available to the manufacturer without any limitation in time or otherwise unless the manufacturer itself chooses not to use the raw material in its excisable product. The credit is, therefore, indefeasible. It should also be noted that there is no correlation of the raw material and the final product, that is to say, it is not as if credit can be taken only on a final product, that is manufactured out of the particular raw material to which the credit is related. The credit may be taken against the excise duty on a final product manufactured on the very day it becomes available. [Para 7]

The High Court of Rajasthan in Hindustan Zinc Ltd. v. Union of India 2008 (223) ELT 149 has held that in case inputs are received in factory and used in manufacture of end product, no excise duty becomes payable on end product. The relevant date for considering exemption from duty of the end product in or in relation to which inputs are used is the date of its receipt in factory and condition is its actual use in or in relation to manufacture of end product by the manufacturer. The chargeability to duty or non-chargeability due to exemption or notified nil rate is to be considered at the stage before goods are actually produced, but on receipt of inputs intended to be used in manufacture of such goods. That being so ultimate clearance of goods at nil rate due to contingency existing at the time of removal does not affect the entitlement that legally arises long before that date. [Para 11]

The above judgments were to be agreed with. Since the language of rule 9(2) of the Cenvat Credit Rules is identical to that of rule 57H(5) of the Excise Rules, the interpretation given by the Apex Court had to apply in the instant case also. It was to be concluded that even though the final product may be exempted from payment of excise, the assessee could not be asked to reverse the Modvat credit already taken by it. [Para 12]

It was for the Board to take an appropriate action against the Commissioner for issuing the alert circular against the instructions issued by the Board and the remedy did not lie in holding all the proceedings invalid and depriving the statutory powers of the revenue officers and also preventing the officers from performing their statutory functions or holding the proceedings in performance of statutory functions invalid. Therefore, there was no substance in the preliminary objections raised by the assessee and the same was to be rejected. [Para 4] The provisions of rule 7 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 and rule 12B of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 would show that it is very important to know as to who was the manufacturer and who was responsible to fulfil all the obligations towards central excise. It was contended that rule 12(b) of the Central Excise Rules would not be applicable to the persons who had already been registered earlier and would be applicable only in respect of the new assessees. However, the rule does not prevent the old manufacturers also from utilizing the facility. Rule 12(b) of the Central Excise Rules envisages four types of situations, namely, a merchant- manufacturer may undertake to fulfil all the obligations himself; the job worker may be authorized by the merchant-manufacturer to fulfil the obligations on his behalf in which situation, the job worker would be virtually acting as an agent for the purpose of manufacture of fabrics of the merchant-manufacturer or alternatively, the merchant-manufacturer may be authorized by the job worker in which case the merchant-manufacturer would be the agent of the job worker. In cases where either the merchant-manufacturer or the job worker had authorized either of them to act on his behalf, obvious conclusion would be that the knowledge of the job worker or the merchant-manufacturer about the existence of the other would be irrelevant, since either of them would be an agent of the other. Therefore, in cases where the job worker or the merchant- manufacturer has been authorized as contemplated under rule 12(b) of the Central Excise Rules, the obvious conclusion would be that when the goods are received under the invoice, the fulfilment of obligations under rule 7(2) of the Cenvat Credit Rules is complete only if the obligation is fulfilled in respect of the person who has supplied the goods to the merchant-manufacturer or the job worker who, in turn, supplied goods to the other. Therefore, if the merchant- manufacturer has authorized the job worker to fulfil his obligations under central excise law, the fact that the merchant-manufacturer has supplied the goods under his own invoice or endorsed the invoice issued by another supplier and, therefore, the knowledge of the receiver about the merchant- manufacturer would be sufficient, would not be correct. In such cases the job worker has to necessarily know the supplier and the obligations can be said to be fulfilled only if it is done keeping the supplier of the merchant-manufacturer in mind. In the instant cases this information was not available. The case of the department was that the job worker or the processor was required to know the supplier of the fabrics even where the invoice was endorsed by the merchant- manufacturer or the merchant-manufacturer had issued another invoice. [Para 20.4]

In cases where the invoice is merely endorsed, the issue is settled and in such cases the obligations of the job worker would be fulfilled only if he has taken reasonable steps to ensure that the supplier of the fabrics to the merchant- manufacturer who has endorsed it is in existence. [Para 20.5]

However, where the goods had not travelled directly from the weaver/the manufacturer to the job worker and the invoice had not been endorsed, the question arose as to whether it would be sufficient if the job worker knew the supplier or he was required to know the original manufacturer who had paid the duty, even though another invoice had been issued by the merchant- manufacturer and he had supplied his invoice as well as the original manufacturer’s invoice. In such cases if the job worker was authorized by the merchant-manufacturer for fulfilling of central excise obligations, the job worker would be required to know the supplier of the fabrics to the merchant- manufacturer. Otherwise it would be sufficient if he knew the merchant- manufacturer and was able to show that he had taken the steps envisaged in rule 7 of the Cenvat Credit Rules. [Para 20.6]

Modvat--cannot be denied in routine or by mechanical approach even if documentation is defective so long as duty has been paid on inputs, "... we are unable to appreciate the routine and mechanical approach of the authorities below in rejecting the claim of the Modvat credit only on the ground that more than one endorsement has been made. When the Board themselves have taken a decision to relax the procedural requirement by way of administrative instruction it should be the endeavour of the authorities to extend Modvat credit wherever the duty-paid nature of the goods is evident from the gate passes produced and quantum of duty paid on the inputs could be ascertained from them. A positive approach is called for in this regard."

2. Modvat--credit for goods received against GP I, after three endorsements by different parties can be allowed as long as duty-paid nature of the goods is established. "Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules stipulates that inputs are to be received under the cover of a gate pass, an AR-I, a Bill of Entry or any other document as may be prescribed by the Board. ...However, when this requirement created some difficulties in the ease of Small Scale units to obtain the inputs through intermediaries, the Board appears to have made relaxation to this requirement by permitting one endorsement in the gate pass initially and subsequently based on the representations permitting upto two endorsements in the gate passes. This relaxation made by the Board appears to be purely of administrative nature based on considerations of implementing the Modvat scheme, so long as the duty-paid nature of the goods and duty paid thereon could be established. As seen from the Trade Notice cited by the learned advocate, it is evident that the Government is keen to extend the Modvat credit so long as the goods in factory packed condition as are covered by the gate passes are received by the parties intending to avail Modvat credit...... the department is entitled to make verification or investigation with regard to the genuineness of the gate pass and also on the question whether gate pass has been utilised for availment of Modvat credit at the earliest stages. In this case, no such enquiry appears to have been conducted and the Modvat credit has-been denied only on the ground that more than that of permitted endorsements have been made in the gate passes. Such an order cannot be sustainable in the context of the scheme of Modvat credit read along with the relaxation made by the Board. We, therefore, set aside the order passed by the authorities below and permit availment of credit and while doing so, we allow the liberty to the Assistant Collector to cause any inquiry or investigation to satisfy himself about the genuine nature of the gate passes and also about non-utilisation of the gate passes at the earlier stages of endorsements for availment of Modvat credit."

They entered into lease agreement with JSWPL, a relationship had already been developed prior to October 2005, as evident from CDR Cell report, JSWPL balance sheet etc., for financial accommodation to get loan from UTI Bank Ltd. for setting up C.P.P. and one of the considerations is that electricity would be supplied to SISCOL, which is an integral part of manufacturing activities of SISCOL. [Para 68.4] Credit available : In view of the above discussion, it is proper to allow Cenvat credit to SISCOL from October 2005 on capital goods used in setting up Power Plant for generation of electricity, which was captively consumed within the factory of SISCOL for manufacturing of their final product. II. Minority View [per : Mathew John, Member (T)] - Credit allowable, but, only from 31-8-2006, after merger :

Scheme : Under the Cenvat Credit Scheme a manufacturer of excisable goods is allowed to take credit of excise duty paid on inputs and capital goods used in the manufacture of excisable goods and utilize such credit for payment of excise duty on final products manufactured by him. [Para 36]

Rule 4(4) - Credit only by person paying value/duty : There is no specific provision in the Rules to the effect that credit can be taken by a manufacturer only if duty is paid by him to the supplier of goods. There is a provision in rule 4(4) to the effect that CENVAT credit in respect of capital goods shall not be allowed in respect of that part of the value of capital goods which represents the amount of duty on such capital goods, which the manufacturer claims as depreciation under section 32 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. So prima facie it would appear that the person who is paying for the value of goods and duty thereon is relevant for taking credit. [Para 38]

Receipt in factory : On the other hand definition of capital goods as given in rule 2 (a) and the rule 3 (1) and rule 4 (2) (a) allowing taking of credit are clear enough that credit is to be taken on capital goods received in the factory of the manufacturer. Interestingly there has been amendment to rule 2(a) and rule 4(2) (a) by Notification 3/2011-NT dated 1-3-2011 to the effect that in the case of captive power plants credit can be taken even if the plants are outside the factory. [Para 39]

Payment of value and duty was made by JSWPL - JSWPL neither holding-subsidiary no job-worker : In this case Cenvat credit was taken by SISCOL during the period Sep 05 to July 06. (From 31-08-2006, SISCOL had taken over the power plant from JSWPL.). SISCOL had not paid for the value of the goods or excise duty payable thereon when credit was taken. Such payments could not be seen in the books of account of SISCOL, when credit was taken. The value of the goods and excise duty thereon were paid by JSWPL on the date on which credit was taken by SISCOL. These are two different companies. There is no relationship of one as the holding company of the other which fact existed in some of the decisions relied upon. There is no relationship of SISCOL as job-worker of JSWPL which was the fact in cases where persons not paying for the goods along with duty were allowed to take credit of duty. [Para 40]

The appellant submitted that there is a complete factual error in the findings of the Member (Technical). The power plant is not a separate legal entity. It is a division of appellant-company and is part and parcel of the appellant unit. The assessee on the other hand contended that there are separate financial accounts for the power plant and the manufacturing unit and hence these two are not to be considered as belonging to same legal entity. The power plant belongs to a group company of appellant. [Para 5]

The Supreme Court in the assessee's own case for earlier year in State of UP v. Renusagar Power Co. AIR 1988 SC 1737 observed that in the facts of case Hindalco and Renusagar were inextricably linked up together. Renusagar had in reality no separate and independent existence apart from and independent of Hindalco. Therefore, the Supreme Court opined that the corporate veil must be lifted and Hindalco and Renusagar should be treated as one concern and if that was taken, the consumption of energy by Hindalco must be regarded as consumption of energy from its own source of generation.

The Delhi High Court in its order dated 9-7-1993 followed the above decision in allowing exemption to electricity supplied by Renusagar to appellant. In any case, further development in this matter made the position amply clear. The Bombay High Court vide order dated 22-4-1993 in company Petition No. 128 of 1993 approved the scheme of amalgamation which resulted in the merger of Hindalco and Renusagar. As such, there can be no dispute about the fact that power plant at Renusagar is belonging to the appellant. Hence, the basis of Technical Member's finding that the power plant belongs to subsidiary unit is factually incorrect. Hence, the reasoning followed is untenable. [Para 6]

Considering the other aspects regarding Hindalco's eligibility for input service credits, it is noted that neither the impugned orders nor the show cause notices have disputed the services in question for their eligibility and coverage under Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. Credit of input service is with reference to manufacturer, not with reference to factory.

In the appellant's own case, the Tribunal vide Final Order No. A/1357/2012-EX(BR), dated 11-12-2012 has held that though initially the power plant was owned by Renusagar, this company had been amalgamated with the appellant company in the year 1993. Thus, during the period of dispute Renusagar was fully owned by Hindalco. Thus, the ratio of the judgments of the Apex Court are squarely applicable to the facts of the case, as the Renusagar, which is a captive power plant of Hindalco, together with cement factory of the Hindalco constitute one integrated unit. [Para 7]

In view of the factual position as explained above there is no ground or reason to deviate from the earlier decisions of the Tribunal. [Para 8]

Thus, the credits of duty paid on services availed with reference to Renusagar are rightly eligible to Hindalco. The view of member (Judicial) is legal sustainable in this regard (Para 10]

Rule 9(2) provides for the availment of Cenvat credit by a manufacturer or provider of input/output services on the basis of the documents, which are enumerated in rule 9(1). The said documents on which credit was availed was not in dispute, inasmuch as the delivery invoices on which credit had been availed by the assessee fell within the category of ‘Invoices’ issued by a service provider. The only question was as to whether the provisions of rule 9(2) were attracted in the instant case. Provisions of rule 9(2) can be pressed into service for denial of cenvat credit to the assessee, only if the document does not contain the particulars as required. In the instant case, it was seen from the show-cause notice that only the contravention of rule 9(2) had been indicated, but it was not very clear as to what was the contravention. Proviso to rule 9(2) talks about non-mention of the particulars and the corrective action that can be taken by the jurisdictional Assistant Commissioner and the Deputy Commissioner in the absence of such details. The credit of service tax leviable under section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 is eligible to be taken as Cenvat credit on any input services received by the manufacturer of the final product. The plea of the assessee on provisions of credit rules, invoked for denial of cenvat credit, was not at all addressed by the Commissioner (Appeals) while rejecting the appeal filed by the assessee. It could be seen from the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that the Commissioner had recorded that the invoices in question were received under the Service Tax Rules, 1994. As per rule 4A(1)(ii), the invoices should indicate the name and address of the person who is receiving the taxable services. There was a strong force in the contention of the assessee that the provisions of rule were very clear; it only requires person receiving the taxable services and only address where the taxable services are provided. [Para 7]

It could be seen from the impugned order that the Commissioner (Appeals) had tried to apply rule 2(1)(ii ) to deny Cenvat credit. That allegation was not made out in the show-cause notice and the finding recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) to reject the appeal filed by the assessee, on that ground, was beyond the allegations made in the show-cause notice. [Para 8]

In sum, the assessee had made out a case for credit of service tax paid on the service to its branch offices. In view of the foregoing reasoning, the impugned order was unsustainable and was to be set aside. The appeal was to be allowed. [Para 9]

Though the invoices are not in the name of the assessee but it is in the name of the directors and the employees of the company, credit should be allowed for the reason that all these expenditure were incurred by the assessee company and the same is not under dispute, therefore even though the invoices are not in the name of the company but in the name of the directors/employees and the same has been booked as expenditure in the books of assessee, credit is admissible. [Para 6]

As regard the reason for denying the credit that cenvatable bills/invoices were not available, assessee submitted that now they are in possession of most of the invoices which can be produced before the authority for verification. In such cases the matter needs to be remanded so that assessee can produce invoices before the adjudicating authority and the adjudicating authority after verifying the same can allow the credit to the assessee. [Para 6.1]

As regard the services which were not considered as input services, it is found that services involved are of construction of foundation in the factory, construction of security cabin, construction of scrap yard, shifting of machines, these services are directly related to activity of the manufacturing unit and the same are clearly included in the inclusion part of the definition of the input services therefore credit is admissible on these services. As regard the services of civil work at Mohannagar quarters, Misc. Civil work in HDFC colony, these services are not related to the factory but it is related to the staff quarters, therefore civil work of staff quarters and civil work in HDFC colony cannot be treated as input service. As regard the air fair and cleaning services, it is related to the business activity of the assessee company hence the credit is admissible. [Para 6.2]

In certain invoices Cenvat credit was denied only for want of service tax registration number on the bills/invoices. In this regard, it is viewed that merely non mention of the registration number on the invoice Cenvat credit cannot be denied particularly when there is no dispute that the invoices was raised to the assessee, services were received by the assessee, therefore only on the reason that service tax registration number not mentioned, service tax cannot be disallowed. [Para 6.3]

Regarding denial of Cenvat credit on the bank charges, in the Cenvat Credit Rules, relaxation is specifically provided that for banking services, even if there are no invoices but from any documents of the bank if it is established the payment of service tax, credit must be allowed therefore only because bills are not available Cenvat credit on banking charges cannot be disallowed. [Para 6.4]

Therefore, the assessee is prima facie entitled for the Cenvat credit which was disallowed for various reasons, subject to verification of the invoices which will be produced by the assessee. Therefore, the impugned order is set aside and the matter is remanded to the Original Adjudicating authority to pass denovo adjudication order, keeping in view the above observations. Appeal is disposed of by way of remand in the above terms. [Para 7]

The Adjudicating Authority held that the services on which credit were availed by the assessee were not covered by the scope of 'input service' under rule 2(l). The main point of dispute in the appeal is the determination of 'place of removal' of excisable goods. The assessee categorically stated that it transfers its goods to its warehouses from where it further transports them to the retail outlets or warehouses of its commission agents, from where the goods were sold. Hence, it was pleaded that place of removal in terms of section 4 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 should be retail outlet/warehouses of commission agents. The goods remain in its ownership till the time of sale from these retail outlets owned by it or up to the warehouses of commission agents, as the case may be. Freight also is paid by it up to the retail oulets/commission agents warehouses. [Para 7]

In the appeal, the revenue contended that the services availed at retail outlets cannot be considered for credit to the assessee. The revenue contended that these services used in retail outlets had no remote connection in the manufacture of ready-made garments. The Adjudicating Authority did not appreciate the legal scope of rule 2(l). He presumed that the services should be in or in relation to manufacture of ready made garments, whereas rule 2(l) clearly talks about services used by manufacturers, whether directly or indirectly in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and clearance of final products up to place of removal. A plain reading of the said statutory provision will indicate that the presumption of the Adjudication Authority is not sustainable. [Para 8]

Regarding the dispute relating to registration of the assessee as ISD, one is in agreement with the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals). On examination of provision of rule 2(m), the Commissioner (Appeals) clearly recorded that a manufacturer who wants to avail benefit of service tax should get registered himself as service provider and then he will be able to account for all the input services tax paid in the headquarters and distribute the same to various units. After examining the provisions of rule 7, the Commissioner (Appeals) concluded that as the manufacturer was having various retail outlets and office besides the factory for manufacture, in order to utilise the credit of input service got registered with the department as ISD. [Para 10]

Another dispute in the appeal is relating to credit availed by the assessee on the basis of debit notes, which were found to be ineligible documents. One notes that the assessee issued challans under rule 4A of the Service tax Rule, 1994 which contain all the required details. Even in case certain particulars were found missing in the relevant documents, one notes that substantial benefit of cenvat credit cannot be denied on this ground. In this connection, one refers to proviso to sub-rule (2) of rule 9 which provides for discretionary powers to the Adjudicating Authority regarding allowing the credit in such situation. As such, mention of wrong address of the service tax department on the documents is not a bar to avail the credit. [Para 12]

In view of the aforesaid, the order to the Commissioner (Appeals) deserved to be upheld.

Benefit of Notfn. of 113/74-CE is available as all conditions have been fulfilled. "......Darshan Corporation was acting only as an intermediary. It did not acquire ownership of the spent lye which continued to vest in Raipur Mfg. Co. Ltd. Spent lye was being routed through Darshan Corporation to the appellants for concentration and the concentrate, in turn, was being routed through Darshan Corporation to Raipur Mfg. Co. Ltd. The other condition was that the caustic soda recovered in another factory........was actually returned to the first factory......to which the spent caustic soda lye belonged.
