The Adjudicating Authority has denied cenvat credit alleging that the assessee has not obtained registration as Input Service Distributor (ISD). The assessee has submitted that it has obtained ISD registration in 2008. A copy of the ISD registration is also furnished. Therefore, the disallowance of credit for the reason that the assessee has not obtained ISD registration is unjustified and requires to be set aside. [Paras 9.1 and 9.2]

The Adjudicating Authority has further denied cenvat credit stating that the invoices were raised in the address of Bangalore and Pune office and the credit has been availed in Hosur Unit. The assessee has taken centralized registration incorporating Bangalore and Pune units. In such circumstances, the revenue cannot deny the credit availed on invoices raised in the address of Bangalore and Pune unit. [Para 9.3]

The Adjudicating Authority has also denied cenvat credit on the plea that clearing and forwarding agent services are availed by the assessee outside the factory/place of removal. The definition of input service does not state that the services have to be availed within the factory. The Board Circular No. 999/6/2015-CX, dated 28-1-2015 has also clarified this point. Therefore, the disallowance of credit is unjustified. [Para 9.4]

The assessee has availed credit on debit notes which has been disallowed on plea that these are not valid documents to avail credit. Debit notes can be considered to be valid documents for availing credit when there is no dispute with regard to the service tax paid and the services consumed. In the instant case, the department does not have a contention that the assessee has not discharged the service tax on the said services on which credit has been availed. Therefore, the disallowance of credit on this ground is unjustified. [Para 9.5]

The assessee has availed cenvat credit on photocopies of invoices. The assessee has submitted that the original invoices were misplaced and, therefore, it has availed credit on photocopies. This submission does not find favour. The assessee cannot avail credit on photocopies. These are not valid documents for availing credit. Further if such practice of availing credit on photocopies of invoices is allowed, then it will lead to false claims of credit made by assessees. The claim of assessee on this ground is disallowed. [Para 9.6]

The Adjudicating Authority has disallowed credit on various input services stating that these services are not availed in relation to the activity of manufacture. The assessee has submitted that these services include services like membership charges which are paid for taking membership in industrial association, exhibition stall charges, delegate fee, sales commission, etc. According to assessee, all these services have an integral connection with the manufacture of finished products. These services were consumed to carry out the activity of manufacture effectively and also to provide export of services/goods. The Adjudicating Authority has not made adequate discussion in this regard. The assessee has submitted that it would be able to establish the nexus of the services with the output services/manufacturing activity, if it is given a further chance. Therefore, this issue requires to be remanded to the Adjudicating Authority. [Para 9.7]

In the result, the impugned order is modified to the extent of allowing the credit in respect of the services availed except on photocopies of invoices. The issue with regard to credit disallowed alleging that the services do not have nexus with the manufacturing activity is remanded to the Adjudicating Authority leaving this issue open. [Para 10]

A perusal of the Rule 10 makes it very clear that if manufacturer of the final products shifts his factory to another site, the manufacturer shall be allowed to transfer the Cenvat credit lying unutilized in his accounts to such transferred factory. The said transfer is subject to the condition stipulated in rule 10(3) of the Rules, which provides that such transfer is permitted only if the stock of inputs as such or in process, or the capital goods is also transferred along with the factory or business premises to the new site, on which credit has been availed of are duly accounted for to the satisfaction of the Deputy Commissioner of Central Excise or as the case may be, the Assistant Commissioner of Central Excise. Therefore, once the aforesaid condition is satisfied, the assessee is entitled to the benefit of unutilized Cenvat credit at the transfer site. In the light of the factual findings recorded in the proceedings by the Authorities that the credit has been availed of duly accounted to the satisfaction of the authority, there is no case of double benefit as sought to be made out by the assessing authority. The Commissioner as well as the Tribunal are justified in setting aside the order and restoring the benefit to the assessee. [Para 4]

Capital goods must be received within factory with certain liberalizations - Liberalizations cannot be extended further :

-

Rule 2(a), Rules 3 and 4 (2)(a) provide that credit is to be taken on goods received in the factory of the manufacturer. The cases where deviation from rules has been approved by judicial forums are to be seen in the totality of the facts of the case. Where credit was allowed to be taken by the main manufacturer on capital goods used by the job- worker it is apparent that credit was so allowed because the capital goods were paid for by the main manufacturer and was used in the process of manufacturing his goods though in the factory of the job-worker. In some cases the equipment were used in premises appurtenant to the factory. In one case the goods were used in a wharf area which was belonging to some other entity. [Para 46]

-

Allowing credit in the present case requires going one step further. That is, it is to be ruled that it is not necessary that the manufacturer pays for the goods or that the goods are used in his factory but credit can be taken if there is a nexus between the capital goods on which credit is taken and the final products manufactured. Thus a further liberalization from rules and decisions given so far is involved.

-

This liberalization will bring in certain other consequences. As per the Rules credit can be denied only if the capital goods are exclusively used in the manufacture of exempted products. So if such power plant sells major part of the electricity generated, credit cannot be denied to the neighbour so long as part of such electricity is used by that neighbour. In this case such a situation did not exist and electricity generated was fully used by SISCOL. However such free bending of the Rules is not desirable because it can defeat some of the basic criteria in the Rules like the one that the person who purchased the goods cannot capitalize the duty amount and claim depreciation. The person who pays for the value of goods and duty may take credit and claim, depreciation and another person who uses the goods can claim the credit and the department may not know about the misuse because the books of account of the owner is not audited normally as in this case wherein the owner of the goods is not a Central Excise assessee. The owner may even refuse permission for such audit and the information can be extracted only through a procedure 'of issue of summons'. Further it can also lead to a situation where someone sets up a power plant supplies part of the electricity to a manufacturer who takes credit and sells the rest of the electricity to the public.

-

The next step can be, for illustration, a factory of SAIL can take credit of duty paid on equipment used by NTPC in a power plant for the reason that the power from NTPC is used in the factory of SAIL at least partially. Such benefits are not intended by the scheme. So the proposal for further liberalization of the conditions laid down in the rules was rejected. [Para 47]

It is not in dispute that the assessee while making purchases in question has paid the applicable central excise duty. In the instant case the assessee is the person who issues the invoice. Procedure to be observed by the manufacturer who wants to avail Modvat credit is provided by Rule 57G. The manufacturer who intends to take credit of the duty paid on inputs should file a declaration with the Assistant Commissioner having jurisdiction over his factory indicating the inputs intended to be used in the final product. Such a manufacture who has filed a declaration is allowed to take credit of the duty paid on the inputs received by him. Clause (2) states that no credit shall be taken unless the inputs are received in his factory or any other document as may be prescribed by the Central Government by notification in the Official Gazette in this behalf evidencing payment of duty on such inputs. By Notification No. 23/94, dated 20-5-1994, it was provided that this duplicate copy is the one to be used for taking credit under rule 57G and rule 57T. [Para 9]

Applying the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in various cases to the facts of the instant case, it was to be held that the amendment made in rule 57G of the Rules by insertion of sub-rule (11) vide Notification No. 7/99, dated 9-2-1999 relates to procedure for availing Modvat credit and does not effect any substantive right. [Para 35]

From the conjoint reading of rules 52A, 57G and the amendment made by Notification No. 7/99, dated 9-2-1999 by which sub-rule (11) was inserted in rule 57G, of filing of the documents for availing Modvat credit is only a procedural matter and the amendment made vide Notification No. 7/99, dated 9-2-1999 which inserted sub-rule (11) in rule 57G the position was made clear that Modvat credit should not be denied only on the ground that the documents referred to in sub-rule (2) does not strictly comply with the said rule but contains the details of payment dues, description of goods, assessable value, name and address of the factory or warehouse etc. This position has also been clarified by the Central Board of Excise and Customs by issuing a circular in exercise of its power under section 37B of the Act and made it applicable to all pending cases. [Para 36]

The submission of the revenue that the Notification No. 7/99, dated 9-2-1999 would come into effect on the date of its publication i.e., 9-2-1999 only, may be correct but the benefit of that Notification as directed by the Central Board of Excise and Customs has been extended to all the pending cases. The provision of sub-rule (2) is procedural for availing Modvat credit, the benefit of sub-rule (11) is available to the assessee. [Para 39]

No doubt, for availing credit of capital goods the conditionalities of rule 2(a) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 will require to be satisfied, inter alia, that goods should be used 'in the factory of manufacture of final products'. Strictly interpreting this provision would no doubt appear, at first sight, that in respect of machines which were installed not in the premises of the assessee but in an adjacent unit of 'H', cenvat credit would ordinarily not be available. However, it should also be kept in mind that the assessee stood merged with 'H' with effect from 1-4-2009 and as a result both these premises became a common entity from that date. From the facts on record, it appears that the assessee has availed credit under cover of invoice dated 1-11-2008, which was around five months prior to the date of the said merger. However, at the same time if the assessee had not taken the credit on or around 1-11-2008, but only on or after 1-4-2009, the availment of credit would not have excited any controversy. Therefore, the assessee's right to avail the credit on the said capital goods is very much available with effect from 1-4-2009 and the availment of credit prior to that date does not extinguish such eligibility. At the most, there will arise an interest liability for the period 1-11-2008 to 1-4-2009, i.e., for the period between the date when the credit was availed and the effective date of merger of two entities. This being so, the availment of cenvat credit by the assessee cannot be disturbed. However, the assessee will require to discharge interest liability at applicable rates for the period 1-11-2008 to 1-4-2009. [Para 5.2]

Rule 4(3) - Capital goods were acquired under loan/lease agreement : Rule 4 (3) of CCR 2004 provides that the Cenvat credit in respect of the capital goods shall be allowed to a manufacturer, even if the capital goods are acquired by him on lease, hire purchase or loan agreement, from a financing company. Rule 4(3) has a wide amplitude in so far as it would cover the cases of various types of financial arrangements for availing credit on the capital goods. It is contemplated that under this sub-rule (3) of rule 4 would cover the cases where the ownership of the capital goods does not vest in the manufacturer until the loan is repaid. There must be an agreement for the purpose of acquiring the capital goods. Under meaning part, only services used after input stage or used in manufacture of excisable goods are input services :

•

A combined reading of rule 2(l) (defining input service) and 2(h) (defining final product) shows that input service means any service used by the manufacturer whether directly or indirectly in or in relation to manufacture of excisable goods manufactured or produced from input or said service. That means that only those services will qualify for the input services which are used after input stage or those input services are used in the manufactured or produced from input or said service. That means that only those services will qualify for the input services which are used after input stage or those input services are used in the manufacture of excisable goods by the manufacturer. [Para 8]

Under inclusive part, in case of input, only procurement services and inward transportation are eligible for credit :

•

Further, the procurement of input and inward transportation of input or capital goods are specifically mentioned in the inclusive definition of the input services and will, therefore, qualify for the eligible input services for the Cenvat Credit. The legislature restricted the benefit of the Cenvat Credit for input services used in respect of inputs for these two categories only. Whenever legislature wanted to give the credit of service tax paid on input services in relation to inputs, it has clearly stated so in the rule. [Para 9]

Rule 4(7) must be read with definition of input service under rule 2(l) :

•

Though under rule 4(7) there is no such restriction about the use of input services outside the factory but rule 4(7) is to be read with definition of input service under rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit rules. [Para 10]

Services in relation to storage of input outside factory are not input services :

•

Ammonia was imported by the assessee. After goods were cleared from the port and the goods were delivered to the assessee, the procurement of the input was over after taking such delivery of the goods. Thereafter assessee was eligible for credit of service tax paid on inward transportation of the inputs as per definitions of the input service. [Para 11]

•

However, in this case, the services were used in installation of storage tanks outside the factory. Inclusive definition of input service also includes input services used in relation to storage up to the place or removal. Storage up to place of removal will include the storage of final products and not storage of inputs because whenever legislature wanted to give the benefit, in respect of inputs it has done so by specifically mentioning as procurement of inputs and inward transportation of the inputs. Therefore, input services used in relation to storage of inputs outside the factory will not be eligible for the credit. [Para 12]

The goods, on which Modvat credit had been taken by the appellants irregularly, were consigned to the job worker. In other words the goods were not received by the appellant but by his job worker. The duplicate copy of the gate pass which had accompanied the goods contain the name of the job worker. However, the original which was sent to the appellants contains the name of the appellant, which was written after scoring out the original consignee i.e., the job worker. The adjudicating authority had given a very detailed finding to indicate that there had been manipulation of the consignee’s name in the original copy of the gate pass. But for that manipulation, the appellant would not have got the Modvat credit. In fact actual consignee was only the job worker. Further the adjudicating authority had found that there was no endorsement in name of appellant as rightly found in the duplicate copy of the gate pass in question. The adjudicating authority had observed that Modvat credit can be taken only when both the material as well as duty paying documents are received by the consignee as indicated in the gate pass. In this case, no fraudulent motive was found which could be attributed to the appellant. The appellant along with consigner have taken recourse to certain devices of expediency to avoid irksome procedures. However, when the material had not been received by the appellant and only by some job worker, taking credit on the goods received by the job worker by changing the name of the consignee in the original copy of the gate pass, was serious matter and such scant regard to rules could not be ignored. The appellant was not entitled for the Modvat credit. [Para 6]

It is not disputed that the goods in respect of which Cenvat credit, in question, has been taken are covered by the Chapters 84, 85 & 90 of the Central Excise Tariff or are the item specifically mentioned in rule 2(a) and, accordingly, are covered by the definition of the 'capital goods' as given in rule 2(a) of Cenvat Credit Rules. [Para 5]

In term of the definition of 'capital goods' as given in rule 2(a) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, the capital goods are those goods which are specified in this rule and which (except for office equipment or appliance) are used in the factory of the manufacturer of the final products or for providing of output service. Thus, any item which is covered by the list of the items mentioned in rule 2(a) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, except for office equipment or office appliances, and is used in any manner in the factory of the manufacturer of the final products, would be covered by the definition of the capital goods and, accordingly, would be eligible for Cenvat credit.

There is absolutely no requirement that the capital goods at the time of receipt must be owned by manufacturer or that the same would cease to be capital goods, if they are installed in the factory and become fixed to earth. In fact, most of the capital goods the machinery, equipment or instruments covered by Chapters 84, 85 and 90, pipes and tubes, pollution control equipment refractories, and storage tanks are required to be installed and after installation, the same put together constitute a manufacturing plant, which is fixed to earth structure. Just because after being installed in the factory, the capital goods put together become a plant which is fixed to earth structure, the Cenvat credit cannot be denied on the basis that the plant which is fixed to earth structure, is not excisable. This preposition of the Department is, in fact absurd, as there is no such condition in rule 2(a) for capital goods.

For capital goods Cenvat credit, the items must be among those mentioned in this rule and should have been used in the factory of the manufacturer and how the items are not used relevant. The words used in rule 2(a) are "used in the factory of manufacturer of the final product" not "used in the manufacture of final product". Therefore, once any item received in the factory is 'capital goods' in terms of Rule 2(a) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, and is used in the factory, the manufacturer would be entitled to Cenvat credit of excise duty paid in respect of the same.

If the logic of the Commissioner in the impugned order is accepted, no capital goods Cenvat credit can be allowed in respect of any item of capital goods enumerated in rule 2(a) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, as all the items - various items of machinery covered under Chapters 84, 85 and 90 of the Tariff, pipes and tubes, tanks, pollution control equipments refractories, etc., have to be installed in the factory before being put to use and after installation, the same would become fixed to earth plant. Reading the impugned order gives an impression that the same has been passed without any application of mind.

Therefore, prima facie, impugned order is not sustainable and as such the assessee have strong prima facie case in their favour. The requirement of pre-deposit of the Cenvat credit demand, interest thereon and penalty is, therefore, waived for hearing of the appeal and recovery thereof is stayed till the disposal of the appeal. [Para 6]

A perusal of the definition of 'input' in rule 2(k) clearly shows that the input means and includes accessories of the final product cleared along with the final product. [Para 6]

The Tribunal observed in the case of Jayshree Industries v. Collector of Central Excise 1992 taxmann.com 503 (CEGAT - Mum.), that in case of items supplied along with certain gadget, the item would qualify for credit in the light of the Supreme Court's judgment in the case of Collector of Central Excise v. Jay Engineering Works Ltd. 1989 taxmann.com 1077, provided the answers to the following questions are in the affirmative:

(a)

Whether the items are essentially required for the operational needs of the gadget;

(b)

Whether they are compulsorily supplied with the gadget at the point of delivery through the factory gate;

(c)

Whether its value is included in the value of the gadget at the factory gate. [Para 6.4]

All the conditions are fulfilled in this case inasmuch as barbed wire is essentially required for smooth operation of the transmission tower and secondly, as per the terms and conditions of the agreements, it is necessary for the company to supply barbed wire along with transmission tower and thirdly, the description list of the goods sold is attached with the invoice copy, which clearly shows that the value of the barbed wire has been included in the assessable value and the duty has been paid on the whole amount. Since all the conditions are fulfilled, the assessee is entitled to the credit of duty paid on barbed wire as held in the case of Ultrapack v. CCE 2005 (192) ELT 540 (Trib-Bang). [Para 7]

Further, the respondent supplied barbed wire to all its customers and as per the terms and conditions of the agreement, the price of barbed wire is included in the assessable value. The respondent placed reliance in the case of Coca-Cola India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 22 STT 130 (Bang.) wherein the Bombay High Court has held that burden of service tax may be borne by the ultimate consumer and not by any intermediary and if the value of the input or input service has been included in the assessable value, then credit should not be denied. [Para 8]

Therefore, keeping in view all the facts and circumstances and the law cited, the appeal of the revenue is liable to be dismissed. [Para 9]

Market stocks to be deemed duty paid: Excisable goods purchased from the open market presumed to be duty paid because as per Excise rules, the goods cannot be cleared from the factory gate unless excise duty is paid thereon. "The petitioners have purchased the base dyes from the open market and the petitioners are perfectly justified in claiming that excise duty has been paid on the goods available in the market. Rule 9(1) of the Central Excise Rules, inter-alia, prescribes that the goods shall not be cleared from the factory gate until the excise duty leviable thereon has been paid". (Rule 9(1) of Central Excise Rules, 1944).

2. Proof of payment of duty--Invoices in support of the purchases made from the open market considered sufficient proof for the excise duty paid in respect of excisable goods purchased. "Apart from the presumption which arises in favour of the petitioners, the petitioners have produced before the Department documents to substantiate their claim that duty was paid on the base dyes purchased from the open market. The petitioners have produced invoices in respect of the purchase and that was the requirement prescribed by the Collector of Central Excise by publication of trade notice dated November 25, 1961." (Exemption Notification 180/61 C.E.)

Benefit of Notification 201/79-CE dated 4.6.1979 would be available even if the consumption of raw materials and the manufacture of final products are in different factories, as long as the manufacturer is the same. "...the benefit of the notification would be available even if the manufacture of the final product is in a factory, different from the factory in which the raw materials are consumed so long as both belong to the same manufacturer...."

2. Raw materials, not used directly in the manufacture of the final goods but used in the manufacture of intermediate goods are entitled to the benefit of the notification, as long as the consumption of raw materials and production of the final product are in the same factory. "...so long as the consumption of the raw material and the production of the final product was in the same factory, it would not be in order to deny credit of duty in respect of raw material on the ground that it was not directly used in the manufacture of the final goods, but in the manufacture of intermediate goods, which may be exempt from duty."

ruling.text:
Per Gowri Shankar :

The notice issued to the respondent to these appeals proposed denial of modvat credit on the ground that it had been taken on invoices which was issued to the assessee's head office, and had been endorsed by it from that head office to its factory at Sion. The Assistant Collector confirmed the proposal in the notice and held that credit was not available. On appeal by the assessee from this order, the Commissioner (Appeals) noted that the head office could not avail modvat credit, not having the manufacturing facility. It also could not endorse the gate passes to its own factory, not being a dealer. Hence the very purpose of modvat credit will be denied. He therefore held that it could not be denied. This is appealed by the department.

2. The ground in the department's appeal is the same as was in the show cause notice, that the invoices were addressed, not to factory but to head office of the assessee and the assessee could not endorse these documents to its own factory.

3. I agree that it is meaningless for an assessee to endorse documents to itself. Endorsement of a document is resorted to signify that title to the goods mentioned in that document is passed on. There can be no question of one person passing the title to another person. Endorsement on these invoices therefore has no legal significance.

4. Representative of the respondent cites before me the decision of the Tribunal in Larsen Toubro Ltd. Vs. CCE 1994 (3) RLT 215 (CEGAT)=1994 (72) ELT 948. The question for decision by the Tribunal was whether credit should be taken by Larsen Toubro and the duty shown to have been paid on the bill of entry, which showed as the importer's address at the company's head office. The credit was actually taken by factory elsewhere. The Tribunal noted that the import of the goods was dealt with by the head office and it was natural that the head office should figure on the bill of entry.

5. In my view, the same consideration would apply to the facts before me. The representative of the respondents explains that the purchase of the goods for use in the two factories of the respondent, then situated at Sion and Mankhurd was processed at the head office at Tardeo and the goods therefore first came to the head office and were thereafter sent to the factory. In a case where the invoices are addressed to the head office, which cannot utilise the credit that office merely passes the goods on to the factory, for being utilised there, I do not see there is any contravention of the rules. In these circumstances, I do not find any ground for interference.

6. Appeal dismissed.

Per Justice Shri U.L. Bhat, President :

Appellant, M/s. Heinz India Pvt. Ltd., Bombay with Head Office at Bombay has a factory in Aligarh for manufacture of Complan and other nutrients. Appellant was availing Modvat credit on certain inputs. The dispute arose on scrutiny of monthly RT 12 Return for October 94. Various items of Modvat were objected to. After hearing the appellant, the objection regarding Rs. 53,309 being the duty element of the input covered by Invoice Nos. 1062, 1075 and 1081 issued by the manufacturer was confirmed and corresponding amount of duty demanded, though other objections were dropped. Confirmation of the demand by the Assistant Commissioner having been confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals), the present appeal has been filed.

2. Copies of three invoices in question are before me. They were issued by the manufacturer of inputs to M/s. Heinz India Pvt. Ltd. Bombay. In the column against destination, Aligarh is seen mentioned. The case of the appellant that order for the input was placed by the Head Office at Bombay for use at the factory in Aligarh is not denied by the Department. The lower authorities objected to the admissibility of Modvat credit on the ground that the invoices were endorsed by the Head Office in favour of factory. Being governed by the Central Excise Rules, 1944, central excise licence was taken in respect of the Aligarh factory in the name of Heinz India Pvt. Ltd. Aligarh. This does not mean that there are two different companies called M/s. Heinz India Pvt. Ltd. and M/s. Heinz India Pvt. Ltd. Aligarh. There is only one entity M/s. Heinz India Pvt. Ltd. Bombay with head office at Bombay and this company has factory at several places including the factory at Aligarh. It is evident from the invoices that order was placed by the Head Office at Bombay for supply to and use in the Aligarh unit. That being so, it cannot be said that there is endorsement on the invoices by one entity to another. The expression "endorsement" has been used only loosely in this context. This is not a case of transfer of inputs by one legal entity to a third party. This is a case where supply had been arranged by Head Office for the use of the factory.

There can be no legal objection to the availment of Modvat credit on the basis of invoices issued in the name of the company at its registered Head Office, though used in the factory at Aligarh. This view is supported by the decisions of the Tribunal in the cases of Larsen Toubro Ltd. 1994 (72) ELT 948 (T), Bansal Containers (P) Ltd. 1994 (3) RLT 215(CEGAT) = 1996 (83) ELT 425 (T), Siyaram Platex (P) Ltd. 1994 (73) ELT 915 (T) and Snow Cem India Ltd. 1994 (4) RLT 119 (CEGAT) = 1997 (96) ELT 627 (T).

3. In this view, the appellant was entitled to avail Modvat credit on the basis of the invoices referred to above.

4. The impugned orders are set aside and the appeal is allowed.

1. Being aggrieved with that part of the order of Commissioner (Appeals) vide which he has held in favour of the assessee, Revenue has filed the present appeal. I have heard Shri R.S. Srova, learned JDR appearing for the Revenue and Shri Jitu Motwani, learned advocate appearing for the respondent.

2. For better appreciation I reproduce the relevant para of the impugned order of Commissioner (Appeals) :-

"In respect of invoices issued in the name of head office, I find that the Board in para 4 of the Circular No. 211/45/96-CX., dated 14-5-1996 has decided that credit should not be denied where the invoice is in the name of the Registered office/head office provided that the same is endorsed by the Registered office/head office in favour of the appellants. Further the Hon’ble Tribunal has also allowed credit on Bill of Entry issued in the name of head office in the case of Eveready Inds. India Ltd. - 2007 (219) ELT 333 and Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. - 2008 (228) ELT 224. In this case also the impugned invoices have been endorsed by the head office in the name of the appellants and therefore following the ratio of above decisions, I hold the credit taken on invoices in the name of the head office and subsequently endorsed by the head office as correct. I also agree with the submissions of the appellants’ that the appellants being the only manufacturing unit, the head office could not fall in the category of input service distributor. Accordingly I set aside the impugned order to the extent of demand of duty on credit availed on invoices issued in the name of head office along with interest and the equivalent penalty."

3. The revenue in their grounds has raised only technical grounds that the documents were not in the name of the assessee’s factory situated at Silvassa but the same were issued in the name of the head office of the assessee situated at Mumbai. However, I find that there is otherwise no dispute about the input services received by the assessee. The substantive benefit cannot be denied on the procedural grounds. I do not find any infirmity in the view adopted by Commissioner (Appeals) and accordingly reject the appeal filed by the revenue.

entries made for the same cannot be accepted as reflecting the actual position. As regards the Board's circular he submits that it is admitted fact that their invoice in question has not been endorsed by their head office in [sic] their factory and as such the conditions of the circular are not satisfied. If the goods were transported by a taxi they could have mentioned the taxi number etc. in the invoice itself. In the circumstances he submits that there is no case made up for grant of stay to the applicants. 4. I have considered the submissions made from both the sides. The dispute is limited to only one invoice in question. The Modvat credit has been disallowed by not accepting the said invoice on the ground that the same shows the address of their head office instead of the factory and there is no endorsement by the head office. Further the department has also doubted the actual receipt of the goods in their factory premises because the applicants have failed to produce any documents showing the actual receipt and [since] the transporters' column in the invoices [having been]left blank. However, I find that the applicants have explained before the Assistant Commissioner, vide their reply to the show cause notice, that the input in question was transported personally by one of their employees in asmuchas the same was only 115.3 K.gs. of stainless steel wire for which a regular transport was not required. They had also produced the good's receipt report. I have seen the photocopy of the report produced on record. The same is carrying a printed serial number and is duly signed by their store-keeper. I also find that the cardex maintained by them reflects the receipt of the above material. Further, there is no dispute or doubt about the fact that the said material was duly entered in their RG-23A Part-I record. Having entered the goods in their Modvatable raw material register, the applicants could not have escaped to show the utilisation of the same in the manufacture of final product and to clear the final product on payment of duty. It is not a case where the applicants have availed the Modvat credit in their Part-II register without the corresponding receipt of raw material in their part I register. As such I find that the failure on the part of the applicants to show the transporters' mode in the invoice, to take the goods first to their head office, got the invoice endorsed in their factory and then transport the goods to their factory are no reasons for denial of benefit of Modvat credit to them. Endorsement of the invoice by their own head office is a rectifiable defect in any case. Taking all these issues into consideration I hold that the applicants had made out a prima facie case for granting them unconditional stay. I Order accordingly.

5. As only above points are involved in the appeal, I take up the appeal itself and allow the same. The impugned order is set aside.

1. Heard both sides. It is claimed that the applicant has more than one manufacturing unit. Their registered/Corporate office is at Village - Narsinghpur, Gurgaon and another unit is at Plot No. 48, Sector 3, IMT Manesar, Gurgaon. Applicant claimed that they have received consignment in the name of the applicant's company indicating the address of the corporate office where they also had another unit. He claimed that the goods have been directly received in the' factory of the applicant at IMT Manesar, Gurgaon and for payment purposes, the bills have been addressed in the name of the corporate office.

2. After hearing both the sides, I find that there is no dispute about the duty paid character of the inputs, their receipt in the factory premises and their utilisation in the manufacture of final products. Merely because the corporate office address is given in the invoice, cannot be made the reason to deny the credit otherwise available to the assessee. I find no justifiable reason to uphold the impugned order of the authorities below. The same are accordingly set aside and appeals allowed with consequential relief to them.

Per T. Anjaneyulu : This appeal is filed by M/s. Cadila Pharmaceuticals Ltd., 342, Nanikadi, Taluka Kadi, Dist. Mehsana, Gujarat, against an Order-in-Appeal dated 21.08.2003 passed by the Commissioner of Central Excise (Appeals), Ahmedabad.

2. The facts of the case in brief are that the appellants had filed a refund claim of Rs. 2,15,951/- on the ground that they have received raw materials from M/s. Cadila Pharmaceuticals Ltd., Ankleshwar, and M/s. Universal Capsules Ltd., Mumbai, under duty paying documents. The supplier had wrongly mentioned the name of the consignee as Dholka instead of Kadi. As per the direction of the Excise authorities, they had debited Rs. 2,15,951/- vide RG 23A Pt. II Entry No. 840 dated 15.10.2001, being the credit of duty wrongly availed on invalid documents. The adjudicating authority rejected the refund claim, which has been confirmed in the Order-in-Appeal.

3. The ld. counsel for the appellants contends that the inputs are actually received and consumed in their Kadi factory and the Certificate is enclosed as per page No. 36. It is condonable procedure by mistake Gate Pass is to said to have prepared at Dholka address. It is the submission that all the three factories belong to one owner. Consignee is not other than the supplier of the goods. In this context, he relied upon a decision reported in 2001 (135) ELT 405 (Tri.-Kolkata) in the case of M/s. Chrome Chemical Industries Vs. Commissioner of Central Excise, Calcutta-IV. It is observed that invoice issued in the name of the head office of the manufacturing unit and not the factory or its non-endorsement by the head office as stipulated in the C.B.E. C. Circular No. 211/45/96-CX. dated 14.05.96 [reported in 1996 (14) RLT M83] are only condonable procedural lapses as long as it is not in dispute that the inputs were actually received and utilized in the manufacture of final products and there is no allegation of any mala fides.

4. The ld. Departmental Representative pointed out the observations made by the ld. Commissioner of Appeals in para 4.1 of the impugned order, which is extracted hereunder:

"4.1 I have gone through the facts of the case and submissions of the appellant and find that the adjudicating authority has rejected the appellant's refund claim observing that in said invoices, the name of the consignee is shown as M/s. Cadila Pharmaceuticals Ltd., Dholka, by the consignor, M/s. Cadila Pharmaceuticals Ltd., Ankleshwar and M/s. Universal Capsules Ltd., Mumbai. Since the consignee of the receiptant goods are at Dholka, credit at Kadi unit is not admissible as the same are invalid documents from them. In this regard, I find that the Hon'ble CEGAT, Mumbai, in the case of M/s. Goyal Electro Steel Castings reported at 2003 (57) RLT 468 held that, "Modvat Credit - Rule 57G of C.Ex. Rules, 1944 - Gate pass - not in the name of appellants and also not endorsed in their favour - credit not admissible though supplier has confirmed receipt of inputs by the appellants - appeal rejected".

5. But the facts on hand are distinguishable from the case law relied upon by the Commissioner (Appeals). In the instant case, the goods are received at Kadi and they are actually consumed, but mistakenly the Gate Passes were prepared at the factory address of Dholka and that it is relevant to note that all the three units belong to one manufacturer. Therefore, I find the impugned order is erroneous, in the result, the appeal is allowed.

Per Archana Wadhwa :

Modvat credit of Rs. 2,560/- has been disallowed and penalty of Rs. 500/- has been imposed on the applicant/appellant by the authorities below. The reason for disallowing the credit on the stainless steel wire received by the applicant from M/s. Hindustan Wire Ltd. under cover of invoice No. A-1158 dt. 24.9.94 is that the same mentions the address of the head office of the applicant company instead of mentioning the factory address. It has also been alleged that the column meant for transporter in the invoice has been left blank. The said invoice has not been further endorsed by the applicants' head office in favour of their factory, thus showing the receipt of the inputs in the factory premises.

2. Shri B.N. Chattopadhyay, Ld. Consultant appearing for the applicant/appellant submits that the invoice in question shows the address of the head office because the Order was placed from their head office and the goods were transported from the input manufacturer's premises to their factory premises directly by one of their employee in a taxi and that is the reason that the transporters mode has not been reflected in the invoice. He submits that to meet the department's allegations that the inputs have not been received by them in their factory, they had produced serial numbered goods receipt report and cardex maintained by them in the ordinary course of their business. These documents have been discarded by the adjudicating authority as well as by the first appellate authority on the basis of assumptions and presumptions and by observing that these are private documents of the Company. He further submits that the goods were duly entered in their RG-23A part-I register on the same day i.e. on the day of receipt of the goods in their factory. He submits that there is absolutely no ground for doubting these documents and giving the findings that the goods were not received in their factory. He submits that the applicants are paying revenue to the tune of six crores from their P.L.A. apart from paying duty from their RG-23A Part-II account. As such it is not expected from the appellant to manipulate the documents for a small amount of Rs. 2,560/-. He also makes reference to the Board's circular No. 211/45/96-CX dt. 14.5.96, wherein the invoices raised in the name of registered Office/head office have [been] recognised as proper invoices for the purposes of availing of Modvat credit in the factory premises. He also submits that the non-endorsement of the invoice issued in the name of head office by the head office is only a rectifiable defect on the basis of which Modvat credit should not be disallowed to them. He explains that this endorsement could not be made because the inputs were directly transported from the manufacturer's factory to the appellants' factory without ever going to the head office. In the circumstances he prays for allowing the stay petition unconditionally.

3. Countering the arguments Shri T.P. Kumar, Ld. SDR submits that the Assistant Commissioner had allowed the Modvat in respect of two other invoices where the applicants had produced the evidence of transportation of the inputs to their factory. However, in respect of the invoice in question, the applicant failed to substantiate their submission of transportation of the goods to their factory premises directly. As regards other co-lateral evidences produced by them he submitted that these are in the nature of private records maintained by the applicant themselves and entries made for the same cannot be accepted as reflecting the actual position. As regards the Board's circular he submits that it is admitted fact that their invoice in question has not been endorsed by their head office in [sic] their factory and as such the conditions of the circular are not satisfied. If the goods were transported by a taxi they could have mentioned the taxi number etc. in the invoice itself. In the circumstances he submits that there is no case made up for grant of stay to the applicants.

Per S.L. Peeran : This appeal arises from Order-in-Appeal No. 86/2003-CE, dated 31.1.2003 by which the Modvat Credit has been denied on invoices which has been endorsed in favour of the Head Office. The department has taken a stand that there is no endorsement in favour of factory for the purpose of availing of Modvat Credit by the factory. It is, therefore, a demand of Rs. 39,530/- under Rule 57I of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 has been invoked. The appellant has relied on large number of judgments, which are noted in para 3 (e), of Commissioner (Appeals) order, which are reproduced herein below:-

(a)

Amai Rasayan Ltd. Vs. CCE - 1993 (67) ELT 133 (T)

(b)

Eicher Tractors Vs. CCE - 1996 (87) ELT 252 (T)

(c)

Bansal Containers P. Ltd. Vs. CCE - 1996 (83) ELT 425 (T)

(d)

Subros Ltd. Vs. Commr. - 1997 (96) ELT 602 (T)

(e)

Chamundi Rolling Mills Vs. Commr. - 1994 (3) RLT 855 (CEGAT-B)=1996 (81) ELT 563 (T)

(f)

Shree Acids Chemicals Vs. Commr. - 1997 (95) ELT 114 (T)

(g)

Commr. Vs. Jay Enn Castings Ltd. - 1997 (22) RLT 210 (CEGAT)=1997 (95) ELT 82 (T)

(h)

Ramgarh Chini Mills Vs. Commr. of Central Excise, Kanpur - 1998 (26) RLT 169 (CEGAT)=1998 (103) ELT 65 (T).

Despite these citations the Commissioner (Appeals) did not accept the plea and proceeded to decide on the basis of Trade Notice No. 57/96, dated 4.6.96 to deny the taking of Modvat Credit.

2. Ld. Advocate Shri Hasan Khan submit that the ratio of the judgments rendered in the case of Ramgarh Chini Mills Vs. Commissioner of Central Excise, Kanpur reported in 1998 (26) RLT 169 (CEGAT)=1998 (103) ELT 65 (Tri.) and Chrome Chemical Industries Vs. Commissioner of Central Excise, Calcutta-IV reported in 2001 (135) ELT 405 (Tri. Kolkata) directly applies to the facts of the case and all the citations already noted. He submits that the invoices being in the Head Office name, it has been held to be condonable procedural lapse. As, it is not the dispute that the inputs were actually received and utilised in the manufacture of final products and there is no allegation of malafide. He submits that the appeal is required to be allowed in the light of these judgments.

3. Ld. JDR Shri C. Mani, reiterates the view expressed by the authorities. In so far as the citations are concerned, he leaves the matter to the discretion of the Bench.

4. On a careful consideration, I notice that there is no allegation of any malafides against the appellants in misusing the inputs. The inputs has been received and utilised in the manufacture of the final product. The only issue was that the invoices stood in the name of the Head Office and not in the name of the factory. The Tribunal in the case of Chrome Chemical Industries Vs. Commissioner of Central Excise, Calcutta-IV have dealt in identical situation, wherein, it was found that the invoices was in the name of Head Office and it was found that it is a condonable lapse. As there is no allegation of malafides and that the inputs were actually received and utilised in the manufacture of the final products, this Bench is bound by the ratio of the co-ordinate Benches. Therefore, respectfully following the ratio of the above noted judgments, the impugned order is set aside and the appeal is allowed with consequential relief, if any.

Per S.S. Kang : Appellants filed this appeal against the order-in-appeal passed by the Commissioner (Appeals).

2. In this case, the benefit of MODVAT Credit was denied to the appellants on the ground that there was cutting and tempering in the name and address of the appellants in the invoices.

3. Heard both sides.

4. The contention of the appellants is that they are engaged in the manufacture of fungicides and pesticides and their head office is at Srinagar and the manufacturing unit is at Jammu. Appellants purchased the inputs from various manufacturers and the invoices were issued in the name of their head office and when the matter was brought to the notice of their manufacturer, the manufacturer corrected the address in their invoice. Appellants produced certain certificate from the manufacturers where they confirmed that the name and address in the invoice was changed by them. In these circumstances, the impugned order is not sustainable on the ground that there was cutting and manipulation in the invoice.

5. Even on merit, when the invoice is in the name of the registered office and the goods were used in the factory, which was at different address, the manufacturer is entitled for the benefit of credit. The Tribunal in the case of Bihar Tubes Ltd. vs. CCE., Noida reported in 2003 (54) RLT 419 allowed the credit where the invoice was in the name of registered head office. In view of above discussion, the impugned order is set aside and the appeal is allowed.

1. Cenvat credit of service tax paid has been denied to the factory on the ground that the invoice issued by the service provider is in the name of the registered office and not in the name of the factory. According to the Revenue, the registered office should have taken registration as in input service distributor and should have issued separate invoices to facilitate availment of cenvat credit by the factory.

2. Heard both the sides. Since the issue involved is short and both the sides were heard in detail and both the sides have no objection to decide the issue itself finally, the requirement of pre-deposit is waived and the appeal itself is taken up for final decision.

3. The learned counsel on behalf of the appellant submitted that the appellant has only one factory and therefore the question of distribution does not arise. He also submitted that it is not the case of the department, that service has not been received. He relies upon the decisions of the Tribunal in the case of CC&CE v. DNH Spinners [2010] 25 STT 295 (Ahd.-CESTAT) and Modern Petrofils v. CCE [2010] 29 STT 111 (Ahd.-CESTAT) to submit that just because credit has been availed on the basis of invoice not containing name of the factory, credit cannot be disallowed and when there is no dispute on receipt of services by the factory, credit cannot be denied on the technical ground that document is in the name of head office/registered office situated elsewhere. The learned SDR would rely upon the decisions of the Tribunal in the case of Khaitan Electricals Ltd. v. CCE [2011] 32 STT 234/12 taxmann.com 338 (Kol.-CESTAT), Philips Electronics (India) Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 22 STT 332 (Ahd.-CESTAT) and Vimal Enterprise v. Union of India 2006 (195) ELT 267 (Guj.). The learned SDR with the support of above decisions sought to submit that according to these decisions, registration of input service distributor is a must and if the input service distributor is not registered credit is not admissible.

4. After considering the submissions and records I find that the decisions relied upon by the learned SDR are not applicable to the facts of the case. In all these cases a view was taken that the input service distributor is required to be registered and the effective date of such registration was also required to be considered as held in the case of Philips Electronics (India) Ltd. (supra). In all those cases there was no dispute that input distributor was required to be registered. The dispute had arisen as to the effective date of registration, exercise of discretionary powers for allowing credit deficiencies in documents issued by the input service distributor etc. In the present case the dispute is totally different. The dispute is not as to whether the document issued by the distributor is a valid document or not. But the issue is whether the registered office of the appellant is required to be registered at all when they have only one factory and when the credit has been taken by the factory on the basis of invoices issued by service providers. There is also no indication or no allegation in the show cause notices or in the findings that appellant's factory did not receive the service. In the decisions cited by the learned counsel, a view was taken that credit cannot be denied and the invoice is in the name of registered office/head office provided the same is endorsed. For this purpose the circular issued by the Board on 14-5-1996 was taken note of in the case of DNH Spinners (supra). 6. We have heard rival submissions. On careful consideration of the submissions made, we agree with the contention of the Id. Counsel of the appellant that the three issues present themselves for decision in this case.

7. The first issue is whether modvat credit could be taken on the strength of the Gate Passes issued prior to 1.4.94 and endorsed subsequently upto 30.6.94. Following the ratio of the decision of the Tribunal in the case, we hold that modvat credit will be admissible on the strength of Gate Passes issued prior to 1.4.94 and endorsed subsequently upto 30.6.94.

8. On the second issue i.e., taking of modvat credit on the strength of invoices issued by depots/distributors. We find that Notfn. No. 15/94-CE permits taking of modvat credit on the strength of invoices issued by the factory or its depots or its distributors. This notification was issued on 31.3.94. Modvat credit on the strength of invoices has been taken before 12.5.94. We have also seen the clarification given by the C.B.E.C. We have also perused the case law in the case of M/s. Fine Core Cables (P) Ltd. cited above. Following the ratio of the decision of this Tribunal in the case of Fine Core Cables (P) Ltd. and the clarification of the C.B.E.C, we hold that modvat credit could be taken on the strength of invoices issued by depots of the manufacturer and his distributors before 12.5.94.

9. The third issue is about taking of modvat credit on the strength of documents received at the factory Head office address. We note that the issue is covered by the decision of this Tribunal in the case of M/s. Ramgarh Chini Mills cited above. Following the ratio of the decision, we hold that modvat credit will be admissible to the appellants.

1. The appellant M/s. Industrial Electronics is a unit of LML Ltd., situated at Gurgaon having their Head Office functioning at Kanpur. In November 1996, the Head Office imported a consignment of 55 packages of raw materials which were according to the appellants, sent straight to their Gurgaon Factory although the concerned Bill of Entry travelled to their Head Office at Kanpur. Their contention is that they also have a factory manufacturing scooters in Kanpur and which is a part of the Head Office itself in which mistakenly modvat credit was taken on 23.3.1997. However, realizing the mistake on 25.3.1997, the credit was reversed and fresh invoices were issued under Rule 52A on the basis of the packing list attached with the Bill of Entry and the same were dispatched to Gurgaon Factory. In view of the above although according to the applicants the goods had physically reached Gurgaon factory in November 1996, the credit was taken by them only in March 1997.

2. The learned counsel for the applicants has argued that since the goods had in any case reached the destination, their not following the procedure should not make any difference and they are, therefore, eligible for the benefit of modvat credit. In this connection, he also refers to the Central Board of Excise and Customs Circular dated 29.2.1996 which has laid down two conditions in similar circumstances: (i) that the entire consignment covered by the said Bill of Entry is to be received in the factory in original packed condition and (ii) the triplicate copy of the Bill of Entry/duplicate copy of the Bill of Entry generated on EDI system is endorsed by the registered office/Head Office to the effect that the consignment covered by Bill of Entry are delivered to the manufacturing unit for availing credit. He admits that while they have fulfilled the condition (i), he admits that condition (ii) has not been fulfilled, which he terms as technical lapse . He also admits that there is a short-coming, since as instead of endorsing the same Bill of Entry, the applicants had issued fresh invoices. However, the credit was taken well within the time stipulated under the modvat regulations.

3. The Revenue s only objection is that the goods never moved alongwith 16 invoices issued by the Head Office and as such, the said documents cannot be held to be valid documents for the purpose of Cenvat credit.

4. Apart from the fact that the goods were received by the appellant directly whereas the credit was wrongly availed by the Head office and the said mistake was subsequently rectified by issuance of reverse invoices on the basis of which the present appellant took credit, I also note that the credit was availed in March 97 and was duly reflected by the appellant in their Return filed for the said period. The Show Cause Notice stands issued on 04.02.2002 i.e. beyond the normal period of limitation. The appellant has also filed the reconciliation statement on record and the Revenue is not disputing the fact of the goods having reached the Gurgaon Factory directly. In such a scenario, the non-following of the procedure by itself cannot be held to be a ground for denial of credit. Accordingly, I set aside the impugned order on merits as also on limitation and allow the appeal with consequential relief to the appellant.

Per Gowri Shankar : The question for consideration in this appeal is the eligibility to modvat credit by the appellant of the duty that is shown to have been paid on the invoices issued by the dealers of the inputs. After hearing both sides, we deal with each of the grounds on which modvat has been denied, as follows:-

2. A sum of Rs. 2.21 lakhs had been denied on the ground that the invoice bore the address of the appellant's head office and not that of the factory. Counsel for the appellant says that there was only one manufacturing unit located at Pune, the head office being in Mumbai. The head office could not have taken the credit, not being a factory. Endorsement of invoices is also not permissible. The goods had been received in the appellant's factory and utilised in the manufacture. Therefore the failure, if any, is most technical and should not stand in the way. The departmental representative emphasises that the invoice is not in the name of the manufacturing unit.

3. In a situation of this kind where there is only one factory, we are of the view that the drawback in the invoice that it did not contain the factory's name, should not result in the invoice being held invalid. The head office was not a factory and so could not have utilised the credit. The provisions of Rule 57F (1), permitting removal of the inputs for home consumption as such, would also not be available to it. It is not as if, by containing the heading office's name, credit could have been taken by the recipient in more than one factory; as we have noted, the factory was only one. There is no dispute that the goods were not received and utilised in the factory. In this situation, we do not think that the credit should be denied.

4. Invoices issued by dealers for a total of Rs. 7.49 lakhs have been held invalid on the ground that they were not marked duplicate or original and they were "extra copies". The invoices were issued between the period from 3rd August 1994 to 4th January 1995. The contention of the counsel for the appellant is that the requirement that credit must be been taken on duplicate invoices came on the statute book by way of amendment of sub-rule (4) of Rule 57GG on 19.1.1995. The trade notice that was issued in November 1994 by the Commissioner, Pune, insisting upon this requirement had no legal authority.

5. Although the departmental representative relies on the trade notice, the appellant's contention has to be accepted. In the absence of any legal authority, the denial of the credit is not justified. This is the view taken by the Tribunal in its decisions in Lauls Ltd. Vs. CCE 2000 (41) RLT 213 and Parikh Chemical Industries Vs. CCE 1997 (95) ELT 598. Another objection raised with regard to these invoices is that they did not contain details of the mode of transport and time. The Commissioner has confirmed that these invoices did not indicate the mode and time of transport. Counsel for the appellant points out, rightly, that the proforma prescribed under sub-rule (4) of Rule 57GG did not contain time and mode of transport. Column 1 (i) of the proforma specifies "date and time of issue both in words and figures of the invoice of registered person issuing the invoice." This refers to the date of issue of the invoice and not the date and time of despatch of the goods from the premises. The contention of the departmental representative that some of the invoices did not contain this also may be true; that however was not the basis for proposing to disallow these invoices. The basis was very clear that time and mode of transport had not been shown. We therefore do not think that this was a valid objection and credit ought not to have been denied.

6. The credit of 36000/- has been objected to on the ground that it was a customer copy of an invoice issued by Steel Authority of India Ltd. (SAIL for short) and not a duplicate. We do not see how reliance made on a Circular 86/86/94-CX dated 22.12.1994 of the Board helps the appellant. This only provides that SAIL can issue invoices from the depot recognised for modvat credit purposes and has anything to do with any copy. There being no other ground, the denial of the credit is in order.

7. The appeal is accordingly allowed in part.

So far as this ground is concerned, I find that the credit cannot be disallowed on the basis that the invoice is not in the name of the factory. It is obvious that several transporters would be involved in the process of transporting these goods and it cannot be a case that, all the transporters have lost the duplicate copy of invoice in transit. Under Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, procedure to be observed by the manufacturer is laid down and it is, inter-alia, provided by sub-rule (3) thereof that, no credit under sub-rule (2) shall be taken by the manufacturer unless the inputs are received in the factory under the cover of the documents enumerated therein including at clause (e), being an invoice issued by a "first stage dealer" of excisable goods, registered under Rule 174. Rule 174, deals with registration of certain persons including dealers storing in private store-room or warehouse or otherwise, excisable goods. There appears to be no statutory provision to the effect that modvat credit can be denied, if the goods are not first taken to the premises of the registered dealer and then brought to the factory of the manufacturer. The scheme of the Act and rules appears to be focusing on the movement of the goods for which purpose it regulates the place where they can be stocked, before delivery to the manufacturer who wants to avail of modvat credit thereon and appropriate records are required to be maintained. This is why, the premises have to be got registered by the registered dealer and the necessary inward and outward entries are required to be made, just as the relevant statutory records are to be maintained by the original manufacturer of such goods and their movement from the factory is required to be shown. However, keeping in view the inconvenience experienced by the trade, it appears that, by Trade Notice No. 10/95 dated 21.2.1995 issued by the Mumbai Commissionerate-I, provisions for transit sale were made. It was provided in the notice that where a registered person places an order on a manufacturer for supply and delivery of the goods directly to a consumer and the goods are accordingly transported from the manufacturer's premises to the user's premises without being brought to the registered person's premises, the manufacturer will issue an invoice under Rule 57A which will contain, in addition to the prescribed details including the consignee's name and address, mentioned therein, the registered person's name and address, on whose instructions the goods have been dispatched. The consignee in such a case will be the end-user. In such a situation the registered person's invoice is not required for availment of modvat credit. In such cases the goods need not be brought to the premises of the registered person (dealer). Invoice of registered person/dealer is not required for availing the cenvat credit by the consignee. For this purpose, invoice book of different series such cenvatable invoice of dealer was required to be maintained.

specific and mandatory in character. The amended portion of this Rule enacts as under:-

"No credit shall be taken unless the inputs are received in the factory under the cover of an invoice, issued under Rule 52-A and AR-1 or Bill of Entry, a certificate issued by an appraiser of the Customs posted in Foreign Post Office, or any other document as prescribed by the Central Government by Notification in the Official Gazetted in this behalf evidencing payment of duty on such inputs." Therefore, under these circumstances, it is neither permissible nor justifiable legally to infer the deemed facility of endorsement in respect of the invoices after 1.4.94, as was available earlier on the gate passes, so as to make those invoices as valid documents for claiming modvat credit. The Tribunal being not a law making body has no power to allow from its own side any endorsement on the invoices and to declare that the invoice bearing endorsements would not be accepted as valid documents for taking modvat credit. Moreover, it is well settled that while construing a fiscal statute, plain meaning of the language has to be looked into and there is no room for any fiscal legislation. Unless there is ambiguity, it would not be open to the court to deviate from the rule of construction which is that the intention of the Legislature should be primarily gathered from the words which are used. It is only when the words used are ambiguous that they were sought to be examined and construed in the light of the surrounding circumstances and constitutional principles and practice. Even the Apex Court in Commissioner of Wealth Tax Vs. Smt. Hashmatunissa Begum AIR 1989 SC 1024=1989 (40) ELT 239 (SC) has ruled as under:-

"The rule of construction that if the statutory provision is susceptible or admits of two reasonably possible views then the one which would promote its constitutionality should be preferred on the ground that the legislature is presumed not to have intended an excess of its own jurisdiction, is subject to the further rule that it applies only where two views are reasonably possible on the statutory language. If the words of the Statute, on a proper construction, can be read only in a particular way, then it cannot be read in another way by a Court of construction anxious to avoid the unconstitutionality."

18. In the instant case there is no ambiguity in the language used in the Notification No. 15/94 dated 30.3.94 and the amendment on its basis made in Rule 57-G of the Central Excise Rules. Rather the language of the notification and the amended provisions of Rule 57-G is quite clear and leaves no doubt in our mind that endorsement of the invoices had not been intended to be allowed by the legislature. Only the issuance of the fresh invoice by the dealer or trader after having received the goods from the manufacturer, had been made permissible under Rule and that to on a prescribed proforma giving full details referred therein. If the intention of the legislature was to allow the endorsement of the invoices, as was earlier made permissible regarding the gate passes by the Board, such a provision must have been made in Rule 57-G itself or by issuing a separate notification or circular by the Central Government. But having not so done it becomes quite clear that the endorsed invoices after 1.4.94 cannot be legally considered to be valid document for claiming the modvat credit.

19. The arguments of the learned counsel that by endorsement the invoice does not become invalid as it remains the invoice and that the duty paid character of the goods cleared under the invoice can be verified by the Excise department and as such endorsement of the invoice should be held to be permissible, cannot be accepted in the light of the facts and circumstances discussed above. The endorsement of the invoice cannot be made permissible, as it would be lacking in the particulars and details which are required to be given in the subsequent invoice to be issued by a dealer or a trader to a third party, the proforma of which prescribed by the Central Government and referred to above (Annexure 2E) stands appended to the Rules. He is also required to maintain stock account in the form RG.23D and to make entry regarding receipt and despatch of the goods in the register and also to make available that register for inspection on demand by the Excise Officer, as is clear from the provisions of Rule 57-GG which have been inserted by Notification 32/94 dated 4.7.94. All this was not required to be done before 1.4.94 when endorsed gate passes were accepted as valid documents. The verification of the duty paid character of the goods in the case of endorsed invoices would also be not possible by the Excise department as in the endorsement no particulars are recorded by the person making the endorsement.
