INPUT SERVICE DISTRIBUTOR

In this article, the author has discussed the provisions relating to ‘input service distributor’ including amendment carried out in 2008.

Introduction

1. ‘Input service distributor’ is the beautiful and utilitarian concept introduced by the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. In this article, we shall discuss the provisions relating to ‘input service distributor’.

Definition

2. Rule 2(m ) of the Rules defines ‘input service distributor’ as under :—

"(m)‘Input service distributor’ means an office of the manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service, which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services and issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider, as the case may be;"

Important criteria for input service provider

3. Important criteria for input service provider are :—

(i)It has an office as the manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service. In other words, an office of manufacturer of excisable goods or taxable service provider can be registered as input service distributor.

(ii)It has to receive invoices towards purchase of services. The services might have been received by one of the units manufacturing goods or premises providing services or other offices.

(iii)It can issue invoice or bill or challan for the purpose of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the services to the manufacturing unit or service providing unit.

It is to be noted that the input service provider can be registered as head office, registered office, branch, depot, regional office, zonal office, etc.

Regional marketing office was registered as input service distributor and credit was distributed to manufacturing units. It was held by the Tribunal in its prima facie view, that the distribution was in order in Jaypee Rewa Plant v. CCE 2007 (218) ELT 576 (Delhi - Trib.).

It is possible that one company may have many input service distributors.

Example

4. ABC Ltd. has three manufacturing units. Its head office has taken Fire Insurance Policy covering the manufacturing units and paid insurance premium and service tax of Rs. 10,300. Head Office can distribute the service tax paid by it to the manufacturing units and manufacturing units can take the credit on receipt of Invoice from the head office and utilise this amount like any other Cenvat credit.

Conditions

5. Rule 7 deals with distribution of credit by input service distributor. The input service provider can distribute service tax paid by it subject to the following conditions :—

(i)The credit distributed shall not exceed the amount of service tax paid by it. (Is it possible to distribute more than the credit availed?)

(ii)The credit of service tax attributable to service used in an unit exclusively engaged in manufacture of exempted goods or providing of exempted services shall not be distributed.

It is important to note that there is no requirement to distribute the credit proportionately. The input service distributor can distribute to various units as the circumstances warrants. There is no rule regarding periodicity of distribution and it is advisable to distribute monthly.

Registration

6. Input service distributors have to obtain registration from the service tax authorities. They have to apply in Form No. ST-1 and have to obtain Registration Certificate in Form No. ST-2.

Maintenance of records

7. Rule 9 of the Rules deals with maintenance of records by the input service distributor. The records maintained by it must contain the following :—

(i)Serial number and date of the document on which the Cenvat credit is availed.

(ii)Service tax registration number and name of input service provider.

(iii)Description and value of input service.

(iv)Service tax credit availed.

(v)Basis of allocation/apportionment of credit amount.

(vi)Service tax utilised for distributing the credit.

(vii)Balance credit available for distribution.

Issue of Invoice

8. After making the payment of service charges and service tax, input service distributor can avail the credit provided service received is input service and distribute it to various manufacturing units or service providing units.

Rule 4A(2) of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 deals with the issue of invoice by the input service distributor. The invoice shall be serially numbered and contain the following particulars :

(i)the name, address and registration number of the person providing input services and the serial number and date of invoice;

(ii)the name and address of the input service distributor;

(iii)the name and address of the recipient of the credit distributed; and

(iv)the amount of the credit distributed.

It is learnt that in some cases, the department is taking a view that in such cases, registration as Input Service Distributor and distribution of credit is mandatory.

The issue involved is whether such registration and/or distribution is compulsory or optional.

Who is Input Service Distributor ?

2. As per rule 2(m ) of CENVAT Credit Rules, an entity is ‘input service distributor’ if it satisfies the following three conditions—

"(a )office managing the business of manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service,

(b )which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services and

(c )issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be,

there are factories or places for provision of service in another places. In such cases, the input services received at main factory are recorded there itself and credit is availed in the main factory without ‘distributing’ to other factories or other places providing output services.

It is learnt that in some cases, the department is taking a view that in such cases, registration as Input Service Distributor and distribution of credit is mandatory.

The issue involved is whether such registration and/or distribution is compulsory or optional. Who is Input Service Distributor ?

2. As per rule 2(m ) of CENVAT Credit Rules, an entity is ‘input service distributor’ if it satisfies the following three conditions—

"(a )office managing the business of manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service,

(b )which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services and

(c )issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider, as the case may be."

The word used is ‘and’. Thus, an entity is ‘input service distributor’ only if all the three conditions are satisfied. If an assessee has office or premises which receives invoices and it does not issue any invoice, bill or challan for distributing credit of service tax, it is not ‘Input Service Distributor’.

Service Tax (Registration of Special Category of Persons) Rules, 2005 issued vide Notification No. 27/2005-ST, dated 7-6-2005 provide for registration of ‘Input Service Distributor’. Rule 2(c) of these Rules states that ‘input service distributor’ shall have the meaning assigned to it in rule 2(m) of CENVAT Credit Rules.

It is, thus, clear that the Service tax (Registration of Special Category of Persons) Rules, 2005 apply when an entity falls within the definition of rule 2(m). If the office or main factory does not issue any invoice or challan for distribution of CENVAT credit, it does not fall within the definition of ‘Input Service Distributor’. In such case, the rules in respect of registration and issue of invoice by Input Service Distributor do not apply at all.

Provision is not a mandatory requirement

3. Rule 7 of the CENVAT Credit Rules uses the words ‘Input Service Distributor may distribute credit’. ‘May’ cannot be read as ‘must’.

Rule 9(1) of CENVAT Credit Rules gives list of seven types of documents eligible for availing CENVAT credit, out of which invoice of input service distributor is one of the eligible documents. Thus, the invoice of input service distributor is not the only eligible document for availing CENVAT credit. Credit can be availed on basis of other eligible documents also.

As discussed below, distribution can be in any ratio. Thus, even if main factory is registered as ‘Input Service distributor’ it can legally allocate entire CENVAT credit to itself, which would be an exercise in futility.

Facility cannot be a compulsion

4. ‘Input Service Distributor’ is a facility provided to assessee. It is nowhere stated that it is a mandatory requirement. This ‘facility’ cannot be thrust upon an unwilling assessee.

In CIT v. Mahendra Mills [2000] 243 ITR 56/109 Taxman 225 (SC), it was observed, ‘A privilege cannot be to a disadvantage and an option cannot become an obligation’.

Can CENVAT credit be denied in such cases

5. Even assuming for the sake of argument that registration as Input Service Distributor and distribution of credit is mandatory (though really it is not), non-registration and non-distribution may at the most lead to penalty for violation of rules. How can it lead to complete denial of CENVAT credit?

Is there any provision to deny CENVAT credit for violation of such a procedural provision?

T 242 (CESTAT), it was held that credit of duty paid on inputs meant for ‘matador’ vehicle can be used for payment of duty on other motor vehicle ‘tempo-traveller’.

CBE&C, vide para 2(viii) of Circular No. 33/33/94-CX dated 4-5-1994 has confirmed that there is no one to one correlation between input and final product under the CENVAT scheme for utilisation of credit. Definition of ‘input service’ expanded

8. Definition of ‘input service’ as per rule 2(1) of CENVAT Credit Rules is very wide in view of the inclusive part of the definition. Any service in relation to business is ‘input service’.

The second part of the definition of ‘input service’ covers various services like advertisement or sales promotion, market research, activities relating to business, such as accounting, auditing, financing, recruitment and quality control, coaching and training, computer networking, credit rating, share registry and security.

These input services have hardly any relation with ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of output service’.

Main factory can ‘distribute’ entire credit to itself

9. In some cases, office and main factory are situated at one place and other factories are situated at different places. In such case, if the office is registered as ‘Input Service Distributor’, it is perfectly legal to distribute all CENVAT credit to the main factory itself. Thus, registering office as ‘Input Service Distributor’ and ‘distributing’ all CENVAT credit to the main factory itself is an exercise in futility. Instead of that, the credit of services at office can be utilised in main office itself. As explained above, definition of ‘input service’ does not require any relation with ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of output service’. CENVAT Credit Rules do not require one-to-one relationship.

What is not required in the main definition cannot be brought in through the mechanism of ‘input service distributor’.

All provisions have to be read in cohesive manner

10. Any provision in law cannot be read in isolative manner. The provision of ‘Input Service Distributor’ cannot be read in isolation of other provisions relating to CENVAT credit.

Interpretation must depend on the text and the context . They are the basis of interpretation. One may well say, if the text is the texture, context is what gives the colour. Neither can be ignored. The interpretation is best which makes the textual interpretation match the contextual. A statute is best interpreted when we know why it is enacted. With this knowledge, the statute must be read, first as a whole and then section by section, clause by clause, phrase by phrase and word by word. If a statute is looked at, in the context of its enactment, with the glasses of the statute-maker, provided by such context, its scheme, the sections, clauses, phrases and words may take colour and appear different than when statute is looked at without the glasses of context. With those glasses, we must look at the Act as a whole and discover what each section, each clause, each phrase and each word is meant and designed to say as to fit into the scheme of the entire Act. No part of a statute can be construed in isolation. Statutes have to be construed so that every word has a place and everything is in its place - RBI v. Peerless General Finance & Investment Co. Ltd. AIR 1987 SC 1023/[1987] 1 SCC 424/[1987] 61 Comp. Cas. 663 (SC) - quoted with approval in J.K. Industries Ltd. v. Chief Inspector of Factories [1996] 89 Taxman 321 (SC), Indian Handicrafts Emporium v. UOI AIR 2003 SC 3240/[2003] 7 SCC 589, National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh AIR 2004 SC 1531/[2004] 3 SCC 257, Prakash Kumar v. State of Gujarat AIR 2005 SC 1075.

Conclusion

11. In conclusion, it can be stated as follows—

u Input Service Distributor is a facility, not a compulsion.

u CENVAT Credit Rules do not require one-to-one relationship.

u Provision of ‘Input Service Distributor’ also does not envisage one-to-one relationship.

u Any service in relation to business of assessee is his ‘input service’.

u CENVAT credit can be utilised at one place without distributing it.

u Even if distribution is done, ‘distribution’ of credit can be in any ratio. Entire credit can be allocated to one of the factories/places of provision of output services, if assessee so desires.

u The only requirement is that ‘input service’ should be in relation to business of assessee. Any relation with ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of output service’ is not required.

Service tax was demanded from the assessee for activity of bottling of liquor as packaging activity under section 65(76b). The assessee challenged the validity of said section in writ petition. In the course of hearing, the assessee contended that the Division Bench in Vindhyachal Distilleries (P.) Ltd. v. State of MP [2006] 5 STT 254 (MP) had not appropriately considered the decision rendered in case of Som Distilleries & Breweries (P.) Ltd. v. State of MP 1997 (1) JLJ 319 and various other aspects which deserved consideration. The Division Bench thought it apposite to refer the matter to a Larger Bench referring the question as to whether bottling of liquor amounts to manufacture of liquor or only packaging so as to attract service tax.

The High Court held that on a scrutiny of the definition of ‘packaging activity’, it is quite clear that packaging activity means packaging of goods including pouch-filling, bottling, labelling or imprinting of the package but the definition does not stop there, as the provision expressly shows that it does not include any packaging activity that amounts to manufacture within the meaning of clause (f) of section 2 of the 1944 Act. In Circular No. 249/1/2006, it was mentioned that as alcohol beverages are not covered under the Central Excise Law, the production of beverages would not fall within the meaning of the term ‘manufacture’ as conceptualized under clause (f) of section 2. The Board re-examined the matter in detail after receipt of the response and issued Circular F. No. 249/1/2006-CX.4, dated 27-10-2008 which relates to levy of service tax on production of alcoholic beverages on job work basis.

As per High Court, the basic aspect of manufacture as contained in section 2(f) conveys that the term ‘manufacture’ would include ‘any process incidental or ancillary with the completion of manufactured product’. The definition clause further expands the scope of manufacture to include certain goods which are specified in the section. The first limb of the inclusive definition of the term ‘manufacture’ under section 2(f) has a very wide connotation. As the definition clause lays down an inclusive facet, the term ‘manufacture’ has to be construed in a natural and plain manner and would include any process incidental or ancillary to the completion of a manufactured product. Keeping in view the context in which the term ‘manufacture’ has been used, it would take in its fold the incidental or ancillary process in the manufacture or finishing of any manufactured product. It does not leave any room for doubt that an allied process should be an integral and inextricable part of manufacture for completeness and presentability of the manufactured product.

Thus, as per definition, [See under Heading Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Condition for allowing] the Cenvat credit in respect of transportation can be availed up to the place of removal. The CBEC has also clarified this provision in Circular No. 97/8/2007-ST, dated 23-8-2007, in the following manner:

"8. CENVAT Credit

(c )ISSUE - Up to what stage a manufacturer/consignor can take credit on the service tax paid on goods transport by road?

COMMENTS - This issue has been examined in great details by the CESTAT in the case of Gujarat Ambuja Cements Ltd. v. CCE [2007] (6) STR 249/8 STT TRI-Delhi. In this case, CESTAT has made the following observations:—

"…The post sale transport of manufactured goods is not an input in manufacturer. The two clauses in the definition take care to circumscribe input credit by stating that service used in relation to the clearance from the place of removal and service used for outward transportation upto the place of removal are to be treated as input service. The first clause does not mention transport service in particular. The second clause restricts transport service credit upto the place of removal. When these two clauses are read together, it becomes clear that transport service credit cannot go beyond transport upto the place of removal. The two clauses, the one dealing with general provision and other dealing with a specific item, are not to be read disjunctively as to bring about conflict to defeat the laws’ scheme. The purpose of interpretation is to find harmony and reconciliation among the various provisions". (p. 127)

Similarly, in the case of Ultratech Cement Ltd. v. CCE [2007] 8 STT 152 (Ahd. - CESTAT), it was held that after the final products are cleared from the place of removal, there will be no scope of subsequent use of service to be treated as input. The above observations and views explain the scope of the relevant provisions clearly, correctly and in accordance with the legal provisions. In conclusion, a manufacturer/consignor can take credit on the service tax paid on outward transport of goods up to the place of removal and not beyond that.

Whether garden maintenance service (With using materials/without using materials) is taxable? If yes, under which services it is taxable?

It should come under ‘Management, Maintenance or repair’ service , since that head covers both movable as well as immovable property. It does not make any difference whether it is with materials or without materials. You can claim deduction in respect of materials like plants, etc., but not in respect of consumables.

CENTRALISED OPERATIONS We are a Gas Distribution Company based at Gujarat. We are having CNG Station at various locations. We obtain excise Separate Registration of each CNG Station. Our queries are (1) Whether we are able to take CENVAT Credit on Excise Payable for Capital Goods? If yes, then whether only CENVAT credit on particular Capital goods used for a particular station only can be claimed? (2) Shall we claim excise on common pipe line which is partly used for CNG and partly for domestic gas, inspite of fact that domestic gas is not excisable goods? (3) Whether regarding the supplier invoice, the address of CNG Station has to be mentioned or not on that invoice or invoice made to Head Office address is sufficient to take Cenvat Credit?

(1) Since you have separate registration for each location, it is advisable to take separate credit only for each unit in respect of capital goods installed there. (2) Check tariff heading of pipeline. Mostly, it is 72 or 73 and, hence, does not fall within the definition of ‘capital goods’, as defined in the Cenvat Credit Rules. However, if some equipment does fall within the definition, you can take credit even if it is only partly used for taxable service. (3) It is highly advisable to mention address of CNG station in supplier’s invoice to avoid disputes and harassment from department. If this is not possible, invoice should be endorsed by HO in favour of CNG station with clear remark that these goods are for the particular unit and they have not taken any Cenvat credit at HO.

One of my clients has centralised registration. He has placed capital goods at various sites of the clients. Can the unit shift the capital goods to other sites of the clients after work at one site is completed ?

In respect of capital goods on which there was no credit taken, obviously no question arises. In other cases, if each unit is registered separately, then the first unit should pay ‘amount’ as per Cenvat credit rules and then other unit can take credit. However, in this case, since there is centralised registration, there is no problem, since there is no question of one unit paying duty and other unit taking credit. At the most, you may write letter informing department suitably (Don’t ask for permission. That will create a mess).

A unit having centralised registration is procuring inputs and input services at the sites where the work of the clients is going on. In view of the fact that the unit has taken centralized registration, will it be able to get credit of inputs and input services in the centralized office, if the billing of the supplier is addressed to this centralized office and inputs/input services are directly received at the work site? Or will the unit be required to avail service tax registration as a distributor for all these sites separately and then transfer the credit to centralized office? Here we would like to clarify that service tax registration certificate at present mentions the addresses of various sites at which work is going on.

Really, input service distributor is a facility and not compulsion. Further, Cenvat Credit Rules do not require one to one relationship. If there is centralised accounting and all records are available in HO, credit can be taken at HO. Of course, harassment from department cannot be ruled out. Hence, it is better to write a letter to the department about informing the procedure you are following.

We have branches at various places. Each branch is separately registered for purpose of service tax. In some cases, capital goods installed in one branch have to be shifted to other branch for various purposes like shortages, urgency, etc. We have received a demand that in such cases, Cenvat credit has to be reversed. Please advise.

It is true that technically, you should pay ‘amount’ while removing capital goods from one branch under ‘invoice’ and then take credit in other branch. However, practically, at operational level, such deep knowledge of service tax laws is difficult. You can argue that paying ‘amount’ in one branch and taking credit in other branch will be a revenue neutral exercise. There are many Tribunal decisions that substantive benefit cannot be lost for procedural lapses, particularly when the whole exercise is revenue neutral.

Coverage beyond manufacturing/service provision stage

2. Inclusive definition clause of rule 2(l) extends scope of ‘input services’ even beyond stage of ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of service’. The inclusive clause makes it clear that services much earlier to manufacture or provision of service or even after manufacture and after provision of provision of service will be eligible for service tax credit.

Services which do not have even any casual relation with manufacture of goods or provision of service have been covered by the definition of ‘input service’. In fact, any service in relation to business of assessee is ‘input service’.

Thus, though the words used in rule 2(l)(ii) are ‘used by the manufacturer, whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and clearance of final products from the place of removal’, in view of the word ‘includes’, the scope of definition is much wider than ‘in or in relation to manufacture’ and would cover even services unrelated to ‘manufacture’. This is also clear from the fact that service tax paid at Head Office and branches/depots can be utilised as Cenvat credit through the mechanism of ‘input service distributor’.

. The assessee availed Cenvat credit on the quantity of LSHS. The Commissioner disallowed the credit holding that since fertilizers were exempted goods, credit on LSHS, even though used as fuel within the factory, was not allowable. On appeal, the Larger Bench of the Tribunal following the decision in CCE&C v. Gujarat Narmada Fertilizers Co. Ltd. 2006 (193) ELT 136 (Guj.) allowed the credit. The Supreme Court held that rule 6(1) is plenary. It restates a principle, namely, that Cenvat credit for duty paid on inputs used in the manufacture of exempted final products is not allowable. This principle is inbuilt in the very structure of the Cenvat Scheme. Sub-rule (1), therefore, merely highlights that principle. Sub-rule (1) covers all inputs, including fuel, whereas sub-rule (2) refers to non-fuel inputs. Sub-rule (2) covers a situation where common Cenvated inputs are used in or in relation to manufacture of dutiable final product and exempted final product but the fuel input is excluded from that sub-rule. However, exclusion of fuel-input vis-a-vis non-fuel input would still fall in sub-rule (1). As stated above, sub-rule (1) is plenary and, hence, it cannot be said that because sub-rule (2) is inapplicable to fuel-input(s), Cenvat credit is automatically available to such inputs even if they are used in the manufacture of exempted goods. The cumulative reading of sub-rules (1) and (2) makes it abundantly clear that the circumstances specified in sub-rule (2), which, inter alia, require separate accounting of input, are not applicable to the fuel-input(s). However, the said sub-rule (2) nowhere says that the legal effect of sub-rule (1) will stand terminated in respect of fuel-inputs which do not fall in sub-rule (2). In other words, the legal effect of sub-rule (1) has to be applied to all inputs including fuel-inputs, only exception being non-fuel-inputs, for which one has to maintain separate accounts or in its absence, pay 8 per cent/10 per cent of the total price of the exempted final products. Therefore, sub-rule (1) of rule 6 shall apply in respect of goods used as ‘fuel’ and on such application, the credit will not be permissible on such quantity of fuel which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods. The above aspect had not been properly appreciated by the Gujarat High Court in the case of Gujarat Narmada Fertilizers Co. Ltd. (supra).

As per Supreme Court, it may be noted that litigation on interpretation of Cenvat Credit Rules has arisen on account of various conflicting decisions given by various Benches of CESTAT, the reason being that the rules have not been properly drafted. In the circumstances, no penalty was leviable, however, in order to decide the amount of duty payable by each of the assessees, the matter was to be remitted to the adjudicating authority to decide the amount of duty payable without penalty on reversal of credit to the extent of the input being used in the manufacture of exempted final products.

We have two units – one unit is paying duty and other unit is in Himachal Pradesh, which is exempt from duty. Is it required that Cenvat credit of services received at HO should be taken on proportionate basis? Please advise.

There is no provision to take credit on ‘proportionate basis’. You cannot apply costing principles for Cenvat credit when rule 7 or any other rule of Cenvat Credit Rules makes no such provision. Further, rule 7(b) of Cenvat Credit Rules provides that if some expenses are exclusively related to exempted product, then no credit is available. Thus, so long as expenses are not exclusively related to exempted final product, Cenvat credit is available. Hence, in my view, entire credit of service tax can be availed at HO, except that which is exclusively related to the unit manufacturing exempted goods.

Input Service Distributor is a facility and not compulsion. Even rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules uses the words ‘may distribute the Cenvat credit’. Thus, law does not say that credit can be availed only through mechanism of Input Service Distributor. Moreover, you can distribute credit in any ratio. Thus, technically, even if you register your HO as input service distributor, you can take entire credit at Pune factory, itself. Cenvat Rules do not require one to one relationship.

To avoid litigation and petty disputes, it may be advisable to register HO as Input Service Distributor, though not legally required.

(ix) Can CENVAT credit be disallowed on appeal being not filed? - Under rule 3 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, a manufacturer or producer of final product is allowed to take credit of input, input services and capital goods as per the conditions laid down therein. The CENVAT credit is a substantive benefit and cannot be denied in the absence of any legitimate reason. The similar issue was recently decided by CESTAT in Magnet Industries (Cal.) (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2008] 12 STT 32 (CESTAT - Kolkata) wherein it was held that CENVAT credit cannot be denied merely for the reason that the same was not claimed in the appeal and that dues cannot be denied, if such dues are legitimate and patent from record. This was also in tune with Circular No. 218/52/96-CX, dated June 4, 1996. The Tribunal held that there cannot be any other conclusion, but only conclusion to be drawn is in consonance with the Circular as aforesaid to grant relief of CENVAT credit to the appellants, claiming or not claiming in appeal and to grant relief is delivers of due to the deserved on the facts and circumstances of each case. Uniformity and consistency as well as majesty being ordain of justice, the due cannot be denied, if such due is legitimate and patent from record. Therefore, the authorities below, denying CENVAT credit to the appellants and levy of penalty as well as interest had deprived the appellants from the due process of justice. Such injustice could only be ruled out setting aside the order of the authorities below to meet the ends of justice. Thus, in such cases, CENVAT credit cannot be denied.

(x) Utilization of CENVAT Credit in Capital Goods - The assessee can take full credit of duty paid on capital goods but utilize only 50 per cent thereof as provided in the CENVAT Credit Rules as per the restriction provided in rule 4 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. As such, the assessee can utilize the credit to the extent of limit of 50 per cent allowed as per law. There is no wrong utilization of the CENVAT credit nor there is any evidence of fraud or mis-statement or suppression of facts. There is no scope for levy of penalty by the department under rule 15 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. A similar view was taken by the Tribunal in CCE, Rohtak v. Surya Vinayak Industries (P.) Ltd. [(2007) (CESTAT - New Delhi)] and Delphi Automotive Systems v. CCE, Noida [2004 (163) ELT 47 (CESTAT, New Delhi)] relying upon the Apex Court judgment in P & B Pharmaceuticals (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2003 (153) ELT 14 (SC)].

(xi) Denial of CENVAT Credit when invoices issued from Unregistered Premises - A dealer has to issue a valid invoice and there is no condition in the CENVAT credit rules/excise rules that the invoices issuing office of the dealer should be registered with the department. However, the dealer must be registered with the Central Excise Department. In CCE v. Myrorn Electricials (P.) Ltd. [2007 (207) ELT 664 (Punj. & Har.)], the High Court held that CENVAT credit cannot be denied on the ground that invoices have been issued by the dealer from the premises other that for which Central Excise registration had been granted in view of Central Excise Notification No. 7/99-CE, which amended earlier rule 57G of Central Excise Rules, 1944. The Supreme Court also dismissed the departmental appeal on the same issue 2007 (215) ELT A76. Therefore, it can be said that what is important is raising of an invoice by a registered dealer and not a raising of an invoice from a registered premises.

CENVAT CREDIT RULES

13. Increase in time-limit for availment of Cenvat credit from six months to one year

Till 10.07.2014, there was no restriction on availment of Cenvat credit. From 11.07.2014, the Cenvat credit can be taken only upto six months from the date of issue of document as contained in rule 9(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. From 01.03.2015, the time-limit for availment of Cenvat credit has been increased from six months to one year.

14. Credit on goods directly dispatched to job worker

As per rule 4(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, 'the CENVAT credit in respect of inputs may be taken immediately on receipt of the inputs in the factory of the manufacturer or in the premises of the provider of output service'.

In case where the goods are directly dispatched to the premises of job worker on the direction of the manufacturer or the provider of output service, credit can be taken only when the said goods are received in the factory of the manufacturer or in the premises of the provider of output service. This was the interpretation done by the department and various Courts.

In order to streamline the said provision, rule 4(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 w.e.f 01.03.2015 states that the CENVAT credit in respect of inputs may be taken immediately on receipt of the inputs in the factory of the manufacturer or in the premises of the provider of output service or in the premises of the job worker, in case goods are sent directly to the job worker on the direction of the manufacturer or the provider of output service, as the case may be;

Similarly, w.e.f 01.03.2015, with respect of capital goods, rule 4(2)(a) now states that the CENVAT credit in respect of capital goods received in a factory or in the premises of the provider of output service or outside the factory of the manufacturer of the final products for generation of electricity for captive use within the factory or in the premises of the job worker, in case capital goods are sent directly to the job worker on the direction of the manufacturer or the provider of output service, as the case may be at any point of time in a given financial year shall be taken only for an amount not exceeding fifty per cent of the duty paid on such capital goods in the same financial year.

AVAILMENT OF CENVAT CREDIT

In this article, the author has outlined the situations where service tax paid cannot be denied on the ground that service tax is not applicable in the light of relevant case-laws. The other issues discussed here include : applicability of the time-limit for taking CENVAT credit and utilization of CENVAT credit in case of payment of advance capital goods and centralised registration.

Service Tax Paid - Cannot be denied on the ground that service tax is not applicable : relevant case-laws

1. (i) In Maersk India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [Order No. A/475 (Mum.) of 2008, dated 16-5-2008] - The appellant was registered under the category of ‘Storage & warehousing service’ and ‘Maintenance and repair services’. It got a part of its empty containers repaired through its sub-contractors. The sub-contractors charged service tax on the ‘repair charges’ charged to the appellant and, in turn, the appellant had taken credit of the service tax paid.

CENVAT credit was denied on the ground that sub-contractors did not have service tax liability. It was held by the Tribunal that once service tax has been paid by the service provider, the same cannot be questioned at the receiver’s end and, accordingly, credit cannot be denied.

(ii) Vodafone Essar Digilink Ltd. v. CCE [S.O. No. 15 (Delhi) of 2008 dated 2-1-2008] - BSNL provided service to the appellant and paid service tax on port and space charges. The appellant had taken credit of the service tax paid and credit was denied on the ground that BSNL was not liable to pay service tax in respect of port and space charges.

It was held by the Tribunal that since the payment of service tax by BSNL was not challenged, credit cannot be denied. In this case, pre-deposit of tax and penalty was waived.

(iii) CCE v. Purity Flexpack Ltd. [T.A. No. 92 (Guj.) of 2006 dated 23-11-2006] - The manufacturer had paid Excise duty at the rate of 24 per cent instead of the correct rate of 16 per cent and the buyer of the goods had taken credit of the full amount. It was held that the assessee was entitled to take full credit, as the department had not initiated any action at the supplier’s, i.e., manufacturers’, end.

Supply of components and parts and erection of plant

2. In Rajarambapu Patil SSK Ltd. v. CCE [2008] 11 STR 437 (Trib. - Mum.), the appellant entered into two contracts with a contractor - one for supply of components and parts and another for erection at the appellant’s site. He had taken credit of the duty paid on the components and parts which were used in setting up of the plant and the department held that he was not entitled to credit and the components and parts were inputs of the contractor who supplied and assembled them at the appellant’s site since it was he who used it to manufacture the plant.

The Tribunal held that the contention of the department was incorrect and the appellant was eligible to avail the credit of the duty paid on the parts and components.

Bill without name of service receiver

3. In CCE v. Diamond Cements [2009] 18 STT 151 (New Delhi - CESTAT), the Tribunal held that a certificate from the service provider that the service had been rendered to the appellant can be accepted as a valid document for availing CENVAT credit where the bills did not mention the name and address of the appellant. However, it will be advisable to ask the service provider to enter the name and address of the service receiver in the bills instead of taking separate letter.

Time-Limit

4. Rule 4 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 provides for rules for taking CENVAT credit. The relevant rules are reproduced below for ready reference.

Input : Rule 4(1) - CENVAT credit in respect of inputs may be taken immediately on receipt of the inputs in the factory of the manufacturer or in the premises of the provider of output service.

Input Service : Rule 4(7) - CENVAT credit in respect of input service shall be allowed, on or after the day on which payment is made of the value of input service and the service tax is paid or payable as is indicated in invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan referred to in rule 9.

the question of availing either of the options provided under rule 6(3) would not arise.

Insertion of rule 7A in 2008

12. By the Cenvat Credit (Amendment) Rules, 2008, rule 7A has been inserted with effect from April 1, 2008 vide Notification No. 10/2008-CE (NT), dated March 1, 2008. Rule 7A reads as under :— "7A. Distribution of credit on inputs by the office or any other premises of output service provider.—(1) A provider of output service shall be allowed to take credit on inputs and capital goods received, on the basis of an invoice or a bill or a challan issued by an office or premises of the said provider of output service, which receives invoices, issued in terms of the provisions of the Central Excise Rules, 2002, towards the purchase of inputs and capital goods.

(2) The provisions of these rules or any other rules made under the Central Excise Act, 1944, as made applicable to a first stage dealer or a second stage dealer, shall mutatis mutandis apply to such office or premises of the provider of output service."

Distribution of excise duty paid

13. Rule 7A enables the service provider to transfer the excise duty paid on the capital goods and inputs. As discussed in the previous paragraphs, the manufacturers and service providers can obtain input service distributor registration and can transfer the credit for service tax paid to their manufacturing units and/or service providing units. However, only the service provider can transfer the credit for excise duty on capital goods and inputs.

If the office of the service provider has received invoice for capital goods or inputs, which is delivered to the service providing unit, i.e., premises from which service is provided, it can issue invoice for transferring the credit to the service providing units like input service distributor. However, rule 7A(2) provides that Rules applicable to a first stage dealer or a second stage dealer shall apply to the office or premises of the provider of output service when he transfers the excise duty paid on inputs or capital goods. The Department has not issued any clarification in this regard till date. Circular DOF No. 334/1/2008-TRU, dated February 29, 2008 states the objective of the insertion of rule 7A in the following words :—

"A new rule 7A is being inserted to prescribe a procedure to enable the provider of output services to take credit on inputs and capital goods on the basis of invoice/bill/challan issued by its other office. This change shall come into effect from April 1, 2008."

ANNEX 12.2

[PARA 12.2-3]

CIRCULAR NO. 179/13/96-CX, DATED 29-2-1996

PROBLEMS FACED IN AVAILING MODVAT ON BILL OF ENTRY IN THE NAME OF REGISTERED OFFICE/HEAD OFFICE BUT CREDIT TO BE AVAILED BY THE FACTORY

Attention of the Board has been invited to the difficulties faced by the manufacturers in availing the credit under rule 57G/57T where :

(i)

the Bill of Entry has been filed in the name of the registered office/head office of the manufacturer for the inputs to be used in his factory.

(ii)

imported goods lying in customs dock area/bonded warehouse are diverted to manufacturing units in whose name Bill of Entry has not been filed.

(iii)

domestic duty paid goods consigned to a manufacturing unit are diverted in whole or part from a duty paid godown of the manufacturer or such diversion is affected in transit.

2. The issue has been examined by the Board.

3. It has been decided that credit should not be denied where the Bill of Entry is in the name of the registered office/head office provided that :—

(a)

the entire consignment covered by the said Bill of Entry is received in the factory in original packed conditions.

(b)

triplicate copy of Bill of Entry/duplicate copy of the Bill of Entry generated on EDI system is endorsed by the registered office/head office to the effect that consignment covered by the Bill of Entry are delivered to the manufacturing unit for availing credit.

4. Where the imported goods are still in Customs dock area and the manufacturer- importer decides to divert/transfer the goods, a declaration by the manufacturer- importer can be made on the reverse of triplicate copy of Bill of Entry/duplicate copy of the Bill of Entry generated on EDI system by the manufacturer-importer that consignments are being delivered to the unit (name of the unit) for availing credit and endorsed by the proper Officer of Customs for enabling the manufacturing unit to avail credit.

5. In cases where the imported goods are lying in the bonded warehouse from where diversion takes place either of entire consignment or part consignment, credit can be permitted provided ex-bond Bill of Entry is filed for such entire/part consignments and that a declaration is made on the reverse of the said ex-bond triplicate copy of the Bill of Entry/duplicate copy of the Bill of Entry generated on EDI system to the effect that consignments are delivered to a unit (name of the unit) for availing credit.

6. In all cases duty-paying documents on the basis of which credit has been availed in aforesaid cases, should be submitted to the Range Superintendent for the necessary verification and defacing/endorsement.

7. In case of split consignments and other types of cases not covered by the preceding paragraphs the inputs can be cleared on the payment of duty as envisaged under rule 57F/57S and on the basis of such duty-paying documents credit can be availed.

41.3-4 Supplementary Invoice by supplier-manufacturer or service provider for differential excise duty/service tax

It is possible that a manufacturer who had supplied input/capital goods and who had paid duty on such inputs/capital goods may have to pay further duty on these inputs/capital goods on account of any demand or audit objection or finalisation of provisional assessment or on account of cost escalation granted by buyer or for any other reason. Similarly, a service provider may be liable to pay additional service tax at a later stage.

In such cases, the other manufacturer who is using that input/capital goods will get further credit of additional duty paid by the supplier of inputs/capital goods or additional service tax paid by service provider.

The manufacturer (supplier) or service provider should issue supplementary invoice to buyer for this purpose, which is document eligible for availing Cenvat Credit [rule 9(1)(b) as existing right from 10-9-2004 and 9(1)(bb) as introduced w.e.f. 1-4-2011]

COMMENTS

10.1

Input Service Distributor

A manufacturer or service provider may have head office/regional office at different place/s. The services may be received at head office/regional office, but ultimately, these will be indirectly used for manufacture or providing output service.

Similarly, a principal manufacturer (brand name owner) may send inputs to job worker who is manufacturing goods under brand name of brand name owner. These goods will be supplied by job worker to principal manufacturer. If the goods are covered under MRP valuation provisions, duty will be payable by job worker on basis of MRP. However, many of input services received by principal manufacturer are indirectly used by the job worker.

Provision has been made to avail Cenvat credit of services received and paid for at head office/regional office. Such head office/regional office can be registered with Central Excise as 'Input Service Distributor' and it can issue invoice on the manufacturer or producer or service provider or outsourced manufacturing unit [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

If assessee intends to use the facility, he has to apply for registration in form ST-1.

Provision for registration was introduced w.e.f. 7-6-2005. Hence, during 10-9-2004 to 7-6-2005, the HO could distribute credit even without registration - prima facie view in Hindustan Coca Cola Beverages v. CCE (2011) 32 STT 176 (Mag) = 266 ELT 347 (CESTAT).

In fact, in my view, registration and distribution of Cenvat credit are independent aspects. Even if registration was obtained later, Cenvat credit of prior period at HO/branches can be distributed, if otherwise eligible.

Who is 'input service distributor' - As per rule 2(m) of Cenvat Credit Rules, "input service distributor" means (a) an office managing the business of manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service, (b) which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services (c) issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider or an outsourced manufacturing unit, as the case may be. [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016].

An office of assessee (manufacturer or service provider) is 'Input Service Distributor' if it satisfies all the three aforesaid requirements. It is not that each and every office of assessee is 'Input Service Distributor' and must register. The office should be registered as 'Input Service Distributor' only if it wants to distribute. There is no law that 'distribution' is the only way of availing Cenvat credit of services received at office of assessee. There are various documents eligible for availing Cenvat credit. Invoice/challan issued by 'Input Service Distributor' is only one of the specified document.

In Jaypee Rewa Plant v. CCE (2007) 218 ELT 576 (CESTAT SMB), regional marketing office was registered as Input Service Distributor and credit was distributed to manufacturing units. In prima facie view, the distribution was held as correct.

Outsourced manufacturing unit - 'Outsourced manufacturing unit' means a job-worker who is liable to pay duty on the value determined under rule 10A of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000 on the goods manufactured for the input service distributor or a manufacturer who manufactures goods, for the input service distributor under a contract, bearing the brand name of such input service distributor and is liable to pay duty on the value determined under section 4A of the Excise Act. [Explanation 4 to rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

Document eligible for Cenvat credit - As per rule 9(1)(g); 'invoice, bill or challan' issued by an 'input service distributor' under rule 4A of Service Tax Credit Rules is an eligible document for purpose of taking Cenvat credit.

In Shriram Pistons v. CCE (2012) 281 ELT 90 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is allowable on the basis of letter issued by Head Office (as Input Service Distributor) even if not mentioned as invoice or challan, if it contains all required details.

ELT 161 (CEGAT), Cenvat credit was permitted when the words 'Duplicate' were used instead of 'Duplicate for transport', or when only tick was marked against appropriate word, as assessee should not be denied credit if there is substantial compliance. In Neera Enterprises v. CCE 1998 (104) ELT 382 (CEGAT), Cenvat credit was permitted when the invoice did not contain time of removal, though date of removal was mentioned. Vehicle number/mode of transport incorrect - In Devidayal Aluminium Industries v. CCE 1997(96) ELT 363 (CEGAT), it was held that Cenvat credit cannot be denied merely because invoice was not re-endorsed with the vehicle number by which goods were re-transported. [In this case, goods left factory in one truck, kept in transporter's godown and delivered to buyer in another truck]. It was held that it is a technical breach and substantial benefit cannot be denied. - similar view in Suprabhat Steel v. CCE 1999 (113) ELT 840 (CEGAT).

In CCE v. Okasa 2002(140) ELT 458 (CEGAT), it was held that Cenvat credit cannot be denied merely because invoice does not show vehicle number and time of removal. It is a remedial defect - same view in SRF Ltd. v. CCE (2012) 278 ELT 505 (CESTAT SMB)

As per section 2(h) of CEA, 'purchase' requires transfer from one person to another for valuable consideration. Hence, transfer from one depot to another on the basis of invoice is permissible. Assessee having only one factory or place of provision of service - Sometimes, an assessee has offices at various places but accounting is done centrally in the factory. Sometimes, there are various factories of assessee but accounting is done in main factory.

In such cases, in my opinion, if assessee has only one factory and/or one centralised registration of service tax, the HO or branches need not be registered and all Cenvat credit can be availed in the factory or place where centralised registration has been taken.

The reason is that Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules reads, 'The input service distributor may distribute the Cenvat credit'. 'May' cannot be read as 'must'. It is nowhere stated that the utilisation should be only through mechanism of Input Service Distributor. A facility cannot be a compulsion.

22.6 A manufacturer or service provider may have head office/regional office at different place/s. The services may be received at head office/regional office, but ultimately, these will be indirectly used for manufacture or providing output service.

These goods will be supplied by job worker to principal manufacturer. If the goods are covered under MRP valuation provisions, duty will be payable by job worker on basis of MRP. However, many of input services received by principal manufacturer are indirectly used by the job worker.

Provision has been made to avail Cenvat credit of services received and paid for at head office/regional office. 21.2-2 Inputs should be stored within the factory. Supervision charges or MOT (Merchant Overtime Charges) are not required to be collected from assessee for storage of finished goods outside the factory. However, any other condition to safeguard revenue may be imposed by Jurisdictional Commissioner before granting permission for storage of non-duty paid goods. - CBE&C circular No. 709/25/2003-CX dated 23-4-2003. Monthly stock statement should be submitted to Range Office. Cenvat credit can be taken only when entire inputs covered by an invoice are received in the factory - similar procedure in CCE, Ahmedabad II TN 93/2004 [179 ELT T15].

In Priyadarshini Polysacks v. CCE (2014) 307 ELT 136 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is available even if permission was not obtained for taking out inputs outside the factory.

Such office will have to be registered with Central Excise and submit returns etc. similar to first stage dealer and second stage dealer [Rule 7A of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2008].

A manufacturer may have central warehouse from which he may be distributing inputs to his various factories.

12.2-2 Supplementary Invoice by supplier-manufacturer or service provider for differential excise duty/service tax

It is possible that a manufacturer who had supplied input/capital goods and who had paid duty on such inputs/capital goods may have to pay further duty on these inputs/capital goods on account of any demand or audit objection or finalisation of provisional assessment or on account of cost escalation granted by buyer or for any other reason. Similarly, a service provider may be liable to pay additional service tax at a later stage.

In such cases, the other manufacturer who is using that input/capital goods will get further credit of additional duty paid by the supplier of inputs/capital goods or additional service tax paid by service provider.

Suppose, S is a manufacturer of an input supplied to B. S had paid duty of Rs. 50,000 while supplying the input to B. On the basis of the duty paid by S, B had utilised Cenvat credit of Rs. 50,000. Now, if S has to pay further duty of say Rs. 15,000, B will be entitled to avail of extra Cenvat credit of Rs. 15,000.

The manufacturer (supplier) or service provider should issue supplementary invoice to buyer for this purpose, which is document eligible for availing Cenvat Credit [rule 9(1)(b) as existing right from 10-9-2004 and 9(1)(bb) as introduced w.e.f. 1-4-2011]

Such supplementary invoice can be issued by manufacturer from his factory or depot, dealer, consignment agent or importer. The supplementary invoice can be in respect of excise duty or CVD paid subsequently.

Similarly, a service provider can issue supplementary invoice.

If supplementary invoice is issued by manufacturer on account of price rise given by buyer, the buyer can avail Cenvat credit - Ispat Industries v. CCE (2008) 221 ELT 540 (CESTAT).

In Andhra Petrochemicals v. CCE (2005) 1 STT 195 = 183 ELT 377 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit can be taken on the basis of supplementary invoice even if differential duty was paid on the directions of Supreme Court.

In CCE v. Himalaya Drug Co. Ltd. (2012) 36 STT 715 = 25 taxmann.com 165 (Karn HC DB), assessee did not pay duty initially as goods were non-excisable. Later, on insistence of department, duty was paid to buy piece of mind and supplementary invoice was issued. It was held that Cenvat credit is available at the end of customer.

In CCE v. MRF Ltd. (2009) 244 ELT 601 (CESTAT), supplementary invoice was issued to rectify incorrect adoption of rate of duty at the time of clearance. Department contended that supplementary invoice is recognised only if it arises from provisional assessment or price escalation. However, it was held that substantial benefit cannot be denied for procedural irregularities and Cenvat credit is available. Basic proposition is that credit has to be varied if amount of duty paid is varied.

In JSW Steel Ltd. v. CCE (2008) 17 STT 196 (CESTAT), the provisions relating to supplementary invoice as contained in rule 9(1)(b) are not applicable to service tax at all [In this case, Cenvat credit was allowed on the basis of invoice issued by service provider (presumably on additional or supplementary invoice, though this aspect is not specified in the order).

Assessee having only one factory or place of provision of service - Sometimes, an assessee has offices at various places but accounting is done centrally in the factory. Sometimes, there are various factories of assessee but accounting is done in main factory.

In such cases, in my opinion, if assessee has only one factory and/or one centralised registration of service tax, the HO or branches need not be registered and all Cenvat credit can be availed in the factory or place where centralised registration has been taken.

The reason is that Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules reads, 'The input service distributor may distribute the Cenvat credit'. 'May' cannot be read as 'must'. It is nowhere stated that the utilisation should be only through mechanism of Input Service Distributor. A facility cannot be a compulsion.

In CIT v. Mahendra Mills 2000 AIR SCW 1016 = AIR 2000 SC 1960 = 243 ITR 56 = 109 Taxman 225 (SC), it was observed, 'A privilege cannot be to a disadvantage and an option cannot become an obligation'.

In Durferrit Asea v. CCE (2010) 258 ELT 414 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that if assessee has only one manufacturing unit, HO need not be registered and Cenvat credit can be taken at factory even if invoices are with address of Head Office. Rule 7 is not compulsory if assessee is not inclined to do so.

In Manipal Advertising Services v. CCE (2010) 25 STT 30 (CESTAT), branch offices were not registered with service tax authorities. Invoices were with address of branch, but payment of made from registered premises. It was held that Cenvat credit is available at HO which had Centralised registration as it had centralised accounting system. It was held that Cenvat credit is available even if address on invoice is of branch office.

Invoice of service in name of HO is eligible. It is not necessary that HO should be registered as Input Service Distributor (when there is only one factory) - CCE v. Samita Conductors (2012) 278 ELT 492 (CESTAT SMB) * Valco Industries Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 42 GST 165 = 31 taxmann.com 360 = 286 ELT 54 (CESTAT SMB).

If assessee has only one manufacturing unit, registration as Input Service Distributor is not required. Assessee can take Cenvat credit even if invoice is with address of Head Office - National Plastic Industries v. CCE (2012) 35 STT 193 = 20 taxmann.com 132 (CESTAT) * Bloom Dekor v. CCE (2013) 38 STT 336 = 29 taxmann.com 357 (CESTAT SMB).

In Doshion Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 288 ELT 291 (CESTAT), it was held that since assessee could distribute Cenvat Credit in any ratio upto 31-3-2012, the HO could distribute credit to its unit without registration as Input Service Distributor.

In WNS Global Services v. CCE (2013) 30 taxmann.com 208 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is allowable even if assessee was not registered as Input Service Distributor.

Capital goods used in EPC project

23.4 Capital goods are used in EPC projects by service provider. Issue is how service receiver can avail Cenvat credit of capital goods used by the service provider in the works contract (EPC project).

This is possible with some planning. The invoice of machinery supplier will be in name of service provider (contractor). If the service receiver (principal) intends to avail Cenvat credit of capital goods used in works contract, the invoice should show name of service receiver as consignee, so that he can avail Cenvat credit. Strictly legally, even endorsed invoice is sufficient for availing Cenvat credit.

In Rajarambhau Patil SSK Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (208) ELT 372 (CESTAT), components and equipments required for sugar plants were purchased/manufactured by contractor and brought to the factory. Name of assessee was shown on the invoices. The sugar plant was erected at site and commissioned. It was held that Cenvat credit is available to assessee.

12.1-9 Is name of user of goods/receiver of services using inputs/input services necessary on Invoice ?

Usually department insists that the Invoice should be in name of manufacturer and Cenvat credit is denied if it is not so. Really, there is no provision in the rules that Invoice should indicate name of buyer who is using the material contained in the Invoice. In fact, such condition would be incorrect, as Excise Duty is on 'manufacture' and 'ownership' is irrelevant, e.g. when a job worker manufactures goods from the raw material supplied by a trader, the job worker has to pay duty on raw material cost plus job work charges. In such cases, it is natural that he will be eligible to avail Cenvat on input supplied by the trader. This can be done only on basis of Invoice of raw material which would obviously be in name of the trader.

Rule 9(1)(a) of Cenvat Credit Rules only specifies that Invoice issued by manufacturer of inputs is an eligible document to avail Cenvat. The rule does not require that invoice should be in name of manufacturer/service receiver.

In Nirayu P Ltd. v. CCE (2012) 34 STT 543 = 18 taxmann.com 270 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that name and address of service recipient is not one of the mandatory requirements under rule 9 and is a condonable omission - same view in Craft Corner Papers v. CCE (2013) 39 STT 865 = 29 taxmann.com 71 (CESTAT), where it was held that in such case, verification may be done by AC/DC as per proviso to rule 9(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

In Essar Oil v. CCE (2014) 309 ELT 336 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit can be availed even if the invoice is in name of contractor/owner.

Requirement of name and address of person receiving the service in bill is not mandatory for purpose of Cenvat credit - Novosymes South Asia P Ltd. v. CCE (2014) 74 VST 144 (CESTAT SMB).

In CCE v. Goodlass Nerolac Paints 1986 (26) ELT 57 (CEGAT) = 1986 (8) ECR 639 - same view in 1990 (45) ELT 701 (CEGAT), it has been held that the Invoice need not show the manufacturer (i.e. user of input) as consignee as the rules do not prescribe such a condition. Such a condition cannot be prescribed by administrative orders and such orders/instructions are not legally enforceable - same view in Deputy General Manager (Taxation), BHEL v. CCE (2007) 211 ELT 135 (CESTAT SMB).

In Prakash Fabricators & Galvanizers (P.) Ltd. v. CCE - 1994 (74) ELT 319 (CEGAT), it was observed : 'The Invoice will be in name of manufacturer if he has himself purchased the goods. However, indeed, Cenvat is available on all inputs, whether or not these are purchased by manufacturer. Cenvat can be availed even if inputs are received by manufacturer and duty is paid on final product manufactured by job worker'. - same view in Mahadev Industries v. CCE 2000 (115) ELT 452 (CEGAT), where it was indeed rightly held that ownership of inputs is not required for purpose of Cenvat credit. The credit is not deniable if inputs purchased by buyer are supplied free of cost to job worker - same view in Suntech Glass P Ltd. v. CCE 2006 (199) ELT 517 (CESTAT SMB).

CCE 2001(128) ELT 496 (CEGAT SMB), it was held that Cenvat credit being a beneficial piece of legislation, department is expected to take a liberal view in case of technical violations but certainly guard against violations of grave nature.

Majestic Auto (2010) 25 STT 293 (CESTAT SMB), the invoice mentioned name of brand name owned of manufacturer (e.g. Hero Puch or Hero Motors) and the address, and not name of the company. It was held that when there is no dispute that goods suffered duty and are used in manufacture and invoice indicates ownership of goods, minor defect is ignorable and Cenvat is allowable.

Invoice in different name - Name of service recipient is not an essential requirement for availment of Cenvat credit. Cenvat credit cannot be denied on that count - Akshar Courier Service v. CCE (2013) 42 GST 293 = 33 taxmann.com 410 (CESTAT).

Mistake in description of goods - In Omax Autos v. CCE (2012) 35 STT 379 = 20 taxmann.com 772 (CESTAT), invoice described the goods as CR sheets though goods actually received were HR sheets. It was held that Cenvat credit cannot be denied on this ground.

In Larsen & Toubro v. CCE 2001(127) ELT 807 (CEGAT SMB), it was held that assessee should not be penalised (by denying Cenvat credit) for mistake of seller of goods.

10.1-2 Invoice for distribution of credit by input service distributor

The 'input service distributor' should issue a 'Invoice, Bill or Challan' on monthly basis after consolidating the service tax paid on services received during the month.

Requirements of Invoice, Bill or Challan - As per rule 4A(2) of Service Tax Rules, requirements of the Invoice, Bill or Challan of input service distributor are as follows :

It shall be signed by authorised person.

The document should be for each recipient of the credit distributed.

Document should be serially numbered.

The invoice should contain following details :

(i)

Name, address and registration number of the person providing input services and Serial Number and date of invoice, Bill or challan issued by service provider under rule 4A(1)

(ii)

Name and address of input service distributor

(iii)

Name and address of the recipient of the credit distributed

(iv)

Amount of credit distributed

Thus, details of all invoices of input services are required to be given, which is going to be very cumbersome for large offices and will be administratively difficult.

For example, a company with HO at Nariman Point, Mumbai has factories at Pune and Chennai and has a premise providing services at Delhi. If the turnover ratio of the three units in 40:35:25, it will have to distribute Cenvat credit of service tax on input services in the ratio of 40:35:25, by preparing three invoices every month. In each invoice, details of all input invoices and ratio to which tax on input services have been allocated to each unit should be given.

In Krishna Wire Products v. CCE 2003 (158) ELT 491 (CESTAT), the goods were dispatched directly to place of manufacturer-buyer directly from place of import, but the dealer's invoice showed that goods were dispatched from godown of the dealer. However, there was co-relation between duty paying documents and invoice of dealer. It was held that buyer can avail Cenvat is available, so long as duty paid nature of goods is not in dispute. In Bellary Steels v. CCE 2003 (157) ELT 324 (CESTAT), the applicant was manufacturer as well as dealer. The purchased goods were dispatched directly but it was shown as received in factory. Invoice was raised by the assessee as if he is manufacturer. This was done as the assessee did not want buyers to know who is the actual manufacturer. Thus, though the procedure was wrong, there was no loss to revenue. Hence, penalty imposed was set aside. [Lucky they got relief. Otherwise, it is a border line case, as assessee had thrown all prescribed procedures to the wind].

In V K Enterprises v. CCE (2010) 249 ELT 462 (CESTAT), goods were neither received nor supplied. Only invoices were issued (to pass on credit). It was rightly held that penalty is imposable.

a gate pass, the gate pass book was required to be authenticated by Excise Officer. Later, in April 1994, gate pass was replaced by invoice and pre-authentication by excise officer was replaced by self authentication. A person who authenticates invoice at the top can also sign the invoice at bottom. This did not seem to serve any useful purpose. Thus, 'authentication' was a hangover of the past. It took 16 years to department to get over the hangover]. Invoice should be in book form - Rule 11(4) of Central Excise Rules [earlier rule 52A(7)] refers to 'Invoice Book'. Hence, invoices should be in book form i.e. bound form. Original and duplicate should be delivered to the consignee and triplicate copy should be retained in the Invoice Book. The invoices can be 'loose leaf' only if Invoices are computerised. Rule 11(3) [earlier rule 52A(3)] states that Invoice shall be marked as ORIGINAL FOR BUYER etc.

Invoice can be taken out for typing - When invoices are type written, the leafs have to be first taken out from book for typing. In such cases, the triplicate copy should be retained in bound book form. - Chapter 4 Part I Para 5.4 of CBE&C's CE Manual, 2005.

Cenvat credit cannot be denied for minor defects - Cenvat credit cannot be denied for minor defects in invoice. See case law under Cenvat.

Invoice required even for exempted goods - Invoice is required for clearance of all 'excisable goods'. The manufactured goods continue to be 'excisable goods' even if they are chargeable to 'Nil' rate of duty or are exempt from duty. Thus, 'excise invoice' is required even if goods are exempt from duty. However no 'invoice' is required if goods are not 'excisable goods'. In CCE v. Pawan Tyres P Ltd. 1998 (101) ELT 140 (CEGAT) and CCE v. Govind Rubber Ltd. 1998(102) ELT 67 (CEGAT), it was held that 'clearance' means removal of both dutiable and exempt goods from approved premises. Both dutiable and exempt goods are 'excisable goods'.

Invoice required only for removal from factory and not from dealer's godown - Excise Invoice is required only for removal of goods from factory. There is no such requirement in respect of goods removed from a dealer's place. A transporter carrying goods delivered by a dealer is under no obligation to produce any duty paying document. - Inland Road Service v. CCE - 1992 (60) ELT 571 (CEGAT). All goods lying in market are presumed to be duty paid. [for case law - refer under 'Demand']

Provisions in respect of computerisation of Invoices - Computerisation of Invoices is freely permitted and no permission is required. If running stationary is used, the stationary should be pre-printed with distinctive names and marks of the assessee. After invoices are prepared, triplicate copy shall be retained in bound book form. - Chapter 4 Part I Para 5.4 of CBE&C's CE Manual, 2005.

If invoices are prepared on computer, generation of serial number by computer at the time of printing of invoice on blank stationery of computer is permitted. However, this is so only if the software is such that computer automatically generates number and same number cannot be generated more than once. - Chapter 4 Part I Para 3.3 of CBE&C's CE Manual, 2005.

In case of computerised invoices, authentication at top and signing of invoice at bottom can be done simultaneously. As per earlier instructions, estimated serial number of invoices likely to be used should be intimated.

No specific requirement that Invoice should accompany goods upto destination - Earlier rule 52A(2) provided that duplicate copy of invoice should be produced en route to destination from the factory. Now, there is no parallel provision in new rules. Hence, in the opinion of author, goods cannot be confiscated merely because they are not accompanied by Invoice. Of course, it is highly advisable to ensure that goods are accompanied by duty paying documents, which in any case, are required under provisions of law relating to sales tax, octroi, entry tax, Motor Vehicles Act etc.

Direct dispatch of goods from manufacturer or importer to final consignee

17.4-2 Often, a person procures inputs or capital goods from a manufacturer or registered dealer but these are to be directly despatched to consignee. In such cases, following are the provisions.

Manufacturer to job worker of buyer-manufacturer - If a buyer-manufacturer or provider of output services purchases the inputs and intends to send the same directly to premises of job worker, the invoice of supplier-manufacturer should indicate name of job worker as consignee - second proviso to rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2015.

41.4

Cenvat on Goods purchased from trader

When the inputs are purchased directly from factory of original manufacturer, there is proof regarding amount of duty paid, in the form of Invoice of manufacturer. If goods are imported directly by manufacturer (who is user of inputs), Bill of Entry is proof of payment of CVD.

However, sometimes, goods are purchased from depot/consignment agent of the manufacturer and not directly from the factory. In some cases, indigenous or imported goods (inputs or capital goods) are purchased by the user of inputs (who wants to avail Cenvat) through trade channel i.e. wholesaler and retailer.

In such cases, a provision has been made to allow dealers/depots/consignment agents to issue Invoice to enable manufacturer (buyer of inputs) to avail Cenvat credit. This Invoice will be documentary evidence enabling the manufacturer to avail Cenvat credit.

All dealers/depots/consignment agents issuing invoice for Cenvat purposes will have to register with central excise authorities under Rule 9 of CE Rules. Only first stage and second stage dealers are allowed to issue Cenvatable Invoices.

41.4-1 Direct dispatch of goods by manufacturer i.e. transit sale

In certain cases, direct dispatch of goods without bringing in the premises of dealer is permitted.

Direct dispatch from manufacturer to final buyer, but sale is through dealer i.e. Transit sale - If whole consignment is despatched to buyer from manufacturer, Cenvat will be permissible, if name of the final buyer is shown as consignee. (Invoice will be in name of dealer). The consignee can avail Cenvat on the basis of duplicate copy of manufacturer issued under rule 11 (that time rule 52A). In such cases, the goods need not be brought to the premises of registered person. Invoice of Registered person (dealer) is not required for availing Cenvat by the consignee -CBE&C Circular No. 96/7/95-CX dated 13-2-1995.

This was also held permissible in CCE v. SSPE Cotton 1999(106) ELT 102 (CEGAT), SWILL Ltd. v. CCE (2008) 232 ELT 802 (CESTAT SMB), CCE v. REC Ispat (2009) 240 ELT 101 (CESTAT).

41.4-2 Buyer cannot be penalised for dealer's mistake or wrong doing

In Elveety Industries v. CCE 2001(130) ELT 199 (CEGAT SMB), assessee had taken Cenvat credit on basis of dealer's invoice. The dealer had taken credit on basis of original invoice of manufacturer (and not on duplicate copy of invoice as was required during that time). It was held that assessee cannot be denied Cenvat credit even if dealer had taken credit wrongly. - similar views in CCE v. Unichem Trading Co. 1998(102) ELT 284 (CEGAT).

Assessee buying goods from registered dealer cannot be expected to go beyond checking identity and address of manufacturer or supplier. He cannot examine whether supplier/manufacturer has actually paid the duty - Transpek Industry v. CCE (2010) 249 ELT 91 (CESTAT SMB).

41.4-3 Receiver not liable if supplier does not pay duty or service tax

CBE&C, vide Circular No. 766/82/2003-CX dated 15-12-2003, has clarified that Cenvat should not be denied to user-manufacturer as long as bona fide nature of the consignee's transaction is not doubted. Further, if the manufacturer-supplier has received payment from the buyer in respect of goods supplied including excise duty, action should be initiated against manufacturer-supplier u/ss 11D and 11DD - same view in Prachi Poly Products v.
