In the case of Marmagoa Steel Ltd. (supra), CENVAT credit of CVD paid on certain inputs imported by one M/s. Essar Gujarat Ltd. was claimed by M/s. Marmagoa Steel Ltd. on the basis of three Bills of Entry. The credit was sought to be denied on the ground that the Bills of Entry were not endorsed in favour of M/s. Marmagoa Steel Ltd. The Hon'ble High Court, after finding evidence of payment of CVD on the imported inputs and also evidence of the inputs having been received by M/s. Marmagoa Steel Ltd. and utilized in their factory, took the view that the credit was admissible. In the present case, the Department has no case that the imported capital goods were not received in the appellant's factory or not used for the purpose of manufacturing excisable goods. The limited ground raised for denying CENVAT credit to the appellant is that the endorsed Bill of Entry is not one of the documents prescribed under Rule 9 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. It is interesting to note that, in the case of Marmagoa Steel Ltd., the Department wanted the Bills of Entry to be endorsed in favour of that company so that the said company can claim CENVAT credit of the CVD paid thereon. The Hon'ble High Court found no provision of law for such endorsement of Bill of Entry. There is no such provision under the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 either. Nevertheless, this was not the relevant consideration for the Hon'ble High Court to take a view in favour of the above company. The Court took note of the fact that the inputs were duly received in the factory and used in the manufacture of excisable products. On this basis, regardless of the nature of the Bills of Entry, the party was held to be eligible for CENVAT credit. In the instant case, it is not even the case of the Department that the capital goods in question were not received in the appellant's factory and not used for manufacture of excisable products. In these circumstances, I am of the view that the CENVAT credit of the CVD paid on the capital goods cannot be denied to the appellant on the ground alleged in the show-cause notice. In the case of Khandelwal Laboratories Ltd. (supra) cited by the learned Additional Commissioner (AR), the Hon'ble High Court was remanding a case to this Tribunal for taking fresh decision on a similar issue in the light of the Court's earlier judgment in Marmagoa Steels Ltd. v. UOI. The decision in Khandelwal Laboratories Ltd. case can be seen as a reaffirmation of the view taken in Marmagoa Steels Ltd. case. Nothing in favour of the revenue flows from the decision cited by the learned Additional Commissioner (AR).

10.1-1 Concept of Input Service Distributor is compulsory w.e.f. 1-4-2012 if assessee has more than one factories or places of provision of service

As per Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules as existing upto 31-3-2012, the Cenvat Credit could be distributed by Input Service Distributor in any ratio. Only restriction was that Cenvat credit distributed should not be more than available credit.

However, after 1-4-2012, the distribution is required to be on basis of turnover.

Assessee having only one factory or place of provision of service - Sometimes, an assessee has offices at various places but accounting is done centrally in the factory. Sometimes, there are various factories of assessee but accounting is done in main factory.

In such cases, in my opinion, if assessee has only one factory and/or one centralised registration of service tax, the HO or branches need not be registered and all Cenvat credit can be availed in the factory or place where centralised registration has been taken.

The reason is that Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules reads, 'The input service distributor may distribute the Cenvat credit'. 'May' cannot be read as 'must'. It is nowhere stated that the utilisation should be only through mechanism of Input Service Distributor. A facility cannot be a compulsion.

In CIT v. Mahendra Mills 2000 AIR SCW 1016 = AIR 2000 SC 1960 = 243 ITR 56 = 109 Taxman 225 (SC), it was observed, 'A privilege cannot be to a disadvantage and an option cannot become an obligation'.

In Durferrit Asea v. CCE (2010) 258 ELT 414 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that if assessee has only one manufacturing unit, HO need not be registered and Cenvat credit can be taken at factory even if invoices are with address of Head Office. Rule 7 is not compulsory if assessee is not inclined to do so.

In Manipal Advertising Services v. CCE (2010) 25 STT 30 (CESTAT), branch offices were not registered with service tax authorities. Invoices were with address of branch, but payment of made from registered premises. It was held that Cenvat credit is available at HO which had Centralised registration as it had centralised accounting system. It was held that Cenvat credit is available even if address on invoice is of branch office.

Invoice of service in name of HO is eligible. It is not necessary that HO should be registered as Input Service Distributor (when there is only one factory) - CCE v. Samita Conductors (2012) 278 ELT 492 (CESTAT SMB) * Valco Industries Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 42 GST 165 = 31 taxmann.com 360 = 286 ELT 54 (CESTAT SMB).

If assessee has only one manufacturing unit, registration as Input service Distributor is not required. Assessee can take Cenvat credit even if invoice is with address of Head Office - National Plastic Industries v. CCE (2012) 35 STT 193 = 20 taxmann.com 132 (CESTAT) * Bloom Dekor v. CCE (2013) 38 STT 336 = 29 taxmann.com 357 (CESTAT SMB).

In Doshion Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 288 ELT 291 (CESTAT), it was held that since assessee could distribute Cenvat Credit in any ratio upto 31-3-2012, the HO could distribute credit to its unit without registration as Input Service Distributor.

In WNS Global Services v. CCE (2013) 30 taxmann.com 208 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is allowable even if assessee was not registered as Input Service Distributor.

Input Service Distributor

22.6 A manufacturer or service provider may have head office/regional office at different place/s. The services may be received at head office/regional office, but ultimately, these will be indirectly used for manufacture or providing output service.

Similarly, a principal manufacturer (brand name owner) may send inputs to job worker who is manufacturing goods under brand name of brand name owner. These goods will be supplied by job worker to principal manufacturer. If the goods are covered under MRP valuation provisions, duty will be payable by job worker on basis of MRP. However, many of input services received by principal manufacturer are indirectly used by the job worker.

Provision has been made to avail Cenvat credit of services received and paid for at head office/regional office. Such head office/regional office can be registered with Central Excise as 'Input Service Distributor' and it can issue invoice on the manufacturer or producer or service provider or outsourced manufacturing unit [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

Who is 'input service distributor' - As per rule 2(m) of Cenvat Credit Rules, "input service distributor" means (a) an office managing the business of manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service, (b) which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services (c) issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider or an outsourced manufacturing unit, as the case may be. [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016].

An office of assessee (manufacturer or service provider) is 'Input Service Distributor' if it satisfies all the three aforesaid requirements. It is not that each and every office of assessee is 'Input Service Distributor' and must register. The office should be registered as 'Input Service Distributor' only if it wants to distribute. There is no law that 'distribution' is the only way of availing Cenvat credit of services received at office of assessee. There are various documents eligible for availing Cenvat credit. Invoice/challan issued by 'Input Service Distributor' is only one of the specified document.

In Jaypee Rewa Plant v. CCE (2007) 218 ELT 576 (CESTAT SMB), regional marketing office was registered as Input Service Distributor and credit was distributed to manufacturing units. In prima facie view, the distribution was held as correct.

Outsourced manufacturing unit - 'Outsourced manufacturing unit' means a job-worker who is liable to pay duty on the value determined under rule 10A of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000 on the goods manufactured for the input service distributor or a manufacturer who manufactures goods, for the input service distributor under a contract, bearing the brand name of such input service distributor and is liable to pay duty on the value determined under section 4A of the Excise Act. [Explanation 4 to rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

Document eligible for Cenvat credit - As per rule 9(1)(g); 'invoice, bill or challan' issued by an 'input service distributor' under rule 4A of Service Tax Credit Rules is an eligible document for purpose of taking Cenvat credit.

Therefore for claiming the modvat credit the end user of the goods covered by the invoices has to satisfy the two conditions. Firstly, that the dealer who issued the invoice or invoices is a registered one, under Rule 174 of the Central Excise Rules and secondly that the goods covered by the invoice or invoices were intended to be used or had been actually used in the production of final product. If the very first condition regarding the registration of the dealer does not stand proved, the end user of the goods cannot claim modvat credit on the basis of the invoices on the simple ground that the goods were intended to be used or had been actually used in the product of final product, as in the invoice proforma under Rule 57-G or 57-T appended by the Board as annexure '2E' to the Central Excise Rules, the details regarding the Central Excise registration No., Sales Tax Registration, Income Tax Registration numbers besides other details regarding the goods, had to be mentioned by the dealer issuing the invoice. It is for end user of the goods before making the purchase to satisfy himself that the dealer with whom he is dealing is registered under the Central Excise Act. If he purchases the goods from an unregistered dealer, then he has to blame himself and not the Revenue department, when he is disallowed modvat credit in respect thereof. He cannot be legally permitted to take the benefit of modvat credit scheme for having simply shown that the goods had been used by him in the manufacture of the final product. The Revenue Officer in that case has no discretion or power to allow the modvat credit and to waive the mandatory condition regarding registration of the dealer who issued the invoice to the end user of the goods under Rule 57-G.

12. In the light of what has been discussed above, invoice/invoices issued by a dealer who had failed to get himself registered upto 31.12.94 cannot be legally treated as a valid document under Rules 57-GG, 57-T and 52-A for claiming modvat credit. Consequently, the law laid down in Sandish Combine Pvt. Ltd. Vs. CCE, Pune, CCE Chandigarh Vs. Colour Coats, Pearl Industries Vs. CCE Raipur, Bengal Safety Industries Vs. CCE, Shiv Iron & Brass Works to the contrary, cannot be held to be correct.

14. The controversy in this issue relates to the admissibility of the endorsed invoices as valid document for claiming modvat credit after 1.4.94. 15. Prior to the issuance of Notification No. 15/94 dated 30.3.94, gate passed besides Bill of Entry, AR-1 or any other document, as may be prescribed by the Central Board of Excise & Customs (CBEC), were accepted as valid documents under Rule 57-G of the Central Excise Rules for claiming modvat credit. Two endorsements on the gate pass were also made permissible by the CBEC vide [circular]dated 8.11.94 but thereafter vide Notification No. 15/94 dated 30.3.94 invoices in place of gate passes had been prescribed as valid documents alongwith AR-1 or Bill of Entry under Rule 57-G by amending this Rule, for claiming modvat credit. However, in order to avoid any inconvenience, difficulty to the genuine end user of the goods, it was made clear through Notification No. 16/94 dated 30.3.94 that modvat credit on the strength of gate passes issued before 1.4.94 could be taken till or before 30.6.94.

They have, further contended that by making endorsement on the invoices, the character of the invoices would not stand altered or changed as the goods covered by the invoices would remain duty paid and the use of those goods can be verified by the department before allowing modvat credit to the concerned assessee.

There was no dispute that the goods in question were received by the assessee and were used in the manufacture of the final product and duly recorded in the register. However, the Assistant Commissioner should ensure that inputs/capital goods have suffered duty and are being used/are to be used in the process of manufacture. In the instant case, there was no dispute that inputs/capital goods had suffered duty and were used in the manufacture of final products. 40.4

Input Service Distributor

A manufacturer or service provider may have head office/regional office at different place/s. The services may be received at head office/regional office, but ultimately, these will be indirectly used for manufacture or providing output service.

Similarly, a principal manufacturer (brand name owner) may send inputs to job worker who is manufacturing goods under brand name of brand name owner. These goods will be supplied by job worker to principal manufacturer. If the goods are covered under MRP valuation provisions, duty will be payable by job worker on basis of MRP. However, many of input services received by principal manufacturer are indirectly used by the job worker.

Provision has been made to avail Cenvat credit of services received and paid for at head office/regional office. Such head office/regional office can be registered with Central Excise as 'Input Service Distributor' and it can issue invoice on the manufacturer or producer or service provider or outsourced manufacturing unit [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

If assessee intends to use the facility, he has to apply for registration in form ST-1.

In my view, registration and distribution of Cenvat credit are independent aspects. Even if registration was obtained later, Cenvat credit of prior period at HO/branches can be distributed, if otherwise eligible.

Who is 'input service distributor' - As per rule 2(m) of Cenvat Credit Rules, "input service distributor" means (a) an office managing the business of manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service, (b) which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services (c) issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider or an outsourced manufacturing unit, as the case may be. [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016].

An office of assessee (manufacturer or service provider) is 'Input Service Distributor' if it satisfies all the three aforesaid requirements. It is not that each and every office of assessee is 'Input Service Distributor' and must register. The office should be registered as 'Input Service Distributor' only if it wants to distribute. There is no law that 'distribution' is the only way of availing Cenvat credit of services received at office of assessee. There are various documents eligible for availing Cenvat credit. Invoice/challan issued by 'Input Service Distributor' is only one of the specified document.

Outsourced manufacturing unit - ' Outsourced manufacturing unit' means a job-worker who is liable to pay duty on the value determined under rule 10A of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000 on the goods manufactured for the input service distributor or a manufacturer who manufactures goods, for the input service distributor under a contract, bearing the brand name of such input service distributor and is liable to pay duty on the value determined under section 4A of the Excise Act. [Explanation 4 to rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

Document eligible for Cenvat credit - As per rule 9(1)(g); 'invoice, bill or challan' issued by an 'input service distributor' under rule 4A of Service Tax Credit Rules is an eligible document for purpose of taking Cenvat credit.

In Shriram Pistons v. CCE (2012) 281 ELT 90 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is allowable on the basis of letter issued by Head Office (as Input Service Distributor) even if not mentioned as invoice or challan, if it contains all required details.

Distribution of credit even if invoices prior to registration as ISD - There is no bar in rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules for distributing of credit of invoices prior to date of registration as Input Service Distributor - Beico Industries v. Storage of inputs outside the factory

21.2-2 Inputs should be stored within the factory. However, if manufacturer is unable to store the inputs inside the factory for want of space, hazardous nature of goods etc., he can store the inputs outside the premises. The storage point will be treated as extension of the factory. Permission from Assistant / Deputy Commissioner is necessary. [Rule 8 of Cenvat Credit Rules].

Supervision charges or MOT (Merchant Overtime Charges) are not required to be collected from assessee for storage of finished goods outside the factory. However, any other condition to safeguard revenue may be imposed by Jurisdictional Commissioner before granting permission for storage of non-duty paid goods. - CBE&C circular No. 709/25/2003-CX dated 23-4-2003. [Instructions in case of storage of finished goods, but principle will apply to storage of inputs outside the factory also].

As per Pune Commissionerate TN No. 67/96 dated June 96, a register in prescribed form has to be maintained at the godown as well as factory. Inputs from outside godown should move under challan in prescribed form. As per Chandigarh-II Commissionerate TN 13/97-CE dated 17-11-1997, intimation in D-3 form is necessary within 24 hours of receipt of each consignment. Monthly stock statement should be submitted to Range Office. Cenvat credit can be taken only when entire inputs covered by an invoice are received in the factory - similar procedure in CCE, Ahmedabad II TN 93/2004 [179 ELT T15].

No assessee would like to store goods outside factory except under compelling circumstances as storage outside is open to many vagaries of nature including theft, pilferage etc. Hence, shortage of space outside factory is an exceptional circumstance, and application for storage of goods outside factory should be considered, as per guidelines of CBE&C vide circular No. 206/40/96-CE dated 1-5-1996 - Anutone Accoustics v. CCE (2010) 250 ELT 590 (CESTAT).

HELD: There was no dispute that the goods in question were received by the assessee and were used in the manufacture of the final product and duly recorded in the register. The Central Board of Excise & Customs vide Circular No. 441/7/99-CX, dated 23-2-1999 clarified that in terms of sub-rule (11) in rule 57G, and sub-rule (13) of rule 57T of the erstwhile Central Excise Rules, 1944, the Assistant Commissioner of Central Excise may allow the credit of duty paid on inputs/capital goods in minor procedural lapses in filing the declaration or in the invoices/documents, based on which credit is to be taken. In the instant case, there was no dispute that inputs/capital goods had suffered duty and were used in the manufacture of final products. Accordingly, no reason was found to interfere with the order of the Commissioner (Appeals). The appeal filed by the revenue was to be rejected. [Para 4]

[Para 9] For availing the credit of duty, what is required to be established under rule 57G is that the inputs received are in fact duty paid. The procedure set out in rule 57G is to ensure that the credit is taken on the basis of duty paid documents. The bill of entry is one such document set out in rule 57G. The said rule does not require that the bill of entry should be in the name of the person claiming credit of duty. It is not in dispute that the goods imported and cleared on payment of duty by one person can be used as inputs and credit of duty can be claimed by another person by establishing that the imported duty paid goods have been received as inputs and that the importer has not taken credit of that duty. In the instant case, it was established that the duty paid goods were received as inputs, however, the credit was denied on the ground that the Bill of entry was not endorsed in the name of the appellant. Rule 57G does not require that for taking credit of duty, the bill of entry should be endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the absence of any provision regarding endorsement on the bill of entry, the credit of duty cannot be denied on the ground that the bill of entry is not endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the facts of the instant case, the evidence on record i.e., the bills of entry together with the certificates issued by excise authorities, clearly showed that the goods imported and cleared under the bills of entry on payment of duty were received and utilized by the appellant as inputs in its factory and that the importer had not utilized the credit of duty paid on the said goods. Thus, the appellant had established that the inputs received under the bills of entry were duty paid and, therefore, the authorities below were not justified in denying the credit of duty to the appellant. Background

1. In industries like pharmaceuticals and agro-chemicals many times near-about expired goods, defective goods or damaged goods (for the sake of convenience let us say "defective goods") are sent again by various marketing depots (not registered under excise) for reprocessing. Usually it happens that the original goods have been manufactured by let us say factory A, B and C but the defective goods are returned to only one factory, let us say factory D for reprocessing. This is so because it will be impractical to send the defective goods for reprocessing to the very same factory which had manufactured the original goods due to logistical costs as well as difficulties in identifying them on one-to-one basis.

In such scenario, only document available will be copy of excise invoice issued by the original factory. Had the defective goods been returned to the same factory, manufacturer could have easily claimed CENVAT credit on the basis of originally issued invoice (as the excise invoice was issued by the same factory). However, here the case is different. Factory D wants to claim CENVAT credit of returned defective goods on the basis of excise invoice issued by other factories.

Critical Issues

2. Following critical issues arise in this set-up:

2.1 Whether CENVAT credit can be claimed by factory D when the invoices on the basis of which credit will be claimed has been issued by factory A, B and C ?

2.2 W.e.f. 11-07-2014, third proviso has been added to rule 4(1) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 which provides that credit cannot be claimed after a period of six months from the date of issuance of any document (in our case excise invoice) on the basis of which credit is claimed. In our case, as we are dealing with near-expired or defective goods, in all likelihood excise invoice issued by original manufacturer would have been dated beyond statutory period of six months. Issue is whether the third proviso will apply to the present case ?

2.3 What are the procedures one needs to follow to claim the said credit ?

3. Legal Analysis

3.1 To answer the first question, i.e., whether factory D can avail CENVAT credit on the basis of invoices issued by factory A, B and C for defective goods which are received back, one has to refer to rule 16 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. Relevant extract is reproduced below for ready reference:

"Rule 16. Credit of duty on goods brought to the factory.—(1) Where any goods on which duty had been paid at the time of removal thereof are brought to any factory for being re-made, refined, re-conditioned or for any other reason, the assessee shall state the particulars of such receipt in his records and shall be entitled to take CENVAT credit of the duty paid as if such goods are received as inputs under the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2002 and utilize this credit according to the said rules.

(2) If the process to which the goods are subjected before being removed does not amount to manufacture, the manufacturer shall pay an amount equal to the CENVAT credit taken under sub-rule (1) and in any other case the manufacturer shall pay duty on goods received under sub-rule (1) at the rate applicable on the date of removal and on the value determined under sub-section (2) of section 3 or section 4 or section 4A of the Act, as the case may be.

[Explanation.—The amount paid under this sub-rule shall be allowed as CENVAT credit as if it was a duty paid by the manufacturer who removes the goods.]

3.2 Careful reading of above rule provides that CENVAT credit will be available of any goods on which duty has been paid and are brought to any factory for re-making, refining, re-conditioning or for any other reason as inputs. Thus, only condition to be fulfilled for claiming credit is that duty should have been paid on said goods. It is not necessary that goods should be received back in the same factory. It can be received in any factory. Further, goods can be brought back for reprocessing under rule 16 even if shelf life has expired (CCE v. Rako Agrochem (P.) Ltd. 2010 (260) ELT 479 (Trib. - Delhi)). Thus, credit can be claimed of goods received by factory D on the basis of invoices issued by original manufacturers. One may also refer to Board's Circular 607/44/2001-CX, dated 13-12-2001 which confirms the above view. Thus, CENVAT credit can be claimed on basis of manufacturers invoice available with depot to the extent of quantity received by factory D.

12.2-2 Supplementary Invoice by supplier-manufacturer or service provider for differential excise duty/service tax

It is possible that a manufacturer who had supplied input/capital goods and who had paid duty on such inputs/capital goods may have to pay further duty on these inputs/capital goods on account of any demand or audit objection or finalisation of provisional assessment or on account of cost escalation granted by buyer or for any other reason. Similarly, a service provider may be liable to pay additional service tax at a later stage.

In such cases, the other manufacturer who is using that input/capital goods will get further credit of additional duty paid by the supplier of inputs/capital goods or additional service tax paid by service provider.

Suppose, S is a manufacturer of an input supplied to B. S had paid duty of Rs. 50,000 while supplying the input to B. On the basis of the duty paid by S, B had utilised Cenvat credit of Rs. 50,000. Now, if S has to pay further duty of say Rs. 15,000, B will be entitled to avail of extra Cenvat credit of Rs. 15,000.

The manufacturer (supplier) or service provider should issue supplementary invoice to buyer for this purpose, which is document eligible for availing Cenvat Credit [rule 9(1)(b) as existing right from 10-9-2004 and 9(1)(bb) as introduced w.e.f. 1-4-2011]

Such supplementary invoice can be issued by manufacturer from his factory or depot, dealer, consignment agent or importer. The supplementary invoice can be in respect of excise duty or CVD paid subsequently.

Similarly, a service provider can issue supplementary invoice.

Basic proposition is that credit has to be varied if amount of duty paid is varied.

The definition of "input" makes it clear that, "input" means all goods used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final products or not and includes lubricating oils, greases, cutting oils, coolants, accessories of the final products cleared along with the final product, goods used as paint, or as packing material, or as fuel, or for generation of electricity or steam used in or in relation to manufacture of final products or for any other purpose, within the factory of production. [Para 8]

The word "factory" has been defined in the Central Excise Act at section 2(e). It is an inclusive definition. For the purpose of Central Excise Act, a 'factory' means more than one premises. [Para 9]

Rule 6, of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 makes it clear that the CENVAT Credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of goods which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods. However, exception is carved out in sub-Rule (2). Sub-Rule (2) of Rule 6 provides- where a manufacturer or provider of output service avails CENVAT Credit in respect of any inputs except the input intended to be used as fuel and manufactures such final products or provides such output service which are chargeable to duty or tax as well as exempted goods or services, then, an obligation is cast on the assessee to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory or input and input service meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service and the quantity of input meant for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services. However he would be entitled to CENVAT credit only on that quantity of input or input service which is intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods. Therefore, it is clear that the assessee manufacturer is entitled to CENVAT Credit on "inputs" which is used in the manufacture of dutiable goods. [Para 11]

In view of clear language in the statutory provisions coupled with the fact that the factory includes more than one premises to be eligible for CENVAT Credit, an assessee has to use the input in the manufacture of dutiable goods in his factory. If the factory includes more than one unit and if the assessee uses this input in the manufacturing of excisable goods in both the units, he would be entitled to CENVAT Credit. [Para 12]

The definition of 'input' brings within its fold the inputs used for generation of electricity or steam, provided such electricity or steam is used within the factory of production for manufacture of final products or for any other purpose. Therefore, it follows the term "within the factory of production" cannot be confined to a single unit. In view of the definition of factory in the act which means more than one premises, it has to be construed as the factory owned by the assessee. If the assessee owns more than one unit, all the units if they are situated at a place would constitute "a factory". If the electricity or steam generated within the factory of production means within the factory premises which may include more than one unit. If such electricity or steam generated within the factory of production is utilized by the assessee in more than one unit and if those units are manufacturing excisable goods, then, the assessee would be entitled to the benefit of CENVAT credit to the entire extent of utilization of such electricity or steam in all the units of its factory premises. Therefore, whatever goes into generation of electricity or steam which is placed within the factory which may consists of more than one unit would be an input for the purposes of obtaining credit on the duty payable thereon. [Para 15]

In the instant case, the assessee is having two units; one DTA unit and another EOU unit. Both are situated in the same factory premises. Both are manufacturing excisable goods. The assessee has purchased furnace oil from which, the steam is generated within the said factory premises. The said steam is utilized by the assessee in manufacturing excisable goods in both the units which are situated within the same compound, which falls within the definition of the word "factory" and therefore, the assessee is entitled to CENVAT credit in respect of entire volume of steam used in the manufacture of excisable goods by both the units. That is precisely what the appellate authorities have held and granted relief to the assessee. [Para 16]

Hence, impugned order was confirmed. [Para 17]

4. On the basis of aforesaid case law and statutory, it can be concluded as follows.

Eligibility of Transit sale – In case of transit sale, the Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer, which is eligible document under rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I) of Cenvat Credit Rules. That rule does not require that invoice should be in name of the end user.This has been confirmed in the CBE&C circulars issued in 1995 and 1996. These circulars are not statutory provisions. The circulars only explain and confirm the legal provision. These are still valid as there is no change in that rule.

Intermediary dealer need not be registered - Since Cenvat credit is available on basis of invoice of manufacturer itself, the intermediary dealer is not required to issue any Cenvatable invoice. Hence, he need not be registered under Central Excise.

Invoice need not be in name of manufacturer – Tribunal has consistently held that invoice need not be in name of manufacturer, Even showing name of end user as consignee is not a statutory requirement. There is no such requirement of rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

Proviso to rule 11(2) is only additional facility to registered dealer – The proviso to rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2015 is only additional facility to registered dealer. That rule is applicable only to registered dealers and not to unregistered dealers. The additional facility does not mean that the earlier provisions become invalid.

The proviso is added 'to increase ease of doing business' and not to create more hurdles in business.

If assessee intends to be safe, he may inform department accordingly, though there is no such legal requirement.

12.1-9 Is name of user of goods/receiver of services using inputs/input services necessary on Invoice ?

Usually department insists that the Invoice should be in name of manufacturer and Cenvat credit is denied if it is not so. Really, there is no provision in the rules that Invoice should indicate name of buyer who is using the material contained in the Invoice. In fact, such condition would be incorrect, as Excise Duty is on 'manufacture' and 'ownership' is irrelevant, e.g. when a job worker manufactures goods from the raw material supplied by a trader, the job worker has to pay duty on raw material cost plus job work charges. In such cases, it is natural that he will be eligible to avail Cenvat on input supplied by the trader. This can be done only on basis of Invoice of raw material which would obviously be in name of the trader.

Rule 9(1)(a) of Cenvat Credit Rules only specifies that Invoice issued by manufacturer of inputs is an eligible document to avail Cenvat. The rule does not require that invoice should be in name of manufacturer/service receiver.

One of the documents on which Cenvat credit is allowed as mentioned in clause (a) of subject rule 9(1) is an invoice issued by manufacturer for clearance of inputs or capital goods from his factory. In the instant case, invoices, on which credit was disputed was issued by manufacturer and the appellant's name is clearly appearing as consignee. Therefore, the invoices in question squarely covered by clause (a) of sub-rule 1 of Rule 9. The Revenue's contention that in case of purchase of input from dealer, invoices should be issued by first stage dealer or second stage dealer, is not agreeable. Only in case where the input is purchased directly from a dealer on his invoices and the manufacturer invoices does not indicate the name of the recipient as consignee, the first stage dealer or second stage dealer, as case may be, who is registered with Central Excise, should issue invoices as provided under rule 11 of Central Excise Rules, 2002. However, in the instant case invoices on which credit was taken issued by manufacturer and appellant's name is appearing as consignee, in such cases credit is admissible on these invoices and there is no need of separate invoices to be issued by the registered dealer for taking credit. The contention of the Revenue that since appellant has not made payment for purchase of the input of the manufacturer supplier, Cenvat credit is not admissible, is absurd for the reason that manufacturer supplier as per the invoices, sold the goods to the dealers and in turn dealers sold the goods to appellant in such transactions there are sale purchase transactions is involved, i.e., one from manufacturer supplier to dealers and second from dealers to the appellant. Therefore, the appellant made payment to dealers and cannot make payment of the bills to manufacturer supplier. Therefore, contention of the Revenue on this count is not acceptable. However, for taking Cenvat credit on input it is not mandatory that payment towards purchase of the input has to be made. There are number of transactions in the trade such as procurement input from group company, sister concern on payment of duty, procurement of input for job work, etc. In such transaction there is no transaction of any payments towards supply of inputs. Despite this position, Cenvat credit is admissible and cannot be disputed so long input is duty paid, received in the factory and used in the manufacture. The appellant has correctly and legally availed the Cenvat credit on the invoices wherein appellant name is appearing as consignee and name of the dealers as buyer; therefore, the impugned order is set aside. 10.1-2 Invoice for distribution of credit by input service distributor

The 'input service distributor' should issue a 'Invoice, Bill or Challan' on monthly basis after consolidating the service tax paid on services received during the month.

Requirements of Invoice, Bill or Challan - As per rule 4A(2) of Service Tax Rules, requirements of the Invoice, Bill or Challan of input service distributor are as follows :

It shall be signed by authorised person.

The document should be for each recipient of the credit distributed.

Document should be serially numbered.

The invoice should contain following details :

(i)

Name, address and registration number of the person providing input services and Serial Number and date of invoice, Bill or challan issued by service provider under rule 4A(1)

(ii)

Name and address of input service distributor

(iii)

Name and address of the recipient of the credit distributed

(iv)

Amount of credit distributed

Thus, details of all invoices of input services are required to be given, which is going to be very cumbersome for large offices and will be administratively difficult.

For example, a company with HO at Nariman Point, Mumbai has factories at Pune and Chennai and has a premise providing services at Delhi. If the turnover ratio of the three units in 40:35:25, it will have to distribute Cenvat credit of service tax on input services in the ratio of 40:35:25, by preparing three invoices every month. In each invoice, details of all input invoices and ratio to which tax on input services have been allocated to each unit should be given.

On appeal to the Tribunal by the revenue:

HELD: The benefit of MODVAT credit could not be denied to the assessee merely on the ground that there was change in the address from Kota to Ghaziabad. Issues relating to CENVAT credit on inputs with reference to decided case laws

6. The issues relating to availing of CENVAT credit on inputs are discussed as below with reference to decided case laws:

6.1 Denial of credit :

6.1-1 In Rico Auto Industries Ltd. v. CCE 2003 (157) ELT 170 (Tri. - Delhi) - It was held that when inputs are subjected to certain processes and the processed inputs are cleared on payment of duty which is more than credit taken, credit cannot be denied on the ground that the processes undertaken by the assessee did not amount to manufacture.

6.1-2 In Markwell Paper Plast Private Ltd. v. CCE&CE 2012 (285) ELT 76 (Tri. - Delhi) - The Tribunal held that undisputedly the appellants used duty paid inputs for the production of their final product which was cleared to the customers on payment of excise duty. Admittedly, the department accepted the excise duty on the final product without any protest nor the appellants were informed that their final products were not subject to excise duty as it emerged from the process not amounting to manufacture as defined under Section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act. The department tried to justify the impugned order disallowing the CENVAT credit availed by the appellants on the inputs on the plea that the final product had not emerged from the process which could be termed as manufacture. Such an argument could not be sustained as it was against the tenets of equity and justice. The department having accepted that the excise duty on the final products could not be permitted to deny CENVAT credit on the inputs used for the manufacture of the final products on such a technical plea. If such an argument was allowed to sustain it would negate the entire object of the CENVAT credit scheme which had been put in place with a view to protect the assessee from double taxation. Thus, on this count also, the impugned orders were not sustainable.

6.1-3 In Indian Oil Corpn. Ltd. v. CCE 2013 (292) ELT 210 (Tri.- Mum) - The short question to be dealt with by the Tribunal was whether the credit of the duty paid on tin containers received in the packing unit of the assessee and used in the manufacture of their marketable product, viz., canned lubricating oil during the material period was liable to be denied to them? The Tribunal found that it was not in dispute that packing units were covered by a single registration, thereby meaning that both the units were parts of the registered factory. Receipt of containers in the packing unit during the said period was receipt of input in the factory. Hence, there was no question of denial of credit for the material period.

6.2 Generation of electricity or steam :

6.2-1 In Maruti Suzuki Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 22 STT 54 - The Supreme Court held that the definition of an 'input' brings within its fold inputs used for generation of electricity or steam used within the factory of production for manufacture of final products or for any other purpose. The important point to be noted was that, in the present case, excess electricity had been cleared by the assessee at the agreed rate from time-to-time in favour of its joint ventures, vendors, etc., for a price and had also cleared such electricity in favour of the grid for distribution. To that extent in the view of Supreme Court, the assessee was not entitled to CENVAT credit.

5.1 Rule of harmonious construction - In Jagdish Singh v. Lt. Governor [1997] AIR SCW 2106 = AIR 1997 SC 2239, it was observed -

"It is a cardinal principle of construction that efforts should be made in construing the different provisions, so that, each provision will have its play and in the event of any conflict a harmonious construction should be given. Further, a statute or a rule made thereunder should be read as a whole and one provision should be construed with reference to the other provision so as to make the rule consistent and any construction which would bring any inconsistency or repugnancy between one provision and the other should be avoided. One rule cannot be used to defeat another rule in the same Rules, unless it is impossible to effect harmonisation between them. - - A construction that reduces one of the provisions to a ‘dead letter’ is not a harmonious construction as one part is being destroyed and consequently, Court should avoid such construction". - similar views in British Airways Plc.v. UOI AIR 2002 SC 391 = 2001 AIR SCW 5197 = (2002) 2 SCC 95 = 139 ELT 6 (SC).

Input Service Distributor

7. A manufacturer or service provider may have head office/regional office at different place/s. The services may be received at head office/regional office, but ultimately, these will be indirectly used for manufacture or providing output service. Provision has been made to avail Cenvat credit of services received and paid for at head office/regional office. Such head office/regional office will be registered with Central Excise as ‘Input Service Distributor’ and it will have to issue invoice to the manufacturer or producer or service provider. They have to apply for registration in form ST-1.

7.1 Who is ‘input service distributor’ - As per rule 2(m), "input service distributor" means an office managing the business of manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service, which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services and issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider, as the case may be.

Document eligible for Cenvat credit - As per rule 9(1)(g); ‘invoice, bill or challan’ issued by an ‘input service distributor’ under rule 4A of Service Tax Credit Rules is an eligible document for purpose of taking Cenvat credit.

The word "factory" has been defined in the Central Excise Act at section 2(e). It is an inclusive definition. For the purpose of Central Excise Act, a 'factory' means more than one premises. [Para 9]

Rule 6, of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 makes it clear that the CENVAT Credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of goods which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods. However, exception is carved out in sub-Rule (2). Sub-Rule (2) of Rule 6 provides- where a manufacturer or provider of output service avails CENVAT Credit in respect of any inputs except the input intended to be used as fuel and manufactures such final products or provides such output service which are chargeable to duty or tax as well as exempted goods or services, then, an obligation is cast on the assessee to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory or input and input service meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service and the quantity of input meant for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services. However he would be entitled to CENVAT credit only on that quantity of input or input service which is intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods. Therefore, it is clear that the assessee manufacturer is entitled to CENVAT Credit on "inputs" which is used in the manufacture of dutiable goods. [Para 11]

In view of clear language in the statutory provisions coupled with the fact that the factory includes more than one premises to be eligible for CENVAT Credit, an assessee has to use the input in the manufacture of dutiable goods in his factory. If the factory includes more than one unit and if the assessee uses this input in the manufacturing of excisable goods in both the units, he would be entitled to CENVAT Credit. [Para 12]

Therefore, it follows the term "within the factory of production" cannot be confined to a single unit. In view of the definition of factory in the act which means more than one premises, it has to be construed as the factory owned by the assessee. If the assessee owns more than one unit, all the units if they are situated at a place would constitute "a factory". If the electricity or steam generated within the factory of production means within the factory premises which may include more than one unit. V.S. DATEY

Often, an assessee has office at a place different from the factory or place from which service is provided. Such small offices maintain only basic information. The accounting records including invoices, etc., are sent to main factory and final accounting and record-keeping is done in the main factory/office. Sometimes, office and main factory is at one place, but there are factories or places for provision of service in another places. In such cases, the input services received at main factory are recorded there itself and credit is availed in the main factory without ‘distributing’ to other factories or other places providing output services. It is learnt that in some cases, the department is taking a view that in such cases, registration as Input Service Distributor and distribution of credit is mandatory.

The issue involved is whether such registration and/or distribution is compulsory or optional.

It was also not in dispute that ‘E’ Ltd. had not taken credit of the duty paid on shredded steel scrap which was given on loan to the appellant. It was also not in dispute that the appellant had used the said shredded steel scrap taken on loan from ‘E’ Ltd. as inputs in its factory. The certificate issued by a Superintendent of Central Excise to the effect that ‘E’ Ltd. had not taken credit of duty paid on the said shredded steel scrap, was not doubted by the Excise authorities. Similarly, the certificate issued by another Superintendent to the effect that the quantity of shredded steel scrap received by the appellant from ‘E’ Ltd. had been used as inputs in the factory of the appellant, was also not doubted by the Excise authorities. In these circumstances, the appellant had established that the credit of duty on receipt of imported shredded steel scrap from ‘E’ Ltd. had been taken in accordance with law. [Para 9]

For availing the credit of duty, what is required to be established under rule 57G is that the inputs received are in fact duty paid. The procedure set out in rule 57G is to ensure that the credit is taken on the basis of duty paid documents. The bill of entry is one such document set out in rule 57G. The said rule does not require that the bill of entry should be in the name of the person claiming credit of duty. It is not in dispute that the goods imported and cleared on payment of duty by one person can be used as inputs and credit of duty can be claimed by another person by establishing that the imported duty paid goods have been received as inputs and that the importer has not taken credit of that duty. In the instant case, it was established that the duty paid goods were received as inputs, however, the credit was denied on the ground that the Bill of entry was not endorsed in the name of the appellant. Rule 57G does not require that for taking credit of duty, the bill of entry should be endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the absence of any provision regarding endorsement on the bill of entry, the credit of duty cannot be denied on the ground that the bill of entry is not endorsed in the name of the claimant. In the facts of the instant case, the evidence on record i.e., the bills of entry together with the certificates issued by excise authorities, clearly showed that the goods imported and cleared under the bills of entry on payment of duty were received and utilized by the appellant as inputs in its factory and that the importer had not utilized the credit of duty paid on the said goods. Thus, the appellant had established that the inputs received under the bills of entry were duty paid and, therefore, the authorities below were not justified in denying the credit of duty to the appellant. HELD: Rule 57G clearly shows that the credit of duty can be taken on inputs by establishing that the duty has been paid on the said inputs on the basis of documents such as invoice, AR-1, Bill on Entry, etc. In the instant case, it was not in dispute that the appellant had received imported shredded steel scrap from ‘E’ Ltd. on which countervailing duty had been paid by ‘E’ Ltd. Inclusive Part

5. The expression viz., ‘used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ in the specific/substantive part of the definition is so wide that it would cover innumerable items as ‘input’ and to avoid such contingency the Legislature has incorporated the inclusive part after the substantive part qualified by the place of use. For example, one of the categories mentioned in the inclusive part is ‘used as packing material’. Packing material by itself would not suffice till it is proved that the term is used in the course of manufacture of final product. Mere fact that the item is a packing material whose value is included in the accessible value of final product will not entitle the manufacturer to take credit. Oils and lubricants mentioned in the definition are required for smooth running of machines and, hence, they are included as they are used in relation to manufacture of final product. The intention of the Legislature is that inputs falling in the inclusive part must have nexus with the manufacture of the final product.

In Indo Rama Synthetics (India) Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (219) ELT 122 (Bom.), the High Court held that the credit of duty paid on the goods or fuel used in the generation of electricity is available, provided the electricity is used for the manufacture of final product. The use of electricity must have nexus with goods manufactured in the factory.

5.1 Primary packing material - In Wrigley India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (255) ELT 201 (Punj. & Har.), it was held that it is not a matter of dispute that chewing gum/bubble gums manufactured by the assessees are directly or primarily packed with the printed aluminium foils without tattoos. It means, putting a ‘boomer-tattoo’ in the package material of bubble gum is an additional step in aid used for promotional material and it is not termed as a packing material, as such, especially when it is depicted on the packing that ‘free tattoo inside’. The primary function of putting the ‘tattoo’ in the wrapped bubble gum is to promote the trade and to attract the children rather than to be used for the purpose of packing ‘tattoo’.

Again it is not a matter of dispute that these printed ‘tattoos’ are not used for initial packing in the real sense, rather they are wrapped. Therefore, it cannot possibly be said that the ‘Boomer-tattoo’ is used as initial packing material, meaning thereby the wrapper of the ‘tattoo’ on the bubble gum is not at all required in the form of primary packing. There is no direct and indirect use of the ‘tattoo’ in or in relation to the manufacture of the product, rather it is separately known tattoo in the market, has a separate identity, specific purpose of promotion of the product and for the purpose of advertisement. Hence, it is not a packing material and cannot be considered as inputs within the meaning and definition considered as ‘inputs’ as contemplated under the relevant Rules.

In CCE v. International Tractors Ltd. - 2010 (255) ELT 203 (Punj. & Har.), the respondent was the manufacturer of traction and tractor components. The components manufactured by the respondent were duly packed in boxes and thereafter were sold. The Tribunal had allowed the credit on the goods of full packing of boxes. It had been observed by the Tribunal that duty was paid on the boxes.

The revenue contended that the respondent never received inputs in the packing of boxes and in fact the goods were delivered to the respondent in pallets and, hence, the respondent was not entitled to any credit.

It was held that CESTAT could allow availment of CENVAT credit in respect of duty paid on the packing material.

Place of use

6. The third part of the definition of ‘input’ is the ‘place of use’. Rule 2(k)( i) mandatorily requires that the goods meant for input should be used in the process of manufacture within the premises of the factory. It is a condition precedent to avail CENVAT credit on ‘inputs’ that the product should be manufactured within the premises of the factory. But, at the same time, it is not mandatory for the output service provider to utilize the inputs within the premises of the output service provider. Even if the input is used outside the premises of the service provider, CENVAT credit is allowed for such inputs.

The High Court held that even as a matter of first principle on a plain and literal construction of rule 3(1) the Tribunal was not justified in holding that Deepak Fertilisers was not entitled to avail of the CENVAT credit in respect of services utilized in relation to ammonia storage tanks on the ground that they were situated outside the factory premises. The High Court further observed that rule 2(l) initially provides that input service means any services of the description falling in sub-clauses (i) and (ii). Rule 2(l) then provides an inclusive definition by enumerating certain specified services. Among those services were services pertained to the procurement of inputs and inward transportation of inputs. The first part of rule 2(l), inter alia , covers any services used by the manufacturer directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products. The inclusive part of the definition enumerates certain specified categories of services. Whereas rule 3(1) allows a manufacturer of final products to take credit of excise duty and service tax among others paid on any input or capital goods received in the factory of manufacture of the final product, insofar as any input service is concerned, the only stipulation is that it received the final product. This was needed to be read with the broad and comprehensive meaning of the expression 'input service' in rule 2(l).

The Court finally held that the input services in this case were used by Deepak Fertilisers, whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of the final products and the storage and use of Ammonia was an intrinsic part of that process.

4.1 Final verdict/Judgment - The High Court allowed the input tax credit on the services received in connection with the activity of installation of storage tanks.

Conclusion

5. A manufacturer/service provider uses capital goods such as plants and machinery, inputs such as raw materials and input services such as security services, management, maintenance or repair services, etc., to make a final product. The excise duty/service tax paid on any of these three items is credited and accumulated under a CENVAT credit account. Whenever the manufacturer has to pay duty on finished goods and service tax on output services, it can utilise the accumulated CENVAT credit for the payment, subject to fulfilment of certain conditions. This ensures that the inputs are taxed only once.

Input services also include services used in relation to: modernisation, renovation or repairs of a factory, premises of provider of output service or an office relating to such factory or premises, advertisement or sales promotion, market research, storage up to the place of removal, procurement of inputs, accounting, auditing, financing, recruitment and quality control, coaching and training, computer networking, credit rating, share registry, security, business exhibition, legal services, inward transportation of inputs or capital goods and outward transportation up to the place of removal.

Since inputs may be stored outside the factory as per rule 8 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, therefore, any services availed in relation to such storage should also be allowed as credit.

There is controversy raging in respect of eligibility of Cenvat credit in respect of transit sale through dealer not registered under Central Excise and also through dealer registered under Central Excise. The issues discussed in this article.

Background of the issue

1. Often the end user (manufacturer consumer) purchases goods through dealer and not through the original manufacturer. If the goods are purchased by dealer and then sold on piecemeal basis, there is provision to issue Cenvatable invoice by first stage dealer and second stage dealer.

However, when entire consignment is to be sold as it is, the dealer instruct the original manufacturer of excisable goods to dispatch the goods directly to the end used (consumer manufacturer). Invoice of Manufacturers invoice is in name of dealer as the buyer. Name and address of end user (manufacturer consumer) is shown as consignee.

The end user (consumer manufacturers) avail CENVAT credit on the basis of such invoice of original manufacturer.

This is standard practice, going on at least since 1995.

In the recent budget, a proviso has been added to rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules w.e.f. 1-3-2015, which reads as follows - "Provided also that if the goods are directly sent to any person on the direction of the registered dealer, the invoice shall also contain the details of the registered dealer as the buyer and the person as the consignee, and that person shall take CENVAT credit on the basis of the registered dealer's invoice:"

1.1 Controversy arising out of this proviso: On the basis of this proviso inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2015, a view has been expressed that the Cenvat credit cannot be availed in case of transit sale, if the intermediate buyer is not registered under Central Excise.

A view is also expressed by some assessees that Cenvat credit cannot be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer, if sale is through registered dealer. The registered dealer has to issue another Cenvatable invoice.

In my view, there is no such change in rules. In case of transit sale, Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer, even if the intermediate buyer is not registered dealer. Even if intermediate buyer is registered dealer, he need not issue Cenvatable invoice as Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer.

Reasons for my view are stated below.

Statutory provisions

2. Rule 9(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules prescribes that Cenvat Credit can be taken on the basis of any of the documents prescribed in that sub-rule. The relevant extract from the rule are as follows –

Rule 9(1) Documents and accounts - The CENVAT credit shall be taken by the manufacturer or the provider of output service or input service distributor, as the case may be, on the basis of any of the following documents, namely:–

(a)

An invoice issued by -

(i)

a manufacturer for clearance of— (I) inputs or capital goods from his factory or depot or from the premises of the consignment agent of the said manufacturer or from any other premises from where the goods are sold by or on behalf of the said manufacturer (II) inputs or capital goods as such

(ii)

not relevant

(iii)

not relevant

(iv)

a first stage dealer or a second stage dealer, as the case may be, in terms of the provisions of Central Excise Rules, 2002.

2.1 Invoice of manufacturer is eligible document for Cenvat credit: It can be seen that invoice issued by manufacturer for clearance of inputs or capital goods from his factory is eligible document for availing Cenvat credit, as per rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

The rule does not state that the invoice should be in name of buyer-manufacturer or consumer-manufacturer. The rule even does not state that name of end user (final consumer-manufacturer) should be shown in the invoice.

Of course, it has to be 'input' or 'capital goods' of the consumer-manufacturer.

2.2 Transit Sale through dealer not registered under Central Excise: In transit sale, goods are despatched directly from place of original manufacturer to final user manufacturer (end user) though invoice is in name of the intermediary dealer.

In that case, Cenvat credit is available on basis of invoice of manufacturer under rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I) of Cenvat Credit Rules itself.

INPUT SERVICE DISTRIBUTOR

In this article, the author has discussed the provisions relating to ‘input service distributor’ including amendment carried out in 2008.

Introduction

1. ‘Input service distributor’ is the beautiful and utilitarian concept introduced by the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. In this article, we shall discuss the provisions relating to ‘input service distributor’.

Definition

2. Rule 2(m ) of the Rules defines ‘input service distributor’ as under :—

"(m)‘Input service distributor’ means an office of the manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service, which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services and issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider, as the case may be;"

Important criteria for input service provider

3. Important criteria for input service provider are :—

(i)It has an office as the manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service. In other words, an office of manufacturer of excisable goods or taxable service provider can be registered as input service distributor.

(ii)It has to receive invoices towards purchase of services. The services might have been received by one of the units manufacturing goods or premises providing services or other offices.

(iii)It can issue invoice or bill or challan for the purpose of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the services to the manufacturing unit or service providing unit.

It is to be noted that the input service provider can be registered as head office, registered office, branch, depot, regional office, zonal office, etc.

Regional marketing office was registered as input service distributor and credit was distributed to manufacturing units. It was held by the Tribunal in its prima facie view, that the distribution was in order in Jaypee Rewa Plant v. CCE 2007 (218) ELT 576 (Delhi - Trib.).

It is possible that one company may have many input service distributors.

Example

4. ABC Ltd. has three manufacturing units. Its head office has taken Fire Insurance Policy covering the manufacturing units and paid insurance premium and service tax of Rs. 10,300. Head Office can distribute the service tax paid by it to the manufacturing units and manufacturing units can take the credit on receipt of Invoice from the head office and utilise this amount like any other Cenvat credit.

Conditions

5. Rule 7 deals with distribution of credit by input service distributor. The input service provider can distribute service tax paid by it subject to the following conditions :—

(i)The credit distributed shall not exceed the amount of service tax paid by it. (Is it possible to distribute more than the credit availed?)

(ii)The credit of service tax attributable to service used in an unit exclusively engaged in manufacture of exempted goods or providing of exempted services shall not be distributed.

It is important to note that there is no requirement to distribute the credit proportionately. The input service distributor can distribute to various units as the circumstances warrants. There is no rule regarding periodicity of distribution and it is advisable to distribute monthly.

Registration

6. Input service distributors have to obtain registration from the service tax authorities. They have to apply in Form No. ST-1 and have to obtain Registration Certificate in Form No. ST-2.

Maintenance of records

7. Rule 9 of the Rules deals with maintenance of records by the input service distributor. The records maintained by it must contain the following :—

(i)Serial number and date of the document on which the Cenvat credit is availed.

(ii)Service tax registration number and name of input service provider.

(iii)Description and value of input service.

(iv)Service tax credit availed.

(v)Basis of allocation/apportionment of credit amount.

(vi)Service tax utilised for distributing the credit.

(vii)Balance credit available for distribution.

Issue of Invoice

8. After making the payment of service charges and service tax, input service distributor can avail the credit provided service received is input service and distribute it to various manufacturing units or service providing units.

Rule 4A(2) of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 deals with the issue of invoice by the input service distributor. The invoice shall be serially numbered and contain the following particulars :

(i)the name, address and registration number of the person providing input services and the serial number and date of invoice;

(ii)the name and address of the input service distributor;

(iii)the name and address of the recipient of the credit distributed; and

(iv)the amount of the credit distributed.

2. As per rule 2(m ) of CENVAT Credit Rules, an entity is ‘input service distributor’ if it satisfies the following three conditions—

"(a )office managing the business of manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service,

(b )which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services and

(c )issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be,

there are factories or places for provision of service in another places. In such cases, the input services received at main factory are recorded there itself and credit is availed in the main factory without ‘distributing’ to other factories or other places providing output services.

It is learnt that in some cases, the department is taking a view that in such cases, registration as Input Service Distributor and distribution of credit is mandatory.

The issue involved is whether such registration and/or distribution is compulsory or optional. Who is Input Service Distributor ?

2. As per rule 2(m ) of CENVAT Credit Rules, an entity is ‘input service distributor’ if it satisfies the following three conditions—

"(a )office managing the business of manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service,

(b )which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services and

(c )issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider, as the case may be."

The word used is ‘and’. Thus, an entity is ‘input service distributor’ only if all the three conditions are satisfied. If an assessee has office or premises which receives invoices and it does not issue any invoice, bill or challan for distributing credit of service tax, it is not ‘Input Service Distributor’.

Service Tax (Registration of Special Category of Persons) Rules, 2005 issued vide Notification No. 27/2005-ST, dated 7-6-2005 provide for registration of ‘Input Service Distributor’. Rule 2(c) of these Rules states that ‘input service distributor’ shall have the meaning assigned to it in rule 2(m) of CENVAT Credit Rules.

It is, thus, clear that the Service tax (Registration of Special Category of Persons) Rules, 2005 apply when an entity falls within the definition of rule 2(m). If the office or main factory does not issue any invoice or challan for distribution of CENVAT credit, it does not fall within the definition of ‘Input Service Distributor’. In such case, the rules in respect of registration and issue of invoice by Input Service Distributor do not apply at all.

Provision is not a mandatory requirement

3. Rule 7 of the CENVAT Credit Rules uses the words ‘Input Service Distributor may distribute credit’. ‘May’ cannot be read as ‘must’.

Rule 9(1) of CENVAT Credit Rules gives list of seven types of documents eligible for availing CENVAT credit, out of which invoice of input service distributor is one of the eligible documents. Thus, the invoice of input service distributor is not the only eligible document for availing CENVAT credit. Credit can be availed on basis of other eligible documents also.

As discussed below, distribution can be in any ratio. Thus, even if main factory is registered as ‘Input Service distributor’ it can legally allocate entire CENVAT credit to itself, which would be an exercise in futility.

Facility cannot be a compulsion

4. ‘Input Service Distributor’ is a facility provided to assessee. It is nowhere stated that it is a mandatory requirement. This ‘facility’ cannot be thrust upon an unwilling assessee.

In CIT v. Mahendra Mills [2000] 243 ITR 56/109 Taxman 225 (SC), it was observed, ‘A privilege cannot be to a disadvantage and an option cannot become an obligation’.

Can CENVAT credit be denied in such cases

5. Even assuming for the sake of argument that registration as Input Service Distributor and distribution of credit is mandatory (though really it is not), non-registration and non-distribution may at the most lead to penalty for violation of rules. How can it lead to complete denial of CENVAT credit?

Is there any provision to deny CENVAT credit for violation of such a procedural provision?

CBE&C, vide para 2(viii) of Circular No. 33/33/94-CX dated 4-5-1994 has confirmed that there is no one to one correlation between input and final product under the CENVAT scheme for utilisation of credit. Definition of ‘input service’ expanded

8. Definition of ‘input service’ as per rule 2(1) of CENVAT Credit Rules is very wide in view of the inclusive part of the definition. Any service in relation to business is ‘input service’.

The second part of the definition of ‘input service’ covers various services like advertisement or sales promotion, market research, activities relating to business, such as accounting, auditing, financing, recruitment and quality control, coaching and training, computer networking, credit rating, share registry and security.

These input services have hardly any relation with ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of output service’.

Main factory can ‘distribute’ entire credit to itself

9. In some cases, office and main factory are situated at one place and other factories are situated at different places. In such case, if the office is registered as ‘Input Service Distributor’, it is perfectly legal to distribute all CENVAT credit to the main factory itself. Thus, registering office as ‘Input Service Distributor’ and ‘distributing’ all CENVAT credit to the main factory itself is an exercise in futility. Instead of that, the credit of services at office can be utilised in main office itself. As explained above, definition of ‘input service’ does not require any relation with ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of output service’. CENVAT Credit Rules do not require one-to-one relationship.

What is not required in the main definition cannot be brought in through the mechanism of ‘input service distributor’.

All provisions have to be read in cohesive manner

10. Any provision in law cannot be read in isolative manner. The provision of ‘Input Service Distributor’ cannot be read in isolation of other provisions relating to CENVAT credit.

Interpretation must depend on the text and the context . They are the basis of interpretation. One may well say, if the text is the texture, context is what gives the colour. Neither can be ignored. The interpretation is best which makes the textual interpretation match the contextual. A statute is best interpreted when we know why it is enacted. With this knowledge, the statute must be read, first as a whole and then section by section, clause by clause, phrase by phrase and word by word. If a statute is looked at, in the context of its enactment, with the glasses of the statute-maker, provided by such context, its scheme, the sections, clauses, phrases and words may take colour and appear different than when statute is looked at without the glasses of context. With those glasses, we must look at the Act as a whole and discover what each section, each clause, each phrase and each word is meant and designed to say as to fit into the scheme of the entire Act. No part of a statute can be construed in isolation. Statutes have to be construed so that every word has a place and everything is in its place - RBI v. Peerless General Finance & Investment Co. Ltd. AIR 1987 SC 1023/[1987] 1 SCC 424/[1987] 61 Comp. Cas. 663 (SC) - quoted with approval in J.K. Industries Ltd. v. Chief Inspector of Factories [1996] 89 Taxman 321 (SC), Indian Handicrafts Emporium v. UOI AIR 2003 SC 3240/[2003] 7 SCC 589, National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh AIR 2004 SC 1531/[2004] 3 SCC 257, Prakash Kumar v. State of Gujarat AIR 2005 SC 1075.

Conclusion

11. In conclusion, it can be stated as follows—

u Input Service Distributor is a facility, not a compulsion.

u CENVAT Credit Rules do not require one-to-one relationship.

u Provision of ‘Input Service Distributor’ also does not envisage one-to-one relationship.

u Any service in relation to business of assessee is his ‘input service’.

u CENVAT credit can be utilised at one place without distributing it.

u Even if distribution is done, ‘distribution’ of credit can be in any ratio. Entire credit can be allocated to one of the factories/places of provision of output services, if assessee so desires.

u The only requirement is that ‘input service’ should be in relation to business of assessee. Any relation with ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of output service’ is not required.
