3. The Respondents have sought for decision of the appeal based on records and also based on their submissions in their Paper Book. They in their submissions before the Collector (Appeals) in the grounds of appeal have urged as under: c) Rule 57G (2) stipulates that credit can be taken only if the inputs are received under the cover of an Invoice, an AR-I, Bill of Entry etc. evidencing the payment of duty of the inputs. Neither this Rule nor any of other Central Excise Rule requires that the duty paying document should be made only in the name of the manufacturer using the inputs. All that is required according to both the spirit and the letter of the Rule is that the document should evidence the payment of duty on the input. Indeed, as held by the CEGAT in Collector Vs. Good lass Nerolac Paints -1986 (26) ELT 57 (T) - not only is it not necessary for the duty paying document to show the manufacturer as the Consignee, even the endorsement in favour of the manufacturer is not required. Hence the disallowance of Modvat Credit from endorsed invoices has no legal sanction.

4. I have considered the pleas made by both the sides. It is observed that the learned lower authority has in his order held that the Board in the case of Gate Pass has allowed endorsements twice on the Gate Passes for the purpose of MODVAT Credit under Rule 57G. The issue here is whether the endorsed invoices issued by the manufacturer of the goods which had been received by the appellants through the agency of a dealer can be accepted as a document for the purpose of taking MODVAT Credit. Earlier the goods were required to be cleared under the Gate Passes from a manufacturer's factory and this position came to be changed with effect from 1.4.1994 when a composite invoice was prescribed as the Central Excise document under which the goods are required to be cleared from the factory in place of the Gate Pass. Earlier, by issue of a Notification under Rule 57G, the Board had authorised taking of MODVAT Credit on endorsed Gate Passes where the goods did not come directly from the manufacturer to the assessee for claiming the benefit of MODVAT Credit. This instruction, with the change of the documentation prescribed, i.e. Invoice in place of Gate Pass, was not made applicable specifically in respect of the goods cleared under the cover of Invoices. The plea of the Revenue is that in as much as no instructions under Rule 57G for acceptance of endorsed invoice had been issued, the learned lower authority should not have allowed the benefit of MODVAT Credit on the strength of this endorsed invoice. The learned lower authority, it is seen, has not examined the issue in depth in the context of the charged provisions of law under which the MODVAT Credit has been authorised to be taken when the goods are received under the cover of the invoice issued by the manufacturer. At the same time by issue of Notification 15/94, a facility has also been provided for taking MODVAT Credit in case the goods were not received directly from the manufacturer but through the agency of the whole-sale dealer and distributor. In that event it has been set out in the notification that MODVAT Credit should be taken based on the invoices issued by the whole sale distributor or dealer which indicates the particulars as set out in this notification. FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of polyester filament yarn. It availed credit of service tax during the period from October, 2005 to March, 2006 on the basis of invoices which were not in the name of its factory. In the impugned order, the Commissioner (Appeals) had held that it was only a procedural omission and therefore, the credit taken by the assessee was in order. On that ground as well as on the ground of limitation, he had dropped the demand and also set aside the penalty but had imposed a penalty of Rs. 10,000 under rule 15(1).

On cross-appeals :

HELD: The Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly followed the decision of the Tribunal in the case of CCE&CE v. DNH Spinners [2010] 25 STT 295 (Ahd. - CESTAT). Even though the assessee had multiple divisions, in the absence of any dispute about the receipt of the services in question by the factory to whom credit had been passed on, the ratio of the cited decision was applicable. In fact, the Commissioner(Appeals) proceeded to say that the assessee should have followed the procedure of issue of invoices by the head office as an input service distributor but observed that as far as the present appeal was concerned, the proceedings were limited by the ground taken in the show-cause notice and the order-in-original which had held that assessee had taken credit wrongly since invoice was not in its name but in the name of its head office. In view of the fact that the invoice was in the name of the head office and there was no dispute raised in the show-cause notice as to the admissibility of input service credit to the factory on the ground that the input service was not relatable to the factory, the omission became a totally curable defect and was a condonable one. Under those circumstances, the conclusion reached by the Commissioner (Appeals) to drop the demand could not be found fault with. The Commissioner (Appeals) also had taken a view that merely because the assessee did not disclose to the department that it had availed credit on the basis of documents not prescribed under rule 9(2), it could not be said that there was suppression of fact, wilful misstatement, etc. He had relied upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (211) ELT 513. In view of the fact that there was no allegation of non-receipt of input service or the allegation of service not relatable to the factory and also in view of the fact that invoice was in the name of head office of the same factory and not in the name of someone else, the decision of the Commissioner (Appeals) that extended period was not invocable also had to be upheld. Since the assessee was eligible for the credit and there was no suppression of facts, extended period was not invocable and, hence, the question of penalty did not arise. Accordingly, the penalty imposed was to be set aside. In view of the above, the appeal filed by the revenue was to be rejected and appeal filed by the assessee was to be allowed. [Para 2]

Per Archana Wadhwa :

This is a condonation of application praying for condoning the delay of one year and five months approximately. Arguing on the application, Shri Srinath Singh, learned Advocate explained that the said appeal has been filed against the Order-in-Appeal No. 312/313/PLE/CHD/95 dated 20.10.95 disposing of two orders passed by the Assistant Collector of Central Excise, Amritsar. He submitted that the original appeal was filed in time and it was only when the first appeal was listed from hearing on 24.4.96 it was objected to and brought to this notice that he was required to file two appeals. As such second appeal was subsequently filed by him. Shri D.K. Nayyar, Learned JDR leaves the matter to the discretion of the Bench. Considered. As the original appeal against the impugned order was filed in time, it was only technical requirement to file the second supplementary appeal. As per the practice followed by the Tribunal I condone the delay in filing the supplementary appeal No. E/451/97-NB and proceed to hear this appeal along with the main Appeal No. E/147/96-NB.

2. These two appeals arise against the same impugned Order-in-Appeal disposing of two appeals against the order of the Assistant Collector. As the issue involved in both the cases is same, the common order is being passed.

3. The appellants took Modvat Credit of duty paid on the inputs under the cover of the invoices and challans. These challans were issued in the name of M/s. XEN Central Stores PSEB, Patiala. As per the appellants the inputs are procured by their Head Office at Patiala and from their they are distributed to the various Workshops. In this case also, the invoices which were originally received in Patiala were subsequently transferred to their Workshop, Verka, Amritsar along with the transfer of the inputs, the invoice under the cover of which the inputs were originally received in Patiala were also transferred to Amritsar. While making such a transfer the invoices were endorsed by Patiala in favour of their Amritsar unit. The Modvat Credit has been denied to Amritsar Central Stores on the ground that endorsement of invoice after 1.4.94 is not permissible and as such the endorsed invoices cannot be considered as valid duty paying documents.

4. Shri Srinath Singh, learned Advocate has appeared on behalf of the appellants and Shri D.K. Nayyar, learned JDR has argued and reiterated the reasoning of the lower authorities.

5. After considering the submissions of both the sides, I agree with the submission of the learned JDR that the invoices cannot be endorsed after 1.4.94. However, I find in this case that the material was originally received by M/s. PSEB under the cover of the invoice which was in their own name. The inputs have been transferred to their own unit at Amritsar along with the invoice. As such the receipt of the material by M/s. PSEB, Amritsar can be considered to be under the cover of an invoice which is also in the name of PSEB except that the place is different. In the circumstances, in fact, no endorsement as such was required at all. In view of this discussion, I hold that the Modvat Credit was rightly taken by the appellants and allow the appeal with consequential relief, if any. Personal penalty of Rs. 6,000/- and Rs. 4,000/- imposed is also set aside. At this stage, learned Advocate points that the quantum of Modvat Credit has been debited in their RG-23 Part A and quantum of personal penalty has also been deposited. I have already ordered for the consequential relied and as such Modvat denied and penalty deposited by them should be paid back to the appellants from the date of receipt of the order within two months.

Applicability of proviso to Rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules

3. Rule 9(1)(iv) of Cenvat Credit Rules states that invoice issued by a first stage dealer or a second stage dealer, as the case may be, in terms of the provisions of Central Excise Rules, 2002.

Rule 11 of Central Excise Rules makes provisions in respect of invoice issued by manufacturer.

Rule 11(7) of Central Excise Rules states that the provision of rule 11 shall apply mutatis mutandis (i.e., after making necessary changes) to goods supplied by a first stage dealer or second stage dealer.

Rule 11(1) of Central Excise Rules are applicable for removal of goods from the factory. As per rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules, the invoice is required to contain various details like, range, classification, time and date of removal, mode of transport and registration number, rate of duty etc.

Thus the rule expected that goods should be dispatched from the godown of the registered dealer (so that time and date of removal, mode of transport etc. can be indicated in the invoice).

Thus, a registered dealer was required to bring goods to his godown and then dispatch goods to his customer under his Cenvatable invoice.

This required double transport of goods, which increased transportation costs. Hence, as a facility to registered dealer, direct dispatch of goods has been permitted vide proviso to rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules, w.e.f. 1-3-2015.

Thus, the proviso is applicable only to invoice issued by registered dealer, who is issuing invoice under rule 9(1)(iv) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

The new proviso only provides that Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of registered dealer even in case of transit sale. Of course, Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer also.

3.1 Providing additional facility does not mean that earlier facility withdrawn: In UOI v. Rajasthan Spg. & Wvg. Mills 2004 (174) ELT 42 (Raj.), it was held that merely providing an alternative method or additional method for availing Cenvat Credit does not take away the entitlement to avail Cenvat credit on the basis of original document evidencing payment of duty on inputs.

In this case, the issue was relating to eligibility of Cenvat credit on basis of endorsed invoice. However, the principle is fully applicable here.

Thus, proviso to rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules is only additional method of availing Cenvat credit on basis of invoice of registered dealer, in case of transit sale.

As per Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules as existing upto 31-3-2012, the Cenvat Credit could be distributed by Input Service Distributor in any ratio. Only restriction was that Cenvat credit distributed should not be more than available credit.

Assessee having only one factory or place of provision of service - Sometimes, an assessee has offices at various places but accounting is done centrally in the factory. Sometimes, there are various factories of assessee but accounting is done in main factory.

In such cases, in my opinion, if assessee has only one factory and/or one centralised registration of service tax, the HO or branches need not be registered and all Cenvat credit can be availed in the factory or place where centralised registration has been taken.

The reason is that Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules reads, 'The input service distributor may distribute the Cenvat credit'. 'May' cannot be read as 'must'. It is nowhere stated that the utilisation should be only through mechanism of Input Service Distributor. A facility cannot be a compulsion.

Finally he relied upon the decision of the Larger Bench in the case of Balmer Lawrie (supra). In reply the learned Advocate submitted that the letter given by Maruti Udyog Ltd. to customs is pasted on the reverse side of the Bill of Entry on which the Customs endorses the transfer of the goods under their signature, and therefore, the Bill of Entry is an endorsed Bill of Entry; that it has been held by the Tribunal in the case of CCE vs. Achutha Vulcanizing Cement P. 4. We have considered the submissions of both the sides. It has not been disputed by the Revenue that the goods imported by Maruti Udyog Ltd. were sent directly to the Appellants on the basis of the endorsement made by the Customs Authorities on the letter given by Maruti Udyog Ltd. A perusal of the said letter reveals that it contains Bill of Entry number, date and name of the factory and address of the Appellants for the purpose of availing the Modvat Credit of the Countervailing duty paid on the imported goods. The said letter also contains the details of Central Excise Range, and Division. Merely because letter has been produced in the records separately, it cannot be claimed by the Revenue that the Bill of Entry was not endorsed. It has been emphasized by the learned Advocate that the said letter is generally pasted on the back side of the Bill of Entry. We are, therefore, in agreement with the learned Advocate that the Bill of Entry was an endorsed Bill of Entry as contemplated in the Board's Circular dated 13.2.95. 2.2-1 Documents eligible for taking CENVAT credit [Rule 9(1)] - The CENVAT credit shall be taken by the manufacturer or the provider of output service or input service distributor, as the case may be, on the basis of any of the following documents, namely :—

Conclusion

4. On the basis of aforesaid case law and statutory, it can be concluded as follows.

Eligibility of Transit sale – In case of transit sale, the Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer, which is eligible document under rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I) of Cenvat Credit Rules. That rule does not require that invoice should be in name of the end user.This has been confirmed in the CBE&C circulars issued in 1995 and 1996. These circulars are not statutory provisions. The circulars only explain and confirm the legal provision. These are still valid as there is no change in that rule.

Intermediary dealer need not be registered - Since Cenvat credit is available on basis of invoice of manufacturer itself, the intermediary dealer is not required to issue any Cenvatable invoice. Hence, he need not be registered under Central Excise.

Invoice need not be in name of manufacturer – Tribunal has consistently held that invoice need not be in name of manufacturer, Even showing name of end user as consignee is not a statutory requirement. There is no such requirement of rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

Proviso to rule 11(2) is only additional facility to registered dealer – The proviso to rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2015 is only additional facility to registered dealer. That rule is applicable only to registered dealers and not to unregistered dealers. The additional facility does not mean that the earlier provisions become invalid.

The proviso is added 'to increase ease of doing business' and not to create more hurdles in business.

13.5

Direct dispatch of goods by manufacturer i.e. transit sale

In certain cases, direct dispatch of goods without bringing in the premises of dealer is permitted.

Direct despatch from manufacturer to final buyer, but sale is through dealer i.e. Transit sale - If whole consignment is despatched to buyer from manufacturer, Cenvat will be permissible, if name of the final buyer is shown as consignee. (Invoice will be in name of dealer). The consignee can avail Cenvat on the basis of duplicate copy of manufacturer issued under rule 11 (that time rule 52A). In such cases, the goods need not be brought to the premises of registered person. Invoice of Registered person (dealer) is not required for availing Cenvat by the consignee -CBE&C Circular No. 96/7/95-CX dated 13-2-1995.

This was also held permissible in CCE v. SSPE Cotton 1999 (106) ELT 102 (CEGAT), SWILL Ltd. v. CCE (2008) 232 ELT 802 (CESTAT SMB), CCE v. REC Ispat (2009) 240 ELT 101 (CESTAT).

In Century Dyeing v. CCE (2012) 35 STT 196 = 19 taxmann.com 281 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that Cenvat credit can be taken on basis of endorsed invoices (by dealers) even if name of manufacturer was not shown as consignee on the invoice, as name of consignee is not one of the essential requirements of rule 9(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

It has been clarified that in case of direct despatch from manufacturer to the end user, the indenting dealer need not be registered with Central Excise, even if his name and address is mentioned in the Invoice. Cenvat can be taken by the buyer on the basis of invoice of manufacturer - CBE&C Circular No. 218/52/96-CX dated 4-6-1996 [Similar instructions were given in earlier MF(DR) Circular No. 207/11/96-CX dated 1-5-1996 and 137/48/95-CX dated 18-7-1995.] - same view in Stadmed P Ltd. v. CCE 1998(102) ELT 466 (CEGAT) * Dr. Curies Labs Ltd. v. CCE 1999(112) ELT 539 (CEGAT) * CCE v. Transformers and Rectifiers (2012) 281 ELT 670 (Guj HC DB).

In CCE v. Balaji Iron (2009) 236 ELT 595 (CESTAT), original manufacturer has consigned goods to unregistered dealer who had consigned the same to the registered dealer. It was held that in such case, the dealer whose name is shown as consignee is 'first stage dealer'. He can take credit and issue Dealer's invoice on the basis of invoice issued by manufacturer (where his name was shown as 'consignee').

Dealer (registered person) should not issue Cenvatable Invoice for transit sales. Such invoices can be issued only when goods are physically received in the godown of dealer. Dealer can issue Non-Cenvatable invoice in case of transit sales. They should maintain different series of Invoice Book for this purpose. Such Invoice should not contain the details which are required for Cenvatable Invoice of dealer. - Pune Commissionerate TN No. 76/95 dated 20-7-1995.

In UOI v. Rajasthan Spinning & Weaving Mills 2004 (174) ELT 42 (Raj HC DB), it was held that credit can be taken on basis of endorsed invoice. Merely providing an alternative method or additional method for availing Cenvat Credit does not take away the entitlement to avail Cenvat credit on the basis of original endorsed document evidencing payment of duty on inputs.

In Krishna Wire Products v. CCE 2003 (158) ELT 491 (CESTAT), the goods were dispatched to place of manufacturer-buyer directly from place of import, but the dealer's invoice showed that goods were dispatched from godown of the dealer. However, there was co-relation between duty paying documents and invoice of dealer. It was held that buyer can avail Cenvat, so long as duty paid nature of goods is not in dispute.

Input Service Distributor

22.6 A manufacturer or service provider may have head office/regional office at different place/s. The services may be received at head office/regional office, but ultimately, these will be indirectly used for manufacture or providing output service.

Similarly, a principal manufacturer (brand name owner) may send inputs to job worker who is manufacturing goods under brand name of brand name owner. These goods will be supplied by job worker to principal manufacturer. If the goods are covered under MRP valuation provisions, duty will be payable by job worker on basis of MRP. However, many of input services received by principal manufacturer are indirectly used by the job worker.

Provision has been made to avail Cenvat credit of services received and paid for at head office/regional office. Such head office/regional office can be registered with Central Excise as 'Input Service Distributor' and it can issue invoice on the manufacturer or producer or service provider or outsourced manufacturing unit [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

Who is 'input service distributor' - As per rule 2(m) of Cenvat Credit Rules, "input service distributor" means (a) an office managing the business of manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service, (b) which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services (c) issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider or an outsourced manufacturing unit, as the case may be. [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016].

An office of assessee (manufacturer or service provider) is 'Input Service Distributor' if it satisfies all the three aforesaid requirements. It is not that each and every office of assessee is 'Input Service Distributor' and must register. The office should be registered as 'Input Service Distributor' only if it wants to distribute. There is no law that 'distribution' is the only way of availing Cenvat credit of services received at office of assessee. There are various documents eligible for availing Cenvat credit. Invoice/challan issued by 'Input Service Distributor' is only one of the specified document.

In Jaypee Rewa Plant v. CCE (2007) 218 ELT 576 (CESTAT SMB), regional marketing office was registered as Input Service Distributor and credit was distributed to manufacturing units. In prima facie view, the distribution was held as correct.

Outsourced manufacturing unit - 'Outsourced manufacturing unit' means a job-worker who is liable to pay duty on the value determined under rule 10A of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000 on the goods manufactured for the input service distributor or a manufacturer who manufactures goods, for the input service distributor under a contract, bearing the brand name of such input service distributor and is liable to pay duty on the value determined under section 4A of the Excise Act. [Explanation 4 to rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

Document eligible for Cenvat credit - As per rule 9(1)(g); 'invoice, bill or challan' issued by an 'input service distributor' under rule 4A of Service Tax Credit Rules is an eligible document for purpose of taking Cenvat credit.

In Shriram Pistons v. CCE (2012) 281 ELT 90 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is allowable on the basis of letter issued by Head Office (as Input Service Distributor) even if not mentioned as invoice or challan, if it contains all required details.

Distribution of credit even if invoices prior to registration as ISD - There is no bar in rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules for distributing of credit of invoices prior to date of registration as Input Service Distributor - Beico Industries v. CCE (2012) 286 ELT 689 (CESTAT SMB) * Dagger Forst Tools v. CCE (2013) 42 GST 225 = 32 taxmann.com 353 (CESTAT) * Bhansali Engg v. CCE (2015) 49 GST 697 = 53 taxmann.com 448 (CESTAT) * CCE v. Dashion Ltd. (2016) 54 GST 32 = 66 taxmann.com 31 (Guj HC DB).

to be 'input' or 'capital goods' of the consumer-manufacturer.

2.2 Transit Sale through dealer not registered under Central Excise: In transit sale, goods are despatched directly from place of original manufacturer to final user manufacturer (end user) though invoice is in name of the intermediary dealer.

In that case, Cenvat credit is available on basis of invoice of manufacturer under rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I) of Cenvat Credit Rules itself. CBE&C Circular No. 218/52/96-CX, dated 4-6-1996 had clarified that in case of direct despatch from manufacturer to the end user, the indenting dealer need not be registered with Central Excise, even if his name and address is mentioned in the Invoice. Cenvat can be taken by the buyer on the basis of invoice of manufacturer.

Similar instructions were given in earlier MF(DR) Circular No. 137/48/95-CX dated 18-7-1995.

The same view has been held in Stadmed (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 1998 (102) ELT 466 (CEGAT), Dr. Curies Labs Ltd. v. CCE 1999 (112) ELT 539 (CEGAT).

In CCE v. Transformers and Rectifiers 2012 (281) ELT 670 (Guj.). It was held that the Circular No. 218/52/96-CX, dated 4-6-1996 applies even though rules have changed.

It may be noted that the CBE&C circulars dated 4-6-1996 and 18-7-1995 are not statutory provisions. They do not 'allow' Cenvat credit in case of transit sale. The circulars only clarify and confirm the statutory provision that Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of original manufacturer itself.

2.3 Transit Sale through dealer registered under Central Excise: CBE&C Circular No. 96/7/95-CX, dated 13-2-1995 has clarified that if whole consignment is despatched to buyer from manufacturer, Cenvat will be permissible, if name of the final buyer is shown as consignee (Invoice will be in name of dealer). The consignee can avail Cenvat on the basis of duplicate copy of manufacturer issued under rule 11 (that time rule 52A). In such cases, the goods need not be brought to the premises of registered person. Invoice of Registered person (dealer) is not required for availing Cenvat by the consignee -

This was also held permissible in CCE v. SSPE Cotton 1999 (106) ELT 102 (CEGAT), SWILL Ltd. v. CCE 2008 (232) ELT 802 (CESTAT SMB), CCE v. REC Ispat 2009 (240) ELT 101 (CESTAT).

Dealer (registered person) should not issue Cenvatable Invoice for transit sales. Such invoices can be issued only when goods are physically received in the godown of dealer. Dealer can issue Non-Cenvatable invoice in case of transit sales. They should maintain different series of Invoice Book for this purpose. Such Invoice should not contain the details which are required for Cenvatable Invoice of dealer - Pune Commissionerate TN No. 76/95, dated 20-7-1995.

Really the CBE&C circular dated 13-2-1995 only clarifies and confirms the law that Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of manufacturer even if the invoice is not in name of end user.

2.4 Even name of end user as consignee is not mandatory requirement: Even name of end user (final customer) is not statutory requirement.

In Century Dyeing& Printing Mills v. CCE [2012] 35 STT 196/19 taxmann.com 281 (CESTAT – Ahd.), it was held that Cenvat credit can be taken on basis of endorsed invoices (by dealers) even if name of manufacturer was not shown as consignee on the invoice, as name of consignee is not one of the essential requirements of rule 9(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

2.5 Case law on that invoice need not be in name of manufacturer: There is sufficient case law that Cenvat credit can be availed even if the invoice is not in name of final consumer manufacturer.

In Collector of Central Excise v. Goodlass Nerolac Paints 1985 taxmann.com 387 (CEGAT – Mum.) same view in S.B.S. Organics (P.) Ltd. v. Collector of Central Excise & Customs 1990 (45) ELT 701 (CEGAT), it has been held that the Invoice need not show the manufacturer (i.e., user of input) as consignee as the rules do not prescribe such a condition. Such a condition cannot be prescribed by administrative orders and such orders/instructions are not legally enforceable – same view in Dy. General Manager (Taxation), BHEL v. CCE 2007 (211) ELT 135 (CESTAT).

HEADNOTE: Modvat credit cannot be denied on account of some minor procedural lapses in duty-paying documents Rule 57A read with rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat credit - Allowability of - Whether Modvat credit can be denied on account of some minor procedural lapses in duty-paying documents - Held, no - Whether benefit of modvat credit could be denied to assessee merely on ground that in invoice there was change in address - Held, no Circulars and Notifications - Notification No. 7/1999 - C.E. (NT), dated 9-2-1999 - Circular No. 441/7/1999-CX, dated 23-2-1999

FACT: The assessee, namely, ‘G’, Ghaziabad availed MODVAT credit on the strength of invoice, which was in the name of ‘G’, Kota. The assessee also availed MODVAT credit on the strength of other invoice in which the buyer’s name was ‘P’, Faridabad; whereas the goods had been consigned to the assessee at Delhi. The Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the MODVAT credit taken by the assessee on the strength of the aforesaid invoices. He held that though there was cutting in consignees’ address but the same had been authenticated by the same person who had prepared the invoice and the address was changed from Kota to Ghaziabad.

He further held that a certificate issued by ‘P’ was also brought on record to show that the goods had been supplied by it to the assessee at Delhi address.

On appeal to the Tribunal by the revenue:

HELD: The benefit of MODVAT credit could not be denied to the assessee merely on the ground that there was change in the address from Kota to Ghaziabad. Further, it had not been disputed by the revenue that the inputs sent by ‘P’ were duty-paid and the same were received in the factory for being used in the manufacture of the final products. Thus, in view of the subsequent amendment made in rule 57G by Notification No. 7/1999-CE (NT) dated 9-2-1999, the MODVAT credit cannot be denied on account of some minor procedural lapses in the duty-paying documents. The Board had also clarified, vide Circular No. 441/7/1999-CX dated 23-2-1999, that Notification No. 7/1999-CE (NT), has been issued so as to empower the Assistant Commissioner, having jurisdiction over the factory of the manufacturer, to allow the credit ignoring minor procedural lapses provided the inputs have suffered duty and are being used in the process of manufacture. Hence, the appeal was liable to be rejected. [Para 3]

Insertion of rule 7A in 2008

12. By the Cenvat Credit (Amendment) Rules, 2008, rule 7A has been inserted with effect from April 1, 2008 vide Notification No. 10/2008-CE (NT), dated March 1, 2008. Rule 7A reads as under :— "7A. Distribution of credit on inputs by the office or any other premises of output service provider.—(1) A provider of output service shall be allowed to take credit on inputs and capital goods received, on the basis of an invoice or a bill or a challan issued by an office or premises of the said provider of output service, which receives invoices, issued in terms of the provisions of the Central Excise Rules, 2002, towards the purchase of inputs and capital goods.

(2) The provisions of these rules or any other rules made under the Central Excise Act, 1944, as made applicable to a first stage dealer or a second stage dealer, shall mutatis mutandis apply to such office or premises of the provider of output service."

Distribution of excise duty paid

13. Rule 7A enables the service provider to transfer the excise duty paid on the capital goods and inputs. As discussed in the previous paragraphs, the manufacturers and service providers can obtain input service distributor registration and can transfer the credit for service tax paid to their manufacturing units and/or service providing units. However, only the service provider can transfer the credit for excise duty on capital goods and inputs.

If the office of the service provider has received invoice for capital goods or inputs, which is delivered to the service providing unit, i.e., premises from which service is provided, it can issue invoice for transferring the credit to the service providing units like input service distributor. However, rule 7A(2) provides that Rules applicable to a first stage dealer or a second stage dealer shall apply to the office or premises of the provider of output service when he transfers the excise duty paid on inputs or capital goods. The Department has not issued any clarification in this regard till date. Circular DOF No. 334/1/2008-TRU, dated February 29, 2008 states the objective of the insertion of rule 7A in the following words :—

"A new rule 7A is being inserted to prescribe a procedure to enable the provider of output services to take credit on inputs and capital goods on the basis of invoice/bill/challan issued by its other office. This change shall come into effect from April 1, 2008."

HEADNOTE: Rule 57G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Procedure to be observed by manufacturer- ‘E’ Ltd. imported a consignment of shredded steel which was cleared under bill of entry on payment of countervailing duty - A portion of said goods imported was given as loan to appellant - Appellant availed credit of duty on goods received from ‘E’ Ltd. - Revenue denied credit of duty to appellant on ground that bill of entry was not endorsed in its name - However, Superintendent of Central Excise issued certificate that ‘E’ Ltd. had not taken credit of duty paid on goods which were given as loan to appellant and goods received by appellant were used in its factory as input - Whether since rule 57G does not require that for taking credit of duty, bill of entry should be endorsed in name of claimant, credit of duty could not be denied on that ground to appellant - Held, yes - Whether, further, since bill of entry together with certificate issued by authority clearly showed that goods imported and cleared under bills of entry on payment of duty, were received and utilized by appellant as inputs in its factory and that assessee had not utilized credit of duty paid on said goods, authorities below were not justified in denying credit of duty to appellant - Held, yes

FACT: E Ltd. had imported a consignment of shredded scrap and cleared the same on payment of duty. Out of the said consignment, ‘E’ Ltd. gave certain quantity of shredded scrap to the appellant as a loan. On receipt of said goods, the appellant took credit of duty of the amount equivalent to customs duty paid by ‘E’ Ltd. on those goods. However, the revenue denied credit of duty to the appellant on the ground that it had taken credit of duty on basis of delivery challans issued by ‘E’ Ltd. but credit of duty could not be taken under rule 57G on that basis. On adjudication, the Commissioner confirmed the demand of duty on the appellant along with penalty. On appeal, the Tribunal also confirmed the demand on the ground that bills of entry were not endorsed in the name of the appellant.

On appeal :

HELD: Rule 57G clearly shows that the credit of duty can be taken on inputs by establishing that the duty has been paid on the said inputs on the basis of documents such as invoice, AR-1, Bill on Entry, etc. In the instant case, it was not in dispute that the appellant had received imported shredded steel scrap from ‘E’ Ltd. on which countervailing duty had been paid by ‘E’ Ltd. It was also not in dispute that ‘E’ Ltd. had not taken credit of the duty paid on shredded steel scrap which was given on loan to the appellant. It was also not in dispute that the appellant had used the said shredded steel scrap taken on loan from ‘E’ Ltd. as inputs in its factory. The certificate issued by a Superintendent of Central Excise to the effect that ‘E’ Ltd. had not taken credit of duty paid on the said shredded steel scrap, was not doubted by the Excise authorities. Similarly, the certificate issued by another Superintendent to the effect that the quantity of shredded steel scrap received by the appellant from ‘E’ Ltd. had been used as inputs in the factory of the appellant, was also not doubted by the Excise authorities. In these circumstances, the appellant had established that the credit of duty on receipt of imported shredded steel scrap from ‘E’ Ltd. had been taken in accordance with law. [Para 9]

Assessee having only one factory or place of provision of service - Sometimes, an assessee has offices at various places but accounting is done centrally in the factory. Sometimes, there are various factories of assessee but accounting is done in main factory.

In such cases, in my opinion, if assessee has only one factory and/or one centralised registration of service tax, the HO or branches need not be registered and all Cenvat credit can be availed in the factory or place where centralised registration has been taken.

The reason is that Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules reads, 'The input service distributor may distribute the Cenvat credit'. 'May' cannot be read as 'must'. It is nowhere stated that the utilisation should be only through mechanism of Input Service Distributor. A facility cannot be a compulsion.

In CIT v. Mahendra Mills 2000 AIR SCW 1016 = AIR 2000 SC 1960 = 243 ITR 56 = 109 Taxman 225 (SC), it was observed, 'A privilege cannot be to a disadvantage and an option cannot become an obligation'.

In Durferrit Asea v. CCE (2010) 258 ELT 414 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that if assessee has only one manufacturing unit, HO need not be registered and Cenvat credit can be taken at factory even if invoices are with address of Head Office. Rule 7 is not compulsory if assessee is not inclined to do so.

In Manipal Advertising Services v. CCE (2010) 25 STT 30 (CESTAT), branch offices were not registered with service tax authorities. Invoices were with address of branch, but payment of made from registered premises. It was held that Cenvat credit is available at HO which had Centralised registration as it had centralised accounting system. It was held that Cenvat credit is available even if address on invoice is of branch office.

Invoice of service in name of HO is eligible. It is not necessary that HO should be registered as Input Service Distributor (when there is only one factory) - CCE v. Samita Conductors (2012) 278 ELT 492 (CESTAT SMB) * Valco Industries Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 42 GST 165 = 31 taxmann.com 360 = 286 ELT 54 (CESTAT SMB).

If assessee has only one manufacturing unit, registration as Input Service Distributor is not required. Assessee can take Cenvat credit even if invoice is with address of Head Office - National Plastic Industries v. CCE (2012) 35 STT 193 = 20 taxmann.com 132 (CESTAT) * Bloom Dekor v. CCE (2013) 38 STT 336 = 29 taxmann.com 357 (CESTAT SMB).

In Doshion Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 288 ELT 291 (CESTAT), it was held that since assessee could distribute Cenvat Credit in any ratio upto 31-3-2012, the HO could distribute credit to its unit without registration as Input Service Distributor.

In WNS Global Services v. CCE (2013) 30 taxmann.com 208 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is allowable even if assessee was not registered as Input Service Distributor.

FACT: The appellant being manufacturer availed Cenvat credit on the invoices wherein the appellant's name appeared as consignee and in the column of the buyer, names of the dealers were mentioned.

The Revenue alleged that, since the appellant was not buyer as per the invoices and the appellant was not making payment of said invoices to the manufacturer-supplier, documents were invalid and credit was not admissible on such documents. Accordingly, it was proposed that Cenvat credit should not be allowed.

The Adjudicating Authority confirmed the demand of imposition of penalty of equal amount and Cenvat credit including interest.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) modified the order inasmuch maintained confirmation of demand of Cenvat Credit. However, he reduced the penalty and maintained the demand of interest.

On second appeal before the Tribunal:

HELD: One of the documents on which Cenvat credit is allowed as mentioned in clause (a) of subject rule 9(1) is an invoice issued by manufacturer for clearance of inputs or capital goods from his factory. In the instant case, invoices, on which credit was disputed was issued by manufacturer and the appellant's name is clearly appearing as consignee. Therefore, the invoices in question squarely covered by clause (a) of sub-rule 1 of Rule 9. The Revenue's contention that in case of purchase of input from dealer, invoices should be issued by first stage dealer or second stage dealer, is not agreeable. Only in case where the input is purchased directly from a dealer on his invoices and the manufacturer invoices does not indicate the name of the recipient as consignee, the first stage dealer or second stage dealer, as case may be, who is registered with Central Excise, should issue invoices as provided under rule 11 of Central Excise Rules, 2002. However, in the instant case invoices on which credit was taken issued by manufacturer and appellant's name is appearing as consignee, in such cases credit is admissible on these invoices and there is no need of separate invoices to be issued by the registered dealer for taking credit. The contention of the Revenue that since appellant has not made payment for purchase of the input of the manufacturer supplier, Cenvat credit is not admissible, is absurd for the reason that manufacturer supplier as per the invoices, sold the goods to the dealers and in turn dealers sold the goods to appellant in such transactions there are sale purchase transactions is involved, i.e., one from manufacturer supplier to dealers and second from dealers to the appellant. Therefore, the appellant made payment to dealers and cannot make payment of the bills to manufacturer supplier. Therefore, contention of the Revenue on this count is not acceptable. However, for taking Cenvat credit on input it is not mandatory that payment towards purchase of the input has to be made. There are number of transactions in the trade such as procurement input from group company, sister concern on payment of duty, procurement of input for job work, etc. In such transaction there is no transaction of any payments towards supply of inputs. Despite this position, Cenvat credit is admissible and cannot be disputed so long input is duty paid, received in the factory and used in the manufacture. The appellant has correctly and legally availed the Cenvat credit on the invoices wherein appellant name is appearing as consignee and name of the dealers as buyer; therefore, the impugned order is set aside. These provisions are in respect of invoices of manufacturers issued under rule 52A as well as invoices issued by registered persons (dealers) under rule 57G. - CBE&C circular No 207/41/96-CX dated 1.5.1996 - similar TN No. 65/96 dated 18.6.1996 of Cochin Commissionerate & 50/96 dated 9-7-1996 of Hyderabad Commissionerate.

12.2-2 Supplementary Invoice by supplier-manufacturer or service provider for differential excise duty/service tax

It is possible that a manufacturer who had supplied input/capital goods and who had paid duty on such inputs/capital goods may have to pay further duty on these inputs/capital goods on account of any demand or audit objection or finalisation of provisional assessment or on account of cost escalation granted by buyer or for any other reason. Similarly, a service provider may be liable to pay additional service tax at a later stage.

In such cases, the other manufacturer who is using that input/capital goods will get further credit of additional duty paid by the supplier of inputs/capital goods or additional service tax paid by service provider.

Suppose, S is a manufacturer of an input supplied to B. S had paid duty of Rs. 50,000 while supplying the input to B. On the basis of the duty paid by S, B had utilised Cenvat credit of Rs. 50,000. Now, if S has to pay further duty of say Rs. 15,000, B will be entitled to avail of extra Cenvat credit of Rs. 15,000.

The manufacturer (supplier) or service provider should issue supplementary invoice to buyer for this purpose, which is document eligible for availing Cenvat Credit [rule 9(1)(b) as existing right from 10-9-2004 and 9(1)(bb) as introduced w.e.f. 1-4-2011]

Such supplementary invoice can be issued by manufacturer from his factory or depot, dealer, consignment agent or importer. The supplementary invoice can be in respect of excise duty or CVD paid subsequently.

Similarly, a service provider can issue supplementary invoice.

If supplementary invoice is issued by manufacturer on account of price rise given by buyer, the buyer can avail Cenvat credit - Ispat Industries v. CCE (2008) 221 ELT 540 (CESTAT).

In Andhra Petrochemicals v. CCE (2005) 1 STT 195 = 183 ELT 377 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit can be taken on the basis of supplementary invoice even if differential duty was paid on the directions of Supreme Court.

In CCE v. Himalaya Drug Co. Ltd. (2012) 36 STT 715 = 25 taxmann.com 165 (Karn HC DB), assessee did not pay duty initially as goods were non-excisable. Later, on insistence of department, duty was paid to buy piece of mind and supplementary invoice was issued. It was held that Cenvat credit is available at the end of customer.

In CCE v. MRF Ltd. (2009) 244 ELT 601 (CESTAT), supplementary invoice was issued to rectify incorrect adoption of rate of duty at the time of clearance. Department contended that supplementary invoice is recognised only if it arises from provisional assessment or price escalation. However, it was held that substantial benefit cannot be denied for procedural irregularities and Cenvat credit is available. Basic proposition is that credit has to be varied if amount of duty paid is varied.

In JSW Steel Ltd. v. CCE (2008) 17 STT 196 (CESTAT), the provisions relating to supplementary invoice as contained in rule 9(1)(b) are not applicable to service tax at all [In this case, Cenvat credit was allowed on the basis of invoice issued by service provider (presumably on additional or supplementary invoice, though this aspect is not specified in the order).

In the case of Marmagoa Steel Ltd. (supra), CENVAT credit of CVD paid on certain inputs imported by one M/s. Essar Gujarat Ltd. was claimed by M/s. Marmagoa Steel Ltd. on the basis of three Bills of Entry. The credit was sought to be denied on the ground that the Bills of Entry were not endorsed in favour of M/s. Marmagoa Steel Ltd. The Hon'ble High Court, after finding evidence of payment of CVD on the imported inputs and also evidence of the inputs having been received by M/s. Marmagoa Steel Ltd. and utilized in their factory, took the view that the credit was admissible. In the present case, the Department has no case that the imported capital goods were not received in the appellant's factory or not used for the purpose of manufacturing excisable goods. The limited ground raised for denying CENVAT credit to the appellant is that the endorsed Bill of Entry is not one of the documents prescribed under Rule 9 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. It is interesting to note that, in the case of Marmagoa Steel Ltd., the Department wanted the Bills of Entry to be endorsed in favour of that company so that the said company can claim CENVAT credit of the CVD paid thereon. The Hon'ble High Court found no provision of law for such endorsement of Bill of Entry. There is no such provision under the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 either. Nevertheless, this was not the relevant consideration for the Hon'ble High Court to take a view in favour of the above company. The Court took note of the fact that the inputs were duly received in the factory and used in the manufacture of excisable products. On this basis, regardless of the nature of the Bills of Entry, the party was held to be eligible for CENVAT credit. In the instant case, it is not even the case of the Department that the capital goods in question were not received in the appellant's factory and not used for manufacture of excisable products. In these circumstances, I am of the view that the CENVAT credit of the CVD paid on the capital goods cannot be denied to the appellant on the ground alleged in the show-cause notice. In the case of Khandelwal Laboratories Ltd. (supra) cited by the learned Additional Commissioner (AR), the Hon'ble High Court was remanding a case to this Tribunal for taking fresh decision on a similar issue in the light of the Court's earlier judgment in Marmagoa Steels Ltd. v. UOI. The decision in Khandelwal Laboratories Ltd. case can be seen as a reaffirmation of the view taken in Marmagoa Steels Ltd. case. Nothing in favour of the revenue flows from the decision cited by the learned Additional Commissioner (AR).

Even though the assessee had multiple divisions, in the absence of any dispute about the receipt of the services in question by the factory to whom credit had been passed on, the ratio of the cited decision was applicable. In fact, the Commissioner(Appeals) proceeded to say that the assessee should have followed the procedure of issue of invoices by the head office as an input service distributor but observed that as far as the present appeal was concerned, the proceedings were limited by the ground taken in the show-cause notice and the order-in-original which had held that assessee had taken credit wrongly since invoice was not in its name but in the name of its head office. In view of the fact that the invoice was in the name of the head office and there was no dispute raised in the show-cause notice as to the admissibility of input service credit to the factory on the ground that the input service was not relatable to the factory, the omission became a totally curable defect and was a condonable one. Under those circumstances, the conclusion reached by the Commissioner (Appeals) to drop the demand could not be found fault with. The Commissioner (Appeals) also had taken a view that merely because the assessee did not disclose to the department that it had availed credit on the basis of documents not prescribed under rule 9(2), it could not be said that there was suppression of fact, wilful misstatement, etc. He had relied upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (211) ELT 513. In view of the fact that there was no allegation of non-receipt of input service or the allegation of service not relatable to the factory and also in view of the fact that invoice was in the name of head office of the same factory and not in the name of someone else, the decision of the Commissioner (Appeals) that extended period was not invocable also had to be upheld. Since the assessee was eligible for the credit and there was no suppression of facts, extended period was not invocable and, hence, the question of penalty did not arise. Accordingly, the penalty imposed was to be set aside. In view of the above, the appeal filed by the revenue was to be rejected and appeal filed by the assessee was to be allowed. [Para 2]

EN MAINTENANCE SERVICES

Whether garden maintenance service (With using materials/without using materials) is taxable? If yes, under which services it is taxable?

It should come under ‘Management, Maintenance or repair’ service , since that head covers both movable as well as immovable property. It does not make any difference whether it is with materials or without materials. You can claim deduction in respect of materials like plants, etc., but not in respect of consumables.

CENTRALISED OPERATIONS We are a Gas Distribution Company based at Gujarat. We are having CNG Station at various locations. We obtain excise Separate Registration of each CNG Station. Our queries are (1) Whether we are able to take CENVAT Credit on Excise Payable for Capital Goods? If yes, then whether only CENVAT credit on particular Capital goods used for a particular station only can be claimed? (2) Shall we claim excise on common pipe line which is partly used for CNG and partly for domestic gas, inspite of fact that domestic gas is not excisable goods? (3) Whether regarding the supplier invoice, the address of CNG Station has to be mentioned or not on that invoice or invoice made to Head Office address is sufficient to take Cenvat Credit?

(1) Since you have separate registration for each location, it is advisable to take separate credit only for each unit in respect of capital goods installed there. (2) Check tariff heading of pipeline. Mostly, it is 72 or 73 and, hence, does not fall within the definition of ‘capital goods’, as defined in the Cenvat Credit Rules. However, if some equipment does fall within the definition, you can take credit even if it is only partly used for taxable service. (3) It is highly advisable to mention address of CNG station in supplier’s invoice to avoid disputes and harassment from department. If this is not possible, invoice should be endorsed by HO in favour of CNG station with clear remark that these goods are for the particular unit and they have not taken any Cenvat credit at HO.

One of my clients has centralised registration. He has placed capital goods at various sites of the clients. Can the unit shift the capital goods to other sites of the clients after work at one site is completed ?

In respect of capital goods on which there was no credit taken, obviously no question arises. In other cases, if each unit is registered separately, then the first unit should pay ‘amount’ as per Cenvat credit rules and then other unit can take credit. However, in this case, since there is centralised registration, there is no problem, since there is no question of one unit paying duty and other unit taking credit. At the most, you may write letter informing department suitably (Don’t ask for permission. That will create a mess).

A unit having centralised registration is procuring inputs and input services at the sites where the work of the clients is going on. In view of the fact that the unit has taken centralized registration, will it be able to get credit of inputs and input services in the centralized office, if the billing of the supplier is addressed to this centralized office and inputs/input services are directly received at the work site? Or will the unit be required to avail service tax registration as a distributor for all these sites separately and then transfer the credit to centralized office? Here we would like to clarify that service tax registration certificate at present mentions the addresses of various sites at which work is going on.

Really, input service distributor is a facility and not compulsion. Further, Cenvat Credit Rules do not require one to one relationship. If there is centralised accounting and all records are available in HO, credit can be taken at HO. Of course, harassment from department cannot be ruled out. Hence, it is better to write a letter to the department about informing the procedure you are following.

We have branches at various places. Each branch is separately registered for purpose of service tax. In some cases, capital goods installed in one branch have to be shifted to other branch for various purposes like shortages, urgency, etc. We have received a demand that in such cases, Cenvat credit has to be reversed. Please advise.

It is true that technically, you should pay ‘amount’ while removing capital goods from one branch under ‘invoice’ and then take credit in other branch. However, practically, at operational level, such deep knowledge of service tax laws is difficult. You can argue that paying ‘amount’ in one branch and taking credit in other branch will be a revenue neutral exercise. There are many Tribunal decisions that substantive benefit cannot be lost for procedural lapses, particularly when the whole exercise is revenue neutral.

5.1 Rule of harmonious construction - In Jagdish Singh v. Lt. Governor [1997] AIR SCW 2106 = AIR 1997 SC 2239, it was observed -

"It is a cardinal principle of construction that efforts should be made in construing the different provisions, so that, each provision will have its play and in the event of any conflict a harmonious construction should be given. Further, a statute or a rule made thereunder should be read as a whole and one provision should be construed with reference to the other provision so as to make the rule consistent and any construction which would bring any inconsistency or repugnancy between one provision and the other should be avoided. One rule cannot be used to defeat another rule in the same Rules, unless it is impossible to effect harmonisation between them. - - A construction that reduces one of the provisions to a ‘dead letter’ is not a harmonious construction as one part is being destroyed and consequently, Court should avoid such construction". - similar views in British Airways Plc.v. Input Service Distributor

7. A manufacturer or service provider may have head office/regional office at different place/s. The services may be received at head office/regional office, but ultimately, these will be indirectly used for manufacture or providing output service. Provision has been made to avail Cenvat credit of services received and paid for at head office/regional office. Such head office/regional office will be registered with Central Excise as ‘Input Service Distributor’ and it will have to issue invoice to the manufacturer or producer or service provider. They have to apply for registration in form ST-1.

7.1 Who is ‘input service distributor’ - As per rule 2(m), "input service distributor" means an office managing the business of manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service, which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services and issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider, as the case may be.

Document eligible for Cenvat credit - As per rule 9(1)(g); ‘invoice, bill or challan’ issued by an ‘input service distributor’ under rule 4A of Service Tax Credit Rules is an eligible document for purpose of taking Cenvat credit.

7.2 Distribution of credit - The ‘Input Service Distributor’ shall distribute Cenvat Credit in respect of service tax, among its manufacturing units providing output service. The credit distributed should not be more than the service tax paid. If an input service is attributable to service used in a unit exclusively engaged in manufacturing of exempted goods or providing exempted services, such credit of service tax shall not be distributed [rule 7].

The input service distributors should issue a invoice, Bill or Challan on monthly basis after consolidating the service tax paid on services received during the month.

Assessee having only one factory or place of provision of service - Sometimes, an assessee has offices at various places but accounting is done centrally in the factory. Sometimes, there are various factories of assessee but accounting is done in main factory.

In such cases, in my opinion, if assessee has only one factory and/or one centralised registration of service tax, the HO or branches need not be registered and all Cenvat credit can be availed in the factory or place where centralised registration has been taken.

The reason is that Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules reads, 'The input service distributor may distribute the Cenvat credit'. 'May' cannot be read as 'must'. It is nowhere stated that the utilisation should be only through mechanism of Input Service Distributor. A facility cannot be a compulsion.

In CIT v. Mahendra Mills 2000 AIR SCW 1016 = AIR 2000 SC 1960 = 243 ITR 56 = 109 Taxman 225 (SC), it was observed, 'A privilege cannot be to a disadvantage and an option cannot become an obligation'.

In Durferrit Asea v. CCE (2010) 258 ELT 414 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that if assessee has only one manufacturing unit, HO need not be registered and Cenvat credit can be taken at factory even if invoices are with address of Head Office. Rule 7 is not compulsory if assessee is not inclined to do so.

In Manipal Advertising Services v. CCE (2010) 25 STT 30 (CESTAT), branch offices were not registered with service tax authorities. Invoices were with address of branch, but payment was made from registered premises. It was held that Cenvat credit is available at HO which had Centralised registration as it had centralised accounting system. It was held that Cenvat credit is available even if address on invoice is of branch office.

Invoice of service in name of HO is eligible. It is not necessary that HO should be registered as Input Service Distributor (when there is only one factory) - CCE v. Samita Conductors (2012) 278 ELT 492 (CESTAT SMB) * Valco Industries Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 42 GST 165 = 31 taxmann.com 360 = 286 ELT 54 (CESTAT SMB).

If assessee has only one manufacturing unit, registration as Input service Distributor is not required. Assessee can take Cenvat credit even if invoice is with address of Head Office - National Plastic Industries v. CCE (2012) 35 STT 193 = 20 taxmann.com 132 (CESTAT) * Bloom Dekor v. CCE (2013) 38 STT 336 = 29 taxmann.com 357 (CESTAT SMB).

In Doshion Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 288 ELT 291 (CESTAT), it was held that since assessee could distribute Cenvat Credit in any ratio upto 31-3-2012, the HO could distribute credit to its unit without registration as Input Service Distributor.

In WNS Global Services v. CCE (2013) 30 taxmann.com 208 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is allowable even if assessee was not registered as Input Service Distributor.

In such cases, the other manufacturer who is using that input/capital goods will get further credit of additional duty paid by the supplier of inputs/capital goods or additional service tax paid by service provider.

Suppose, S is a manufacturer of an input supplied to B. S had paid duty of Rs. 50,000 while supplying the input to B. On the basis of the duty paid by S, B had utilised Cenvat credit of Rs. 50,000. Now, if S has to pay further duty of say Rs. 15,000, B will be entitled to avail of extra Cenvat credit of Rs. 15,000.

The manufacturer (supplier) or service provider should issue supplementary invoice to buyer for this purpose, which is document eligible for availing Cenvat Credit [rule 9(1)(b) as existing right from 10-9-2004 and 9(1)(bb) as introduced w.e.f. 1-4-2011]

Such supplementary invoice can be issued by manufacturer from his factory or depot, dealer, consignment agent or importer. The supplementary invoice can be in respect of excise duty or CVD paid subsequently.

Similarly, a service provider can issue supplementary invoice.

If supplementary invoice is issued by manufacturer on account of price rise given by buyer, the buyer can avail Cenvat credit - Ispat Industries v. CCE (2008) 221 ELT 540 (CESTAT).

In Andhra Petrochemicals v. CCE (2005) 1 STT 195 = 183 ELT 377 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit can be taken on the basis of supplementary invoice even if differential duty was paid on the directions of Supreme Court.

In CCE v. Himalaya Drug Co. Ltd. (2012) 36 STT 715 = 25 taxmann.com 165 (Karn HC DB), assessee did not pay duty initially as goods were non-excisable. Later, on insistence of department, duty was paid to buy piece of mind and supplementary invoice was issued. It was held that Cenvat credit is available at the end of customer.

In CCE v. MRF Ltd. (2009) 244 ELT 601 (CESTAT), supplementary invoice was issued to rectify incorrect adoption of rate of duty at the time of clearance. Department contended that supplementary invoice is recognised only if it arises from provisional assessment or price escalation. However, it was held that substantial benefit cannot be denied for procedural irregularities and Cenvat credit is available. Basic proposition is that credit has to be varied if amount of duty paid is varied.

In JSW Steel Ltd. v. CCE (2008) 17 STT 196 (CESTAT), the provisions relating to supplementary invoice as contained in rule 9(1)(b) are not applicable to service tax at all [In this case, Cenvat credit was allowed on the basis of invoice issued by service provider (presumably as additional or supplementary invoice, though this aspect is not specified in the order)].

It was for the Board to take an appropriate action against the Commissioner for issuing the alert circular against the instructions issued by the Board and the remedy did not lie in holding all the proceedings invalid and depriving the statutory powers of the revenue officers and also preventing the officers from performing their statutory functions or holding the proceedings in performance of statutory functions invalid. Therefore, there was no substance in the preliminary objections raised by the assessee and the same was to be rejected. [Para 4] The provisions of rule 7 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 and rule 12B of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 would show that it is very important to know as to who was the manufacturer and who was responsible to fulfil all the obligations towards central excise. It was contended that rule 12(b) of the Central Excise Rules would not be applicable to the persons who had already been registered earlier and would be applicable only in respect of the new assessees. However, the rule does not prevent the old manufacturers also from utilizing the facility. Rule 12(b) of the Central Excise Rules envisages four types of situations, namely, a merchant- manufacturer may undertake to fulfil all the obligations himself; the job worker may be authorized by the merchant-manufacturer to fulfil the obligations on his behalf in which situation, the job worker would be virtually acting as an agent for the purpose of manufacture of fabrics of the merchant-manufacturer or alternatively, the merchant-manufacturer may be authorized by the job worker in which case the merchant-manufacturer would be the agent of the job worker. In cases where either the merchant-manufacturer or the job worker had authorized either of them to act on his behalf, obvious conclusion would be that the knowledge of the job worker or the merchant-manufacturer about the existence of the other would be irrelevant, since either of them would be an agent of the other. Therefore, in cases where the job worker or the merchant- manufacturer has been authorized as contemplated under rule 12(b) of the Central Excise Rules, the obvious conclusion would be that when the goods are received under the invoice, the fulfilment of obligations under rule 7(2) of the Cenvat Credit Rules is complete only if the obligation is fulfilled in respect of the person who has supplied the goods to the merchant-manufacturer or the job worker who, in turn, supplied goods to the other. Therefore, if the merchant- manufacturer has authorized the job worker to fulfil his obligations under central excise law, the fact that the merchant-manufacturer has supplied the goods under his own invoice or endorsed the invoice issued by another supplier and, therefore, the knowledge of the receiver about the merchant- manufacturer would be sufficient, would not be correct. In such cases the job worker has to necessarily know the supplier and the obligations can be said to be fulfilled only if it is done keeping the supplier of the merchant-manufacturer in mind. In the instant cases this information was not available. The case of the department was that the job worker or the processor was required to know the supplier of the fabrics even where the invoice was endorsed by the merchant- manufacturer or the merchant-manufacturer had issued another invoice. [Para 20.4]

In cases where the invoice is merely endorsed, the issue is settled and in such cases the obligations of the job worker would be fulfilled only if he has taken reasonable steps to ensure that the supplier of the fabrics to the merchant- manufacturer who has endorsed it is in existence. [Para 20.5]

However, where the goods had not travelled directly from the weaver/the manufacturer to the job worker and the invoice had not been endorsed, the question arose as to whether it would be sufficient if the job worker knew the supplier or he was required to know the original manufacturer who had paid the duty, even though another invoice had been issued by the merchant- manufacturer and he had supplied his invoice as well as the original manufacturer’s invoice. In such cases if the job worker was authorized by the merchant-manufacturer for fulfilling of central excise obligations, the job worker would be required to know the supplier of the fabrics to the merchant- manufacturer. Otherwise it would be sufficient if he knew the merchant- manufacturer and was able to show that he had taken the steps envisaged in rule 7 of the Cenvat Credit Rules. [Para 20.6]

In cases where either the merchant-manufacturer or the job worker had authorized either of them to act on his behalf, obvious conclusion would be that the knowledge of the job worker or the merchant-manufacturer about the existence of the other would be irrelevant, since either of them would be an agent of the other. Therefore, in cases where the job worker or the merchant- manufacturer has been authorized as contemplated under rule 12(b) of the Central Excise Rules, the obvious conclusion would be that when the goods are received under the invoice, the fulfilment of obligations under rule 7(2) of the Cenvat Credit Rules is complete only if the obligation is fulfilled in respect of the person who has supplied the goods to the merchant-manufacturer or the job worker who, in turn, supplied goods to the other. Therefore, if the merchant- manufacturer has authorized the job worker to fulfil his obligations under central excise law, the fact that the merchant-manufacturer has supplied the goods under his own invoice or endorsed the invoice issued by another supplier and, therefore, the knowledge of the receiver about the merchant- manufacturer would be sufficient, would not be correct. In such cases the job worker has to necessarily know the supplier and the obligations can be said to be fulfilled only if it is done keeping the supplier of the merchant-manufacturer in mind. In the instant cases this information was not available. The case of the department was that the job worker or the processor was required to know the supplier of the fabrics even where the invoice was endorsed by the merchant- manufacturer or the merchant-manufacturer had issued another invoice. [Para 20.4]

In cases where the invoice is merely endorsed, the issue is settled and in such cases the obligations of the job worker would be fulfilled only if he has taken reasonable steps to ensure that the supplier of the fabrics to the merchant- manufacturer who has endorsed it is in existence. [Para 20.5]

However, where the goods had not travelled directly from the weaver/the manufacturer to the job worker and the invoice had not been endorsed, the question arose as to whether it would be sufficient if the job worker knew the supplier or he was required to know the original manufacturer who had paid the duty, even though another invoice had been issued by the merchant- manufacturer and he had supplied his invoice as well as the original manufacturer’s invoice. In such cases if the job worker was authorized by the merchant-manufacturer for fulfilling of central excise obligations, the job worker would be required to know the supplier of the fabrics to the merchant- manufacturer. Otherwise it would be sufficient if he knew the merchant- manufacturer and was able to show that he had taken the steps envisaged in rule 7 of the Cenvat Credit Rules. [Para 20.6]

Under these circumstances, the conclusion reached by the Commissioner to drop the demand cannot be found fault with. The Commissioner also has taken a view that merely because the appellants did not disclose to the department that they have availed credit on the basis of documents not prescribed under rule 9(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, it can be said that there was suppression of fact will full misstatement etc. He has relied upon the decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (211) ELT 513. In view of the fact that there is no allegation of non-receipt of input service or the allegation of service not relatable to the factory and also in view of the fact that invoice was in the name of head office of the same factory and not in the name of some one else, the decision of the Commissioner that extended period is not invocable also has to be upheld. Since I have taken a view that appellants are eligible for the credit and suppression of facts and extended period are not invocable, the question of penalty does not arise. HEADNOTE: Rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Documents and accounts - Assessee-manufacturer placed a purchase order with a supplier for procurement of input, i.e., HR sheets - Though assessee physically received H.R. sheets, description mentioned in invoice was CR sheets instead - Whether in absence of any allegation that assessee had procured same clandestinely without cover of invoice, it was entitled to Cenvat credit on same although description of goods did not match with actual receipt of goods - Held, yes [Para 6] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacturing business of motor vehicle parts. During the course of manufacturing activity, it was procuring inputs such as HR sheets. For that, the assessee placed a purchase order with its supplier for HR sheets and the said HR sheets had been supplied by the supplier but in the invoices, these HR sheets were shown as CR sheets and against which the assessee took Cenvat credit. In such circumstances, the revenue alleged that the assessee has contravened Rule 9. Therefore show-cause notice was issued, on adjudication of which demand along with interest and equivalent amount of penalty was confirmed. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the adjudicating authority.

On appeal:

HELD: It is an admitted fact that the assessee has placed a purchase order for HR sheets and physically received HR sheets in its factory which have been used by it in the manufacture of its final products. The only description mentioned in the invoice is CR sheets instead HR sheets. As per provisions of Rule 9 where it has been clarified that the documents contains the details of duty or service tax, description of the goods or assessable value, Central Excise or Service Tax registration number of the person issuing the invoice, name and address of the factory or warehouse or premises, the assessee is entitled to take Cenvat credit. We have two units – one unit is paying duty and other unit is in Himachal Pradesh, which is exempt from duty. Is it required that Cenvat credit of services received at HO should be taken on proportionate basis? Please advise.

There is no provision to take credit on ‘proportionate basis’. You cannot apply costing principles for Cenvat credit when rule 7 or any other rule of Cenvat Credit Rules makes no such provision. Further, rule 7(b) of Cenvat Credit Rules provides that if some expenses are exclusively related to exempted product, then no credit is available. Thus, so long as expenses are not exclusively related to exempted final product, Cenvat credit is available. Hence, in my view, entire credit of service tax can be availed at HO, except that which is exclusively related to the unit manufacturing exempted goods.

We have Head Office at Mumbai and factories in Pune and Goa. All our HO expenses are accounted for in our factory in Pune and all credit of service tax is taken at Pune. We have received a letter from department that Cenvat credit cannot be availed since Mumbai office is not registered as Input Service Distributor. Please advise, if the objection of service tax department is correct.

Input Service Distributor is a facility and not compulsion. Even rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules uses the words ‘may distribute the Cenvat credit’. Thus, law does not say that credit can be availed only through mechanism of Input Service Distributor. Moreover, you can distribute credit in any ratio. Thus, technically, even if you register your HO as input service distributor, you can take entire credit at Pune factory, itself. Cenvat Rules do not require one to one relationship.

To avoid litigation and petty disputes, it may be advisable to register HO as Input Service Distributor, though not legally required.

7. In CCE v. Sai Ram Industries 2010 (255) ELT 256 (Trib. - Delhi), the goods had been manufactured by Swastika Pipes Ltd., Rohtak who had sold goods to Rameswar Das Devi Dayal, Faridabad. The invoice issued by Swastika Pipes Limited mentioned that the goods were sold to Rameswar Das Devi Dayal, though the same were consigned to Gautam Steel Trader.

As per the definition of ‘First stage dealer’ given in rule 2(ii) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, the ‘First stage dealer’ means the dealer who purchases the goods directly from the manufacturer or from the depots of the manufacturers or the premises of consignment agent of the said manufacturer or from any premises from where the goods are sold by or on behalf of the said manufacturer or from an importer or from the premises of consignment agent of such importer. In this case, Gautam Steel Trader had not purchased the goods directly from the manufacturer but had purchased the same from Rameswar Das Devi Dayal and the manufacturer’s invoice mentioned Rameswar Das Devi Dayal as the buyer, and, thus, Gautam Steel Trader cannot be called ‘First stage dealer’ within the meaning defined in rule 2(ii) of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Since Golden Steel Co. had purchased the goods from Gautam Steel Trader and Gautam Steel Trader was not ‘First stage dealer’, Golden Steel Co. would not be covered by the definition of ‘Second stage dealer’ as the term ‘Second stage dealer’ as defined in rule 2(s) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 means a dealer who purchases goods from the first stage dealer.

In view of this, the invoice issued by Golden Steel Co. cannot be said to be a valid duty paying document for taking credit in terms of rule 9. Therefore, the Commissioner of Central Excise (Appeals)’s order permitting CENVAT credit on the basis of this invoice was not correct.

It applied for registration as an Input Service Distributor (ISD) on 4-5-2006 in respect of its Delhi office and the registration was granted to it on 26-5-2006. A show-cause notice was issued to the assessee for recovery of allegedly wrongly taken Cenvat credit along with interest and penalty on ground that Delhi office of the assessee could not issue invoices to factory at Hapur for passing on service tax credit as Input Service Distributor when no registration in that regard had been obtained.
