HEADNOTE: Rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Documents and accounts - Period from February, 2004 to February, 2005 - Assessee, a manufacturer, availed Cenvat credit on inputs received by it through registered dealers - Lower authority denied said credit on ground that dealer from whom assessee purchased inputs never existed at address mentioned in invoice - Whether since dealer who had issued invoice had shifted his premises from where invoices were issued, said dealer did not have any office or business activity going on and further since inputs which were procured by assessee were duty paid and were received and consumed by assessee in its factory premises, Cenvat credit could not be denied to assessee - Held, yes [Para 3] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee, a manufacturer, availed Cenvat credit on the inputs received by it through registered dealers. The revenue authorities took view that it was a case of irregular availment of Cenvat credit as the dealer from whom the assessee had purchased inputs never existed at the address mentioned in the invoice. Accordingly, demand was confirmed on the assessee along with interest and penalty. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the inputs which were purchased by the assessee were duty paid and consumed by the assessee in the factory premises and it could not be denied the Cenvat credit and, therefore, it set aside the order of the adjudicating authority.

On appeal:

HELD: The material on record clearly discloses that the dealer who has issued the invoice has shifted the premises and that the premises from where the invoices are issued are the premises where the dealer did not have any office or business activity going on. However, there is no denial of the fact that the inputs which were procured by the assessee are duty paid and they were received and consumed by the assessee in the factory premises. The assessee is required to give all the particulars of the goods procured by it and the details of the duty paying documents. The invoice produced by the assessee contains all the necessary particulars. The authority has not recorded any finding that there is no such dealer in existence or that no inputs are supplied by him or that no duty is paid on such inputs. There is also no finding that the inputs are not received in the factory premises or same are not used in the manufacturing process. In absence of any such finding and all those facts having been established, the Tribunal held that the benefit of Cenvat credit cannot be denied. In that view of the matter, there is no justification to interfere with the well-considered order passed by the Tribunal. [Para 3]

CENVAT CREDIT

Input Service Distributor - Facility or compulsion

V.S. DATEY

Often, an assessee has office at a place different from the factory or place from which service is provided. Such small offices maintain only basic information. The accounting records including invoices, etc., are sent to main factory and final accounting and record-keeping is done in the main factory/office. Sometimes, office and main factory is at one place, but there are factories or places for provision of service in another places. In such cases, the input services received at main factory are recorded there itself and credit is availed in the main factory without ‘distributing’ to other factories or other places providing output services. It is learnt that in some cases, the department is taking a view that in such cases, registration as Input Service Distributor and distribution of credit is mandatory. This article examines the statutory provisions and concludes that Input Service Distributor is a facility, not a compulsion. Even ‘distribution’ of credit is a facility and not compulsion and the only requirement is that input service should be in relation to the business of the assessee.

Introduction

1. Often, an assessee has office at a place different from the factory or place from which service is provided. Such small offices maintain only basic information. The accounting records including invoices, etc., are sent to main factory and final accounting and record-keeping is done in the main factory/office.

Sometimes, office and main factory is at one place, but there are factories or places for provision of service in another places. In such cases, the input services received at main factory are recorded there itself and credit is availed in the main factory without ‘distributing’ to other factories or other places providing output services.

It is learnt that in some cases, the department is taking a view that in such cases, registration as Input Service Distributor and distribution of credit is mandatory.

The issue involved is whether such registration and/or distribution is compulsory or optional.

Issues relating to CENVAT credit on inputs with reference to decided case laws

6. The issues relating to availing of CENVAT credit on inputs are discussed as below with reference to decided case laws:

6.1 Denial of credit :

6.1-1 In Rico Auto Industries Ltd. v. CCE 2003 (157) ELT 170 (Tri. - Delhi) - It was held that when inputs are subjected to certain processes and the processed inputs are cleared on payment of duty which is more than credit taken, credit cannot be denied on the ground that the processes undertaken by the assessee did not amount to manufacture.

6.1-2 In Markwell Paper Plast Private Ltd. v. CCE&CE 2012 (285) ELT 76 (Tri. - Delhi) - The Tribunal held that undisputedly the appellants used duty paid inputs for the production of their final product which was cleared to the customers on payment of excise duty. Admittedly, the department accepted the excise duty on the final product without any protest nor the appellants were informed that their final products were not subject to excise duty as it emerged from the process not amounting to manufacture as defined under Section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act. The department tried to justify the impugned order disallowing the CENVAT credit availed by the appellants on the inputs on the plea that the final product had not emerged from the process which could be termed as manufacture. Such an argument could not be sustained as it was against the tenets of equity and justice. The department having accepted that the excise duty on the final products could not be permitted to deny CENVAT credit on the inputs used for the manufacture of the final products on such a technical plea. If such an argument was allowed to sustain it would negate the entire object of the CENVAT credit scheme which had been put in place with a view to protect the assessee from double taxation. Thus, on this count also, the impugned orders were not sustainable.

6.1-3 In Indian Oil Corpn. Ltd. v. CCE 2013 (292) ELT 210 (Tri.- Mum) - The short question to be dealt with by the Tribunal was whether the credit of the duty paid on tin containers received in the packing unit of the assessee and used in the manufacture of their marketable product, viz., canned lubricating oil during the material period was liable to be denied to them? The Tribunal found that it was not in dispute that packing units were covered by a single registration, thereby meaning that both the units were parts of the registered factory. Receipt of containers in the packing unit during the said period was receipt of input in the factory. Hence, there was no question of denial of credit for the material period.

6.2 Generation of electricity or steam :

6.2-1 In Maruti Suzuki Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 22 STT 54 - The Supreme Court held that the definition of an 'input' brings within its fold inputs used for generation of electricity or steam used within the factory of production for manufacture of final products or for any other purpose. The important point to be noted was that, in the present case, excess electricity had been cleared by the assessee at the agreed rate from time-to-time in favour of its joint ventures, vendors, etc., for a price and had also cleared such electricity in favour of the grid for distribution. To that extent in the view of Supreme Court, the assessee was not entitled to CENVAT credit.

HEADNOTE: Rule 57 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat Credit (Modvat) - Modvat - Raw material can be transferred to another unit which can get credit - Inputs need not be used directly as per settled law, as there is no requirement of direct use if inputs are fully utilised - CE Rule 57F(2)

FACT: The appellants have their factory at Mandideep in M.P. They have another factory at Ankleshwar in Gujarat. They manufacture Cephalexin and Cephadroxil falling under Chapter 29 of CETA. Penicillin GK is the main input for the final product, which the appellants import as also procure locally. With the approval of the Assistant Collector they sent Penicillin to Ankleshwar factory direct where the same was converted into "7ADCA", which was then received at the factory at Mandideep for manufacture of the final product. They had similar approval in respect of other raw materials used in the manufacture of "7ADCA" for being sent to the factory at Ankleshwar. They were availing of the Modvat credit in respect of all the raw materials at Mandideep when "7ADCA" along with other documents was received from Ankleshwar. The Collector of CE, Indore after issuing a show cause notice and hearing the appellants, held that appellants had wrongly availed of the Modvat credit at Mandideep by deliberately suppressing the fact by not making a proper declaration of use of inputs in as much as "7ADCA" was never declared as an input. According to the Collector, in the absence of such a declaration they were not entitled to Modvat credit which could have been availed of by the Ankleshwar factory which received the declared raw materials. He therefore disallowed Modvat credit of Rs. 79,38,597.50 and also imposed a penalty of Rs. 5 lakhs.

HELD: The appellants were legally entitled to send the raw material to Ankleshwar factory and to avail of Modvat credit when "7ADCA" was received at Mandideep factory. "Since the appellant had filed the declaration the appellant was legally entitled to send the raw materials to Ankleshwar factory and avail of the credit in respect of such raw materials when 7ADCA manufactured by the appellant at its Ankleshwar factory from such raw materials was received by the appellant at its Mandideep factory."

2. Since there was no requirement to use raw material directly in the manufacture of final product the denial of Modvat credit was uncalled for and contrary to judicial pronouncements. "Since there was no requirement to use raw materials directly in the manufacture of final product the denial of modvat credit by the Collector was clearly uncalled for and contrary to judicial pronouncements which has settled this position beyond any pale of doubt."

3. There was no violation of Rule 57F(2). "We, therefore, hold that there was no violation of Rule 57F(2) which postulates that a manufacturer assessee engaged in the manufacture of final product can send the raw materials directly to a job worker, request such job worker to convert the raw materials into an intermediate product and then receive such intermediate product in his factory for manufacture of final dutiable products."

4. No justification for denying the credit because all raw materials were used in the manufacture of final product. "There is no justification for denying the credit because it was not in dispute that the entirety of the raw materials were, in fact, used in the manufacture of final dutiable product. The appellant had filed before the Collector a certificate from the Chartered Accountant certifying that the total quantity of raw materials received at Ankleshwar was used in the manufacture of 7ADCA which, in turn, was used in the manufacture of Cephalexin at Mandideep. Every ounce of the material was thus fully accounted for."

5. Appellants entitled to Modvat credit of Rs. 79,38,597.50. Penalty imposed set side. "We, therefore, hold that the appellants are entitled to the benefit of modvat credit of Rs. 79,38,597.50. For the same reason, we also set aside the penalty imposed by the adjudicating authority."

Therefore for claiming the modvat credit the end user of the goods covered by the invoices has to satisfy the two conditions. Firstly, that the dealer who issued the invoice or invoices is a registered one, under Rule 174 of the Central Excise Rules and secondly that the goods covered by the invoice or invoices were intended to be used or had been actually used in the production of final product. If the very first condition regarding the registration of the dealer does not stand proved, the end user of the goods cannot claim modvat credit on the basis of the invoices on the simple ground that the goods were intended to be used or had been actually used in the product of final product, as in the invoice proforma under Rule 57-G or 57-T appended by the Board as annexure '2E' to the Central Excise Rules, the details regarding the Central Excise registration No., Sales Tax Registration, Income Tax Registration numbers besides other details regarding the goods, had to be mentioned by the dealer issuing the invoice. It is for end user of the goods before making the purchase to satisfy himself that the dealer with whom he is dealing is registered under the Central Excise Act. If he purchases the goods from an unregistered dealer, then he has to blame himself and not the Revenue department, when he is disallowed modvat credit in respect thereof. He cannot be legally permitted to take the benefit of modvat credit scheme for having simply shown that the goods had been used by him in the manufacture of the final product. The Revenue Officer in that case has no discretion or power to allow the modvat credit and to waive the mandatory condition regarding registration of the dealer who issued the invoice to the end user of the goods under Rule 57-G.

In the light of what has been discussed above, invoice/invoices issued by a dealer who had failed to get himself registered upto 31.12.94 cannot be legally treated as a valid document under Rules 57-GG, 57-T and 52-A for claiming modvat credit. 8. Definition of ‘input service’ as per rule 2(1) of CENVAT Credit Rules is very wide in view of the inclusive part of the definition. Any service in relation to business is ‘input service’.

The second part of the definition of ‘input service’ covers various services like advertisement or sales promotion, market research, activities relating to business, such as accounting, auditing, financing, recruitment and quality control, coaching and training, computer networking, credit rating, share registry and security.

These input services have hardly any relation with ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of output service’.

Main factory can ‘distribute’ entire credit to itself

9. In some cases, office and main factory are situated at one place and other factories are situated at different places. In such case, if the office is registered as ‘Input Service Distributor’, it is perfectly legal to distribute all CENVAT credit to the main factory itself. Thus, registering office as ‘Input Service Distributor’ and ‘distributing’ all CENVAT credit to the main factory itself is an exercise in futility. Instead of that, the credit of services at office can be utilised in main office itself. As explained above, definition of ‘input service’ does not require any relation with ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of output service’. CENVAT Credit Rules do not require one-to-one relationship.

What is not required in the main definition cannot be brought in through the mechanism of ‘input service distributor’.

All provisions have to be read in cohesive manner

10. Any provision in law cannot be read in isolative manner. The provision of ‘Input Service Distributor’ cannot be read in isolation of other provisions relating to CENVAT credit.

Interpretation must depend on the text and the context . They are the basis of interpretation. One may well say, if the text is the texture, context is what gives the colour. Neither can be ignored. The interpretation is best which makes the textual interpretation match the contextual. A statute is best interpreted when we know why it is enacted. With this knowledge, the statute must be read, first as a whole and then section by section, clause by clause, phrase by phrase and word by word. If a statute is looked at, in the context of its enactment, with the glasses of the statute-maker, provided by such context, its scheme, the sections, clauses, phrases and words may take colour and appear different than when statute is looked at without the glasses of context. With those glasses, we must look at the Act as a whole and discover what each section, each clause, each phrase and each word is meant and designed to say as to fit into the scheme of the entire Act. No part of a statute can be construed in isolation. Statutes have to be construed so that every word has a place and everything is in its place - RBI v. Peerless General Finance & Investment Co. Ltd. AIR 1987 SC 1023/[1987] 1 SCC 424/[1987] 61 Comp. Cas. 663 (SC) - quoted with approval in J.K. Industries Ltd. v. Chief Inspector of Factories [1996] 89 Taxman 321 (SC), Indian Handicrafts Emporium v. UOI AIR 2003 SC 3240/[2003] 7 SCC 589, National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh AIR 2004 SC 1531/[2004] 3 SCC 257, Prakash Kumar v. State of Gujarat AIR 2005 SC 1075.

Conclusion

11. In conclusion, it can be stated as follows—

u Input Service Distributor is a facility, not a compulsion.

u CENVAT Credit Rules do not require one-to-one relationship.

u Provision of ‘Input Service Distributor’ also does not envisage one-to-one relationship.

u Any service in relation to business of assessee is his ‘input service’.

u CENVAT credit can be utilised at one place without distributing it.

u Even if distribution is done, ‘distribution’ of credit can be in any ratio. Entire credit can be allocated to one of the factories/places of provision of output services, if assessee so desires.

u The only requirement is that ‘input service’ should be in relation to business of assessee. Any relation with ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of output service’ is not required.

INPUT SERVICE DISTRIBUTOR

In this article, the author has discussed the provisions relating to ‘input service distributor’ including amendment carried out in 2008.

Introduction

1. ‘Input service distributor’ is the beautiful and utilitarian concept introduced by the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. In this article, we shall discuss the provisions relating to ‘input service distributor’.

Definition

2. Rule 2(m ) of the Rules defines ‘input service distributor’ as under :—

"(m)‘Input service distributor’ means an office of the manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service, which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services and issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider, as the case may be;"

Important criteria for input service provider

3. Important criteria for input service provider are :—

(i)It has an office as the manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service. In other words, an office of manufacturer of excisable goods or taxable service provider can be registered as input service distributor.

(ii)It has to receive invoices towards purchase of services. The services might have been received by one of the units manufacturing goods or premises providing services or other offices.

(iii)It can issue invoice or bill or challan for the purpose of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the services to the manufacturing unit or service providing unit.

It is to be noted that the input service provider can be registered as head office, registered office, branch, depot, regional office, zonal office, etc.

Regional marketing office was registered as input service distributor and credit was distributed to manufacturing units. It was held by the Tribunal in its prima facie view, that the distribution was in order in Jaypee Rewa Plant v. CCE 2007 (218) ELT 576 (Delhi - Trib.).

It is possible that one company may have many input service distributors.

Example

4. ABC Ltd. has three manufacturing units. Its head office has taken Fire Insurance Policy covering the manufacturing units and paid insurance premium and service tax of Rs. 10,300. Head Office can distribute the service tax paid by it to the manufacturing units and manufacturing units can take the credit on receipt of Invoice from the head office and utilise this amount like any other Cenvat credit.

Conditions

5. Rule 7 deals with distribution of credit by input service distributor. The input service provider can distribute service tax paid by it subject to the following conditions :—

(i)The credit distributed shall not exceed the amount of service tax paid by it. (Is it possible to distribute more than the credit availed?)

(ii)The credit of service tax attributable to service used in an unit exclusively engaged in manufacture of exempted goods or providing of exempted services shall not be distributed.

It is important to note that there is no requirement to distribute the credit proportionately. The input service distributor can distribute to various units as the circumstances warrants. There is no rule regarding periodicity of distribution and it is advisable to distribute monthly.

Registration

6. Input service distributors have to obtain registration from the service tax authorities. They have to apply in Form No. ST-1 and have to obtain Registration Certificate in Form No. ST-2.

Maintenance of records

7. Rule 9 of the Rules deals with maintenance of records by the input service distributor. The records maintained by it must contain the following :—

(i)Serial number and date of the document on which the Cenvat credit is availed.

(ii)Service tax registration number and name of input service provider.

(iii)Description and value of input service.

(iv)Service tax credit availed.

(v)Basis of allocation/apportionment of credit amount.

(vi)Service tax utilised for distributing the credit.

(vii)Balance credit available for distribution.

Issue of Invoice

8. After making the payment of service charges and service tax, input service distributor can avail the credit provided service received is input service and distribute it to various manufacturing units or service providing units.

Rule 4A(2) of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 deals with the issue of invoice by the input service distributor. The invoice shall be serially numbered and contain the following particulars :

(i)the name, address and registration number of the person providing input services and the serial number and date of invoice;

(ii)the name and address of the input service distributor;

(iii)the name and address of the recipient of the credit distributed; and

(iv)the amount of the credit distributed.

Cenvat on Goods purchased from trader

When the inputs are purchased directly from factory of original manufacturer, there is proof regarding amount of duty paid, in the form of Invoice of manufacturer. If goods are imported directly by manufacturer (who is user of inputs), Bill of Entry is proof of payment of CVD.

However, sometimes, goods are purchased from depot/consignment agent of the manufacturer and not directly from the factory. In some cases, indigenous or imported goods (inputs or capital goods) are purchased by the user of inputs (who wants to avail Cenvat) through trade channel i.e. wholesaler and retailer.

In such cases, a provision has been made to allow dealers/depots/consignment agents to issue Invoice to enable manufacturer (buyer of inputs) to avail Cenvat credit. This Invoice will be documentary evidence enabling the manufacturer to avail Cenvat credit.

All dealers/depots/consignment agents issuing invoice for Cenvat purposes will have to register with central excise authorities under Rule 9 of CE Rules. Only first stage and second stage dealers are allowed to issue Cenvatable Invoices.

41.4-1 Direct dispatch of goods by manufacturer i.e. transit sale

In certain cases, direct dispatch of goods without bringing in the premises of dealer is permitted.

Direct dispatch from manufacturer to final buyer, but sale is through dealer i.e. Transit sale - If whole consignment is despatched to buyer from manufacturer, Cenvat will be permissible, if name of the final buyer is shown as consignee. (Invoice will be in name of dealer). The consignee can avail Cenvat on the basis of duplicate copy of manufacturer issued under rule 11 (that time rule 52A). In such cases, the goods need not be brought to the premises of registered person. Invoice of Registered person (dealer) is not required for availing Cenvat by the consignee -CBE&C Circular No. 96/7/95-CX dated 13-2-1995.

This was also held permissible in CCE v. SSPE Cotton 1999(106) ELT 102 (CEGAT), SWILL Ltd. v. CCE (2008) 232 ELT 802 (CESTAT SMB), CCE v. REC Ispat (2009) 240 ELT 101 (CESTAT).

41.4-2 Buyer cannot be penalised for dealer's mistake or wrong doing

In Elveety Industries v. CCE 2001(130) ELT 199 (CEGAT SMB), assessee had taken Cenvat credit on basis of dealer's invoice. The dealer had taken credit on basis of original invoice of manufacturer (and not on duplicate copy of invoice as was required during that time). It was held that assessee cannot be denied Cenvat credit even if dealer had taken credit wrongly. - similar views in CCE v. Unichem Trading Co. 1998(102) ELT 284 (CEGAT).

Assessee buying goods from registered dealer cannot be expected to go beyond checking identity and address of manufacturer or supplier. He cannot examine whether supplier/manufacturer has actually paid the duty - Transpek Industry v. CCE (2010) 249 ELT 91 (CESTAT SMB).

41.4-3 Receiver not liable if supplier does not pay duty or service tax

CBE&C, vide Circular No. 766/82/2003-CX dated 15-12-2003, has clarified that Cenvat should not be denied to user-manufacturer as long as bona fide nature of the consignee's transaction is not doubted. Further, if the manufacturer-supplier has received payment from the buyer in respect of goods supplied including excise duty, action should be initiated against manufacturer-supplier u/ss 11D and 11DD - same view in Prachi Poly Products v. CCE 2005 (186) ELT 100 (CESTAT SMB) - followed in Bhuwalka Steel Industries v. CCE (2007) 212 ELT 63 (CESTAT SMB) - same view in CCE v. Anand Arc Electrodes (2010) 252 ELT 411 (CESTAT SMB) * CCE v. On appeal : HELD: Concept of Input Service Distributor was introduced for the first time in 2004 Rules effective from 10-9-2004, read with 1994 Rules. Rule 2(m ) of the 2004 Rules, defines an ‘Input Service Distributor’ as an office of the manufacturer or producer of final product or provider of output service, which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the 1994 Rules, towards purchases of input services and issues invoices, bills or, as the case may be, challans for the purpose of distributing the credit of service tax paid on such services to such manufacturer or producer or provider, as the case may be. Rule 4 of the 1994 Rules, provides for obtaining registration by the persons liable for paying the service tax. This rule does not contain any provision regarding obtaining of registration by Input Service Distributor and it provides for registration of only the persons liable for paying the service tax.

From a plain reading of sub-rule (2) of rule 4A of the 1994 Rules, it is clear that there is no provision in this sub-rule that an Input Service Distributor before issue of invoice, bill or challan for passing on the service tax credit must have a registration and should quote such registration number in the invoices, bills or challans issued by him. Though rule 4A in its present form had come into effect from 10-9-2004, there is no provision in sub-rule (2) of rule 4A that this sub-rule will be effective only when the procedure for obtaining registration by Input Service Distributor is notified or that it is necessary for an Input Service Distributor as defined in rule 2(1)(ccc) of the 1994 Rules, read with rule 2(m) of the 2004 Rules, to obtain registration before he could issue the invoices, bills or challans for passing on the Cenvat credit.

By Notification No. 27/05-ST, dated 7-6-2005, the Service Tax (Registration of Special Category of Persons) Rules, 2005 were notified and rule 3(1) of these Rules provided for an Input Service Distributor to make an application to the Jurisdictional Central Excise Superintendent for obtaining registration within the period of thirty days from the commencement of business or 16-6-2005, whichever is later. Simultaneous with the issue of Notification No. 27/05-CE (NT), dated 7-6-2005, another Notification No. 28/05-CE (NT), dated 7-6-2005 was issued by which 2004 Rules were amended and in rule 9(1) of the 2004 Rules clause (e) was amended and sub-rule (10) of rule 9 was substituted by new rule which provided that the Input Service Distributor would furnish a half yearly return in such form as may be prescribed by notification issued by the Board.

FACT: The assessee, a 100 per cent export oriented unit (EOU) was granted permission for manufacturing ship building and the services of ship repairs/refit within the private bonded warehouse as per Letter of Permission (LOP) issued by the Development Commissioner. It fabricated a dry dock for manufacturing ship and repair services.

It availed cenvat credit on input services, input and capital goods used for fabrication of the dry dock amongst others. It utilised cenvat credit towards the output services mainly repair services and export of the goods and claimed refund of unutilised cenvat credit under rule 5.

The adjudicating authority denied the cenvat credit on input services, inputs and capital goods a on the ground that the final product 'ship' was classified under Central Excise Tariff Heading 8901 chargeable to nil rate of duty and, therefore, they were not eligible to avail cenvat credit for manufacturing of the exempted final product. HELD: Cenvat Credit on dry dock

The definition of 'input service' under rule 2(l) precisely covers any service used by a provider of taxable service for providing an output service, any service used by a manufacturer in or in relation to manufacture of final product and inclusive part of the definition, services used in relation to setting up, modernisation, renovation or repair of a factory, premises of a provider of output service or an office relating to such factory or premises, etc. The expression 'any service' read with 'for providing an output service' would cover wide encompass of the definition of input service. The Supreme Court in the case of Indian Chamber of Commerce v. CIT AIR 1976 SC 348 observed that the expression 'for' has to be interpreted as 'for the purpose of'. Cenvat credit availed on input service, input and capital goods for setting up dry dock would be allowed for providing output service namely repair/refit service. This is also covered in the inclusive part of the definition of 'input service'. Hence, the finding of the adjudicating authority, that the appellant is exclusively engaged in the manufacture of exempted final product 'Ships' and Cenvat credit on input, capital goods is inadmissible, cannot be sustainable. [Para 7]

12.1-9 Is name of user of goods/receiver of services using inputs/input services necessary on Invoice ?

Usually department insists that the Invoice should be in name of manufacturer and Cenvat credit is denied if it is not so. Really, there is no provision in the rules that Invoice should indicate name of buyer who is using the material contained in the Invoice. In fact, such condition would be incorrect, as Excise Duty is on 'manufacture' and 'ownership' is irrelevant, e.g. when a job worker manufactures goods from the raw material supplied by a trader, the job worker has to pay duty on raw material cost plus job work charges. In such cases, it is natural that he will be eligible to avail Cenvat on input supplied by the trader. This can be done only on basis of Invoice of raw material which would obviously be in name of the trader.

Rule 9(1)(a) of Cenvat Credit Rules only specifies that Invoice issued by manufacturer of inputs is an eligible document to avail Cenvat. The rule does not require that invoice should be in name of manufacturer/service receiver.

In Nirayu P Ltd. v. CCE (2012) 34 STT 543 = 18 taxmann.com 270 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that name and address of service recipient is not one of the mandatory requirements under rule 9 and is a condonable omission - same view in Craft Corner Papers v. CCE (2013) 39 STT 865 = 29 taxmann.com 71 (CESTAT), where it was held that in such case, verification may be done by AC/DC as per proviso to rule 9(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

Requirement of name and address of person receiving the service in bill is not mandatory for purpose of Cenvat credit - Novosymes South Asia P Ltd. v. CCE (2014) 74 VST 144 (CESTAT SMB).

Such a condition cannot be prescribed by administrative orders and such orders/instructions are not legally enforceable - same view in Deputy General Manager (Taxation), BHEL v. CCE (2007) 211 ELT 135 (CESTAT SMB).

In Prakash Fabricators & Galvanizers (P.) Ltd. v. CCE - 1994 (74) ELT 319 (CEGAT), it was observed : 'The Invoice will be in name of manufacturer if he has himself purchased the goods. However, indeed, Cenvat is available on all inputs, whether or not these are purchased by manufacturer. Cenvat can be availed even if inputs are received by manufacturer and duty is paid on final product manufactured by job worker'. - same view in Mahadev Industries v. Rule 9(2) provides for the availment of Cenvat credit by a manufacturer or provider of input/output services on the basis of the documents, which are enumerated in rule 9(1). HEADNOTE: Rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Documents and Accounts - Period 1-4-2005 to 31-5-2005 - Whether branch offices are not registered with service tax authorities and they do not discharge service tax liability - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, if a person discharges service tax liability from registered premises for services provided by branches, benefit of Cenvat credit on service tax cannot be denied only on ground that invoices are in name of branch offices - Held, yes [Para 7]

FACT: The assessee was registered as provider of advertisement services. According to the adjudicating officer, it had contravened the provisions of rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 inasmuch as it had availed credit on the documents which were not addressed to its registered premises but addressed to the branch office of the assessee. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the adjudicating authority. Before the Tribunal, the assessee’s case was that it had taken service tax registration with the authorities on the ground that it had got centralized accounting system and centralized billing was done from the address of its registered premises.

HELD: The assessee was not having any service tax registration in respect of branch office on whose name the invoices were issued by the service provider; it had centralized billing and centralized accounting system at its registered office. Rule 4 of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 provides for an assessee to get himself registered as service provider. It was seen that in the instant case, the assessee had taken registration under the category of ‘Service provider of advertising services’.

It can be seen from rule 4(2) that an option is given to an assessee to register the premises where centralized billing or centralized accounting systems are located. It was found from the records that there was no dispute that the assessee’s office at Manipal had got the centralized billing and accounting systems. If that be so, registration taken by the assessee was in accordance with the Rules. [Para 6]

If a person is discharging service tax liability from his registered premises, the benefit of Cenvat credit on the service tax paid cannot be denied only on the ground that the said invoices are in the name of branch office. There was no dispute that the branch office was not registered with the service tax authorities and it was not discharging the service tax liability, obviously, as the assessee was discharging service tax liability on the services provided by branch. [Para 7]

It was found that though the document on basis of which the assessee had taken the service tax credit was in the name of branch office, tax was actually paid from the premises wherein the service tax registration had been taken. [Para 8]

In view of the findings, the impugned order was unsustainable and the same was to be set aside and the appeal was to be allowed. [Para 9]

PL SUBRAMANIAN*

AVAILMENT OF CENVAT CREDIT

In this article, the author has outlined the situations where service tax paid cannot be denied on the ground that service tax is not applicable in the light of relevant case-laws. The other issues discussed here include : applicability of the time-limit for taking CENVAT credit and utilization of CENVAT credit in case of payment of advance capital goods and centralised registration.

Service Tax Paid - Cannot be denied on the ground that service tax is not applicable : relevant case-laws

1. (i) In Maersk India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [Order No. A/475 (Mum.) of 2008, dated 16-5-2008] - The appellant was registered under the category of ‘Storage & warehousing service’ and ‘Maintenance and repair services’. It got a part of its empty containers repaired through its sub-contractors. The sub-contractors charged service tax on the ‘repair charges’ charged to the appellant and, in turn, the appellant had taken credit of the service tax paid.

CENVAT credit was denied on the ground that sub-contractors did not have service tax liability. It was held by the Tribunal that once service tax has been paid by the service provider, the same cannot be questioned at the receiver’s end and, accordingly, credit cannot be denied.

(ii) Vodafone Essar Digilink Ltd. v. CCE [S.O. No. 15 (Delhi) of 2008 dated 2-1-2008] - BSNL provided service to the appellant and paid service tax on port and space charges. The appellant had taken credit of the service tax paid and credit was denied on the ground that BSNL was not liable to pay service tax in respect of port and space charges.

It was held by the Tribunal that since the payment of service tax by BSNL was not challenged, credit cannot be denied. In this case, pre-deposit of tax and penalty was waived.

(iii) CCE v. Purity Flexpack Ltd. [T.A. No. 92 (Guj.) of 2006 dated 23-11-2006] - The manufacturer had paid Excise duty at the rate of 24 per cent instead of the correct rate of 16 per cent and the buyer of the goods had taken credit of the full amount. It was held that the assessee was entitled to take full credit, as the department had not initiated any action at the supplier’s, i.e., manufacturers’, end.

Supply of components and parts and erection of plant

a carrier or other bailee (whether named by the buyer or not) for the purposes of transmission to the buyer and does not reserve the right of disposal, he is deemed to have unconditionally appropriated the goods to the contract. What is the import of the words "reserve the right of disposal" ? Please clarify. The expression "reserves the right of disposal" as used in section 23(2) of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 means "ownership", i.e., "right to sell/dispose". If the property in goods passes onto the buyer at the factory gate, i.e., seller no longer has the right to dispose of the goods as he likes, then credit is available only upto the factory gate.

However, if the seller retains the right to dispose of the goods till delivery, i.e., the property passed onto the buyer at buyer's premises (FOR sales) and the transit risk is of the seller, then the credit would be available upto the buyer's premises.

This is what is sought to be clarified by the CBEC Circular referred to in your query.

Statutory Provision

1. The expression 'input service' is defined in rule 2(l) as follows :

"(l) "input service" means any service, —

(i)

used by a provider of taxable service for providing an output service; or

(ii)

used by the manufacturer, whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and clearance of final products, up to the place of removal, and includes services used in relation to setting-up modernization, renovation or repairs of a factory, premises of provider of output service or an office relating to such factory or premises, advertisement or sales promotion, market research, storage up to the place of removal, procurement of inputs, activities relating to business, such as accounting, auditing, financing, recruitment and quality control, coaching and training, computer networking, credit rating, share registry, and security, inward transportation of inputs or capital goods and outward transportation up to the place of removal."

Rule 3(1) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 provides that a manufacturer or producer of final products or a provider of taxable service shall be allowed to take credit, inter alia, of the service tax leviable under section 66 of the Finance Act, paid on the following :

"(i)

any input or capital goods received in the factory of manufacture of final product or premises of the provider of output service on or after the 10th day of September, 2004; and

(ii)

any input service received by the manufacturer of final product or by the provider of output services on or after the 10th day of September, 2004."

2. Facts and Issues involved in the case

Deepak Fertilisers & Petrochemicals Corpn. Ltd. was engaged in the manufacture of excisable goods.

Deepak Fertilisers & Petrochemicals Corpn. Ltd. installed storage tanks for storing Ammonia at its premises situated at Raigad.

Deepak Fertilisers & Petrochemicals Corpn. Ltd. claimed that it was eligible for the CENVAT credit of service tax paid on input services used for the Ammonia storage tanks installed at Raigad, since the input/raw material stored there was intended for manufacture of the final product at Taloja (i.e., factory place).

Deepak Fertilisers & Petrochemicals Corpn. Ltd. availed of the CENVAT credit with respect of the services of consulting engineers, technical inspection and certification, construction, erection, commissioning and installation services for the installation of the Ammonia storage tanks.

A show-cause notice was issued to Deepak Fertilisers & Petrochemicals Corpn. Ltd. denying such Cenvat credit.

Department's contention

3. The department denied credit arguing that services received in connection with the activity of installation of storage tank which was immovable property and outside factory premises was not an input service.

High Court's observations in the case

4. The High Court observed that rule 3(1) allows a manufacturer of final products to take credit, inter alia, of service tax which is paid on : (i) any input or capital goods received in the factory of manufacturer of the final product; and (ii) any input service received by the manufacturer of the final product.

Clause (i) cited above provides that the service tax paid on any input or capital goods received in the factory of manufacture of the final product. Such a restriction, however, was not imposed with regard to input services since the only stipulation in clause (ii) was that the input services received by the manufacturer of the final product.

The High Court held that even as a matter of first principle on a plain and literal construction of rule 3(1) the Tribunal was not justified in holding that Deepak Fertilisers was not entitled to avail of the CENVAT credit in respect of services utilized in relation to ammonia storage tanks on the ground that they were situated outside the factory premises.

(viii) Can a trader avail input service tax credit? - Where the manufacturer of excisable goods has no exempted final product but has trading activity, it is worthwhile to note that rule 6 does not cover such cases specifically. The credits in respect of inputs used for manufacture can be claimed as there is manufacturing involved. In respect of input services, the assessee can examine following the procedure given below, that is, to split the input services that are common in nature into two categories. (i )16 services specified under rule 6 which would be eligible to full credits.

(ii )Those services which cannot be related to any specific activity and in such cases, the credits can be apportioned between the trading activity and the manufacturing activity on a reasonable basis. Basis could be relative turnovers or the usage of the internal resources of the organization where that would be more appropriate. This can be followed where the assessee is risk averse.

(iii )The other view could be that trading activity is distinct from manufacture of exempted goods or provision of exempted services and, in such cases, exclude the said trading turnover from the formula explained above. This, however, could be taken up under intimation to the department to be on the safer side of the law.

(ix) Can CENVAT credit be disallowed on appeal being not filed? - Under rule 3 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, a manufacturer or producer of final product is allowed to take credit of input, input services and capital goods as per the conditions laid down therein. The CENVAT credit is a substantive benefit and cannot be denied in the absence of any legitimate reason. The similar issue was recently decided by CESTAT in Magnet Industries (Cal.) (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2008] 12 STT 32 (CESTAT - Kolkata) wherein it was held that CENVAT credit cannot be denied merely for the reason that the same was not claimed in the appeal and that dues cannot be denied, if such dues are legitimate and patent from record. This was also in tune with Circular No. 218/52/96-CX, dated June 4, 1996. The Tribunal held that there cannot be any other conclusion, but only conclusion to be drawn is in consonance with the Circular as aforesaid to grant relief of CENVAT credit to the appellants, claiming or not claiming in appeal and to grant relief is delivers of due to the deserved on the facts and circumstances of each case. Uniformity and consistency as well as majesty being ordain of justice, the due cannot be denied, if such due is legitimate and patent from record. Therefore, the authorities below, denying CENVAT credit to the appellants and levy of penalty as well as interest had deprived the appellants from the due process of justice. Such injustice could only be ruled out setting aside the order of the authorities below to meet the ends of justice. Thus, in such cases, CENVAT credit cannot be denied.

(x) Utilization of CENVAT Credit in Capital Goods - The assessee can take full credit of duty paid on capital goods but utilize only 50 per cent thereof as provided in the CENVAT Credit Rules as per the restriction provided in rule 4 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. As such, the assessee can utilize the credit to the extent of limit of 50 per cent allowed as per law. There is no wrong utilization of the CENVAT credit nor there is any evidence of fraud or mis-statement or suppression of facts. There is no scope for levy of penalty by the department under rule 15 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. A similar view was taken by the Tribunal in CCE, Rohtak v. Surya Vinayak Industries (P.) Ltd. [(2007) (CESTAT - New Delhi)] and Delphi Automotive Systems v. CCE, Noida [2004 (163) ELT 47 (CESTAT, New Delhi)] relying upon the Apex Court judgment in P & B Pharmaceuticals (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2003 (153) ELT 14 (SC)].

(xi) Denial of CENVAT Credit when invoices issued from Unregistered Premises - A dealer has to issue a valid invoice and there is no condition in the CENVAT credit rules/excise rules that the invoices issuing office of the dealer should be registered with the department. However, the dealer must be registered with the Central Excise Department. In CCE v. Myrorn Electricials (P.) Ltd. [2007 (207) ELT 664 (Punj. & Har.)], the High Court held that CENVAT credit cannot be denied on the ground that invoices have been issued by the dealer from the premises other that for which Central Excise registration had been granted in view of Central Excise Notification No. 7/99-CE, which amended earlier rule 57G of Central Excise Rules, 1944. The Supreme Court also dismissed the departmental appeal on the same issue 2007 (215) ELT A76. Therefore, it can be said that what is important is raising of an invoice by a registered dealer and not a raising of an invoice from a registered premises.

2. As per rule 2(m ) of CENVAT Credit Rules, an entity is ‘input service distributor’ if it satisfies the following three conditions—

"(a )office managing the business of manufacturer or producer of final products or provider of output service,

(b )which receives invoices issued under rule 4A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 towards purchases of input services and

(c )issues invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan for the purposes of distributing the credit of service tax paid on the said services to such manufacturer or producer or provider, as the case may be."

The word used is ‘and’. Thus, an entity is ‘input service distributor’ only if all the three conditions are satisfied. If an assessee has office or premises which receives invoices and it does not issue any invoice, bill or challan for distributing credit of service tax, it is not ‘Input Service Distributor’.

Service Tax (Registration of Special Category of Persons) Rules, 2005 issued vide Notification No. 27/2005-ST, dated 7-6-2005 provide for registration of ‘Input Service Distributor’. Rule 2(c) of these Rules states that ‘input service distributor’ shall have the meaning assigned to it in rule 2(m) of CENVAT Credit Rules.

It is, thus, clear that the Service tax (Registration of Special Category of Persons) Rules, 2005 apply when an entity falls within the definition of rule 2(m). If the office or main factory does not issue any invoice or challan for distribution of CENVAT credit, it does not fall within the definition of ‘Input Service Distributor’. In such case, the rules in respect of registration and issue of invoice by Input Service Distributor do not apply at all.

Provision is not a mandatory requirement

3. Rule 7 of the CENVAT Credit Rules uses the words ‘Input Service Distributor may distribute credit’. ‘May’ cannot be read as ‘must’.

Rule 9(1) of CENVAT Credit Rules gives list of seven types of documents eligible for availing CENVAT credit, out of which invoice of input service distributor is one of the eligible documents. Thus, the invoice of input service distributor is not the only eligible document for availing CENVAT credit. Credit can be availed on basis of other eligible documents also.

As discussed below, distribution can be in any ratio. Thus, even if main factory is registered as ‘Input Service distributor’ it can legally allocate entire CENVAT credit to itself, which would be an exercise in futility.

Facility cannot be a compulsion

4. ‘Input Service Distributor’ is a facility provided to assessee. It is nowhere stated that it is a mandatory requirement. This ‘facility’ cannot be thrust upon an unwilling assessee.

In CIT v. Mahendra Mills [2000] 243 ITR 56/109 Taxman 225 (SC), it was observed, ‘A privilege cannot be to a disadvantage and an option cannot become an obligation’.

to apply accountancy concept to Cenvat credit. This is not envisaged in rules at all. Rules do not require any relation of input service and manufacturing. What you are saying is your figment of imagination, not envisaged in Cenvat Credit Rules.

Firstly, definition of ‘input service’ is very wide. Any service in relation to your business is your ‘input service’. Any relation to manufacturing or provision of service is not envisaged in the inclusive part of the definition. Secondly, Cenvat Credit rules do not require one-to-one correlation. If you refer to Cenvat Credit Rules, all duties and taxes mentioned in rule 3(1) form a pool termed as ‘Cenvat Credit’. Credit from this ‘pool’ can be utilised for payment of any tax or duty as specified in rule 3(4). Only exceptions are those contained in rule 3(7). The rule 3(7) does not envisage bifurcation of ‘input service’ as you are envisaging from accountant’s perspective.

The pool of credit is common. It can be used for payment of excise duty or service tax or any other eligible tax or duty as specified in rule 3(4).

11. We agree that the issue is litigation prone. However, our views are as follows —

uInput Service Distributor is a facility. A facility cannot be a compulsion. It is required only when you want to ‘distribute’ Cenvat credit to more than one factories/service centre.

uDefinition of ‘input service’ is very wide. Any service in relation to business is your ‘input service’ for purpose of Cenvat credit.

uProvisions relating to distribution of Cenvat credit of input service by Head Office do not require that the distribution should be in a particular ratio or on a particular basis. Even if you register your HO as ‘Input Service Distributor, it is legally permissible to ‘distribute’ (allocate) entire credit to your HO factory itself, as is being done by you now.

uThus, getting registration as ‘Input Service Distributor’ and then ‘distributing’ entire credit to your HO factory itself will be an exercise in futility.

uThus, what you are doing today is perfectly legal and, in any case, ‘revenue neutral’.

In short, what you are doing is OK. However, to avoid unnecessary disputes, it is advisable to register HO as ‘Input Service Distributor’ and then ‘distribute the credit’. You should concentrate on work of value addition, instead of fritting away your energy on fruitless controversies.

There is controversy raging in respect of eligibility of Cenvat credit in respect of transit sale through dealer not registered under Central Excise and also through dealer registered under Central Excise. The issues discussed in this article.

Background of the issue

1. Often the end user (manufacturer consumer) purchases goods through dealer and not through the original manufacturer. If the goods are purchased by dealer and then sold on piecemeal basis, there is provision to issue Cenvatable invoice by first stage dealer and second stage dealer.

However, when entire consignment is to be sold as it is, the dealer instruct the original manufacturer of excisable goods to dispatch the goods directly to the end used (consumer manufacturer). Invoice of Manufacturers invoice is in name of dealer as the buyer. Name and address of end user (manufacturer consumer) is shown as consignee.

The end user (consumer manufacturers) avail CENVAT credit on the basis of such invoice of original manufacturer.

This is standard practice, going on at least since 1995.

In the recent budget, a proviso has been added to rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules w.e.f. 1-3-2015, which reads as follows - "Provided also that if the goods are directly sent to any person on the direction of the registered dealer, the invoice shall also contain the details of the registered dealer as the buyer and the person as the consignee, and that person shall take CENVAT credit on the basis of the registered dealer's invoice:"

1.1 Controversy arising out of this proviso: On the basis of this proviso inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2015, a view has been expressed that the Cenvat credit cannot be availed in case of transit sale, if the intermediate buyer is not registered under Central Excise.

A view is also expressed by some assessees that Cenvat credit cannot be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer, if sale is through registered dealer. The registered dealer has to issue another Cenvatable invoice.

In my view, there is no such change in rules. In case of transit sale, Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer, even if the intermediate buyer is not registered dealer. Even if intermediate buyer is registered dealer, he need not issue Cenvatable invoice as Cenvat credit can be availed on basis of invoice of original manufacturer.

Reasons for my view are stated below.

Statutory provisions

2. Rule 9(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules prescribes that Cenvat Credit can be taken on the basis of any of the documents prescribed in that sub-rule. The relevant extract from the rule are as follows –

Rule 9(1) Documents and accounts - The CENVAT credit shall be taken by the manufacturer or the provider of output service or input service distributor, as the case may be, on the basis of any of the following documents, namely:–

(a)

An invoice issued by -

(i)

a manufacturer for clearance of— (I) inputs or capital goods from his factory or depot or from the premises of the consignment agent of the said manufacturer or from any other premises from where the goods are sold by or on behalf of the said manufacturer (II) inputs or capital goods as such

(ii)

not relevant

(iii)

not relevant

(iv)

a first stage dealer or a second stage dealer, as the case may be, in terms of the provisions of Central Excise Rules, 2002.

2.1 Invoice of manufacturer is eligible document for Cenvat credit: It can be seen that invoice issued by manufacturer for clearance of inputs or capital goods from his factory is eligible document for availing Cenvat credit, as per rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

The rule does not state that the invoice should be in name of buyer-manufacturer or consumer-manufacturer. The rule even does not state that name of end user (final consumer-manufacturer) should be shown in the invoice.

Of course, it has to be 'input' or 'capital goods' of the consumer-manufacturer.

2.2 Transit Sale through dealer not registered under Central Excise: In transit sale, goods are despatched directly from place of original manufacturer to final user manufacturer (end user) though invoice is in name of the intermediary dealer.

In that case, Cenvat credit is available on basis of invoice of manufacturer under rule 9(1)(a)(i)(I) of Cenvat Credit Rules itself.

The consignee in such a case will be the end-user. In such a situation the registered person's invoice is not required for availment of modvat credit. The assessee-company was engaged in providing service of industrial construction. It availed Cenvat credit on mobile phone bills. The original authority disallowed the Cenvat credit on ground that mobile phone bills were not issued in the name of the assessee but were issued in the names of staff and employees of the assessee and, therefore, the assessee was not eligible to take the credit. The Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the order.

On appeal :

Facts

The assessee is engaged in the manufacture of motor vehicle parts and is availing the benefit of Cenvat credit of duty paid on the various inputs used in the manufacture of their finished excisable goods.

The assessee had purchased inputs from Haryana Steel & Alloy Ltd. (HSAL) engaged in the manufacture of stainless steel flats.

On search at premises of HSAL, department found that -

while there was clearance of flats and other products manufactured by them without payment of duty to various manufacturers of Delhi,

however, Cenvatable invoices were being issued in the name of other manufacturer, without actually dispatching the goods to them, so as to pass on the wrongful credit to them.

HSAL's executive director admitted that -

they had not sent any goods to assessee and had only issued the Cenvatable invoices to them to cover up some quantities of stainless steel dispatched to Jodhpur manufacturer without invoices ;

some of the transporters have kept the blank GR books in their factory and the same were being used to show transportation of the goods in question ;

one transporter company was not in existence and their GR book was supplied to them by some other transport company at Rs. 200 per GR.

The transporter admitted that no goods were actually transported to assessee.

One of the authorised signatories of assessee as well director of the assessee-company agreed that they have availed the Cenvat credit against invoices of HSAL without receiving the goods physically.

The Department denied Cenvat credit in hands of the assessee and sought levy of interest and penalty.

Assessee's Arguments

Revenue's finding that the inputs were not received by assessee is based upon presumption inasmuch as they have made the payments through cheques and there is no evidence of any flow back of money by the assessee.

Extended period of limitation was not invocable.

Since they have voluntarily debited the involved Cenvat credit prior to the issuance of the show-cause Notice, penalty should not have been imposed.

Issue Involved

Whether assessee had actually received inputs so as to be entitled to credit ?

The Adjudicating Authority has denied cenvat credit alleging that the assessee has not obtained registration as Input Service Distributor (ISD). The assessee has submitted that it has obtained ISD registration in 2008. A copy of the ISD registration is also furnished. Therefore, the disallowance of credit for the reason that the assessee has not obtained ISD registration is unjustified and requires to be set aside. [Paras 9.1 and 9.2]

The Adjudicating Authority has further denied cenvat credit stating that the invoices were raised in the address of Bangalore and Pune office and the credit has been availed in Hosur Unit. The assessee has taken centralized registration incorporating Bangalore and Pune units. In such circumstances, the revenue cannot deny the credit availed on invoices raised in the address of Bangalore and Pune unit. [Para 9.3]

The Adjudicating Authority has also denied cenvat credit on the plea that clearing and forwarding agent services are availed by the assessee outside the factory/place of removal. The definition of input service does not state that the services have to be availed within the factory. The Board Circular No. 999/6/2015-CX, dated 28-1-2015 has also clarified this point. Therefore, the disallowance of credit is unjustified. [Para 9.4]

The assessee has availed credit on debit notes which has been disallowed on plea that these are not valid documents to avail credit. Debit notes can be considered to be valid documents for availing credit when there is no dispute with regard to the service tax paid and the services consumed. In the instant case, the department does not have a contention that the assessee has not discharged the service tax on the said services on which credit has been availed. Therefore, the disallowance of credit on this ground is unjustified. [Para 9.5]

The assessee has availed cenvat credit on photocopies of invoices. The assessee has submitted that the original invoices were misplaced and, therefore, it has availed credit on photocopies. This submission does not find favour. The assessee cannot avail credit on photocopies. These are not valid documents for availing credit. Further if such practice of availing credit on photocopies of invoices is allowed, then it will lead to false claims of credit made by assessees. The claim of assessee on this ground is disallowed. [Para 9.6]

The Adjudicating Authority has disallowed credit on various input services stating that these services are not availed in relation to the activity of manufacture. The assessee has submitted that these services include services like membership charges which are paid for taking membership in industrial association, exhibition stall charges, delegate fee, sales commission, etc. According to assessee, all these services have an integral connection with the manufacture of finished products. These services were consumed to carry out the activity of manufacture effectively and also to provide export of services/goods. The Adjudicating Authority has not made adequate discussion in this regard. The assessee has submitted that it would be able to establish the nexus of the services with the output services/manufacturing activity, if it is given a further chance. Therefore, this issue requires to be remanded to the Adjudicating Authority. [Para 9.7]

In the result, the impugned order is modified to the extent of allowing the credit in respect of the services availed except on photocopies of invoices. The issue with regard to credit disallowed alleging that the services do not have nexus with the manufacturing activity is remanded to the Adjudicating Authority leaving this issue open. [Para 10]

Computation of input tax credit

After the commencement of the Act, where any dealer registered as a VAT dealer or where the authority prescribed registers any dealer as a VAT dealer under rule 3, such dealer shall be eligible for input tax credit as provided under section 20 of the Act. (a)

The dealer claiming such input tax credit must be registered under the Act.

(b)

The VAT dealer claiming input tax credit, shall make an inventory of all goods in hand, on the Appointed Day, which has suffered the incidence of tax under the Repealed Act, and shall file his claim for input tax credit in Form JVAT 401 along with the evidences, including the 6[statement of] purchase or sale invoice(s) 7[or] 8[***] copies of the Declaration (s) in Form IX-C issued/received under the Repealed Act.

(c)

The VAT dealer claiming input tax credit, in the circumstances he is a manufacturer or a miner and has purchased his Inputs or the raw-materials under sub-section (1) of section 13 of the Repealed Act, shall make an inventory of all such goods in hand, on the Appointed Day, which has suffered the incidence of tax under the Repealed Act, and shall file his claim for input tax credit in Form JVAT 401 along with the evidences, including the purchase or sale invoice(s) and the evidences/copies of the Declaration (s) in Form IX issued/received under the Repealed Act.

(d)

In the circumstances, the tax paid purchase invoices reflect the amount of taxes realised and paid separately, input tax credit to the extent of 100% of such amount of tax shall be admissible.

12. Changes in provisions relating to supplying of goods

Under rule 11(2) of the Central Excise Rules, 2002, under mentioned provisos have been inserted which are self-explanatory:

If goods are directly sent to a job worker on the direction of a manufacturer or the provider of output service, the invoice shall also contain the details of the manufacturer or the provider of output service, as the case may be, as buyer and the details of job worker as the consignee.

If the goods are directly sent to any person on the direction of the registered dealer, the invoice shall also contain the details of the registered dealer as the buyer and the person as the consignee, and that person shall take CENVAT credit on the basis of the registered dealer's invoice.

CENVAT CREDIT RULES

13. Increase in time-limit for availment of Cenvat credit from six months to one year

Till 10.07.2014, there was no restriction on availment of Cenvat credit. From 11.07.2014, the Cenvat credit can be taken only upto six months from the date of issue of document as contained in rule 9(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. From 01.03.2015, the time-limit for availment of Cenvat credit has been increased from six months to one year.

14. Credit on goods directly dispatched to job worker

As per rule 4(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, 'the CENVAT credit in respect of inputs may be taken immediately on receipt of the inputs in the factory of the manufacturer or in the premises of the provider of output service'.

In case where the goods are directly dispatched to the premises of job worker on the direction of the manufacturer or the provider of output service, credit can be taken only when the said goods are received in the factory of the manufacturer or in the premises of the provider of output service. This was the interpretation done by the department and various Courts.

In order to streamline the said provision, rule 4(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 w.e.f 01.03.2015 states that the CENVAT credit in respect of inputs may be taken immediately on receipt of the inputs in the factory of the manufacturer or in the premises of the provider of output service or in the premises of the job worker, in case goods are sent directly to the job worker on the direction of the manufacturer or the provider of output service, as the case may be;

Similarly, w.e.f 01.03.2015, with respect of capital goods, rule 4(2)(a) now states that the CENVAT credit in respect of capital goods received in a factory or in the premises of the provider of output service or outside the factory of the manufacturer of the final products for generation of electricity for captive use within the factory or in the premises of the job worker, in case capital goods are sent directly to the job worker on the direction of the manufacturer or the provider of output service, as the case may be at any point of time in a given financial year shall be taken only for an amount not exceeding fifty per cent of the duty paid on such capital goods in the same financial year.

FACT: Facts

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of excisable goods and provision of output services.

The assessee installed ammonia Storage tank facility at their premises at Raigad for storage of imported ammonia, which was raw material meant for manufacturing of final product at their Taloja factory.

The assessee availed Cenvat Credit of service tax paid on input services (Consulting Engineers, Technical Inspection and certification service, Construction service, erection, commissioning and installation service, etc.) used for installation of said ammonia storage tank.

The department denied credit arguing that services received in connection with the activity of installation of storage tank which was immovable property and outside factory premises were not input services.

Issue Involved

Whether the assessee was eligible for CENVAT Credit on input services ?

HELD: There is no condition as to place of receipt of input services - Input services may be received anywhere :

Rule 3(1) allows a manufacturer of final products to take credit inter alia of duty/service tax which is paid on :

(i)

any input or capital goods received in the factory of manufacturer of the final product; and

(ii)

any input service received by the manufacturer of the final product.

Rule 3(1) makes a distinction between inputs or capital goods on the one hand and input services on the other hand.

Clause (i) of rule 3(1) provides that duty should be paid on any input or capital goods received in the factory of manufacture of the final product.

Such a restriction, however, is not imposed in regard to input services since the only stipulation in clause (ii) is that the input services should be received by the manufacturer of the final product.

Hence, even as a matter of first principle on a plain and literal construction of rule 3(1), Tribunal was not justified in holding that assessee would not be entitled to avail of CENVAT credit in respect of services utilized in relation to ammonia storage tanks on the ground that they were situated outside the factory of production. [Para 5]

Storage of input is a part of process of manufacture - Hence, impugned services were input services under rule 2(l) :

The definition of the expression 'input service' covers any services used by the manufacturer, whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products. The words 'directly or indirectly' and 'in or in relation to' are words of width and amplitude. The subordinate legislation has advisedly used a broad and comprehensive expression while defining the expression 'input service'.

Rule 2(l) initially provides that input service means any services of the description falling in sub-clauses (i) and (ii). Rule 2(l) then provides an inclusive definition by enumerating certain specified services. Among those services are services pertaining to the procurement of inputs and inward transportation of inputs.

The Tribunal's interpretation that legislature restricted the benefit of CENVAT credit for input services used in respect of inputs only to these two categories viz. for the procurement of inputs and for the inward transportation of inputs was ex facie contrary to the provisions contained in Rule 2(l).

The first part of Rule 2(l) inter alia covers any services used by the manufacturer directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products. The inclusive part of the definition enumerates certain specified categories of services. However, it would be far-fetched to interpret rule 2(l) to mean that only two categories of services in relation to inputs viz. for the procurement of inputs and for the inward transportation of inputs were intended to be brought within the purview of Rule 2(l). Rule 2(l) must be read in its entirety.

Inclusive Part

5. The expression viz., ‘used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ in the specific/substantive part of the definition is so wide that it would cover innumerable items as ‘input’ and to avoid such contingency the Legislature has incorporated the inclusive part after the substantive part qualified by the place of use. For example, one of the categories mentioned in the inclusive part is ‘used as packing material’. Packing material by itself would not suffice till it is proved that the term is used in the course of manufacture of final product. Mere fact that the item is a packing material whose value is included in the accessible value of final product will not entitle the manufacturer to take credit. Oils and lubricants mentioned in the definition are required for smooth running of machines and, hence, they are included as they are used in relation to manufacture of final product. The intention of the Legislature is that inputs falling in the inclusive part must have nexus with the manufacture of the final product.

In Indo Rama Synthetics (India) Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (219) ELT 122 (Bom.), the High Court held that the credit of duty paid on the goods or fuel used in the generation of electricity is available, provided the electricity is used for the manufacture of final product. The use of electricity must have nexus with goods manufactured in the factory.

5.1 Primary packing material - In Wrigley India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (255) ELT 201 (Punj. & Har.), it was held that it is not a matter of dispute that chewing gum/bubble gums manufactured by the assessees are directly or primarily packed with the printed aluminium foils without tattoos. It means, putting a ‘boomer-tattoo’ in the package material of bubble gum is an additional step in aid used for promotional material and it is not termed as a packing material, as such, especially when it is depicted on the packing that ‘free tattoo inside’. The primary function of putting the ‘tattoo’ in the wrapped bubble gum is to promote the trade and to attract the children rather than to be used for the purpose of packing ‘tattoo’.

Again it is not a matter of dispute that these printed ‘tattoos’ are not used for initial packing in the real sense, rather they are wrapped. Therefore, it cannot possibly be said that the ‘Boomer-tattoo’ is used as initial packing material, meaning thereby the wrapper of the ‘tattoo’ on the bubble gum is not at all required in the form of primary packing. There is no direct and indirect use of the ‘tattoo’ in or in relation to the manufacture of the product, rather it is separately known tattoo in the market, has a separate identity, specific purpose of promotion of the product and for the purpose of advertisement. Hence, it is not a packing material and cannot be considered as inputs within the meaning and definition considered as ‘inputs’ as contemplated under the relevant Rules.

In CCE v. International Tractors Ltd. - 2010 (255) ELT 203 (Punj. & Har.), the respondent was the manufacturer of traction and tractor components. The components manufactured by the respondent were duly packed in boxes and thereafter were sold. The Tribunal had allowed the credit on the goods of full packing of boxes. It had been observed by the Tribunal that duty was paid on the boxes.

The revenue contended that the respondent never received inputs in the packing of boxes and in fact the goods were delivered to the respondent in pallets and, hence, the respondent was not entitled to any credit.

It was held that CESTAT could allow availment of CENVAT credit in respect of duty paid on the packing material.

Place of use

6. The third part of the definition of ‘input’ is the ‘place of use’. Rule 2(k)( i) mandatorily requires that the goods meant for input should be used in the process of manufacture within the premises of the factory. It is a condition precedent to avail CENVAT credit on ‘inputs’ that the product should be manufactured within the premises of the factory. But, at the same time, it is not mandatory for the output service provider to utilize the inputs within the premises of the output service provider. Even if the input is used outside the premises of the service provider, CENVAT credit is allowed for such inputs.

The manufacturer who intends to take credit of the duty paid on inputs should file a declaration with the Assistant Commissioner having jurisdiction over his factory indicating the inputs intended to be used in the final product. [Para 35]

From the conjoint reading of rules 52A, 57G and the amendment made by Notification No. 7/99, dated 9-2-1999 by which sub-rule (11) was inserted in rule 57G, of filing of the documents for availing Modvat credit is only a procedural matter and the amendment made vide Notification No. 7/99, dated 9-2-1999 which inserted sub-rule (11) in rule 57G the position was made clear that Modvat credit should not be denied only on the ground that the documents referred to in sub-rule (2) does not strictly comply with the said rule but contains the details of payment dues, description of goods, assessable value, name and address of the factory or warehouse etc. This position has also been clarified by the Central Board of Excise and Customs by issuing a circular in exercise of its power under section 37B of the Act and made it applicable to all pending cases. [Para 36]

The submission of the revenue that the Notification No. 7/99, dated 9-2-1999 would come into effect on the date of its publication i.e., 9-2-1999 only, may be correct but the benefit of that Notification as directed by the Central Board of Excise and Customs has been extended to all the pending cases. The provision of sub-rule (2) is procedural for availing Modvat credit, the benefit of sub-rule (11) is available to the assessee. [Para 39]
