The credit was taken on basis of documents/invoices of Input Service Distributor.

The Department argued that -

the depots were storing and selling the final products not only manufactured at Borivali plant but also at their other plants ; and

the services used in relation to the final products manufactured at other than Borivali plants cannot be termed as 'Input service' for the Borivali plant ; and

transportation charges involved in delivery of finished goods from such depots to the customers was ineligible for credit, as place of removal is the depot and transportation charges incurred beyond the depots are excluded from the definition of input service.

The assessee argued that there is no bar under Rules in distributing credit to various units of the assessee even if the services might have been availed in another unit of the assessee and not in the unit where the credit is being taken.

Revenue argued that input service tax can be distributed only in respect of services availed by a unit and not in respect of 'input service' which have been availed by another unit as it would amounts to transfer of credit from one unit to the other which is not permissible in law.

Issue Involved

Whether assessee was eligible for impugned credit ?

From the above sequence of movements, of inputs from supplier to the job worker and to the assessee, it is seen that -

they have not received the inputs in their factory but directly supplied from the principal manufacturer to the job workers premises and

after the job work is done the goods were returned back to the assessee factory.

The assessee raised challans to the job workers only after reversing the credit in their books of account and they finally availed the credit only on receipt of the goods from the job workers, and all transactions of movement and receipt are maintained by the assessee.

The original payment of duty on the inputs is made by the principal manufacturer, the duty paying documents is in the name of assessee and the final receipt of the goods from the job workers to the assessee's factory is not disputed by the department.

It is relevant to state that the substantial condition for availing credit on inputs is :

(1)

evidence of duty payment of inputs

(2)

receipt of the inputs and

(3)

usage of the inputs in the excisable goods.

In the present case, all the three conditions have been satisfied. Though the goods have been directly supplied from the principal manufacturer to the job workers premises, the invoices are raised by the principal supplier is in the name of assessee. It is also not in dispute that the assessee had duly received the goods from the job workers premises after carrying out the job work. [Para 8]

Credit cannot be denied on the ground that the inputs were supplied directly to the job workers premises from the principal manufacturers.

The Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly observed the revenue neutrality as there is no loss of revenue and also there is no dispute on the duty paid nature of the inputs duly received by the assessee from the job workers premises.

Therefore, there was no infirmity in the order of the Commissioner (Appeals), in allowing credit on the inputs directly supplied to the job workers premises from the principal manufacturer and subsequently received by the assessee. [Para 10]

The Supreme Court in Collector of Central Excise v. Dai Karkaria Ltd. 1999 (7) SCC 448 held that where a manufacturer obtains credit for the excise duty paid on raw material to be used by him in the production of an excisable product immediately, it should make the requisite declaration and obtain an acknowledgement thereof. It is entitled to use the credit at any time thereafter while making payment of excise duty on the excisable product. There is no provision in the Rules which provides for a reversal of the credit by the Excise Authorities except where it has been illegally or irregularly taken, in which event it stands cancelled or, if utilized, has to be paid for. Where the credit has been validly taken, its benefit is available to the manufacturer without any limitation in time or otherwise unless the manufacturer itself chooses not to use the raw material in its excisable product. The credit is, therefore, indefeasible. It should also be noted that there is no correlation of the raw material and the final product, that is to say, it is not as if credit can be taken only on a final product, that is manufactured out of the particular raw material to which the credit is related. The credit may be taken against the excise duty on a final product manufactured on the very day it becomes available. [Para 7]

The High Court of Rajasthan in Hindustan Zinc Ltd. v. Union of India 2008 (223) ELT 149 has held that in case inputs are received in factory and used in manufacture of end product, no excise duty becomes payable on end product. The relevant date for considering exemption from duty of the end product in or in relation to which inputs are used is the date of its receipt in factory and condition is its actual use in or in relation to manufacture of end product by the manufacturer. The chargeability to duty or non-chargeability due to exemption or notified nil rate is to be considered at the stage before goods are actually produced, but on receipt of inputs intended to be used in manufacture of such goods. That being so ultimate clearance of goods at nil rate due to contingency existing at the time of removal does not affect the entitlement that legally arises long before that date. [Para 11]

The above judgments were to be agreed with. Since the language of rule 9(2) of the Cenvat Credit Rules is identical to that of rule 57H(5) of the Excise Rules, the interpretation given by the Apex Court had to apply in the instant case also. It was to be concluded that even though the final product may be exempted from payment of excise, the assessee could not be asked to reverse the Modvat credit already taken by it. [Para 12]

It is, therefore, clear that for a manufacturer/consignor, the eligibility to avail credit of the service tax paid on the transportation during removal of excisable goods would depend upon the place of removal as per the definition. In case of a factory gate sale, sale from a non-duty paid warehouse, or from a duty paid depot (from where the excisable goods are sold, after their clearance from the factory), the determination of the ‘place of removal’ does not pose much problem. However, there may be situations where the manufacturer/consignor may claim that the sale has taken place at the destination point because in terms of the sale contract/agreement (i) the ownership of goods and the property in the goods remained with the seller of the goods till the delivery of the goods in acceptable condition to the purchaser at his door step; (ii) the seller bore the risk of loss of or damage to the goods during transit to the destination; and (iii) the freight charges were an integral part of the price of goods. In such cases, the credit of the service tax paid on the transportation up to such place of sale would be admissible if it can be established by the claimant of such credit that the sale and the transfer of property in goods (in terms of the definition as under section 2 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 as also in terms of the provisions under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930) occurred at the said place.

n From clause (ii) rule 2(l), it is very clear that service used by a manufacturer whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to clearance of final products from the place of removal is an ‘Input service’. From the place of removal, normally, the final products are removed. So, the first limb of the definition of ‘Input service’ defines the ‘Input service’ as any service used by the manufacturer in or in relation not only to the manufacture of final products, but also to clearance of final products from the place of removal. The place of removal can be either factory or depot. So, it is very clear that rule 2(l)(ii) covers the service which was in dispute. When the place of removal is factory, the service tax paid on the goods transport services availed by the manufacturer from the factory up to the destination of the buyer is definitely included. Similarly, when the depot is the place of removal, the service tax paid on the goods transport services availed by the manufacturer is entitled to credit. This is very clear from the first limb of the definition of ‘Input service’ which is rule 2(l)(ii ).

The High Court held that even as a matter of first principle on a plain and literal construction of rule 3(1) the Tribunal was not justified in holding that Deepak Fertilisers was not entitled to avail of the CENVAT credit in respect of services utilized in relation to ammonia storage tanks on the ground that they were situated outside the factory premises. The High Court further observed that rule 2(l) initially provides that input service means any services of the description falling in sub-clauses (i) and (ii). Rule 2(l) then provides an inclusive definition by enumerating certain specified services. Among those services were services pertained to the procurement of inputs and inward transportation of inputs. The first part of rule 2(l), inter alia , covers any services used by the manufacturer directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products. The inclusive part of the definition enumerates certain specified categories of services. Whereas rule 3(1) allows a manufacturer of final products to take credit of excise duty and service tax among others paid on any input or capital goods received in the factory of manufacture of the final product, insofar as any input service is concerned, the only stipulation is that it received the final product. This was needed to be read with the broad and comprehensive meaning of the expression 'input service' in rule 2(l).

The Court finally held that the input services in this case were used by Deepak Fertilisers, whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of the final products and the storage and use of Ammonia was an intrinsic part of that process.

Conclusion

5. A manufacturer/service provider uses capital goods such as plants and machinery, inputs such as raw materials and input services such as security services, management, maintenance or repair services, etc., to make a final product. The excise duty/service tax paid on any of these three items is credited and accumulated under a CENVAT credit account. Whenever the manufacturer has to pay duty on finished goods and service tax on output services, it can utilise the accumulated CENVAT credit for the payment, subject to fulfilment of certain conditions. This ensures that the inputs are taxed only once.

HELD: No doubt, for availing credit of capital goods the conditionalities of rule 2(a) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 will require to be satisfied, inter alia, that goods should be used 'in the factory of manufacture of final products'. Strictly interpreting this provision would no doubt appear, at first sight, that in respect of machines which were installed not in the premises of the assessee but in an adjacent unit of 'H', cenvat credit would ordinarily not be available. However, it should also be kept in mind that the assessee stood merged with 'H' with effect from 1-4-2009 and as a result both these premises became a common entity from that date. From the facts on record, it appears that the assessee has availed credit under cover of invoice dated 1-11-2008, which was around five months prior to the date of the said merger. However, at the same time if the assessee had not taken the credit on or around 1-11-2008, but only on or after 1-4-2009, the availment of credit would not have excited any controversy. Therefore, the assessee's right to avail the credit on the said capital goods is very much available with effect from 1-4-2009 and the availment of credit prior to that date does not extinguish such eligibility. At the most, there will arise an interest liability for the period 1-11-2008 to 1-4-2009, i.e., for the period between the date when the credit was availed and the effective date of merger of two entities. This being so, the availment of cenvat credit by the assessee cannot be disturbed. However, the assessee will require to discharge interest liability at applicable rates for the period 1-11-2008 to 1-4-2009. [Para 5.2]

Background

1. In industries like pharmaceuticals and agro-chemicals many times near-about expired goods, defective goods or damaged goods (for the sake of convenience let us say "defective goods") are sent again by various marketing depots (not registered under excise) for reprocessing. Usually it happens that the original goods have been manufactured by let us say factory A, B and C but the defective goods are returned to only one factory, let us say factory D for reprocessing. This is so because it will be impractical to send the defective goods for reprocessing to the very same factory which had manufactured the original goods due to logistical costs as well as difficulties in identifying them on one-to-one basis.

In such scenario, only document available will be copy of excise invoice issued by the original factory. Had the defective goods been returned to the same factory, manufacturer could have easily claimed CENVAT credit on the basis of originally issued invoice (as the excise invoice was issued by the same factory). However, here the case is different. Factory D wants to claim CENVAT credit of returned defective goods on the basis of excise invoice issued by other factories.

Critical Issues

2. Following critical issues arise in this set-up:

2.1 Whether CENVAT credit can be claimed by factory D when the invoices on the basis of which credit will be claimed has been issued by factory A, B and C ?

2.2 W.e.f. 11-07-2014, third proviso has been added to rule 4(1) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 which provides that credit cannot be claimed after a period of six months from the date of issuance of any document (in our case excise invoice) on the basis of which credit is claimed. In our case, as we are dealing with near-expired or defective goods, in all likelihood excise invoice issued by original manufacturer would have been dated beyond statutory period of six months. Issue is whether the third proviso will apply to the present case ?

2.3 What are the procedures one needs to follow to claim the said credit ?

3. Legal Analysis

3.1 To answer the first question, i.e., whether factory D can avail CENVAT credit on the basis of invoices issued by factory A, B and C for defective goods which are received back, one has to refer to rule 16 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. Relevant extract is reproduced below for ready reference:

"Rule 16. Credit of duty on goods brought to the factory.—(1) Where any goods on which duty had been paid at the time of removal thereof are brought to any factory for being re-made, refined, re-conditioned or for any other reason, the assessee shall state the particulars of such receipt in his records and shall be entitled to take CENVAT credit of the duty paid as if such goods are received as inputs under the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2002 and utilize this credit according to the said rules.

(2) If the process to which the goods are subjected before being removed does not amount to manufacture, the manufacturer shall pay an amount equal to the CENVAT credit taken under sub-rule (1) and in any other case the manufacturer shall pay duty on goods received under sub-rule (1) at the rate applicable on the date of removal and on the value determined under sub-section (2) of section 3 or section 4 or section 4A of the Act, as the case may be.

[Explanation.—The amount paid under this sub-rule shall be allowed as CENVAT credit as if it was a duty paid by the manufacturer who removes the goods.]

3.2 Careful reading of above rule provides that CENVAT credit will be available of any goods on which duty has been paid and are brought to any factory for re-making, refining, re-conditioning or for any other reason as inputs. Thus, only condition to be fulfilled for claiming credit is that duty should have been paid on said goods. It is not necessary that goods should be received back in the same factory. It can be received in any factory. Further, goods can be brought back for reprocessing under rule 16 even if shelf life has expired (CCE v. Rako Agrochem (P.) Ltd. 2010 (260) ELT 479 (Trib. - Delhi)). Thus, credit can be claimed of goods received by factory D on the basis of invoices issued by original manufacturers. One may also refer to Board's Circular 607/44/2001-CX, dated 13-12-2001 which confirms the above view. Thus, CENVAT credit can be claimed on basis of manufacturers invoice available with depot to the extent of quantity received by factory D.

There is no condition as to place of receipt of input services - Input services may be received anywhere :

Rule 3(1) allows a manufacturer of final products to take credit inter alia of duty/service tax which is paid on :

(i)

any input or capital goods received in the factory of manufacturer of the final product; and

(ii)

any input service received by the manufacturer of the final product.

Rule 3(1) makes a distinction between inputs or capital goods on the one hand and input services on the other hand.

Clause (i) of rule 3(1) provides that duty should be paid on any input or capital goods received in the factory of manufacture of the final product.

Such a restriction, however, is not imposed in regard to input services since the only stipulation in clause (ii) is that the input services should be received by the manufacturer of the final product.

Hence, even as a matter of first principle on a plain and literal construction of rule 3(1), Tribunal was not justified in holding that assessee would not be entitled to avail of CENVAT credit in respect of services utilized in relation to ammonia storage tanks on the ground that they were situated outside the factory of production. [Para 5]

Storage of input is a part of process of manufacture - Hence, impugned services were input services under rule 2(l) :

The definition of the expression 'input service' covers any services used by the manufacturer, whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products. The words 'directly or indirectly' and 'in or in relation to' are words of width and amplitude. The subordinate legislation has advisedly used a broad and comprehensive expression while defining the expression 'input service'.

Rule 2(l) initially provides that input service means any services of the description falling in sub-clauses (i) and (ii). Rule 2(l) then provides an inclusive definition by enumerating certain specified services. Among those services are services pertaining to the procurement of inputs and inward transportation of inputs.

The Tribunal's interpretation that legislature restricted the benefit of CENVAT credit for input services used in respect of inputs only to these two categories viz. for the procurement of inputs and for the inward transportation of inputs was ex facie contrary to the provisions contained in Rule 2(l).

The first part of Rule 2(l) inter alia covers any services used by the manufacturer directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products. The inclusive part of the definition enumerates certain specified categories of services. However, it would be far-fetched to interpret rule 2(l) to mean that only two categories of services in relation to inputs viz. for the procurement of inputs and for the inward transportation of inputs were intended to be brought within the purview of Rule 2(l). Rule 2(l) must be read in its entirety.

The input services in the present case were used by the Appellant whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products. The assessee was manufacturing dutiable final products and the storage and use of ammonia is an intrinsic part of that process.

Hence, assessee was eligible for input service credit. [Para 5]

[Para 8] In 2000, the MODVAT Rules were replaced by the CENVAT Rules by the Central Excise (Second Amendment) Rules, 2000. Basically there was a re-arrangement of the earlier rules which in substance remained the same.

It is clear that sub-rule (d ) of rule 57AA (as introduced in 2000) had merely reframed rule 57B to include all the ingredients of inputs while at the same time broadening the base not only by referring to ‘all goods’ but also by using the word ‘includes’. [Para 9]

Rule 57AC provides for the conditions for allowing CENVAT credit in respect of inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer. [Para 10]

Initially, rule 57J of the MODVAT Rules was deleted. Consequently, with the intention of re-introducing the benefit granted earlier under rule 57J, rule 57AB was introduced under the heading ‘CENVAT credit’. [Para 11]

Rule 57AB effectively duplicates the substance of rule 57J(1) and (2) and deals with a situation where inputs are received by a job worker for production of intermediate goods which are used in the manufacture of a final product. [Para 12]

In J.K. Udyog Ltd.’s case (supra), three reasons were given by the Supreme Court for holding that credit could be taken only on inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer of the final product. First, the Court held that the definition of input given in sub-rule(d) of rule 57AA was entirely different from the manner in which the said word had been expounded in the Explanation to rule 57A of the MODVAT Rules. However, there was only a re-arrangement of the several provisions of rule 57B in rule 57AA. Rule 57AA is in fact more broad based than rule 57B.

Second, the Court proceeded on the basis that under the CENVAT scheme, there was no provision similar to rule 57J of the MODVAT scheme. However, rule 57J was replaced in substance by rule 57AB. That provision was overlooked.

Another reason given by the Court in J.K. Udaipur Udyog case (supra ) for holding that the CENVAT scheme was different from the MODVAT Scheme was rule 57AC(1). However, that rule was limited to inputs received in the factory of the manufacturer and did not impinge on rule 57AB at all.

The schemes of MODVAT and CENVAT Credit are not, therefore, different and the conclusion of the Court in J.K. Udaipur Udyog that the decision in Jaypee Rewa Cement (supra ) would have no application to CENVAT Rules could not be accepted. [Para 14]

The CENVAT Rules in effect substitute the MODVAT Rules and the decision in Jaypee Rewa Cement would continue to apply. The decision in CCE v. J.K. Udaipur Udyog Ltd. (supra ) holding to the contrary, was not good law. [Para 15]

Assessee's Arguments

When the assessee establishes two units in the same compound, both of them falls within the definition of "premises" under the Act and when both the units are manufacturing excisable goods, the steam manufactured in the factory of production even if it is used in the other unit, is eligible for CENVAT Credit.

When the assessee who manufacture the steam, use the same in the factory of manufacturing and also utilized the steam in its another unit which is situated in the same compound, is he entitled to CENVAT Credit proportionately to the extent which was used in the other unit ?

26.2-2 Earlier, it was clarified that goods should be brought to premises of the dealer and then sold. This involves transportation cost and time/Hence, rule 11(2) of Central Excise Rules, as amended w.e.f. 1-3-2015, allows direct dispatch of goods from the factory of supplier manufacturer to the user manufacturer. The invoice shall contain details of registered dealer as buyer and user manufacturer as consignee. The user manufacturer can avail Cenvat credit on basis of invoice of original manufacturer.

This amended rule envisages direct dispatch of entire consignment. However, CBE&C circular No. 1003/10/2015-CX dated 5-5-2015 has clarified as follows - (a) If entire consignment is transferred from factory of original manufacturer to user manufacturer, Cenvat credit can be taken on basis of invoice of original manufacturer itself. (b) If the consignment is split, the registered dealer can issue Cenvatable invoice, even if goods are not received in the godown of registered dealer [what they probably mean is that the manufacturer clears goods under one invoice and later the dealer splits the consignments outside, without bring goods in his godown]. - - It has been clarified that the new facility is to meant to improve ease of doing business.

Earlier, Registered Dealer was expected to bring the goods in his godown and then sell from there. Now, even if goods are despatched directly from original manufacturer to consignee (user manufacturer), registered dealer can issue Cenvatable invoice.

[Earlier, Direct despatch from manufacturer to buyer was permitted only if whole consignment is despatched from manufacturer to ultimate buyer. In such case, dealer was not required to issue Cenvatable Invoice at all as buyer could take Cenvat credit on basis of the manufacturer's invoice, if his name was shown as consignee. This facility is continuing even after 1-3-2015, as clarified in CBE&C circular No. 1003/10/2015-CX dated 5-5-2015]

II. Minority View [per : Mathew John, Member (T)] - Credit allowable, but, only from 31-8-2006, after merger :

Scheme : Under the Cenvat Credit Scheme a manufacturer of excisable goods is allowed to take credit of excise duty paid on inputs and capital goods used in the manufacture of excisable goods and utilize such credit for payment of excise duty on final products manufactured by him. [Para 36]

Rule 4(4) - Credit only by person paying value/duty : There is no specific provision in the Rules to the effect that credit can be taken by a manufacturer only if duty is paid by him to the supplier of goods. There is a provision in rule 4(4) to the effect that CENVAT credit in respect of capital goods shall not be allowed in respect of that part of the value of capital goods which represents the amount of duty on such capital goods, which the manufacturer claims as depreciation under section 32 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. So prima facie it would appear that the person who is paying for the value of goods and duty thereon is relevant for taking credit. [Para 38]

Receipt in factory : On the other hand definition of capital goods as given in rule 2 (a) and the rule 3 (1) and rule 4 (2) (a) allowing taking of credit are clear enough that credit is to be taken on capital goods received in the factory of the manufacturer. Interestingly there has been amendment to rule 2(a) and rule 4(2) (a) by Notification 3/2011-NT dated 1-3-2011 to the effect that in the case of captive power plants credit can be taken even if the plants are outside the factory. [Para 39]

Payment of value and duty was made by JSWPL - JSWPL neither holding-subsidiary no job-worker : In this case Cenvat credit was taken by SISCOL during the period Sep 05 to July 06. (From 31-08-2006, SISCOL had taken over the power plant from JSWPL.). SISCOL had not paid for the value of the goods or excise duty payable thereon when credit was taken. Such payments could not be seen in the books of account of SISCOL, when credit was taken. The value of the goods and excise duty thereon were paid by JSWPL on the date on which credit was taken by SISCOL. These are two different companies. There is no relationship of one as the holding company of the other which fact existed in some of the decisions relied upon. There is no relationship of SISCOL as job-worker of JSWPL which was the fact in cases where persons not paying for the goods along with duty were allowed to take credit of duty. [Para 40]

Issue Involved

When the assessee who manufacture the steam, use the same in the factory of manufacturing and also utilized the steam in its another unit which is situated in the same compound, is he entitled to CENVAT Credit proportionately to the extent which was used in the other unit ? HELD: The definition of "input" makes it clear that, "input" means all goods used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final products or not and includes lubricating oils, greases, cutting oils, coolants, accessories of the final products cleared along with the final product, goods used as paint, or as packing material, or as fuel, or for generation of electricity or steam used in or in relation to manufacture of final products or for any other purpose, within the factory of production. [Para 8]

The word "factory" has been defined in the Central Excise Act at section 2(e). It is an inclusive definition. For the purpose of Central Excise Act, a 'factory' means more than one premises. [Para 9]

Rule 6, of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 makes it clear that the CENVAT Credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of goods which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods. However, exception is carved out in sub-Rule (2). Sub-Rule (2) of Rule 6 provides- where a manufacturer or provider of output service avails CENVAT Credit in respect of any inputs except the input intended to be used as fuel and manufactures such final products or provides such output service which are chargeable to duty or tax as well as exempted goods or services, then, an obligation is cast on the assessee to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory or input and input service meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service and the quantity of input meant for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services. However he would be entitled to CENVAT credit only on that quantity of input or input service which is intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods. Therefore, it is clear that the assessee manufacturer is entitled to CENVAT Credit on "inputs" which is used in the manufacture of dutiable goods. [Para 11]

In view of clear language in the statutory provisions coupled with the fact that the factory includes more than one premises to be eligible for CENVAT Credit, an assessee has to use the input in the manufacture of dutiable goods in his factory. If the factory includes more than one unit and if the assessee uses this input in the manufacturing of excisable goods in both the units, he would be entitled to CENVAT Credit. [Para 12]

The definition of 'input' brings within its fold the inputs used for generation of electricity or steam, provided such electricity or steam is used within the factory of production for manufacture of final products or for any other purpose. Therefore, it follows the term "within the factory of production" cannot be confined to a single unit. In view of the definition of factory in the act which means more than one premises, it has to be construed as the factory owned by the assessee. If the assessee owns more than one unit, all the units if they are situated at a place would constitute "a factory". If the electricity or steam generated within the factory of production means within the factory premises which may include more than one unit. If such electricity or steam generated within the factory of production is utilized by the assessee in more than one unit and if those units are manufacturing excisable goods, then, the assessee would be entitled to the benefit of CENVAT credit to the entire extent of utilization of such electricity or steam in all the units of its factory premises. Therefore, whatever goes into generation of electricity or steam which is placed within the factory which may consists of more than one unit would be an input for the purposes of obtaining credit on the duty payable thereon. [Para 15]

In the instant case, the assessee is having two units; one DTA unit and another EOU unit. Both are situated in the same factory premises. Both are manufacturing excisable goods. The assessee has purchased furnace oil from which, the steam is generated within the said factory premises. The said steam is utilized by the assessee in manufacturing excisable goods in both the units which are situated within the same compound, which falls within the definition of the word "factory" and therefore, the assessee is entitled to CENVAT credit in respect of entire volume of steam used in the manufacture of excisable goods by both the units. That is precisely what the appellate authorities have held and granted relief to the assessee. [Para 16]

Hence, impugned order was confirmed. [Para 17]

Assessee having Centralised registration for service tax - Assessee having Centralised registration for service tax (and either having no manufacturing unit or having manufacturing unit only at the place where assessee has centralized registration for service tax) can avail entire Cenvat Credit of input services at one place. In my view, in such cases, distribution of Cenvat credit is not required, as he has centralized accounting.

In case of Centralised registration, the Cenvat credit is also centralised and that credit can be utilised by any of taxable output services - ratio of B E Billimoria & Co. Ltd. v. CST (2013) 39 STT 315 = 29 taxmann.com 271 (CESTAT).

Distribution of credit without registration - In Doshion Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 288 ELT 291 (CESTAT), it was held that since assessee could distribute Cenvat Credit in any ratio upto 31-3-2012, the HO could distribute credit to its unit without registration as Input Service Distributor [In my view, the principle will be valid even after 1-4-2012, if assessee has only one factory].

In WNS Global Services v. CCE (2013) 30 taxmann.com 208 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is allowable even if assessee was not registered as Input Service Distributor.

In a contrary view, in Khaitan Electricals v. CCE (2011) 32 STT 234 (Mag) = 12 taxmann.com 338 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that manufacturing unit cannot avail Cenvat credit of services availed at depot if depot is not registered as Input Service Distributor.

Cenvat credit available even if a particular unit was not included in Centralised Registration - In Tech Mahindra Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 39 STT 785 = 33 taxmann.com 354 (CESTAT), it was held that even if a unit was not registered under centralised registration, the Cenvat credit is available of input services received by such unit.

Position till 31-3-2012 - Till 31-3-2012, in my view, the main factory could directly take Cenvat credit of service tax on the basis of documents, even if there were more than one factories or places of provision of service of the assessee.

Till 31-3-2012, law did not even specify that there must be distribution of Cenvat credit or that the distribution should be in some specified ratio. If no 'distribution' is necessary, there should not be any need of 'Input Service Distributor'.

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of automobile parts. It registered itself with Central Excise Department on 28-11-2006 for manufacture of automobile components. The assessee set up its new factory by awarding the contract of construction thereof to a contractor. During the period from January 2007-08, the assessee availed cenvat credit on service tax paid on the construction services on the strength of 12 invoices issued by the contractor. Out of 12 invoices, invoices involving cenvat credit were issued prior to 28-11-2006 and remaining were issued after 28-11-2006, i.e. the date on which the assessee was registered with the Central Department. The Commissioner allowed the credit relating to the invoices which were issued subsequent to 28-11-2006, however, disallowed the credit in relation to the invoices which were issued prior to 28-11-2006 on the ground that the assessee was not registered with the Department at the time of issuance of those invoices and secondly, on the ground that the invoices were issued in the earlier name of assessee and not in the current name of the assessee.

On appeal:

The Adjudicating Authority held that the services on which credit were availed by the assessee were not covered by the scope of 'input service' under rule 2(l). The main point of dispute in the appeal is the determination of 'place of removal' of excisable goods. The assessee categorically stated that it transfers its goods to its warehouses from where it further transports them to the retail outlets or warehouses of its commission agents, from where the goods were sold. Hence, it was pleaded that place of removal in terms of section 4 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 should be retail outlet/warehouses of commission agents. The goods remain in its ownership till the time of sale from these retail outlets owned by it or up to the warehouses of commission agents, as the case may be. Freight also is paid by it up to the retail oulets/commission agents warehouses. [Para 7]

In the appeal, the revenue contended that the services availed at retail outlets cannot be considered for credit to the assessee. The revenue contended that these services used in retail outlets had no remote connection in the manufacture of ready-made garments. The Adjudicating Authority did not appreciate the legal scope of rule 2(l). He presumed that the services should be in or in relation to manufacture of ready made garments, whereas rule 2(l) clearly talks about services used by manufacturers, whether directly or indirectly in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and clearance of final products up to place of removal. A plain reading of the said statutory provision will indicate that the presumption of the Adjudication Authority is not sustainable. [Para 8]

Regarding the dispute relating to registration of the assessee as ISD, one is in agreement with the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals). On examination of provision of rule 2(m), the Commissioner (Appeals) clearly recorded that a manufacturer who wants to avail benefit of service tax should get registered himself as service provider and then he will be able to account for all the input services tax paid in the headquarters and distribute the same to various units. After examining the provisions of rule 7, the Commissioner (Appeals) concluded that as the manufacturer was having various retail outlets and office besides the factory for manufacture, in order to utilise the credit of input service got registered with the department as ISD. [Para 10]

Another dispute in the appeal is relating to credit availed by the assessee on the basis of debit notes, which were found to be ineligible documents. One notes that the assessee issued challans under rule 4A of the Service tax Rule, 1994 which contain all the required details. Even in case certain particulars were found missing in the relevant documents, one notes that substantial benefit of cenvat credit cannot be denied on this ground. In this connection, one refers to proviso to sub-rule (2) of rule 9 which provides for discretionary powers to the Adjudicating Authority regarding allowing the credit in such situation. As such, mention of wrong address of the service tax department on the documents is not a bar to avail the credit. [Para 12]

In view of the aforesaid, the order to the Commissioner (Appeals) deserved to be upheld.

Jay Engineering Works Ltd. 1989 taxmann.com 1077, provided the answers to the following questions are in the affirmative:

(a)

Whether the items are essentially required for the operational needs of the gadget;

(b)

All the conditions are fulfilled in this case inasmuch as barbed wire is essentially required for smooth operation of the transmission tower and secondly, as per the terms and conditions of the agreements, it is necessary for the company to supply barbed wire along with transmission tower and thirdly, the description list of the goods sold is attached with the invoice copy, which clearly shows that the value of the barbed wire has been included in the assessable value and the duty has been paid on the whole amount. It engaged engineering and management consultants from abroad. During the period-in-question, it made certain payments to those consultants and paid service tax. Subsequently, the assessee filed refund application claiming return of service tax paid on ground that the assessee was not liable to pay the tax, but the provider, i.e., the foreign consultants were liable to pay the tax and it was only with effect from 1-1-2005, that the service recipient became liable for payment of the tax, in the light of the Notification No. 36/2004, dated December 31, 2004. The original authority rejected the said application. On appeal, the first appellate authority upheld the order of the original authority. On second appeal, the Tribunal held that there was no dispute at all that the tax was attracted during the relevant period on the services received by the assessee. There was also no dispute about the amount of tax paid. It was found from the agreements between the foreign consultants and the assessee that the local taxes were to be over and above the consultation fees. The agreements clearly stated that ‘above fees was net and free of all local taxes’. The agreements provided that the foreign consultants would raise their invoices excluding taxes. Thus, under the scheme of the agreements, the assessee was to bear the cost of consultancy as well as the cost of all local taxes. In this scheme of the agreements, the tax amounts could either be remitted by the assessee to the foreign consultants who paid it to the Government or the same could be deposited by the assessee directly to the Government. In the instant case, the latter course was adopted and the assessee deposited the tax amounts. Such payment could only be treated as payment made on behalf of the foreign consultants who were liable to deposit the amount. In this view of the matter, there was no merit in the claims for refund. A refund at instant, belated stage would not be in the interests of justice. A refund at instant stage would only lead to the assessee receiving an undue advantage, while the revenue would not be able to recover the tax due from the foreign consultants. In the facts of the instant case, such a course was not advisable or necessary.

The assessee availed Cenvat credit of service tax paid on mobile phone services in respect of the phones used by its own employees and officers. The department sought to deny the benefit on the ground that the phones were not installed in the factory premises and, therefore, could not be treated as input service in terms of the Board’s Circular No. 59/8/2003 dated 20-6-2003.

On appeal :

The definition of "input" makes it clear that, "input" means all goods used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final products or not and includes lubricating oils, greases, cutting oils, coolants, accessories of the final products cleared along with the final product, goods used as paint, or as packing material, or as fuel, or for generation of electricity or steam used in or in relation to manufacture of final products or for any other purpose, within the factory of production. [Para 8]

The word "factory" has been defined in the Central Excise Act at section 2(e). It is an inclusive definition. For the purpose of Central Excise Act, a 'factory' means more than one premises. [Para 9]

Rule 6, of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 makes it clear that the CENVAT Credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of goods which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods. However, exception is carved out in sub-Rule (2). Sub-Rule (2) of Rule 6 provides- where a manufacturer or provider of output service avails CENVAT Credit in respect of any inputs except the input intended to be used as fuel and manufactures such final products or provides such output service which are chargeable to duty or tax as well as exempted goods or services, then, an obligation is cast on the assessee to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory or input and input service meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service and the quantity of input meant for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services. However he would be entitled to CENVAT credit only on that quantity of input or input service which is intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods. Therefore, it is clear that the assessee manufacturer is entitled to CENVAT Credit on "inputs" which is used in the manufacture of dutiable goods. [Para 11]

In view of clear language in the statutory provisions coupled with the fact that the factory includes more than one premises to be eligible for CENVAT Credit, an assessee has to use the input in the manufacture of dutiable goods in his factory. If the factory includes more than one unit and if the assessee uses this input in the manufacturing of excisable goods in both the units, he would be entitled to CENVAT Credit. [Para 12]

The definition of 'input' brings within its fold the inputs used for generation of electricity or steam, provided such electricity or steam is used within the factory of production for manufacture of final products or for any other purpose. Therefore, it follows the term "within the factory of production" cannot be confined to a single unit. In view of the definition of factory in the act which means more than one premises, it has to be construed as the factory owned by the assessee. If the assessee owns more than one unit, all the units if they are situated at a place would constitute "a factory". If the electricity or steam generated within the factory of production means within the factory premises which may include more than one unit. If such electricity or steam generated within the factory of production is utilized by the assessee in more than one unit and if those units are manufacturing excisable goods, then, the assessee would be entitled to the benefit of CENVAT credit to the entire extent of utilization of such electricity or steam in all the units of its factory premises. Therefore, whatever goes into generation of electricity or steam which is placed within the factory which may consists of more than one unit would be an input for the purposes of obtaining credit on the duty payable thereon. [Para 15]

In the instant case, the assessee is having two units; one DTA unit and another EOU unit. Both are situated in the same factory premises. Both are manufacturing excisable goods. The assessee has purchased furnace oil from which, the steam is generated within the said factory premises. The said steam is utilized by the assessee in manufacturing excisable goods in both the units which are situated within the same compound, which falls within the definition of the word "factory" and therefore, the assessee is entitled to CENVAT credit in respect of entire volume of steam used in the manufacture of excisable goods by both the units. That is precisely what the appellate authorities have held and granted relief to the assessee. [Para 16]

Hence, impugned order was confirmed. [Para 17]

The definition of 'input' is to be construed as within the factory of production, if the assessee owns more than one unit and they are situated at one place.

The salient points of the Strategic Alliance Agreement are as follows :

(a)

assessee manufactures alloy and non-alloy steel billets and blooms;

(b)

Kalyani Steels Limited manufacture pig iron (solid) and pig iron (hot metal) which is an intermediary product and in turn this intermediary product is also used by assessee for production of final product in terms of the Strategic Alliance Agreement dated 16-5-1998 for production of steel through an integrated steel plant.

Therefore, logically, the corporate entities had entered to Strategic Alliance Agreement for manufacture of steel in an integrated steel plant. [Para 8]

Admittedly, Praxiar has supplied oxygen and nitrogen in pipelines and the CENVAT credit has been availed of only by the assessee. Though the CENVAT credit was claimed only by the assessee, the input i.e., oxygen and nitrogen were used by both the companies. [Para 9]

It is well settled that a manufacturing unit can have one or more units to manufacture intermediary raw materials to manufacture a final product. In the instant case, by the Strategic Alliance Agreement, the corporate entities had entered into a joint venture agreement to manufacture steel products. The records disclose that whatever was manufactured by Kalyani in the ratio agreed to between the parties was finally made over to the assessee herein for manufacture of final product. Therefore, it appears, the companies joined hands to manufacture the final products in terms of the Strategic Alliance Agreement. In the circumstances, CENVAT cannot be deemed on the ground that credit is being availed by one factory and material inputs are used by three factories, because the CENVAT able input is being used for common share and continuous purpose of manufacturing dutiable goods.

Though there are three separate units with separate registrations, the entire raw material is being converted into final dutiable product in continuous, inter connected and integrated process conforming to the definition of a single factory under section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act. [Para 10]

Hence, Tribunal order was affirmed. [Para 11]

Credit only if value and duty paid by person taking credit : In various decisions, credit was allowed to be taken by the job-worker, when the goods were owned by the main manufacturer, apparently for the reason that the capital goods were in the factory of the job-worker and there was no condition in the rules that the job-worker should have paid duty from his funds for the reason that the capital goods were in fact used in its factory. So essentially what is being canvassed on this issue is a further extension of the decisions already given and not a simple application of the decisions already given. Such extension can lead to unintended benefits and is not warranted. [Para 45]

Capital goods must be received within factory with certain liberalizations - Liberalizations cannot be extended further :

-

Rule 2(a), Rules 3 and 4 (2)(a) provide that credit is to be taken on goods received in the factory of the manufacturer. The cases where deviation from rules has been approved by judicial forums are to be seen in the totality of the facts of the case. Where credit was allowed to be taken by the main manufacturer on capital goods used by the job- worker it is apparent that credit was so allowed because the capital goods were paid for by the main manufacturer and was used in the process of manufacturing his goods though in the factory of the job-worker. In some cases the equipment were used in premises appurtenant to the factory. In one case the goods were used in a wharf area which was belonging to some other entity. [Para 46]

-

Allowing credit in the present case requires going one step further. That is, it is to be ruled that it is not necessary that the manufacturer pays for the goods or that the goods are used in his factory but credit can be taken if there is a nexus between the capital goods on which credit is taken and the final products manufactured. Thus a further liberalization from rules and decisions given so far is involved.

-

This liberalization will bring in certain other consequences. As per the Rules credit can be denied only if the capital goods are exclusively used in the manufacture of exempted products. So if such power plant sells major part of the electricity generated, credit cannot be denied to the neighbour so long as part of such electricity is used by that neighbour. In this case such a situation did not exist and electricity generated was fully used by SISCOL. However such free bending of the Rules is not desirable because it can defeat some of the basic criteria in the Rules like the one that the person who purchased the goods cannot capitalize the duty amount and claim depreciation. The person who pays for the value of goods and duty may take credit and claim, depreciation and another person who uses the goods can claim the credit and the department may not know about the misuse because the books of account of the owner is not audited normally as in this case wherein the owner of the goods is not a Central Excise assessee. The owner may even refuse permission for such audit and the information can be extracted only through a procedure 'of issue of summons'. Further it can also lead to a situation where someone sets up a power plant supplies part of the electricity to a manufacturer who takes credit and sells the rest of the electricity to the public.

-

The next step can be, for illustration, a factory of SAIL can take credit of duty paid on equipment used by NTPC in a power plant for the reason that the power from NTPC is used in the factory of SAIL at least partially. Such benefits are not intended by the scheme. So the proposal for further liberalization of the conditions laid down in the rules was rejected. [Para 47]

Collector take the credit of the duty paid on the inputs received by him. On going through the records we find that on 31.3.1986 the petitioner has addressed a communication to the Asst. Collector purporting to be a declaration under Rule 57-G of the Modvat Rules. This was presented with the Range Supdt., Hyderabad and has been acknowledged by him on 31.3.1986. place of removal depends upon the facts as to whether the property or the ownership in the goods has passed to the buyer or not and in the case of FOB/CIF sale, the property passes only after the goods are loaded for the purpose of transportation or when the goods reach the destination as the case may be. Thus, from the circular, it is quite clear that in a case where the sale is on FOB/CIF basis, the place of removal has to be the load port only. The Tribunal held that the phrase ‘place of removal’ has not been defined, in CENVAT Credit Rules. In terms of sub-rule (t) of rule 2 of the said Rules, if any words or expressions are used in the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 and are not defined therein but are defined in the Central Excise Act, 1944 or the Finance Act, 1994, they shall have the same meaning for the CENVAT Credit Rules as assigned to them in those Acts. Further, the definition of ‘input services’ also has been defined to mean any service rendered in relation to outward transportation up to the place of removal. Since input service includes services rendered for outward transportation up to the place of removal, all the service tax paid to facilitate goods to reach the place of removal has to be eligible for the benefit of CENVAT credit. Further, the definition of ‘input service’ also includes any service used for manufacture directly or indirectly in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and clearance of final products from the place of removal. There is no dispute that the CHA services are required to facilitate clearance of final products from the place of removal, i.e., the load port. Hence, the Tribunal held that the appeals filed by the department were without merit.

Rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Input service - Rent-a-cab scheme operator

5.15 The assessee-manufacturer took credit of service tax paid by rent-a-cab scheme operator. The Deputy Commissioner denied the said credit on ground that said service was not provided in or in relation to production/manufacture of finished goods directly or indirectly. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that since rent-a-cab service was exclusively used for bringing and dropping the staff engaged in the production activity of the factory, the same had to be considered in or in relation to the manufacturing business; as such, hiring of cars would not have been required, if the assessee had not been manufacturing excisable goods in its factory.

The Tribunal held that from the definition of ‘input service’, it is very clear that the input service besides being used in or in relation to manufacture of final products and clearance of final products from the place of removal includes a plethora of other services such as services used in relation to setting up, modernization, renovation or repairs of factory or premises, of provider of input service or an office relating to such factory or premises, advertisement or sales, activities of business, accounting, auditing, financing, recruitment, quality control, training and coaching, etc., and, therefore, its scope is much larger than being used directly or indirectly in relation to manufacture. Since rent-a-cab service was used for bringing employees to work in the factory for manufacture of goods, it had to be considered as being used indirectly in relation to the manufacture or as part of business activity for promoting the business as any facility given to the employees would result in greater efficiency and promotion of business.

HEADNOTE: Rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Input service - Whether assessee was entitled to input credit on LPG used in its canteen where such canteen, as per Factories Act, was necessarily required to run manufacturing activity - Held, yes [Para 6]

FACT: The assessee was the manufacturer of Scooters. It had availed the Cenvat credit on Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG). LPG was also used in its canteen for providing meals to the workers and staff members. The department held that the quantity of LPG which was used in canteen was not eligible for the Modvat credit as it was not used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final products. The assessee was asked to reverse inadmissible credit of LPG used in the canteen. However, on appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the demand of duty.

On appeal :

HELD: In the instant case, there was no doubt that the assessee was required to maintain a canteen in its factory as per the Factories Act and to provide canteen facilities to its workers to run its factory which was a statutory requirement. In M.M.R. Khan v. Union of India AIR 1990 SC 937, the Apex Court had given a clear-cut findings that providing canteen was an integral part of the manufacturing activity of the assessee and as per the decision in Maruti Suzuki Ltd.'s v. CCE [2009] 22 STT 54 (SC) also any input which has gone into manufacturing of the final product directly or indirectly is entitled to input credit. Relying on both the decisions, it was to be held in the instant case also that the assessee was entitled to input credit on LPG used in the canteen, which as per the Factories Act was necessarily required to run its manufacturing activity. Accordingly, there was no infirmity in the impugned order and the same was to be upheld and the appeal filed by the revenue was to rejected. [Para 6]

On appeal :

. The assessee availed Cenvat credit on the quantity of LSHS. The Commissioner disallowed the credit holding that since fertilizers were exempted goods, credit on LSHS, even though used as fuel within the factory, was not allowable. On appeal, the Larger Bench of the Tribunal following the decision in CCE&C v. Gujarat Narmada Fertilizers Co. Ltd. 2006 (193) ELT 136 (Guj.) allowed the credit. The Supreme Court held that rule 6(1) is plenary. It restates a principle, namely, that Cenvat credit for duty paid on inputs used in the manufacture of exempted final products is not allowable. This principle is inbuilt in the very structure of the Cenvat Scheme. Sub-rule (1), therefore, merely highlights that principle. Sub-rule (1) covers all inputs, including fuel, whereas sub-rule (2) refers to non-fuel inputs. Sub-rule (2) covers a situation where common Cenvated inputs are used in or in relation to manufacture of dutiable final product and exempted final product but the fuel input is excluded from that sub-rule. However, exclusion of fuel-input vis-a-vis non-fuel input would still fall in sub-rule (1). As stated above, sub-rule (1) is plenary and, hence, it cannot be said that because sub-rule (2) is inapplicable to fuel-input(s), Cenvat credit is automatically available to such inputs even if they are used in the manufacture of exempted goods. The cumulative reading of sub-rules (1) and (2) makes it abundantly clear that the circumstances specified in sub-rule (2), which, inter alia, require separate accounting of input, are not applicable to the fuel-input(s). However, the said sub-rule (2) nowhere says that the legal effect of sub-rule (1) will stand terminated in respect of fuel-inputs which do not fall in sub-rule (2). In other words, the legal effect of sub-rule (1) has to be applied to all inputs including fuel-inputs, only exception being non-fuel-inputs, for which one has to maintain separate accounts or in its absence, pay 8 per cent/10 per cent of the total price of the exempted final products. Therefore, sub-rule (1) of rule 6 shall apply in respect of goods used as ‘fuel’ and on such application, the credit will not be permissible on such quantity of fuel which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods. The above aspect had not been properly appreciated by the Gujarat High Court in the case of Gujarat Narmada Fertilizers Co. Ltd. (supra).

As per Supreme Court, it may be noted that litigation on interpretation of Cenvat Credit Rules has arisen on account of various conflicting decisions given by various Benches of CESTAT, the reason being that the rules have not been properly drafted. In the circumstances, no penalty was leviable, however, in order to decide the amount of duty payable by each of the assessees, the matter was to be remitted to the adjudicating authority to decide the amount of duty payable without penalty on reversal of credit to the extent of the input being used in the manufacture of exempted final products.

1.2 Service need not be received in factory or premises from where output service provided - In case of inputs and capital goods, Cenvat credit is available to manufacturer only if these are received in the factory. However, in case of input service, there is no such requirement. Input service need not be received in factory or premises of service provider.

In case of service provider, even there is no requirement that inputs and capital goods should be received in premises of service provider.

Coverage beyond manufacturing/service provision stage

2. Inclusive definition clause of rule 2(l) extends scope of ‘input services’ even beyond stage of ‘manufacture’ or ‘provision of service’. The inclusive clause makes it clear that services much earlier to manufacture or provision of service or even after manufacture and after provision of provision of service will be eligible for service tax credit.

Services which do not have even any casual relation with manufacture of goods or provision of service have been covered by the definition of ‘input service’. In fact, any service in relation to business of assessee is ‘input service’.

Thus, though the words used in rule 2(l)(ii) are ‘used by the manufacturer, whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and clearance of final products from the place of removal’, in view of the word ‘includes’, the scope of definition is much wider than ‘in or in relation to manufacture’ and would cover even services unrelated to ‘manufacture’. This is also clear from the fact that service tax paid at Head Office and branches/depots can be utilised as Cenvat credit through the mechanism of ‘input service distributor’.

2.1 Services covered in inclusive part of definition - The services that will be covered are services in relation to —

(a)Setting up, modernization, renovation or repairs of a factory, premises of provider of output service or an office relating to such factory or premises

(b)Advertisement or sales promotion

(c)Market research

(d)Storage up to the place of removal

(e)Procurement of inputs

(f)Activities relating to business, such as accounting, auditing, financing, recruitment and quality control, coaching and training, computer networking, credit rating, share registry and security, inward transportation of inputs or capital goods and outward transportation up to the place of removal.

2.2 Wide scope due to use of word ‘includes’ - The word used in Explanation is ‘includes’. As it has been seen earlier, the word ‘includes’ denotes that scope is expanded beyond normal meaning of term ‘in relation to manufacture or clearance of final products’ or ‘in relation to providing an output service’.

Provisions in respect of computerisation of Invoices - Computerisation of Invoices is freely permitted and no permission is required. [Para 39] Explanatory note by Harmonised System of Nomenclature (HSN) to Heading 21.06 proves the integral link between concentrate manufactured by the assessee and the beverage (aerated water) manufactured by the bottler from it. The concentrate manufactured by the assessee in question had been classified and assessed to Cenvat (excise duty) under heading 21.06 by the Schedule to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985. That heading is identical to heading 21.06 of organised system of nomenclature issued by WCO. In fact the Excise Tariff is based on HSN. Therefore, the Supreme Court has repeatedly emphasized that the Explanatory Notes of HSN are valuable material for understanding the scope of various headings in the Central Excise Tariff. The Explanatory Note of HSN of Heading 21.06 demonstrates that the concentrates contain the flavouring ingredient that are characteristics of a particular beverage. The beverage in question is obtained simply by diluting the preparation with water, sugar and carbondioxide gas. From the Explanatory Note it is, therefore, clear that there is a link between the concentrate and the beverage made from that. The above Explanatory Note also explains the rational for business being arranged in this industry in a particular manner. This method of doing business avoids unnecessary transport of large quantity of water. In addition, the bottles and crates have to be collected back from the shop keepers or dealers and taken back to the factory for filling the fresh batch on a constant basis. At all times, the quality of beverage was maintained and marketing support to the beverages was provided by the brand name holder-cum-concentrate manufacturer. [Para 42]

It follows from the above discussion that the credit is availed on the tax paid on the input service, which is advertisement and not on the contents of the advertisement. Thus, it is not necessary that the contents of the advertisement must be that of the final product manufactured by the person advertising, as long as the manufacturer can demonstrate that the advertisement services availed have an effect or impact on the manufacture of the final product and establish the relationship between the input service and the manufacture of the final product. The manufacturer thereby can avail the credit of the service tax paid by him. Once the cost incurred by the service has to be added to the cost, and is so assessed, it is a recognition by the revenue of the advertisement services having a connection with the manufacture of the final product. This test will also apply in the case of sales promotion. [Para 43]

Therefore, services of advertising and marketing procured by the assessee in respect of advertisements for aerated waters are covered by the definition of the words ‘input services’ as defined in rule 2(l) when admittedly the assessee manufactured concentrates which were exclusively used for the manufacture of the respective aerated waters which were advertised by the assessee. The advertisement or sales promotion of aerated waters undertaken by manufacturer of concentrate was covered by the inclusive part of the definition of ‘input service’ contained in rule 2(l ). [Para 43]

In the light of the above, the impugned order of the Commissioner, and the order of the Tribunal were set aside, and the matter was restored to the Commissioner, to pass appropriate order in the light of what had been set out above. [Para 44]

The notification does not prohibit the use of an intermediary, who received the concentrated liquor but never acquired the ownership of the goods, and the processed goods were returned to the textile mill from which the spent lye had been received. "......Darshan Corporation was acting only as an intermediary. It did not acquire ownership of the spent lye which continued to vest in Raipur Mfg. Co. Ltd. Spent lye was being routed through Darshan Corporation to the appellants for concentration and the concentrate, in turn, was being routed through Darshan Corporation to Raipur Mfg. Co. Ltd. This evidence has not been controverted by the Department. The notification itself does not place a prohibition on the presence of an intermediary as in this case. What it required was that the ownership of the spent caustic soda lye should continue to vest in the factory where it was obtained, .....The evidence on record points to the fulfilment of this condition. The other condition was that the caustic soda recovered in another factory........was actually returned to the first factory......to which the spent caustic soda lye belonged. The evidence on record points to the fulfilment of this condition also."
